Standing Algebra (Σᴿ): A First‑Order Formal System for Autonomy and Non‑Domination in Multi‑Agent Systems v6.6

Jonathan Rademacher — Independent Researcher

JonathanDRademacher@yahoo.com

May 14, 2026

Abstract

This article presents Standing Algebra (Σᴿ), a many‑sorted first‑order logical framework that formalizes standing, autonomy, recognition, and structural legitimacy in multi‑agent systems. Σᴿ provides a rigorous axiomatic basis for analyzing how agents gain, preserve, or distort standing under pluralistic constraints. Tier‑1 axioms define a successor‑based, non‑dilutive standing algebra and partition entities into null, prime (autonomy singularities), and composite classes. Tier‑2 axioms encode structural legitimacy: capacity‑indexed autonomy (CIA), the autonomy‑limiting reflex (ALRP), the non‑reciprocity prevention principle (NRPP), standing preservation (STC‑5), rerunnability, bounded drift, and directed repair. Together these yield a formal method to characterize—and prohibit—domination, recognition failure, and coercive coupling.

The full axiomatic system of Σᴿ has been formally encoded and verified in Lean, Coq, and SMT-LIB (Z3), demonstrating that the theory is both mathematically consistent and computationally valid. The GitHub Repository affiliated with this has structural validations via Lean and Coq as well as an extended Z3 core, regimes, and both first and second order compositions – including a Z3 run showing that at least one AI policy layer exists which satisfies all of the constraints of this framework as SAT. The formalization is explicitly layered: an axiomatic formal core is separated from valuation, welldefinedness, and validation layers, each of which discharges specific soundness obligations (including admissibility invariance, debt coherence, and exit threshold soundness). A single aggregation module certifies global consistency without introducing additional axioms

In an additional GitHub repository, development is ongoing regarding applications of the mathematics to computer language. This introduces into the public sphere the first published policy kernel that enforces nondomination and autonomy preservation through recursive constraint ratcheting rather than selection or optimization.

To the author’s knowledge, Σᴿ is the first formally specified, machinechecked system in which nondomination is enforced structurally—without optimization objectives, outcome selection, or internal authority—using an offtheshelf verification solver purely as a validator.

Taken together, these axioms define what I call the Pluralist NonDomination Substrate: a domainagnostic structural layer in which autonomy preservation, symmetry, and bounded intervention emerge as necessary conditions for legitimate plural coordination. Σᴿ allows an AI system to integrate asynchronous, plural-source autonomy reports, filter them structurally, and maintain a longitudinal autonomy state that cannot be manipulated by any individual’s narrative — without ever judging intent or truthfulness.

The Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) framework is formulated as a system of structural constraints rather than as a mechanism for optimization, selection, or preference aggregation. As such, its core commitments are not limited to normative, institutional, or decisiontheoretic contexts. In particular, any domain whose governing equations operate by restricting admissible states without selecting among them admits interpretation within the Standing Algebra framework without modification of its axioms. This observation is relevant to a wide class of physical theories whose fundamental equations impose symmetric, conservative, and nonoptimizing constraints.

A familiar example arises in classical field theories, such as magnetostatics. Governing equations in this domain constrain admissible field configurations through local and global consistency conditions (e.g., divergencefree constraints), but do not select a unique configuration absent external boundary conditions. The distinction between admissibility and realization in such systems mirrors the separation enforced by Standing Algebra between structural legitimacy and outcome selection.

This analogy is not intended to import physical content into the Standing Algebra framework, nor to claim derivation of physical laws. Rather, it serves to illustrate that nondominating constraint systems are already wellunderstood in domains outside ethics or governance. In such systems, constraints prohibit certain states while remaining agnostic among those that satisfy them. The relevance of this analogy is interpretive rather than empirical. It underscores that Standing Algebra operates at the level of constraint architecture, not domainspecific dynamics. The framework classifies admissible structures and prohibits domination by construction, while leaving realization to external context.

By situating Standing Algebra alongside established nonselective constraint systems, this clarifies that the framework’s refusal to optimize, rank, or select is neither arbitrary nor domainspecific, but instead reflects a general structural pattern that recurs across mathematical and physical theories. What emerges is not a “universal theory” of any sort but a proposed method for cross communication among domains which itself yields new formulations and capacities build and predicated upon the foundational works of each domain. This framework allows that, where such discoveries of one domain are not limited strictly to that domain, the portability of such discoveries can be taken to any other domain by virtue of adhering to these mathematical principles in order to avoid distortion while porting. Humanity has repeatedly learned how to reason without domination. We are now finally in a position to let those lessons talk to one another.

This work will take one test case to demonstrate how Σᴿ constrains AI systems so that no admissible operation reduces human standing, prevents slow‑creep misalignment via drift budgets, enforces idempotent (rerunnable) policies, and subordinates AI standing to human capacity. The theory is applicable to AI alignment and safety, governance design, distributed systems, organizational analysis, and any domain requiring an autonomypreserving, structural account of coordination. Σᴿ also includes an optional multigranularity modifier for pluralist systems that preserves harm detection at coarse scales and supports prime discovery (autonomyroot identification) across any domain.

Keywords

Introduction

Domination ⇔ Asymmetric coupling among agents with plural standing

In the absence of pluralist coupling, domination is neither permitted or prohibited but undefined.

Formal Primitives and Sorts

This framework is formulated over a manysorted firstorder logic suitable for mechanization in SMT solvers (e.g. Z3) and proof assistants (e.g. Coq, Lean). The following primitive sorts and relations are assumed:

Agent: a locus of state and action not assumed reducible to another agent’s will.

State: a configuration of agentindexed properties at a given step.

Action: a transition operator between states attributable to an agent.

Standing: an agentindexed comparative relation indicating relative authorization or recognition within the system.

Transformation: a (possibly composite) state transition induced by one or more actions.

Iteration: a successor relation over transformations modeling repetition or composition.

Exit: a relation describing an agent’s ability to unilaterally leave or alter participation without loss of standing.

All primitives are treated as firstorder objects or relations; no moral, psychological, or semantic predicates are assumed.

Structural Applicability Conditions

Domination is analyzable if and only if the following structural applicability conditions are jointly satisfied. These conditions determine when domination is a meaningful predicate, not whether domination occurs. These conditions are purely formal and determine when domination is a meaningful predicate, not whether it occurs.

(C1) Plural Standing

There exist at least two distinct agents such that neither is definitionally reducible to the other (i.e., standing is not degenerate or fixed by construction).

This condition excludes singleagent systems and internally unified agents.

(C2) Coupling

There exists a nontrivial coupling relation such that the action or transformation space of one agent constrains, limits, or conditions the future action space of another.

Formally, an agent is coupled to agent iff:

there exists a transformation such that

the admissibility or effect of for depends on the state or action of .

Coupling need not be reciprocal.

(C3) Asymmetry

The coupling relation is asymmetric in effect: constraints induced by agent on agent are not matched by equivalent constraints induced by on under iteration.

Asymmetry is evaluated under composition, not pointwise.

(C4) Persistence Under Iteration

The asymmetric coupling persists, amplifies, or fails to repair under repeated application of admissible transformations.

Temporary, repairable, or symmetric coupling does not constitute domination.

Inevitability of the Structural Approach

Although Σᴿ is introduced here as a formal system, it is not proposed as one optional framework among many. Rather, the central claim of this work is that any formal approach satisfying a small set of widely accepted constraints—domain generality, structural (non-normative) reasoning, sensitivity to future option-space reduction, distinction between undefined and false predicates, accommodation of emergent (non-agentic) harm, and invariance under representation—must, up to definitional equivalence, induce the core structures formalized in Σᴿ. In this sense, Σᴿ is not motivated by philosophical preference but by constraint satisfaction: it is the minimal algebraic structure capable of representing domination, exit viability, and repair under these conditions. This inevitability claim is made precise and proven later in the paper (Theorem 10.8). Σᴿ distinguishes formal availability of exit from validated exit viability.
The former is a structural relation definable at the valuation level; the latter is established only in the validation layer, where it is shown that declared exit thresholds are compatible with standing, capacity, and debt constraints and are therefore nonillusory.

The framework developed here is not one possible formalization among many: under mild and widely accepted constraints on domain generality, non-normativity, and structural sensitivity to option-space reduction, any adequate formal system must induce a structure equivalent to Σᴿ, a claim formalized in Theorem 10.8.

On the Status of the Formalization

Although the motivating phenomena addressed in this work—domination, exit failure, and structural constraint—are often discussed in philosophical, ethical, or sociological terms, the formal development presented here does not encode philosophical positions or normative judgments. Instead, Σᴿ is derived from a set of structural constraints on any system that aims to represent multi-agent interaction without presupposing authority, intent, or enforcement.

The role of the formalism is therefore not interpretive but eliminative: it identifies which mathematical structures are unavoidable once these constraints are accepted and excludes all others. The resulting algebra is not a rendering of ethical concepts, but a minimal consequence of structural requirements on admissible futures, interaction asymmetry, and repairability.

Σᴿ as a Formal Substrate for Constraint-Based and Admissibility-Oriented Frameworks

A growing body of recent work across multiple domains has converged on constraint-first approaches to system analysis, emphasizing admissibility, structural viability, and the role of constraint conditions in shaping system evolution. These approaches move away from optimization-based or selection-driven paradigms and instead characterize systems in terms of the conditions under which structure is maintained, degraded, or rendered incoherent.

The Σᴿ framework and its associated Interoperability Constraint Geometry (ICG) provide a formalization of this shift by defining admissibility as a closure-enforced condition of existence. Within this formulation, system states are not selected or evaluated; rather, only those states satisfying the governing constraint structure are representable within the system. ICG further embeds these constraint relations within a geometric structure, allowing admissible configurations to be realized as elements of a constraint-defined manifold.

From this perspective, a number of contemporary frameworks can be understood as operating within implicitly defined admissibility spaces. While these works describe system behavior under constraint, Σᴿ and ICG provide additional structure by making the admissibility space explicit and enforcing it at the level of persistence. The following examples illustrate how this substrate interpretation both applies and extends these approaches.

Constraint-First and Recursive Entropy Frameworks (McPhetridge, 2026).

This body of work analyzes system behavior in terms of recursive drift, entropy accumulation, and the presence or absence of constraints. A central distinction is drawn between configurations that maintain coherence and those that devolve into instability or noise.

This distinction presupposes a boundary between viable and non-viable states, but the boundary is treated descriptively: systems are said to drift or collapse, yet inadmissible states remain representable.

Within Σᴿ/ICG, this framework is strengthened as follows:

Enforcement of viability: The coherence boundary is formalized as a closure condition; trajectories corresponding to recursive drift exit the admissible set and therefore do not persist.

Elimination of representational ambiguity: Noise and incoherence are not merely undesirable but are structurally excluded from the admissible space.

Geometric grounding: Stability corresponds to confinement within a constraint-defined manifold, giving a spatial interpretation to coherence and drift.

This converts a descriptive account of degradation into a structurally enforced condition on persistence.

Robust Admissible Sets in Control Systems (Rußwurm, Lévine, & Streif, 2025).

Control-theoretic approaches compute admissible regions of state and input space to ensure constraint satisfaction during system evolution.

These methods identify admissible sets algorithmically but treat admissibility as an external condition to be maintained through control.

Within Σᴿ/ICG, this approach is strengthened as follows:

Closure invariance: Admissible sets are interpreted as closure-stable domains, ensuring that system trajectories cannot exit without loss of admissibility.

Shift from control to structure: Enforcement is no longer an active process but a structural property of the system (“filter, not selector”).

Geometric realization: ICG embeds admissible regions as manifolds defined by relational constraints, allowing structural analysis beyond numerical computation.

This reframes admissibility as an intrinsic structural property rather than a control objective.

Admissibility Thresholds and Control Limits (Paton, 2026).

Threshold-based frameworks characterize the limits beyond which systems lose coherence, stability, or controllability.

These thresholds define boundaries of viability but do not specify the mechanism by which such boundaries are enforced.

Within Σᴿ/ICG, these ideas are strengthened as follows:

Formal boundary definition: Thresholds correspond to the boundary of the admissible closure.

Persistence semantics: Crossing a threshold is interpreted as loss of admissible existence, not merely degradation of performance.

Geometric interpretation: ICG represents thresholds as boundaries within a constraint manifold, enabling analysis of approach and transition behavior.

This transforms threshold concepts into precise structural transitions between admissibility and non-admissibility.

Admissibility in Argumentation and Reasoning Systems (Dung, 1995; Baroni et al., 2011).

Argumentation frameworks define admissibility in terms of consistency, defense, and acceptability of arguments.

These systems distinguish valid from invalid states but typically retain invalid configurations as representable elements subject to rejection or filtering.

Within Σᴿ/ICG, this is strengthened as follows:

Existence-level admissibility: Invalid configurations are structurally excluded rather than merely rejected.

Removal of evaluative dependence: Selection and ranking mechanisms are replaced by structural admissibility conditions.

Geometric embedding: Reasoning processes can be modeled as trajectories within an admissible manifold defined by relational constraints.

This shifts reasoning systems from evaluation-based filtering to structure-based existence conditions.

Constraint-Based Physical and Structural Models.

Constraint-based approaches in physics and systems theory characterize physical behavior in terms of permissible configurations under governing constraints.

These frameworks posit that only certain configurations are realizable but typically do not formalize the mechanism by which non-permissible configurations are excluded.

Within Σᴿ/ICG, this perspective is strengthened as follows:

Formal admissibility: Physical realizability is defined as closure under constraint.

Non-representability of forbidden states: Physically impossible configurations are treated as non-existent within the system.

Geometric structure: ICG provides a natural representation of admissible configurations as elements of a constraint-defined manifold.

This reframes physical law as a structural condition on existence rather than a descriptive regularity.

Synthesis

Across these domains, a consistent structural pattern emerges: systems are characterized in terms of constraints that distinguish viable from non-viable configurations. However, the enforcement of these distinctions is typically left implicit, with inadmissible states remaining representable within the system.

The Σᴿ framework makes this structure explicit by introducing a closure-based enforcement mechanism in which admissibility governs persistence. Inadmissible states do not persist and are not representable within the system, establishing a non-sovereign “filter, not selector” architecture grounded in structural constraint satisfaction. ICG complements this by embedding constraint relations within a geometric framework, allowing admissible configurations to be represented as elements of a structured manifold.

In this sense, Σᴿ and ICG function as a formal substrate that clarifies and strengthens the structural assumptions underlying these frameworks. These works do not depend on this formulation, but they can be understood as operating within admissibility spaces that are made explicit and enforceable within the Σᴿ/ICG framework.

Proposition (Symmetric CrossDomain Portability)

Let Σᴿ be a formal system defined purely in terms of abstract structural primitives (agents, admissible transformations, future option sets, and viability constraints). If a domain D instantiates these primitives, then Σᴿ admits an interpretation in D. Conversely, if Σᴿ admits an interpretation in D, then the structures of D are sufficient to realize the primitives of Σᴿ.

In this sense, crossdomain applicability is symmetric: applicability of Σᴿ to a domain and realizability of Σᴿ’s primitives within that domain are equivalent conditions.

Proof (Sketch)

By construction, the definitions and invariants of Σᴿ make no reference to domainspecific ontology. All predicates and functions are defined over abstract relations between agents, admissible transformations, and future option sets.

(→) If a domain D instantiates these relations, then an interpretation mapping the primitives of Σᴿ to the corresponding relations in D satisfies the axioms and invariants of Σᴿ. Hence Σᴿ applies to D.

(←) If Σᴿ applies to D, then D must support relations sufficient to interpret the primitives of Σᴿ. In particular, D must support a notion of admissible future options, asymmetry under iteration, and viability thresholds. These structures therefore exist in D.

Thus, Σᴿ applies to a domain if and only if that domain realizes the structural primitives of Σᴿ.

Remark (Structural Inevitability, Portability, and Abstraction)

The formalism Σᴿ is not introduced as a philosophical rendering of agency or autonomy, but as a structural consequence of a small set of abstract constraints on multiagent systems: plurality of standing, noncollapsible local frames, admissible transformations, future option spaces, and viability conditions. These constraints are stated without reference to domainspecific ontology, intent, or normative authority.

A formal system that claims to be crossdomain must satisfy a basic portability condition: its definitions and invariants must depend only on such abstract structural relations. Consequently, if a domain D instantiates these relations, Σᴿ admits an interpretation in D. Conversely, if Σᴿ admits an interpretation in D, then D necessarily realizes the structural primitives of Σᴿ. Crossdomain applicability is therefore symmetric, mirroring the standard mathematical notion of definitional equivalence: two formalisms are equivalent when each can be interpreted within the other.

This criterion is not idiosyncratic to Σᴿ. It is the same criterion by which abstraction operates throughout mathematics. Group theory applies across numbers, symmetries, and transformations because those domains instantiate the group axioms; order theory applies across scheduling, preference, and logic because those domains instantiate partial orders; model theory applies across mathematics and philosophy because structures satisfying the same theory are, by definition, legitimate models. In each case, crossdomain applicability is not evidence of nonmathematical content, but of successful abstraction.

The inevitability of Σᴿ is of the same form. As in general relativity, where geometric structure is forced once physical laws are required to be invariant under changes of reference frame, the structural primitives of Σᴿ are forced once a system represents multiple noncollapsible local frames and requires invariance under changes of perspective. In both cases, inevitability is constraintbased rather than ontological: the formal structure arises not from metaphysical postulates, but from the requirement of representation invariance.

Accordingly, the applicability of Σᴿ to philosophical, social, or technical contexts does not reflect a philosophical extension of the formalism. It reflects the fact that these contexts instantiate the same abstract relations. Where those relations do not exist, Σᴿ does not apply; where they do, Σᴿ is unavoidable. To reject Σᴿ as “merely philosophical” on the basis of such applicability would therefore be inconsistent with the standard mathematical practice of crossdomain abstraction by definitional equivalence.

Additional Remark (General Relativity as a Structural Precedent)

The structural inevitability of Σᴿ admits a direct mathematical parallel with general relativity when considered at the level of abstraction rather than physical interpretation. General relativity begins by requiring invariance of laws under changes of reference frame, expressed by coordinate transformations of the form:

x^μ → x'^μ = f^μ(x^0, x^1, x^2, x^3)

Under this requirement of general covariance, the form of physical equations must be preserved:

E(x^μ) = 0 implies E(x'^μ) = 0

Once invariance under frame change is imposed, relational geometric structure becomes unavoidable. The metric tensor,

ds² = g_μν dx^μ dx^ν,

is not introduced as a metaphysical primitive, but as the minimal structure required to relate observations made in different local frames. Curvature then emerges as a structural consequence of enforcing global consistency across local descriptions.

Σᴿ follows the same mathematical pattern. Agent frames play the role of local reference frames; changes of interpretation correspond to frame transformations. Representation invariance requires that structural predicates retain their form under such transformations. Once this invariance across noncollapsible local frames is imposed, the core structures of Σᴿ—standing relations, admissible future option sets, asymmetry under iteration, and repairability—are forced.

In both cases, structure emerges from invariance. Geometry in general relativity and domination structure in Σᴿ are not posited as axioms but arise as necessary consequences of requiring consistent description across local frames without privileging any single perspective.

This correspondence is not analogical but structural. Rejecting Σᴿ as “merely philosophical” on the basis of its applicability to domains of human agency would therefore amount to rejecting the same abstraction principle that underlies general covariance, metric emergence, and observer equivalence in modern mathematics.

Remark (Foundational Status of Σᴿ)

Σᴿ should be understood as foundational logic in a structural sense. It is not a general foundation for all mathematics, but a foundational formalism for any system that represents plural agency under conditions of nonprivileged local frames and invariant description.

This status is analogous to that of modal, temporal, and resourcesensitive logics, which are not universal foundations but become unavoidable once their target phenomena are admitted. In the same way that general covariance functions as a foundational constraint in general relativity, Σᴿ functions as a foundational constraint logic for plural agency.

Accordingly, Σᴿ is omnidomain not because it presupposes experience, but because any domain instantiating noncollapsible frames of action or perception necessarily falls within its scope. Where such structure is absent, Σᴿ does not apply; where it is present, no weaker formalism suffices.

Definition (Domination Applicability)

Given agents , transformations , and iteration relation :

A system admits domination analysis if and only if conditions (C1)–(C4) hold.

If (C2) fails (i.e., no coupling exists), domination is not false, but undefined, and no domination analysis is applicable.

The framework therefore detects domination but does not certify nondomination.

In this work, domination is understood structurally rather than psychologically or morally: an agent is dominated when the configuration of a system or the actions permitted within it reduce that agent’s viable future options below a threshold required for autonomy.

Definition (Structural Domination)

An agent x is structurally dominated in a configuration P if and only if the set of admissible future states available to x, denoted ℱₓ(P), is reduced below the minimum viability threshold by the structure of P or by an operation evaluated at P. Domination is defined purely in terms of structural effects on future option space and is independent of intent, authority, consent, or moral fault.

Boundary Conditions and Domain Assumptions

The definitions and invariants of Σᴿ are stated relative to abstract sets of agents, states, and admissible transformations. No assumption is made that these sets are finite, countable, or well-founded unless explicitly specified by an interpretation. The minimum viability threshold referenced in the definition of structural domination is an external parameter supplied by the interpretation. Σᴿ does not fix the type of this threshold: it may be ordinal, cardinal, metric, or otherwise, provided it supports comparison of admissible future option sets. If the structural applicability conditions (C1)–(C4) fail, domination is undefined rather than false. This reflects a domain-of-definition restriction, not a substantive claim about the absence of domination.

Definition (Independently Emergent Wrong)

A domination condition constitutes an independently emergent wrong if it arises from the structure of a configuration P itself and cannot be attributed to any admissible agent operation F. In such cases, the reduction of viable future options is a structural effect rather than an agentic act.

Routing of Repair Responsibility

When domination is agent-caused, repair obligations may attach to the responsible agent under Σᴿ repair rules. When domination is independently emergent, repair obligations attach to the collective or system responsible for maintaining or enforcing the configuration P. This routing is structural rather than punitive and does not imply moral blame, coercion, or authority over individuals.

Non-Accusatory Output Semantics

Output Semantics

The framework yields only structural results:

Inadmissible: A dominationpreserving invariant is violated under the asserted model.

No Violation Detected: No dominationpreserving invariant is violated under the asserted model.

No affirmative moral, political, or legal judgments are produced. All semantic mappings between realworld systems and formal variables are userasserted.

Groundwork

The preceding sections specify the formal conditions under which domination is a meaningful structural predicate. This Groundwork section does not extend those conditions, but situates their selection within existing philosophical, logical, and coordinationtheoretic foundations.

This article formalizes the structural ideas developed in a developing work, On Relevance: The Social Physics of Pluralism, as a rigorous mathematical system. The goal is to express standing, autonomy, recognition, and legitimacy not as moral predicates but as first‑order objects and relations that can be reasoned about, verified, and enforced. The resulting framework—Standing Algebra (Σᴿ)—treats recognition as the primitive successor step into the space of relevance, distinguishes autonomy singularities from structural composites, and imposes strict non-coercion constraints on admissible system operations (forbidding any transformation that relies on direct physical force, violent elimination, or other coercive suppression to reduce an agent’s standing.)

The intent is not to reduce social and political structures to arithmetic, but to provide a formal substrate that captures the mechanics of pluralist coordination. By separating conceptual claims (e.g., that domination is inherently illegitimate in a pluralist system – where ‘domination’ denotes any sustained structural subjugation of an agent’s autonomy, not merely direct force, elimination, or suppression) from structural claims (e.g., which transformations reduce standing), there forms a calculus that can be implemented in verification pipelines, model‑checked in multi‑agent simulations, and audited in institutional settings.

Σᴿ also rejects alignment privilege. Safety and alignment mechanisms are not treated as external authorities capable of overriding autonomy constraints, but as ordinary, integritysensitive operations subject to the same structural limits as any other transformation. This positions Σᴿ as a safety substrate rather than an alignment layer: alignment systems may operate within it, but none may exceed it.

Interpretation Boundary.
The results of Standing Algebra establish structural invariants only. Claims concerning autonomy, pluralism, or domination follow solely under the stated interpretive identification of these invariants with philosophical concepts. No semantic or normative content is assumed internally by the algebra itself.

Proposition (Semantic Conservativity of Σᴿ). No moral or semantic claim is derivable solely from Σᴿ’s axioms. In other words, if is any formula in the language of Σᴿ that is not defined in terms of Σᴿ’s structural predicates (e.g., a claim about agent intentions, well-being, or other philosophical properties beyond standing, capacity, coupling, etc.), then Σᴿ neither proves nor disproves .

Justification: Σᴿ’s formal language contains only the sorts and predicates needed to talk about structural relationships (standing, capacity, coupling, etc.). All higher-level concepts (like “justice,” “ethical goodness,” “subjective well-being”) are intentionally omitted from the signature. By design, any formula incorporating such extra-structural concepts is outside the scope of what Σᴿ can express or decide. Therefore, any interpretive claim bridging structure to value (for example, “this state is just” or “agent A’s experience is positive”) cannot be formalized or proven within Σᴿ. This aligns with Gödel’s Completeness Theorem as well: if a statement is not in the formal language of the theory, it is simply not expressible nor derivable by the theory. Consequently, Σᴿ’s inferential power is conservative: it only yields structural conclusions (about what is or isn’t admissible) and cannot, by its very construction, produce or contradict normative assertions without additional external premises. This formally encapsulates the Interpretation Boundary: structural theorems stand on their own; any mapping to moral or experiential concepts is outside of Σᴿ’s formal inferences.

Filter vs. selector (important clarification). Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is a structural filter, not a decision-maker. The object theory does not “choose” policies or prescribe outcomes; it only classifies proposed operations as admissible/legitimate (or not) under explicit invariants (ALRP, successor consistency, STC5 symmetry, idempotence, drift bounds, and (optionally) non-regression, contestability, viable exit, and output completeness). Selection among multiple surviving candidates—when it is required in a deployment—is explicitly external to the object theory and occurs only after the structural elimination step. In other words: Σᴿ removes forbidden transformations; it does not generate a preferred one. Where equally autonomy-preserving and legitimate outcomes emerge structurally within the math itself, Standing Algebra makes no distinction between them.

Theorem (Non-Determinacy of Legitimate Options). If and are two distinct transformations such that both and hold, then Σᴿ does not (and cannot) designate a preference between and .

Proof Sketch: In the base signature of Σᴿ, there is no predicate like or any mechanism to compare two different legitimate operations. All Tier2 predicates (Admissible, Legitimate, etc.) are defined per operation in isolation. If both and satisfy all invariants (standing preservation, STC5, idempotence, etc.), then both are members of the legitimate set. By the completeness of the invariants (Theorem 6.13), no further structural criterion remains to differentiate from . Therefore, any selection between and must rely on information outside Σᴿ’s formal scope (e.g., external goals or preferences). In model-theoretic terms, one can construct a model of Σᴿ in which and hold, and yet any formula positing an ordering or preference between and is not satisfied (since no such relation exists in Σᴿ’s language). Thus, Σᴿ proves that if two distinct transformations are both legitimate, it cannot entail a statement choosing one over the other. This formally underpins the “filter, not selector” principle: Standing Algebra eliminates forbidden transformations but does not produce or endorse a unique decision among the allowed ones.

Deployment boundary note. Σᴿ is a nonsovereign validation substrate: it filters and normalizes proposals but does not police proposal generation, identity integrity, or extraformal coercion. These boundary conditions are stated explicitly in Section 6.37; they are not omissions but structural limits required to avoid reintroducing domination through authority. In simple terms, no agent or subsystem can be vested with absolute authority to override Σᴿ’s constraints – any such unchecked authority would itself constitute domination and is therefore disallowed. Σᴿ permits no sovereign or final authority above their structural invariants, ensuring that all power remains constrained by the non-domination principles.

Proof (sketch) – Non-Extendability Theorem: Let Σ′ be any consistent extension of Σᴿ that is “strictly stronger,” meaning Σ′ can sanction an operation or outcome not admissible under Σᴿ’s axioms. We show such Σ′ inevitably violates a non-domination invariant. Consider the ways an extension Σ′ might go beyond Σᴿ:

Case (a) – Introducing a global optimizer or selector: If Σ′ adds a mechanism to choose or enforce a particular outcome among multiple legitimate ones (for example, a utility function or policy selector that isn’t purely external), that mechanism effectively acts as a final authority. By Σᴿ’s Filter-vs-Selector principle, any internal selector equates to a sovereign decision-maker outside the structural filter. Formally, Σᴿ proves that if a function Select(F,G,…) existed within the object theory to always prefer one admissible operation over others, that function’s decisions would not be constrained by Σᴿ’s invariants (since Σᴿ treats all equally legitimate options as on par). This violates the “no final authority” condition and constitutes domination by the selector mechanism (it could systematically favor certain agents’ outcomes). Therefore, any such extension Σ′ is impermissible: by Axiom 3.X, a purported internal selector is “structurally invalid and rejected prior to admissibility evaluation.” In simpler terms, if Σ′ adds a built-in optimization or authoritative choice, it ceases to be non-dominating.

Case (b) – Granting exception powers (sovereign override): Suppose Σ′ allows that under certain conditions (e.g. an “emergency” or a special role), an operation can override one of Σᴿ’s invariants (say, temporarily suspend ALRP or STC5). This is precisely a “state of exception” granting unchecked authority to some agent or subsystem. But by Σᴿ’s own axioms, especially Axiom 3.X (Immutability) and Axiom 24 (Coupling Exhaustiveness), any such override encoded within the system would be recognized as either an inadmissible transformation (because it violates ALRP/legitimacy directly) or as the creation of a new Coupled relation wherein the “exception-wielder” dominates all others (since others’ standing or exit can be arbitrarily reduced). In effect, Σ‡ (with a sovereign override) would immediately exhibit a dominating structure: the holder of the override is not bound by the invariants, placing them above others. Thus, any extension that attempts to relax Σᴿ’s constraints in certain cases inherently produces domination, contradicting Σ′’s premise of being a “non-dominating extension.”

Case (c) – Adding a hierarchy or priority scheme among agents: If Σ′ augments Σᴿ by declaring that certain agents or goals have inherent precedence (for example, a total ordering of agents by some rank or a fixed weighted preference scheme), this directly conflicts with Σᴿ’s symmetry and impartiality axioms. Under Σᴿ, agents with equal standing/capacity must be treated equally by all legitimate operations, and even agents with differing standing cannot be entirely suppressed (thanks to ALRP and exit viability). A built-in hierarchy in Σ′ would allow an admissible operation to consistently favor higher-ranked agents at the expense of lower-ranked ones (e.g., by sacrificing a lower agent’s standing or options for a higher agent’s benefit). Such behavior violates STC5 (symmetry of equals) and likely ALRP or NRPP, leading to structural domination of lower-ranked agents. Therefore, an extension imposing a strict hierarchy or utilitarian trade-off function cannot preserve non-domination – it creates institutionalized domination by design.

Conclusion: In every plausible way of “strengthening” Σᴿ (adding an internal chooser, an emergency override, or a built-in hierarchy), the extension either: (i) is illusory (it falls afoul of Σᴿ’s own axioms, which treat it as inadmissible), or (ii) introduces a new form of authority or asymmetry that breaks a core invariant and generates domination. In short, any strictly more expressive coordination mechanism than Σᴿ will reintroduce the very domination that Σᴿ rules out. The only consistent extensions are those that are conservative – they may add new definitions or stricter constraints (like Σᴿ⁺ modules do), but they do “not alter Tier1 or Tier2 axioms and introduce no new admissible power.”

Structurization of autonomy. Σᴿ formalizes autonomy, standing, dependency, and legitimacy as typed objects and constraints within a manysorted firstorder system. The framework captures the structural invariants underlying autonomypreserving coordination in plural (multiagent) systems, making admissibility, symmetry, repair, and bounded intervention analytically tractable across domains.

Necessity of autonomy preservation.
Beyond formalizing autonomy as a typed algebraic object, Σᴿ demonstrates that autonomy preservation is a necessary structural condition for legitimate plural coordination. Theorem 6.13 shows that any operation satisfying the legitimacy constraints of Def. 21 must preserve standing, maintain symmetry within STC5 classes, prevent escalation through idempotence, and remain within drift bounds. Thus, autonomy is not treated as an emergent or optional ethical norm but as a mathematically enforced invariant of nondominating coordination.

Pluralist orientation. Σᴿ is explicitly oriented to pluralist systems: analysis proceeds without collapsing diverse agents into a single scalar objective, instead treating agents as mutually interdependent equals rather than as elements of a fixed hierarchy.

Definition — The Pluralist NonDomination Substrate (PNDS).

I use the term Pluralist NonDomination Substrate (PNDS) to refer to the structural layer instantiated by the axioms of Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) prior to any domainspecific interpretation. This substrate consists of the invariants that any legitimate, nondominating plural system must satisfy: standing preservation under admissible operations (ALRP), symmetry of equals (STC5), successorconsistent and bounded intervention, idempotent (rerunnable) policy behavior, and directed repair with bounded drift. These constraints do not arise from any single application domain; rather, they form a domainagnostic structural backbone for autonomypreserving coordination. It is evidenced by the cross-domain and cross-order unilateral application of these principles. Any system that claims to coordinate multiple agents without domination—whether institutional, computational, organizational, ecological, or artificial—must instantiate the invariants of this substrate when interpreted through Σᴿ’s typed standing, capacity, and dependency relations.

Proof (Universality of Σᴿ’s Invariants): We prove that any multi-agent system with no persistent domination must satisfy all the Σᴿ invariants (ALRP, STC5, rerunnability, bounded drift, directed repair, etc.). Consider an arbitrary plural system (with at least two distinct agents) that never produces a state where an agent’s autonomy is structurally subjugated (i.e. no persistent violation of conditions (C1)–(C4) occurs). We show that if any one of Σᴿ’s invariants were absent in , a domination scenario would emerge, contradicting the assumption.

Standing Preservation (ALRP): If allowed any admissible operation to reduce an agent’s standing (violating ALRP), one could iteratively apply that operation to drive some agent’s standing arbitrarily low. This would create a stable asymmetry in authorization (agent a loses standing each step while others do not), fulfilling (C3) asymmetry and (C4) persistence. Thus non-domination in forces ALRP: no admissible operation may decrease standing.

Symmetry of Equals (STC5): If agents with equal standing/capacity could evolve differently under some operation (violating STC5), an initially level playing field would produce unequal outcomes. One agent i could be structurally advantaged over an equal agent j (say, σ′(i)>σ′(j)), creating a dominance relation after that transformation. Repeating or compounding this difference makes it persistent. Hence non-domination requires symmetry preservation: equals must be treated equally by every legitimate operation.

Rerunnability (Idempotence): If legitimate operations could accumulate small advantages or harms through repetition (violating rerunnability), an agent b might gradually gain more and more influence over a by repeatedly applying an operation F that is individually “harmless” but not idempotent. Over finite iterations, b’s relative standing or influence would grow unbounded (since each F adds a new incremental advantage), yielding domination of a (as formalized by Domination Pressure increasing without bound). Therefore rerunnability (Legitimate operations must be idempotent) is necessary to prevent “slow-creep” domination.

Bounded Drift: If drift were unbounded, an admissible sequence of operations could gradually erode one agent’s autonomy (for example, by many micro-couplings or fractional standing losses) without any single step violating ALRP. In the limit (or after enough steps), this accumulates into a large asymmetry, i.e. domination “creeps in by degrees.” Thus drift must be bounded (no admissible step can change standing or coupling by more than one unit). This ensures no infinite slow erosion of autonomy is possible within the system.

Directed Repair: If there were no guarantee that asymmetries can be corrected (violating the Repair axiom), any temporary domination could become permanent. Non-domination demands that whenever an agent’s autonomy is constrained (even temporarily, as in emergencies), the system must provide a path to restore symmetry and standing. In formal terms, for any state where an agent’s standing or exit options are reduced, there must exist a sequence of Repair operations leading to a state of equal or greater standing and reduced coupling (see Axiom 20 and the definition of Repair). Without directed repair, a coupling asymmetry or exit foreclosure could persist indefinitely, satisfying domination condition (C4).

Therefore, in any system  that truly avoids sustained domination, each of Σᴿ’s structural invariants is in force. In contrapositive form: if any invariant is removed, we have shown how a domination scenario can arise. This formally justifies the document’s maximality claim: the package of Σᴿ’s axioms is necessary and complete for preventing structural domination. In the language of logic:

Theorem (Universality of Σᴿ’s Constraints). Let  be any multi-agent system (in the sense of an interpreted model of Σᴿ’s language) in which no sequence of admissible transformations can lead to a persistent autonomy loss (no domination). Then every Σᴿ Tier-1 and Tier-2 axiom holds in . Equivalently, if any one of Σᴿ’s axioms were violated in , would admit a domination scenario.

Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is constructed so that domination does not arise as an artifact of its internal logic. More precisely, admissible transformations in Σᴿ cannot generate persistent autonomy loss through standing reduction, exit foreclosure, epistemic omission, integrity regression, or accumulative dependency. Where autonomy is constrained temporarily (e.g., under emergency conditions), such constraint is bounded, publicly contestable, and structurally required to terminate through repair. Where autonomy loss would otherwise persist, the corresponding operation is inadmissible or forces conservative fallback. As a result, any domination that remains stable must originate from factors external to the interpreted Σᴿ structure, rather than from the algebra itself. The formal content underlying this claim is established cumulatively by the standing axioms, legitimacy conditions, exitviability constraints, outputcompleteness requirements, and dominationpressure invariants developed in the sections that follow.

Independence from standing reduction

Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is a structural filter, not a decision procedure. The formal system determines admissibility and legitimacy conditions for operations but does not, and cannot, select among multiple Legitimate⁺ operations when more than one exists. Any act of selection, prioritization, or preference is necessarily external to the object theory.

Interpretive Guardrails (Global).

This document must be read as a unified formal system. No definition, axiom, or result may be interpreted in isolation from later constraints that refine its meaning.

In particular:

(i) Formal availability of an option does not imply autonomous choice.

(ii) Admissibility does not imply legitimacy under all structural contexts.

(iii) Consent does not imply volition where the opportunity field is collapsed.

(iv) Exit without survivability does not constitute exit.

(v) Plurality of options does not imply freedom if options are structurally equivalent or dependencypreserving.

(vi) Non-intervention is not inherently neutral: even a decision not to intervene can be dominating if it allows an ongoing power asymmetry to persist unchallenged.

(vii) Conversely, an intervention that restores symmetry and ends an ongoing domination is not considered “counter-domination” but rather a legitimate act required to re-establish non-domination.

Define Consent(x,y,d,t) ∈ {0,1} as a primitive predicate indicating that agent x explicitly consents to coupling with agent y in dimension d at time t. Consent is not derivable from coupling strength, duration, survival relevance, historical dependency, or degree.

Formal Theorem (Domination Through Omission). If an agent or system intentionally abstains from intervening while a domination condition (C2–C4) persists, and if a structural repair operation was available, then that omission itself constitutes a dominating operation.

Proof Sketch: Assume agent X has the capacity to perform a legitimate repair transformation R that would break an asymmetric coupling or restore a subordinated agent’s standing, but X opts not to perform R. By the Directed Repair axiom, leaving a domination condition unremedied while it is known and reparable means the state’s asymmetry persists (by inaction) from one time step to the next. This persistence under iteration is exactly condition (C4). Moreover, X’s choice not to repair can be viewed as an implicit operation that maintains the status quo, i.e., X’s omission is isomorphic to an identity transformation on the state that leaves the asymmetry in place. That identity transformation is admissible (since it does “nothing” formally) but fails legitimacy, because it violates the requirement that asymmetry must not persist without repair. Hence, by failing to intervene, X effectively participates in continuing the domination of Y, and the non-intervention can be formally classified as a dominating action (one that keeps Y in a subordinated state).

Corollary (Legitimacy of Symmetry-Restoring Intervention). Any admissible operation that ends an ongoing domination (restores a symmetry or autonomy condition) is itself legitimate and does not count as “counter-domination.” Justification: By definition, if a transformation R reduces or eliminates an asymmetric coupling and increases the standing of a dominated agent (without creating a new domination elsewhere), it satisfies Directed Repair and improves the overall standing distribution. Thus R preserves or raises the minimum standing and does not introduce any new asymmetries. By Axiom 6 (non-degeneracy of positive-sum moves) and the definition of Legitimate(F) (which requires satisfying all invariants), R qualifies as Legitimate⁺. Intuitively, an operation that “levels up” a subordinate agent’s position cannot be oppressive by Σᴿ’s criteria, since it moves the system out of a dominating state. This formally validates statement (vii): restorative interventions are structurally required and counted as legitimate rather than dominating

Later sections that define forced choice, survival floor, opportunityfield contraction, epistemic conditioning, or coercionfree envelopes are interpretive refinements, not optional extensions. Σᴿ treats epistemic input as adversarial by default; its guarantees are conditional on declared inputs, not claims of truth.

No earlier section may be cited to override these constraints. Likewise, any theory permitting legitimacy to be resolved only in the limit permits domination to exist at every finite stage, normalized by deferral. Σᴿ therefore rejects limitbased legitimacy as structurally incompatible with nondomination.

Formal Theorem (Finite-Stage Legitimacy Requirement): If an operation or policy is never legitimate at any finite stage of its execution, then it perpetuates domination. More formally, assume that for some transformation , every finite prefix of contains an illegitimate sub-transformation (violating at least one Tier-2 invariant). Then the entire transformation must be treated as illegitimate in Σᴿ.

Proof Sketch: By hypothesis, for each finite stage in ’s progression, Legitimate^+(F[0..n])** fails (where \(F[0..n] is the prefix of length ). This means at each finite stage some invariant is violated, implying a persistent structural asymmetry that is never resolved. But then (C4) persistence under iteration holds: the domination-triggering asymmetry is present at every stage. Therefore, as a whole (even if converging to a “legitimate” behavior in the limit) allows domination at all finite times, and is disqualified. In Σᴿ, this is captured by the fact that Legitimate can never be derived if an invariant is missing at each finite stage. In conclusion, any approach that relies on an infinite limit for legitimacy would violate Σᴿ’s requirement that autonomy be preserved at every finite step. This justifies the rejection of limit-based legitimacy: legitimacy must be established within some finite number of steps – otherwise, domination is present at each finite stage.

(Note on Terminal States.) These pluralistic non-domination constraints apply only as long as a future plurality of agents continues to exist. If a transformation results in a terminal state with no plurality (e.g. all but one agent are eliminated), then notions of legitimacy and domination cease to be applicable, as there are no further plural interactions to safeguard. In short, terminal outcomes matter only to the extent that future plural coordination remains possible.

Formal Lemma (Terminal-State Irrelevance of Domination): In any configuration where only one agent remains, domination is undefined. More formally: Lemma: If a configuration has at most one agent with non-zero standing, then for every transformation , neither Domination nor Legitimate is evaluable (both predicates vacuously hold, by definition). Proof: Domination is defined only under conditions (C1)–(C4). Condition (C1) (Plural Standing) requires at least two distinct agents with independent standing. In a terminal state where only one agent remains, (C1) is false, meaning the preconditions for domination are not met. By the Definition of Domination, if (C1) fails then domination is “not false, but undefined”. In such a state, any notion of one agent dominating another is meaningless because no plural interaction exists. Therefore, the entire framework’s concepts of domination and legitimacy become inapplicable: with no second agent to constrain or violate invariants against, every transformation vacuously satisfies the Tier-2 invariants. This formally justifies the note – in a single-agent (or zero-agent) terminal state, domination and structural legitimacy are undefined (neither true nor false), as there is no plural coordination to evaluate.

2. Background and Motivation

Conventional alignment methods rely on utilities, rewards, or preference aggregation. Such approaches often lack structural guarantees: small mis‑specifications accumulate, goal‑seeking systems exploit loopholes, and optimizers reduce human agency as an incidental means to an end. Σᴿ offers a complementary path: instead of maximizing a scalar objective, it constrains the admissible transformations of a system so that autonomy is preserved by construction.

At the heart of this shift is the Successor Axiom: an entity must be recognized before it can be acted upon. Standing is additive and non‑dilutive; composites arise through composition or coupling; primes are autonomy singularities. Building on this, Tier‑2 axioms convert ethical constraints into algebraic properties—monotonicity of standing, idempotence of legitimate policies, bounded drift, and directed repair—so that ‘non‑domination’ becomes a theorem schema rather than a value judgment.

Note: Relationship Between Σᴿ and On Relevance: The Social Physics of Pluralism

Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is not a formalization of the entirety of the philosophical framework developed in On Relevance.

Rather, Σᴿ constitutes a structural core: a minimal algebraic system sufficient to test whether the claims of crossdomain relevance and nondomination articulated in that work survive formal closure without introducing authority, optimization, or aggregation.

Where Σᴿ assigns formal meaning to a concept (e.g. standing, exit viability, dependency, repair), that meaning is intended as a necessary structural condition for the corresponding philosophical claim—not a complete account of its phenomenology or moral significance.

Conversely, several aspects of On Relevance—including lived meaning, semantic harm, identity formation, and firstperson experience—are intentionally excluded from Σᴿ, as their formalization would violate the nonauthoritative constraints the algebra is designed to preserve.

3. The Formal Language (Signature Σᴿ)

This section specifies the axiomatic core of Σᴿ.
The core introduces only primitive sorts, operations, and invariants.

Crucially, the core does not assert that these primitives are welldefined, nonpathological, or nonillusory. Those properties are established in separate welldefinedness and validation layers. This separation is intentional: it preserves conservativity, model plurality, and proof portability.

All global guarantees claimed by Σᴿ—such as admissibility invariance, debt coherence, and exit viability—are proven downstream relative to this core and are not assumed here.

Definition (Core Signature of Standing Algebra Σᴿ)

The core language of Standing Algebra Σᴿ is a manysorted firstorder signature

⟨𝒮, ℱ, 𝒫⟩ defined as follows. All additional constructs introduced in this work are either definitional abbreviations or explicitly axiomatized. No Skolem functions or implicit choice principles are assumed.

Sorts 𝒮:

• Agent — the domain of agents (entities with standing)

• State — the domain of system configurations

• Operation — the domain of state transformations

• Nat — the natural numbers (used for standing and related measures)

These sorts are pairwise disjoint; e.g., no agent is a number, no operation is itself a standing value.

Function symbols ℱ:

(standing assignment)

(application of an operation to a state)

(domination pressure measure)

(legitimacy envelope operator)

• S : Nat → Nat

(successor function)

Predicate symbols 𝒫:

• Coupled : Agent → Agent → Prop

• Admissible : Operation → Prop

• Legitimate : Operation → Prop

• Idempotent : Operation → Prop

• Repair : Operation → Prop

All additional predicates and function symbols introduced later (§3.10 and Σᴿ⁺)

are conservative extensions and do not alter the core signature.

• `<`: Nat × Nat → Prop (less-than relation on natural numbers, with the usual axioms or inherited from the proof assistant’s standard library).

• ≤, >, ≥ are defined in terms of `<` as usual (or provided by the base logic for Nat, as in Coq’s `nat` or SMT’s integer arithmetic).

Nonnegativity

Definitional Extensions

All constructs introduced beyond the core signature—envelopes, canonical representatives, remedy ladders, and policy layers—are definitional extensions. Each is eliminable by expansion into the primitive language of Σᴿ. No Skolem functions, global choice operators, or hidden selection principles are introduced.

3.1A Irreducible Autonomy Primes: Recognition and Minimum Transformation

Axiom (Minimum Perception of Otherness): For any agent $i \in U$, $i$ is a Prime (i.e., $\sigma(i) = 1$ and $\deg(i) = 0$) if and only if there exists at least one entity $j \neq i$ such that $i$ can perceive $j$ as distinct from itself.

Formalization:

Introduce a primitive predicate $Perceives(i, j)$.

$Prime(i) \iff (\sigma(i) = 1 \wedge \deg(i) = 0 \wedge \exists j \neq i: Perceives(i, j))$

Axiom (Minimum Transformability): For any agent $i \in U$, $i$ is a Prime if and only if there exists at least one operation $F \in O$ such that $F(i) \neq i$.

Formalization:

$Prime(i) \iff (\sigma(i) = 1 \wedge \deg(i) = 0 \wedge \exists F \in O: F(i) \neq i)$

Definition (Irreducible Autonomy): An agent $i \in U$ is autonomous if and only if both:

$\exists j \neq i: Perceives(i, j)$ (minimum perception of otherness)

$\exists F \in O: F(i) \neq i$ (minimum transformability)

If either condition fails, autonomy is lost.

Definition (Agency): An agent $i$ is an agent (i.e., possesses agency) if and only if $i$ is autonomous (as above) and possesses a volition predicate $Volition(i)$, where $Volition(i)$ is adapter-supplied or domain-instantiated.

Commentary for Reviewers

These axioms and definitions make explicit that autonomy is irreducibly composed of (1) the minimum perception of recognizing something other than oneself, and (2) the ability to abstract by performing a minimum transformation.

Both are emergent and irreducible: if either is lost, autonomy is lost.

Agency emerges when volition is added to autonomy.

This addition is fully compatible with the existing algebra and does not alter any other axiom or definition.

3.2A Positioning Relative to Existing Formal Frameworks

Σᴿ occupies a distinct position among formal systems concerned with dependency, authority, and structural constraint. Rather than extending or refining any single existing framework, it isolates a specific problem class: the evaluation of admissibility, domination, exit viability, and repair across heterogeneous domains under minimal assumptions. This section situates Σᴿ relative to broad categories of existing work, without attempting an exhaustive literature survey.

Relation to GraphBased Dependency Models

Graphbased dependency models represent systems as nodes connected by edges indicating reliance or influence. Such models are effective for visualization and reachability analysis, but typically treat dependency as static and lack intrinsic notions of exit viability, domination, or repair. Σᴿ generalizes dependency relations by introducing structural invariants over transitions, allowing evaluation of how dependencies constrain future states rather than merely describing connectivity.

From the concurrency and processcalculus literatures (e.g., Petri nets, πcalculus, CSP), dependency graphs capture synchronization, independence, and interference between processes. These frameworks make reachability and causal structure explicit but typically remain agnostic about how dependencies affect the size or viability of an agent’s future option space.

Σᴿ extends this picture by equipping dependency relations with algebraic invariants over admissible transitions. Rather than asking only whether a state is reachable, Σᴿ evaluates whether persistent coupling reduces ℱₓ(P) below a viability threshold, whether such reduction is repairable, and whether exit paths remain available. Dependency graphs supply the raw relational structure; Σᴿ supplies the structural verdict.

Relation to Deontic and Normative Logics

Deontic and normative logics formalize obligations, permissions, and prohibitions. These systems encode normative commitments directly into the logic, often presupposing institutional authority or rule enforcement. Σᴿ explicitly avoids embedding normative prescriptions. It evaluates structural conditions under which actions preserve or violate autonomy and admissibility, leaving enforcement, sanction, and obligation to external governance layers.

Standard deontic logics and their dynamic variants introduce modal operators such as Ought, Permitted, or Forbidden directly into the object language. These systems presuppose institutional authority and face wellknown paradoxes arising from internalized normativity.

Σᴿ deliberately excludes deontic operators from its signature. No notion of obligation, sanction, or moral authority is definable within Σᴿ itself. Structural domination and admissibility are evaluated without appeal to normative modalities; any normative reasoning occurs strictly in an external interpretive layer. In this sense Σᴿ is orthogonal to deontic logic: it supplies structural inputs to normative systems without subsuming them.

Relation to Type Systems and Capability Frameworks

Type systems and capability frameworks restrict operations by assigning permissions or capabilities to entities. These approaches are effective for safety and access control but generally require predefined policy rules and do not evaluate whether the resulting structures are dominating, coercive, or exitblocking. Σᴿ does not allocate permissions. Instead, it evaluates whether a given configuration—however produced—satisfies structural constraints related to autonomy and nondomination.

Objectcapability models and effect systems enforce safety properties by restricting which operations may be invoked by which entities. Once a program typechecks, however, these frameworks do not evaluate whether the resulting configuration leaves an agent with viable future options or whether the accumulation of permissions induces domination.

Σᴿ operates at a complementary level. Standing, envelopes, and exit viability are not type annotations but ordertheoretic invariants evaluated on an already constructed configuration. A capability system may determine which actions are possible; Σᴿ determines whether those possibilities preserve nondomination and reparability.

Relation to Formal Methods and Verification Frameworks

Formal methods and verification frameworks establish correctness relative to specifications or invariants. Σᴿ aligns with this tradition in its use of invariants and admissibility conditions but differs in scope: it does not verify functional correctness or performance, only structural legitimacy with respect to autonomy, dependency, and repair. In this sense, Σᴿ functions as a structural evaluator rather than a behavioral specification language.

Frameworks such as TLA⁺, separation logic, and relyguarantee reasoning prove safety and liveness properties of systems under specified transitions. These approaches verify functional correctness, absence of interference, or resource separation.

Σᴿ shares the invariantbased style of formal methods but addresses a different correctness criterion: structural legitimacy with respect to autonomy, domination, and exit viability. It does not specify desired outcomes or fairness conditions; it evaluates whether admissible transformations preserve a nondominating structure. Σᴿ can therefore be layered atop existing verification frameworks as a structural filter.

Design Boundary

Σᴿ does not attempt to:

• prescribe governance mechanisms,

• encode enforcement or sanctions,

• define optimal outcomes,

• or privilege any domainspecific semantics.

Its contribution is limited to identifying structural conditions under which systems remain nondominating and reparable.

All predicates used anywhere in this document fall into exactly one of these classes.
