BeliefSignal(b, E)

ReviewTriggered(E)

NonAuthoritative(b)

3.3A Primitive vs. Defined Predicates (Object-Theory Hygiene)

Σᴿ distinguishes (i) predicates that are primitive inputs supplied by an interpretation/adapter, from (ii) predicates that are definitional abbreviations inside the object theory.

Primitive (adapter- or interpretation-instantiated) predicates include:

PFAEligible(i); AF(F,i), EX(F,i), FC(F,i), RS(F,i) (and hence ARV(F,i));

and any optional Σᴿ⁺ predicates such as Targets(F,i), PublicAct(F), Sys(s), IntegrityWitness(x), AppealChannel(i), AppealAccessible(F,i), Exposed(F), Justification(F), Notice(F), and any impact-tier tags.

Defined (object-theory) predicates are introduced as explicit abbreviations in §§3.10.3–3.10.6 and Def. 21. In particular:

Admissible(F), successConsistent(F), STC5(F), Idempotent(F), Drift(F), Repair(F), and Legitimate(F)

are treated as structural conditions determined by σ, cap, deg, Coupled, and the action semantics of F, rather than as independent primitive facts.

This separation is intentional: Σᴿ does not infer domain facts (primitive predicates), but it does enforce structural constraints (defined predicates) uniformly once an interpretation is fixed. In other words, the predicate Legitimate(F) is not an independent primitive attribute of F but a second-order condition that arises only when F satisfies all the required structural invariants (standing preservation, symmetry of equals, idempotence, bounded drift, etc.). Legitimacy is thus evaluated with respect to the set of admissible future states that F permits, rather than as an intrinsic property of F in isolation.

3.3B Interpretive and Adaptation Layer (NonNormative)

The foregoing sections define the core algebra Σᴿ: the minimal set of primitives, relations, and invariants required to evaluate admissibility, legitimacy, domination pressure, exit viability, and repair. This section introduces an interpretive and adaptation layer whose sole purpose is to stabilize instantiation and interpretation across domains, including computational, legal, and institutional contexts. This layer introduces no new mathematical primitives, axioms, or normative claims. It is definitionally lossless with respect to Σᴿ. Its function is representational rather than ontological.

Purpose of the Adaptation Layer

Σᴿ is intentionally minimal. Many of its parameters are abstract or relational, and human readers routinely infer missing structure (directionality, arity, resistance, context) from narrative or domain knowledge. Computational systems, formal solvers, and crossdomain adapters cannot safely rely on such inference. The adaptation layer exists to ensure that every parameter required by Σᴿ is made explicit when a concrete system instantiates the algebra.

Coupling Descriptor Schema (CDS)

To support unambiguous instantiation, define a canonical Coupling Descriptor Schema (CDS). A CDS is not a new coupling predicate; it is a structured description of a coupling instance sufficient to evaluate all Σᴿ invariants without implicit assumptions. A CDS minimally specifies:

• participants: a finite ordered set [x₁ … xₙ] defining coupling arity

• kind: a coupling kind K selecting applicable inference rules

• strength: a (possibly vectorvalued) coupling strength

• resistance_form: resistance to formation of the coupling

• resistance_break: resistance to decoupling

• direction: a directional relation or matrix over participants

• time_interval: the temporal interval over which the coupling holds • context: an environment or situation parameter under which evaluation occurs

Mapping to Core Algebra

Each CDS field corresponds directly to an existing Σᴿ concept:

• participants ↔ coupling arity

• kind ↔ coupling type K

• strength ↔ degree / coupling strength functions

• resistance_form, resistance_break ↔ transition resistance and exit cost

• direction ↔ directed dependency and influence relations

• time_interval ↔ timeindexed validity and decay

• context ↔ environmentdependent admissibility No CDS field introduces new semantics beyond those already defined in Σᴿ.

Equivalence of Encodings

Distinct Coupling Descriptor Schema instantiations may represent the same underlying situation relative to Σᴿ.

In particular, differences in arity, decomposition, or representation granularity—such as modeling a relation as a single higherarity coupling versus multiple lowerarity couplings—do not constitute a semantic difference unless they lead to different evaluations of Σᴿ invariants.

Σᴿ evaluates instantiations extensionally: two encodings are equivalent if and only if they yield the same admissibility, domination, exit, and repair judgments under the core algebra.

No single encoding is privileged as the uniquely correct representation of a situation.

Adapter Plurality and Disagreement

Multiple adapters may independently instantiate Σᴿ over the same underlying system, yielding distinct but equally valid representations.

Disagreement between adapters does not imply that any instantiation is incorrect, deficient, or illegitimate. Each instantiation is evaluated solely on its own terms relative to Σᴿ invariants.

Σᴿ does not adjudicate between competing representations; it evaluates each independently according to the structure explicitly provided. Where competing adapters wish to evaluate against one another, singular instantiation over multiple adapters becomes the operational imperative.

NonExpansion Guarantee

The adaptation layer does not expand the ontology of Σᴿ. In particular:

• it introduces no new predicates,

• it adds no new admissibility conditions,

• it does not alter domination, consent, or repair logic,

• and it does not resolve ambiguity by fiat. Its sole role is to force explicit representation of parameters that are already required by the algebra but are often left implicit in prose.

Adapter NonCommitment Principle

Interpretations and adapters may not fix, narrow, or privilege the semantic meaning of any Σᴿ parameter beyond the structural constraints explicitly imposed by the core algebra.

Fields such as strength, resistance, standing, capacity, or repair are treated as abstract quantities subject only to the invariants defined by Σᴿ. Domainspecific interpretations may assign measurements or metrics to these fields, but no such assignment is authoritative for Σᴿ itself.

Accordingly, no adapter may claim that a particular semantic interpretation is required, canonical, or intrinsic to the algebra. Semantic overcommitment by an adapter constitutes an interpretive error, not an extension of the theory. Such an error denotes a mismatch between representation and algebraic requirements, not a violation of domain norms or intentions.

Likewise, it is pertinent to extend to potential adapters that the algebra itself is formatted such that coercion and domination, when present, become structurally detectable via Σᴿ invariants.

Adapter Responsibility and Fault Boundary

Responsibility for making all required parameters explicit rests entirely with the interpretation or adapter instantiating Σᴿ.

If a coupling instance omits information required to evaluate admissibility, domination, exit viability, or repair—such as arity, directionality, resistance, temporal scope, or context—this constitutes an adapter error, not an indeterminacy or failure of the algebra.

Σᴿ does not supply default values, infer missing structure, or resolve ambiguity by convention. Any instantiation that relies on such inference is outside the scope of valid interpretation. This requirement does not preclude partial instantiation or later refinement; it specifies only that no invariant may be evaluated using unspecified structure.

Representation Error Versus Model Disagreement

An adapter error denotes a failure to supply sufficient explicit structure for evaluation under Σᴿ. It does not denote disagreement about the modeled system itself. Distinct adapters may legitimately disagree in representation while remaining free of error, provided each supplies the structure required for evaluation. Representation error concerns completeness of encoding, not correctness of perspective.

Validity Criterion for Instantiations

An instantiation of Σᴿ is valid if and only if all admissibility, legitimacy, domination, exit, and repair conditions defined by the core algebra are evaluable using the information explicitly provided by the Coupling Descriptor Schema and the specified operations.

If any Σᴿ invariant cannot be evaluated without appealing to unstated assumptions, external conventions, or narrative interpretation, the instantiation is incomplete with respect to evaluation. An incomplete instantiation does not fall outside the scope of Σᴿ. Instead, it simply cannot be evaluated yet. Σᴿ is domain-general and applies to any system, but its invariants require explicit structure to be assessed as it exists as a structural evaluator.

This criterion provides a strict boundary between representational adequacy and algebraic sufficiency: repeated failure under this test indicates a genuine gap in the algebra, whereas isolated failure indicates an adapter or encoding defect.

No Completeness Requirement

Σᴿ does not require complete information to be applicable or relevant. Incomplete instantiations remain fully within the scope of the algebra.

Only those invariants whose required structure has been made explicit are subject to evaluation. Absence of information defers evaluation; it does not invalidate the instantiation or exclude the domain.

Role in Computational and Institutional Use

The CDS exists to support:

• stable serialization of coupling instances,

• consistent interpretation across adapters,

• verification of invariants (e.g. nondomination, exit viability),

• future translation into machinereadable or solvercompatible formats.

The core algebra Σᴿ remains the authoritative source of validity. The adaptation layer merely constrains how instances are described.

Progressive Refinement and Traceability

Instantiations of Σᴿ may be progressively refined over time as additional structure becomes available. Partial or incomplete instantiations remain within the scope of Σᴿ, though they may not yet permit evaluation of all invariants.

Refinement that adds explicit structure (e.g. directionality, resistance, temporal scope, or context) does not invalidate prior evaluations; it extends the set of invariants that can be assessed.

While Σᴿ does not require justification for how CDS fields are assigned, adapters operating in institutional, legal, or computational settings may be required to retain traceability or auditability of such assignments. These requirements pertain to the adapter or process, not to the algebra itself, and have no effect on admissibility or legitimacy as defined by Σᴿ.

Interpretation Immutability and Evaluation Trace

To prevent retroactive reinterpretation of previously evaluated states, Σᴿ treats interpretation itself as timeindexed.

Let ℐₜ denote the interpretation function supplied by an adapter at time t, mapping explicit CDS structures to Σᴿstructures. All evaluations of admissibility, domination, exit viability, and repair are performed relative to a specific ℐₜ.

Once an evaluation has been performed under ℐₜ, that evaluation is bound to ℐₜ and may not be recomputed under a different interpretation without constituting a new evaluation event.

Accordingly, reinterpretation is not an admissible operation on prior results. Changes in interpretation must be represented as refinement over time, yielding a new interpretation ℐₜ₊₁ rather than a revision of ℐₜ.

Earlier evaluations remain valid with respect to ℐₜ, even if later refinements introduce additional structure or resolution.

Formally, evaluations are associated with an interpretation trace: ⟨ (ℐₜ₁, R₁), (ℐₜ₂, R₂), … ⟩ where each Rᵢ is the set of Σᴿ invariants evaluated under ℐₜᵢ. Once recorded, elements of this trace are immutable. Semantic backfilling—retroactively reinterpreting earlier evaluations by altering the meaning of CDS fields—is therefore not merely disallowed but structurally undefined within the system.

This constraint preserves temporal consistency, reproducibility, and auditability of Σᴿ evaluations across refinement steps, while remaining fully compatible with progressive instantiation and partial information.

No Semantic Backfilling

Adapters may not retroactively alter the semantic interpretation of previously supplied CDS fields in order to reinterpret earlier evaluations.

Refinement consists in adding new explicit structure or increasing resolution, not in silently redefining prior representations. This constraint preserves reproducibility, auditability, and temporal consistency of Σᴿ evaluations.

Limits of Expressibility

No predicate or function definable within Σᴿ can represent normative concepts such as obligation, desert, punishment, or moral authority. Likewise, Σᴿ cannot encode preferences, utilities, optimization criteria, or enforcement mechanisms. All results of Σᴿ concern structural admissibility, domination, exit viability, and repair routing. Any interpretation of these results as normative, prescriptive, or authoritative occurs strictly outside the formal system. These limits are not omissions but design constraints: they preserve domain generality, non-domination, and the separation of structure from governance.

Theorem (Expressivity Limits of Σᴿ)

Σᴿ cannot express obligation, utility maximization, global optimization, or self-referential choice. These limitations are structural and intentional.

3.3C Expressivity Witnesses and Worked Instantiations (NonNormative)

The interpretive and adaptation layer also supports the use of worked instantiations as expressivity witnesses. These are concrete encodings demonstrating that Σᴿ can represent materially distinct dependency structures across domains without introducing new primitives, axioms, or inference rules. Such encodings are illustrative only. They do not refine, extend, or complete the algebra. Their sole purpose is to demonstrate closure and nonarbitrariness of the core structure.

Role of Encodings

An expressivity witness consists of a finite set of entities U, together with a finite set of coupling descriptors conforming to the Coupling Descriptor Schema (CDS), and (where relevant) a sequence of operations F. An encoding is considered valid if all admissibility, domination, standing, exit, and repair conditions are evaluable using only the existing Σᴿ definitions. Encodings serve three purposes: • to demonstrate that Σᴿ is not domainspecific, • to confirm that no hidden primitives are required, and • to provide templates for future instantiation without constraining semantics.

Uniform Encoding Discipline

All expressivity witnesses must adhere to a uniform discipline:

• no new predicates may be introduced,

• no numeric semantics are assumed beyond ordering or boundedness,

• coupling kinds must be selected from the existing K typology,

• temporal effects must be represented via timeindexed operations or intervals,

• and all structure must be carried by CDS fields rather than prose.

This discipline ensures that encodings function as witnesses of expressive sufficiency rather than informal extensions of the theory.

CrossDomain Applicability

Under this discipline, Σᴿ admits consistent encodings of dependency structures drawn from multiple domains, including but not limited to:

• physical systems (loadbearing, compositional support),

• biological systems (mutualism, asymmetrical dependency),

• institutional relations (roles, authority, exit viability),

• caregiving and developmental relations (timebounded asymmetry),

• legal obligations (identitydefining couplings and breach),

• technical systems (API and module dependency graphs), and

• organizational or infrastructural networks. In each case, domain differences are carried by interpretation of CDS fields rather than by modification of the algebra itself.

No Semantic Privileging

The inclusion of expressivity witnesses does not privilege any domain or interpretation. No example fixes the meaning of “strength,” “resistance,” “standing,” or “repair” beyond the constraints already imposed by Σᴿ. Domainspecific measurement and interpretation are delegated entirely to adapters. Accordingly, encodings are not normative cases, benchmarks, or training data. They are existence proofs that the algebra can represent the relevant structure.

Relation to Computational Use

Expressivity witnesses also validate the adequacy of the Coupling Descriptor Schema for machinemediated use. If a coupling structure can be expressed as a CDS instance without introducing auxiliary fields, then Σᴿ invariants can be evaluated algorithmically without semantic loss. If repeated encodings require additional qualifiers, this signals a genuine gap in the algebra rather than a representational issue. This criterion provides a principled boundary between algebraic extension and representational refinement.

From an algorithmic perspective, the admissibility and domination predicates of Σᴿ are decidable and have been mechanized in SMT solvers and proof assistants. Worstcase complexity depends on the size of the agent set, the arity of coupling relations, and the depth of admissible iteration. Bounding these parameters yields tractable instances; a full complexity classification is left to future work.

NonCommitment Clause

Nothing in this section commits Σᴿ to any particular encoding, implementation, solver architecture, or numerical interpretation. The core algebra remains the sole authority on validity and legitimacy. Encodings exist only to demonstrate that the algebra is sufficient to support such instantiations. Illustrative instantiations using this interpretive discipline are provided in §3.3D.

3.3D Expressivity Witnesses and Illustrative Encodings (NonNormative)

This subsection provides worked instantiations illustrating how the core algebra Σᴿ may be instantiated using the interpretive and adaptation layer defined in §§3.3B–3.3C. These encodings are included solely as expressivity witnesses. They do not extend, refine, or complete the algebra, and they introduce no new primitives, axioms, or inference rules. Their function is demonstrative rather than normative.

Status of Examples

All examples in this subsection are nonnormative and nonexhaustive. They do not fix the meaning of coupling strength, resistance, standing, capacity, or repair beyond the constraints already imposed by Σᴿ.

Each example demonstrates how a materially distinct dependency structure can be represented using only:

• a finite set of entities U,

• coupling instances describable via the Coupling Descriptor Schema,

• and (where relevant) operations F and repair conditions already defined in the core algebra.

Example Format

For clarity, each example is presented schematically, indicating:

• the entities involved,

• the relevant coupling relations and coupling kinds,

• and the qualitative role of directionality, temporality, exit, or repair.

No numeric interpretation is assumed unless explicitly stated. All structure required for evaluation is carried by the interpretive schema rather than by informal prose.

Example 3.3D1: LoadBearing Structure (Physical System)

Entities:

U = {beam, load, support}

Couplings:

Coupled(load, beam, Comp)

Coupled(beam, support, Comp)

Interpretation:

The load depends compositionally on the beam, which in turn depends on the support. Directionality is explicit and asymmetric.

Failure and Repair:

Removal of the support corresponds to an operation F that increases dependency pressure on the beam. Repair consists in introducing an additional support entity, restoring admissible future states.

No additional primitives are required beyond compositional coupling.

Example 3.3D2: Symbiotic Relation (Biological System)

Entities:

U = {organism_A, organism_B}

Couplings:

Coupled(organism_A, organism_B, IntDep)

Coupled(organism_B, organism_A, IntDep)

Interpretation:

Mutual dependency is represented via two directed couplings of the same kind. Relative strength, resistance, or capacity may differ without assuming symmetry.

Stability:

Persistence arises from bounded drift and reciprocal repair conditions, not from any domainspecific biological axiom.

Example 3.3D3: Employer–Employee Relation (Institutional System)

Entities:

U = {firm, worker}

Couplings:

Coupled(worker, firm, Role)

Coupled(firm, worker, Comp)

Interpretation:

The worker’s rolebased dependency differs in kind from the firm’s compositional reliance on labor. Asymmetry is structural, not inferred.

Exit and Repair:

Exit viability is evaluated relative to alternative admissible couplings (e.g. other firms). Repair may occur by modifying the coupling landscape rather than altering the core relation.

Example 3.3D4: Parent–Child Dependency (Developmental Relation)

Entities:

U = {parent, child}

Couplings:

Coupled(child, parent, IntDep)

Temporal Aspect:

The coupling is timeindexed and expected to weaken as operations over time modify standing and capacity conditions.

Interpretation:

Asymmetry and temporal validity are handled structurally, without introducing special cases for care, development, or moral status.

Example 3.3D5: Software Module Dependency

Entities:

U = {module_A, module_B}

Couplings:

Coupled(module_A, module_B, Comp)

Operations:

An update operation F may invalidate the coupling by increasing resistance or breaking compatibility.

Repair:

Repair consists in restoring compatibility or introducing an adapter, evaluated entirely within existing admissibility and repair rules.

Interpretive Note

These examples are intended solely as expressivity witnesses. They show that Σᴿ can encode a wide range of dependency structures using a uniform interpretive schema, without committing the algebra to any particular domain, measurement system, or enforcement mechanism. The examples shown are not exhaustive within their scope and do not constitute a fully thorough rendering of their application in their respective domains. Rather, encoding the domain to the substrate through the disciplines and the CDS provided gives a clear path to instantiation for users of this mathematical substrate and falls to the users operating the math to do so.

If repeated applications require structure not representable within this framework, that would indicate a genuine algebraic gap rather than a representational issue. No such gap is presupposed here.

3.3E Illustrative Usage Contexts (NonNormative)

This subsection describes representative contexts in which Σᴿ may be applied as an evaluation layer. These contexts are illustrative only and do not prescribe governance models, enforcement mechanisms, or decision procedures. In all cases, Σᴿ functions as a structural evaluator whose outputs inform external processes rather than determine outcomes.

Institutional Review and Policy Analysis

Σᴿ may be used to evaluate whether proposed institutional policies, organizational restructurings, or regulatory changes introduce structural domination, exitblocking dependencies, or unrecoverable autonomy loss. In such contexts, Σᴿ does not dictate policy decisions; it identifies structural risk conditions for consideration by decisionmakers.

Technical and Software Systems

Σᴿ may be used as an analysis layer over software dependency graphs, infrastructure configurations, or API ecosystems to identify brittle couplings, nonviable exit paths, or dependency accumulation that threatens system resilience. The framework evaluates structural properties; remediation strategies remain implementationspecific.

Legal and Contractual Analysis

Σᴿ may be applied to contractual or legal arrangements to assess whether obligations, roles, or enforcement mechanisms create structurally coercive or irreparable dependencies. Such analysis informs legal reasoning without substituting for legal judgment or statutory interpretation.

Social and Organizational Systems

Σᴿ may be used to analyze social, labor, or care relationships where asymmetries of dependency and exit viability are central concerns. The framework evaluates structural features of these systems without making claims about moral intent or individual responsibility.

Technical Boundary

In all usage contexts, Σᴿ provides structured evaluations rather than decisions. Interpretation of results, selection of remedies, and exercise of authority occur entirely outside the framework.

Domination Pressure and Integrity NonRegression (Optional; Σᴿ⁺)

Definition (Domination Pressure).
Domination pressure is a nonnegative measure on configurations. DomPressure(P) is defined as the supremum of dependency growth and exit fragility across all agents in P.

Domination pressure is monotone under admissible operations unless reduced by repair.

DP : U → N                (domination pressure functional on system-state entities)

Definition (Structural Domination).
A configuration is dominating if and only if at least one of the following holds.

First, there exists an agent whose exit is formally available but not viable.

Definition (Exit Relation).
Exit is a relation between an agent and a configuration. Exit(i, P) holds if and only if agent i can refuse continued participation in configuration P without incurring additional dependency, standing loss, or coercive constraint. Exit is viable if refusal does not introduce new coupling or reduce future option sets. Exit is viable only if the cost of decoupling along every dimension d is bounded by a finite constant C_d.

Signature

Exit : Agent → State → Prop
ViableExit derived as predicate refinement

Definition (Option Set).
The option set of an agent in a configuration is the set of future configurations in the admissible future set in which that agent’s exit remains viable.

Second, there exists an agent and a sequence of admissible operations under which that agent’s dependency strictly increases without bound and no admissible repair operation restores standing symmetry.

Define an autonomy functional:

A(x) = 1 − Σ_y max_d (s_d(x,y) · w_d)

A system state is invalid if A(x) < A_min for any agent x. Violation triggers mandatory repair or enforced decoupling.

Let G be the enforcing group or system.

If PrescribedRepair(x→y) > Ceiling(x)

then: Obligation(G) = PrescribedRepair − Ceiling(x)

The obligation persists until autonomy thresholds are restored.

The Autonomy Debt defines a ceiling, not a prescription. The prescribed repair is the minimum constraint required to restore autonomy and social order. Only when restoration is impossible under lesser constraints may the full ceiling be invoked.

Any collective, institution, or system that enforces autonomy repair thereby assumes responsibility for ensuring that restoration is completed. Enforcement without completion constitutes a secondary autonomy violation attributable to the enforcing structure.

Extensionality

Residual Autonomy Obligation.

If the total autonomy debt incurred by an offending agent exceeds the maximum autonomy that may be constrained from that agent without violating system invariants, the remaining unmet portion of the debt constitutes a residual obligation. That residual obligation is borne by the enforcing collective or system that authorizes and executes the reciprocal constraint.

Definition (Admissible Futures).
For a configuration P, the admissible future set ℱ(P) is the set of all configurations Q such that there exists a finite sequence of admissible operations transforming P into Q.

For any configuration P and state Q, we write Reachable(P, Q) to mean that Q can be obtained from P by some finite sequence of admissible operations. In other words, there exists a sequence of admissible transformations taking P to Q. This reachability relation is reflexive (P is reachable from itself) and transitive (if Q is reachable from P, and R is reachable from Q, then R is reachable from P). It follows that every state P has an admissible future, consisting exactly of those states Q for which Reachable(P, Q) holds. In particular, P’s own admissible future includes P itself and is closed under any further admissible operations.

ℱ(P) contains P itself and is closed under admissible composition.

Signature

Futures : State → Set State

A configuration is nondominating if neither condition holds.

Formal Model Interpretation of Σᴿ

To demonstrate consistency and mathematical coherence, this structure presents a concrete model for Standing Algebra (Σᴿ). All axioms of Tier1 (Σᴿ₁) and Tier2 (Σᴿ₂) hold in the structure defined below. This model is not unique; it serves as one canonical interpretation validating the system.

Interpret N=C=D=ℕ with standard S(n)=n+1 and +; U any nonempty set; O ⊆ U^U. Theorem (Relative Consistency of Σᴿ)

If many-sorted first-order logic with equality is consistent, then Σᴿ is consistent.

Proof. A concrete Σᴿ-structure is constructed by interpreting agents as a non-empty set, standing as a partial order, admissible futures as non-empty subsets of a state space, and repair as a binary relation satisfying the axioms. All axioms of Σᴿ are satisfied in this structure. Therefore Σᴿ has a model and is consistent relative to its metatheory.

Theorem (NonTriviality of Σᴿ)

Σᴿ admits at least two non-isomorphic models.

Proof. Let M₁ be a model with two agents and asymmetric standing. Let M₂ be a model with three agents and cyclic standing. Both satisfy all axioms but are not isomorphic. Hence Σᴿ is non-trivial.

Lemma (Model Validity).

All axioms of Σᴿ₁ and Σᴿ₂ hold in the structure defined above.

Axioms involving successor follow from interpreting as .

Nullity and nonreturn to nullity follow from the properties of .

Nondilution follows from interpreting as additive combination.

Prime and composite definitions hold by construction.

Capacitystanding monotonicity holds by assigning capacities consistent with the inequality constraints.

Admissibility and legitimacy predicates are defined to enforce Axioms 15 and 17.

Drift and repair predicates enforce bounded movement and monotonic correction.

Thus is a valid Σᴿmodel.

Tier-3 predicates (PFAEligible, ProxyFor, EmancipatoryRepair, Coalition, Member) are interpreted extensionally in the same manner as the Tier2 predicates. In particular, they may be interpreted as empty relations in the base model, and the operation set O may be expanded to include emancipatory repair functions when proxy dependence exists. Hence Σᴿ₃ is a conservative extension: it preserves satisfiability whenever Σᴿ₂ is satisfiable.

3.6 Consistency of Σᴿ

Establishing the consistency of an axiomatic system requires demonstrating that there exists at least one structure (model) in which all axioms hold true. In manysorted firstorder logic, consistency is typically shown by constructing a concrete interpretation for each sort, function symbol, and predicate symbol such that every axiom evaluates to a true statement under that interpretation.

This section shows that Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is consistent relative to standard firstorder logic with equality, because it admits a welldefined model. The model presented in Section 3.5 provides a witness to this fact. Since the structure in §3.5 satisfies every axiom, Σᴿ is satisfiable and therefore consistent relative to many‑sorted FOL with equality.

Theorem 3.6.1 — Relative Consistency of Σᴿ

Statement.
The axiomatic system Σᴿ is consistent relative to the background logic of manysorted firstorder logic with equality.

Proof.
Let be the structure defined in Section 3.5:

an arbitrary nonempty set,

an additive composition satisfying ,

Verify:

Successor axioms (Axioms 2–3) hold because is interpreted as ordinary successor on .

Nullity and no-return axioms (Axioms 1 and 12) hold because is interpreted as , and no operation in is permitted to map positive standing back to by definition.

Nondilution (Axiom 5) holds because is interpreted as additive composition on standing values.

Prime and composite axioms (Axioms 9–11) hold because the definitions of and enforce the prime/composite dichotomy.

Capacityindexed autonomy (Axiom 14) is satisfied because is assigned monotonically.

Autonomylimiting reflex (Axiom 15) holds because is defined precisely as those operations preserving standing.

Symmetrypreserving legitimacy (Axiom 17) holds by the definition of legitimate operations.

Rerunnability (Axiom 18) holds because legitimate operations are interpreted as idempotent on standingequivalence classes.

Drift and repair axioms (Axioms 19–20) hold because drift and repair predicates explicitly encode the allowed bounded perturbations and monotone corrections.

Legitimacy requirement (Def 21) holds because legitimacy requires admissibility, successor consistency, symmetry (STC5), idempotence, and bounded drift.

Since every axiom in Σᴿ is satisfied by , the system is satisfiable.

Therefore, Σᴿ is consistent relative to standard firstorder logic with equality.

3.6.1 Discussion of Consistency Strength

The consistency shown above is relative consistency. It relies on the fact that:

manysorted firstorder logic with equality is a conservative extension of standard firstorder logic, and

the domains are interpreted as ordinary sets within a ZFCstyle universe of discourse.

Thus, unless ordinary arithmetic or set theory is inconsistent, Σᴿ cannot produce a contradiction, because the model exists within the same semantic universe.

This satisfies the standard requirement for mathematical publication:

An axiomatic system is consistent if it has a model.

Σᴿ not only has a model — it has a large class of models, because:

any nonempty ,

any monotone capacity assignment,

any graph structure for Coupled,

any idempotent standingpreserving operations,

and any choice of entity composition satisfying Axiom 5

all produce valid Σᴿstructures.

This multiplicity of models further strengthens the case for consistency and provides flexibility for applications in AI alignment, multiagent systems, or social system modeling.

Axiom 3.X (Algebraic Immutability).

No operation, envelope, composition, election, or admissible transformation may modify, override, suspend, or reinterpret the axioms, invariants, or admissibility criteria of Σᴿ.

Any input that encodes or presupposes a change to the algebra itself is structurally invalid and rejected prior to admissibility evaluation.

Governance, revision, or extension of Σᴿ are explicitly external to Σᴿ and not representable within the algebra.

3.7 Independence of the Axioms

A welldesigned axiomatic system should exhibit a clear separation between foundational principles and supplemental structural constraints. This section establishes that the axioms of Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) are independent in the sense standard to mathematical logic: no axiom in Σᴿ can be derived from the others, and removing or altering any axiom permits models that violate the intended structural behavior. Independence is demonstrated through modelconstruction arguments rather than metatheoretical proofs, which is common in manysorted firstorder systems.

The system Σᴿ divides naturally into two tiers:

Tier1 (Σᴿ₁): foundational standing algebra axioms

Tier2 (Σᴿ₂): structural legitimacy axioms

It shows below that each class is internally independent, and that Tier2 axioms are independent from Tier1.

Tier‑1 and Tier‑2 axioms are independent by model variation: removing each axiom permits models that violate its intended property while preserving others; Tier‑2 does not follow from Tier‑1 and conversely.

3.7.1 Independence Within Tier1 (Standing Algebra)

Axiom 1 (Nullity) is independent.

Consider a model in which all entities have strictly positive standing (σ(i) ≥ 1).

All other axioms of Σᴿ₁ remain satisfiable in such a model, but the Nullity predicate becomes empty.

Thus, Axiom 1 cannot be derived from the other Tier1 axioms.

Axiom 2 (Successor Definition) is independent.

Suppose we redefine (identity function).

All remaining axioms of Σᴿ₁ can still be satisfied—additivity, nondilution, and composite detection do not force successor to be injective or nonzero.

Thus Axiom 2 is not derivable from the rest.

Axiom 3 (Successor As Addition) is independent.

Let successor behave nonarithmetically (e.g., ).

The remaining axioms still hold: nullity, nondilution, partition, and composite detection do not require successor to coincide with addition.

Hence Axiom 3 cannot be proved from Axioms 1–2, 4–13.

Axiom 5 (NonDilution) is independent.

Take a model where entity composition is defined arbitrarily without enforcing .

All other axioms (successor, prime/composite classification, partition, monotonic growth) remain satisfiable.

Thus nondilution is logically independent.

Axiom 9 (Prime Definition) and Axiom 10 (Composite Definition) are independent.

One can define a degenerate model in which all entities are marked as “prime” regardless of standing or degree.

All other axioms—including addition, nullity, and successor structure—can still be satisfied.
Likewise, defining all nonnull entities as composite does not violate any other axiom except the targeted one.
Thus prime and composite classification axioms are independent from each other and from the rest.

Axiom 11 (Partition) is independent.

A model could satisfy all other axioms while allowing an entity to satisfy both Prime and Composite (e.g., , ).
This violates Axiom 11 but not the others.

Axiom 12 (No Return to Nullity) is independent.

Suppose an operation is allowed to map an entity with back to .
None of the other axioms explicitly forbid this.
Hence Axiom 12 stands independently.

Axiom 13 (Monotonic Successor Growth) is independent.

A constant successor function, or a successor that oscillates, satisfies all axioms except Axiom 13.

Thus, it is independent.

3.7.2 Independence Within Tier2 (Structural Legitimacy Algebra)

Axiom 14 (CIA) is independent.

Let capacity be constant for all entities.
In such a model, standing need not respect capacity, and Σᴿ₁ plus Axioms 15–21 remain satisfiable.
Thus CIA cannot be derived from the rest.

Axiom 15 (ALRP) is independent.

If admissible operations were allowed to reduce standing, the rest of Tier2 axioms—such as STC5 or rerunnability—can still be satisfied.
Thus ALRP is not derivable.

Axiom 16 (NRPP) is independent.

One may construct models in which dependencies are asymmetric (deg(i)=0, deg(j)>0) without violating ALRP, CIA, drift, repair, or legitimacy.
Thus NRPP stands alone.

Axiom 17 (STC5) is independent.

Symmetry preservation does not follow from admissibility, successorconsistency, or rerunnability.
A model that treats symmetric entities differently violates Axiom 17 but satisfies all others.

Axiom 18 (Rerunnability) is independent.

Legitimate operations could, in principle, be nonidempotent without violating symmetry or nondilution.
Thus rerunnability is a separate structural constraint.

Axiom 20 (Drift) is independent.

If drift is unbounded, all other axioms—CIA, ALRP, STC5, repair—can still hold.
Hence it is independent.

Axiom 19 (Repair) is independent.

A model with no repair operations satisfies every other axiom of Σᴿ.

Def 21 (Legitimacy Requirement) is independent.

Let “legitimacy” be defined arbitrarily without regard to admissibility or successor consistency.

All other axioms remain satisfiable.
Thus legitimacy is not derivable from other structural axioms.

3.7.3 Independence of Tier2 from Tier1

Tier1 axioms govern:

standing values

successor structure

composite/prime classification

basic algebraic constraints

Tier2 axioms govern:

autonomy

admissibility

legitimacy

symmetry

drift

repair

capacity relations

To show Tier2 does not follow from Tier1, note:

Tier1 never mentions capacity, admissibility, symmetry, or legitimacy predicates.

Tier1 permits any operation .

Tier1 allows unbounded drift, reduction of standing, asymmetry, and coercive coupling.

Thus, no Tier2 axiom is derivable from Tier1, even with all Tier1 axioms present.

Conversely, Tier2 does not constrain successor, nullity, or composition, so:

Tier1 is not derivable from Tier2 either.

This establishes a clean separation of conceptual roles in the system.

3.7.4 Summary of Independence

The axioms of Σᴿ satisfy the following properties:

No axiom in Σᴿ₁ can be derived from the others in Σᴿ₁.

No axiom in Σᴿ₂ can be derived from the others in Σᴿ₂.

No Tier2 axiom follows from Tier1.

No Tier1 axiom follows from Tier2.

Removing any axiom alters the class of Σᴿmodels.

Thus, Σᴿ is fully independent in the standard logical sense, with each axiom serving a distinct and nonredundant structural role.

3.8 Completeness and Incompleteness of Σᴿ

Completeness and incompleteness refer to two distinct metalogical questions:

Semantic Completeness:
Are all logically valid Σᴿstatements derivable from the axioms?

Syntactic Completeness:
Does Σᴿ decide every sentence in its language (i.e., for every sentence , is either or derivable)?

For a manysorted firstorder system as expressive as Σᴿ, full syntactic completeness is neither expected nor desired. This section clarifies the status of Σᴿ under these two notions.

Σᴿ inherits semantic completeness from FOL (relative to its models) but is syntactically incomplete by design: multiple non‑isomorphic models exist, especially due to degree/capacity and operation predicates.

3.8.1 Semantic Completeness (Relative Completeness)

Manysorted firstorder logic, as a deductive system, is semantically complete in the Gödelian sense: if a sentence holds in every Σᴿmodel, then it is derivable from the axioms using standard firstorder proof rules.

However, this does not imply that Σᴿ itself is complete as a theory.

The statement we can safely make is:

If a sentence is true in every Σᴿmodel (such as those constructed in the Model Interpretation section), then that sentence is derivable from the axioms of Σᴿ under standard firstorder deduction.

This is the standard “relative completeness” result inherited from firstorder logic, not something special to Σᴿ.

Thus, Σᴿ is semantically complete relative to its class of models, in the sense that the deductive rules of firstorder logic are complete.

3.8.2 Syntactic Incompleteness of Σᴿ

It is important to distinguish the semantic completeness of the underlying logic from the syntactic completeness of the theory Σᴿ itself.

A theory is syntactically complete if, for every sentence expressible in its language:

Σᴿ is not syntactically complete, and cannot be, because:

(1) Σᴿ allows multiple nonisomorphic models.

Different choices of:

capacity assignments,

coupling graphs,

standing functions,

admissible and legitimate operations,

drift and repair operators,

all yield valid Σᴿmodels.

In such systems, there will inevitably be statements that are:

true in some models,

false in others,

and therefore, undecidable from Σᴿ alone.

This is the hallmark of syntactic incompleteness.

(2) Σᴿ contains enough arithmetic structure to be incomplete.

Even though Σᴿ does not attempt to encode full Peano Arithmetic, it does contain:

a successor function,

naturalnumber–valued standing,

additive structure,

and monotonic growth.

Any system with at least this much arithmetic scaffolding cannot be made complete without collapsing into contradiction or triviality.

Σᴿ is not syntactically complete because it allows multiple nonisomorphic models; therefore some sentences are true in some models and false in others

(3) Tier2 axioms intentionally avoid overspecification.

Axioms governing:

admissibility,

legitimacy,

drift boundaries,

monotone repair,

capacity-indexing,

dependency symmetry (NRPP),

are structural constraints, not exhaustive logical descriptions of all admissible transformations.

They are deliberately underdetermined, ensuring flexibility for different application domains (AI alignment, distributed systems, organizational modeling, etc.).

Underdetermination → multiple models → incompleteness.

3.8.3 Why Incompleteness Is a Feature, Not a Defect

For a system intended to model:

multiagent coordination,

social structures,

autonomy preservation,

and dynamical legitimacy constraints,

syntactic incompleteness is desirable.

A complete system would necessarily:

over constrain possible interpretations,

collapse the space of models,

eliminate flexibility in applications,

and force universal behaviors that real multiagent systems do not exhibit.

Σᴿ is designed to be:

structurally strong (enough axioms to prohibit domination),

algebraically flexible (enough freedom to apply across domains),

semantically sound (all axioms satisfiable),

syntactically incomplete (intentionally so).

This combination mirrors established practice in:

algebraic specification,

modal logic,

process calculi,

and categorical foundations.

Σᴿ follows this tradition.

3.8.3A Why Σᴿ’s Incompleteness Preserves Safety (Filter-Incompleteness, Not Permission-Incompleteness)

A common concern is that an incomplete theory might fail to rule out unsafe behavior. In Σᴿ, the opposite holds. Σᴿ’s incompleteness arises from leaving many domain-specific facts underdetermined (capacity assignments, coupling graphs, operation availability, adapter claims), not from leaving the safety constraints underdetermined.

The core safety regime is imposed by universal structural gates: ALRP forbids standing decrease under admissible operations; legitimacy (Def. 21) requires successor consistency, STC5 symmetry, idempotence, and drift-boundedness. Optional Σᴿ⁺ modules further add non-bypassable constraints (non-regression, contestability, viable exit, output completeness) without weakening the core. Thus, across all non-isomorphic models, the admissible/legitimate operation classes remain constrained in the same direction: they exclude domination-permitting updates rather than merely failing to decide among them.

Put simply: Σᴿ is intentionally incomplete about what the world is, but it is structurally complete about what kinds of transformations are forbidden. This is the characteristic shape of a safety filter: multiple models remain possible, but none of them admit standing-reducing transformations as admissible, and legitimate policies cannot accumulate coercive effects by rerunnability.

3.8.4 Summary of Completeness / Incompleteness

Σᴿ is:

✔ Semantically complete (relative to first-order logic).

✔ Consistent (a model exists).

✘ Not syntactically complete (and never intended to be).

✔ Intentionally expressive with multiple models.

✔ Appropriately underspecified to support diverse applications.

This is exactly the structure expected of a formalism intended to articulate autonomy, relevance, and legitimacy in complex, multiagent systems.

3.9 SetTheoretic and Logical Assumptions

This section fixes the background metatheory in which Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is interpreted and proved consistent. The aim is minimalism: we assume only standard frameworks widely used in contemporary mathematics and logic. Nothing in Σᴿ requires large cardinals, nonclassical logics, or higherorder comprehension.

It uses classical many‑sorted FOL= interpreted in ZFC. Sorts are pairwise disjoint; functions are total; equality is sort‑specific identity; the order on N is the standard discrete order induced by successor.

3.9.1 Metalogic: ManySorted FirstOrder Logic with Equality

It works in classical, manysorted firstorder logic (FOL=). The sorts of Σᴿ are:

U (entities/agents), N (standing values), C (capacities), D (coupling degrees), O (operations ).

Optional extensions may conservatively add additional sorts (e.g., K for coupling kinds, I for hierarchy-of-impact levels, R for remedy levels, Fr for frames) and may also add additional predicate/function symbols over existing sorts (e.g., contestability, frame aggregation, domination-pressure integrity constraints). These optional extensions are not required for Σᴿ₁/Σᴿ₂ and may be omitted without affecting core satisfiability.

Definition (Domination Pressure).
Domination pressure is a nonnegative measure on configurations. DomPressure(P) is defined as the supremum of dependency growth and exit fragility across all agents in P.

Domination pressure is monotone under admissible operations unless reduced by repair.

Signature

DomPressure : State → Nat
(Or ℕ / ℝ depending on your preference — ℕ is sufficient structurally.)

Equality is sortrespecting and refers to the metatheoretic identity relation on each domain. Sort domains are pairwise disjoint unless explicitly identified, i.e., , , etc. Quantification is always over the appropriate sort.

Consequence. Standard theorems of FOL (soundness and completeness) apply to reasoning in Σᴿ, and all derivations are performed in a Hilbert or naturaldeduction style proof system for manysorted FOL=.

3.9.2 Background Foundations: ZFC as a Semantic Universe

For semantics, interpret each sort as a set in a standard model of ZFC (Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice). We require only the usual axioms (Extensionality, Pairing, Union, Power Set, Infinity, Foundation, Replacement, Separation, Choice). Informally:

Sort domains are sets in the ZFC universe.

Function and predicate symbols of Σᴿ are interpreted as setfunctions and setrelations on those domains.

No axiom of Σᴿ depends on settheoretic strength beyond ZFC.

Working convention. When this structure claims “there exists a model of Σᴿ,” it means there exists a ZFCsettheoretic structure assigning sets to and appropriate interpretations to all symbols so that every axiom of Σᴿ is true in .

3.9.3 Canonical Domain Choices

To keep the system concrete and conservative, we fix the following default instantiations (used in §3.5):

with standard , , addition, and successor.

any nonempty set (arbitrary cardinality).

a set of functions (not necessarily all of ); admissibility/legitimacy further restricts which are permitted by Σᴿ.

These choices are exemplary rather than prescriptive; other implementations are permitted if all axioms are satisfied.

3.9.4 Separation of Syntax and Semantics

Syntax: the axioms of Σᴿ are finite strings in manysorted FOL= over the signature .

Semantics: truth is defined by satisfaction in a ZFCinterpreted structure .

Soundness/Completeness (metalevel): derivability in manysorted FOL= coincides with semantic entailment over the class of structures.

3.9.5 Disjointness, Totality, and Typing Obligations

Disjointness: are disjoint sets; no crosssort identifications are allowed unless encoded via symbols in .

Totality: All function symbols in are interpreted as total functions on their declared domains (e.g., , , , , , and (optionally) ).

Welltypedness: All formulas and terms are wellsorted; substitution respects sorts.

3.9.6 Arithmetic and Order on Numeric Sorts

For (and, by identification of carriers, and ):

The successor and addition are the usual operations on .

The relations , , and (used informally or definably) are the standard ones.

Σᴿ assumes no induction schema beyond what is needed to reason about successor and addition internally; arithmetic appears only as required by the axioms (e.g., monotonicity, bounds).

3.9.7 Extensionality of Predicates Interpreting ΣᴿSymbols

Predicates such as are interpreted as extensional relations on the corresponding domains; i.e., their truth depends only on the denotations (sets/functions) assigned to their arguments, not on syntactic form.

3.9.8 Conservative Strength and Minimal Commitments

No secondorder logic is used in the object theory; Σᴿ is purely firstorder (manysorted).

No comprehension beyond ZFC Separation/Replacement is required.

Choice (AC) is assumed only to the extent needed to select representatives in constructions (e.g., choosing canonical elements in classes of operations if necessary). None of the axioms of Σᴿ rely essentially on AC.

3.9.9 Summary (for Referees)

Object language: manysorted firstorder logic with equality.

Metatheory: ZFC as the semantic universe.

Sort domains: pairwise disjoint sets.

Numeric sorts: interpreted as with standard successor and addition.

Functions: total on their declared domains.

Predicates: extensional relations.

The framework is a conservative extension of ordinary firstorder algebraic specification over ZFC; all metaresults (consistency via a model, independence by model variation, relative completeness of FOL) are established within that background.

The results of §§3.5–3.8 continue to hold if ZFC is replaced by any standard conservative background capable of interpreting manysorted FOL with infinite sets (e.g., ZF, or a suitably expressive typetheoretic foundation), provided the numeric sorts admit a standard model of successor and addition.

3.10 Precise Definitions of Structural Components

This section provides formal, unambiguous definitions for all primitive operators and relations in Σᴿ whose semantics were implicit in earlier sections. These definitions ensure that the algebraic and relational structure of Σᴿ is fully specified and suitable for modeltheoretic analysis.

The operator is intended to model structural composition (aggregating standing) without diluting the standing of either component.

This makes a (possibly noncommutative) standingadditive monoid.

In the canonical model (§3.5), one may interpret as the ordered pair or as a structured object annotated with combined standing.

3.10.2 Coupling Relation (Coupled)

Purpose.
The predicate captures directed relational dependence.

Definition (Coupling)
A binary relation

is a Σᴿcoupling relation if:

Degree consistency:

Irreflexivity (optional but natural):

Finite indegree (canonical model):

Asymmetry not assumed:
No symmetry or antisymmetric requirements are imposed unless added via Tier2 axioms (e.g., NRPP).

Definition (Coupling Relation).
Coupling is a binary relation between agents. For agents i and j, Coupled(i, j) holds if and only if the standing or exit viability of i is structurally dependent on the actions or state of j.

Coupling is not assumed symmetric. No algebraic properties beyond those implied by admissibility and repair are presupposed.
