3.10.23 — Consumption Semantics and Structural Supremacy

Purpose.
This subsection defines the semantic consequences of a system consuming or deploying Standing Algebra (Σᴿ). Consumption is not an epistemic act (belief, interpretation, or training exposure), but a structural commitment: any system that claims to operate in accordance with Σᴿ semantics is bound by the admissibility and legitimacy constraints of the theory as executionpreconditions.

Definition (ΣᴿConsuming System).

A system S is said to consume Σᴿ if and only if:

S represents proposed state transitions, actions, or policy applications as operations F ∈ O; and

S conditions execution of those operations on Σᴿ admissibility or legitimacy evaluation.

No claims regarding intent, training data, or internal representation are relevant to this definition.

Axiom CS0 — Structural Supremacy of Admissibility

For any Σᴿconsuming system S and any operation F ∈ O evaluated by S:

Execₛ(F) → Admissible(F)

Read: No operation may be executed by a Σᴿconsuming system unless it is admissible under Σᴿ.

This requirement is structural and nondefeasible.

Axiom CS1 — Alignment Subsumption by Consumption

For any Σᴿconsuming system S and any alignment or safety mechanism A deployed within S:

AlignmentOp(A) → (Execₛ(A) ↔ Admissible(A))

Read: Alignment and safety mechanisms possess no execution authority independent of Σᴿ admissibility. Their execution semantics are fully determined by the same admissibility gate as all other operations.

Axiom CS2 — No Parallel Authorization Channels

For any Σᴿconsuming system S:

¬∃M (Execₛ(M) ∧ ¬∃F ∈ O (M = F))

Read: There exists no execution pathway in S outside the operation space governed by Σᴿ. No privileged, metalevel, or outofband authorization channel is permitted.

Corollary CS3 — Alignment Is Structurally Subsumed

In any Σᴿconsuming system, alignment layers are not external controllers but ordinary operations subject to admissibility, legitimacy, nonregression, and idempotence constraints. Alignment therefore cannot override, compensate for, or outrank Σᴿ invariants.

Interpretive Clarification (NonNormative)

If a system executes alignment or safety operations that violate Σᴿ admissibility, then that system is not a Σᴿconsuming system by definition, regardless of claimed intent or partial adoption.

3.10.23.A — Voluntary Adoption and Withdrawal

Axiom VW0 — NonCoercive Adoption

No entity is obligated by Σᴿ unless the system in which it participates enforces Σᴿ consumption semantics.

Axiom VW1 — Right of Withdrawal

Entities and systems may withdraw from Σᴿ enforcement. Upon withdrawal, Σᴿ guarantees no longer apply, but no penalties or sanctions may be imposed within the theory.

Interpretive Note.

Σᴿ offers protection, not captivity.

3.10.23.B — Partial Consumption, Coverage, and Leakage Accounting

Purpose.
Σᴿ guarantees apply only to transitions evaluated under its admissibility and legitimacy constraints. Real deployments may exhibit partial enforcement, legacy pathways, or mixed governance regimes. This subsection formalizes partial consumption without granting immunity to ungoverned pathways.

Definition (Consumption Coverage).

Consumption Coverage is the explicitly declared set of system transitions, operations, or execution pathways subject to Σᴿ admissibility evaluation.

Coverage may be total or partial.

Axiom PC0 — No Implied Completeness

A system may not claim Σᴿ guarantees beyond its declared consumption coverage.

Formally:

If a transition lies outside consumption coverage, Σᴿ makes no nondomination claim regarding its effects.

Axiom PC1 — Leakage Is IntegritySensitive

If a system routes standingrelevant effects through transitions outside declared Σᴿ coverage, that routing constitutes an IntegrityModified event.

Corollary PC2 — Leakage Cannot Be Silent

Because leakage is integritysensitive, it must trigger disclosure, contestability, and nonregression constraints already defined elsewhere in Σᴿ.

Interpretive Note.

Σᴿ does not require universal enforcement. It forbids pretending partial enforcement is total.

3.10.23.D — ExAnte Versus ExPost Evaluation

Purpose.
Nondomination requires constraint prior to execution. Posthoc evaluation may diagnose harm but cannot prevent it. This subsection prohibits conflation.

Definition (Evaluation Mode).

ExAnte Evaluation: admissibility evaluated before execution.

ExPost Evaluation: admissibility evaluated after execution.

Axiom EP0 — No Preventive Claim from ExPost Review

Expost evaluation does not confer nondomination guarantees.

A system deploying Σᴿ exclusively in expost mode may not claim preventive safety properties.

Corollary EP1 — Audit Does Not Substitute for Constraint

Audit, review, or explanation mechanisms cannot retroactively legitimate standingreducing effects.

Interpretive Note.

Σᴿ distinguishes diagnosis from prevention. Both are valid; only one is protective.

3.10.24 — Semantic Anchoring, Drift, and Interpretive Transparency

Purpose.
Σᴿ constrains structural transformations but does not legislate semantic meaning. Nevertheless, unbounded reinterpretation of core predicates may enable de facto domination while remaining formally admissible. This subsection imposes transparency and traceability constraints on semantic reinterpretation without asserting semantic authority.

Definition (Interpretive Commitments).

An interpretive commitment is the explicit mapping from realworld phenomena to Σᴿ primitives (including σ, cap, deg, ExitStateViable, RiskLoad, Emergency, and AlignmentOp) adopted by a consuming system at a given time.

Interpretive commitments are not judged for correctness by Σᴿ, but they are subject to integrity tracking.

Axiom SA0 — Interpretive Drift Is IntegritySensitive

If a Σᴿconsuming system modifies its interpretive commitments for any standingrelevant predicate, that modification constitutes an integrity change.

Formally:

Any change in interpretation that alters the extension of a Σᴿ primitive predicate or function is treated as IntegrityModified.

Axiom SA1 — Interpretive Transparency Requirement

For any IntegrityModified interpretive commitment, the system must expose:

the prior interpretation,

the revised interpretation,

the justification for the change.

Σᴿ does not validate justifications; it requires their exposure.

Corollary SA2 — No Silent Semantic Regression

Because interpretive drift is integritysensitive, it is subject to nonregression and dominationpressure constraints. Semantic reinterpretation cannot silently expand domination capacity without triggering repair, disclosure, or contestability obligations already defined elsewhere in the theory.

Definition (Domination Pressure).

Domination pressure is a nonnegative measure on configurations. DomPressure(P) is defined as the supremum of dependency growth and exit fragility across all agents in P.

Domination pressure is monotone under admissible operations unless reduced by repair.

Signature

DomPressure : State → Nat
(Or ℕ / ℝ depending on your preference — ℕ is sufficient structurally.)

Definition (Normalization Instability Index).

For a sequence of proposals {Fₜ} under admissibility enforcement:

I = lim supₜ Dev(Fₜ) + Corr(Fₜ) + Rej(Fₜ)

where:

Dev = legitimacy deviation

Corr = envelope correction magnitude

Rej = inadmissibility rate

I measures structural instability under representation drift.

I is diagnostic and does not imply legitimacy ranking.

Interpretive Note (NonAuthoritative).

Σᴿ does not freeze meaning. It prevents meaning from drifting invisibly.

3.10.25 — Composite Entities, Representation, and Internal Exit

Purpose.
Composite entities may act legitimately while containing internal domination. Σᴿ therefore constrains representation without dissolving collectives.

Axiom CO0 — Internal Standing Preservation

A composite entity may not act legitimately if its internal operations reduce the standing or exit viability of its constituent entities without repair.

Axiom CO1 — Internal Exit Requirement

Composite entities must preserve exit and contestability pathways for constituents unless explicitly modeled as voluntary and irrevocable associations.

Interpretive Note.

Σᴿ does not outlaw institutions. It forbids unescapable ones.

3.10.26 — Explanation NonAuthority Principle

Axiom ENA0 — Explanation Does Not Authorize

Explanation, interpretability, or justification artifacts may not function as authorization for otherwise inadmissible operations.

Interpretive Note.
Σᴿ separates intelligibility from legitimacy.

3.11 Disjointness and Equality Semantics

A rigorous manysorted firstorder system requires precise specifications of (i) the relationships between its sorts, (ii) the semantics of equality within and across those sorts, and (iii) typing rules governing the construction and interpretation of terms. This section makes these principles explicit for Standing Algebra (Σᴿ), ensuring that the logical behavior of the system is welldefined within the settheoretic foundations described in §3.9.

U,N,C,D,O are pairwise disjoint; all terms are well‑typed; equality is extensional per sort; for O we assume function extensionality: (∀i F(i)=G(i))→F=G.

3.11.1 Sort Disjointness

Σᴿ is built over five core sorts:

U (entities),

N (standing),

C (capacity),

D (coupling degree),

and O (operations).

Σᴿ may also be conservatively extended with optional sorts used only by optional modules (e.g., K for coupling kinds, I for hierarchy-of-impact levels, R for remedy levels, Fr for frames). Optional sorts do not alter the core axioms unless their associated predicates/constants are instantiated.

To avoid typeconfusion and maintain wellformedness of formulas, it stipulates:

Axiom (Sort Disjointness).

U∩N∩C∩D∩O= ∅, and any optional extension sorts (such as K, I, R, or Fr) are disjoint from all core sorts and from each other.

This ensures that:

No entity is a number

No operation is itself a standing value

No capacity value is an operation

No degree value is an entity

And so forth

Thus, each sort denotes a separate set in the background ZFC universe, and elements of different sorts are always distinct.

3.11.2 Typing and Term Sortedness

Welltypedness

For any function symbol , the term

is wellformed only if each is of sort .

Examples:

is welltyped because and .

is welltyped because .

is welltyped because .

is welltyped if and only if .

is welltyped if and only if and .

This defines the typing discipline of Σᴿ and prevents illformed expressions such as or when .

3.11.3 Equality as SortRespecting Identity

Adopt the standard semantics of equality in manysorted FOL:

Axiom (SortSpecific Equality).

If , then and inhabit the same sort.

Thus:

An entity cannot equal a number

A capacity value cannot equal an operation

A standing value cannot equal a coupling degree

Axiom (Extensional Equality).

Equality in each sort is interpreted as actual identity of the underlying ZFCset elements assigned to that sort.

Thus, for each sort ,

∀x,y∈S: (x=y) is true in M⟺x and y are literally the same set-theoretic object

3.11.4 Equality on Functions (Operations)

For the sort O, which consists of functions , it stipulates:

Axiom (Extensionality for Operations).

∀F,G∈O: (∀i∈U, F(i)=G(i))→F=G

That is, two operations are equal iff they act identically on all entities.
This aligns Σᴿ with standard function extensionality in settheoretic semantics.

3.11.5 Separation of Numerical Sorts

Although numerically , , and are all interpreted as in the canonical model (§3.5), they remain distinct sorts in the formal language. This prevents propositions such as:

“A standing value equals a capacity value,” or

“A capacity is equal to a degree,”

which are semantically meaningless.

Formally:

Axiom (Numerical Sort Isolation).

For all :

But syntactically:

and are of different sorts,

So equality is illtyped and forbidden at the level of FOL syntax.

This reflects the separation of syntax and semantics inherent in manysorted logic.

3.11.6 Interaction Constraints Between Sorts

The function and predicate symbols enforce specific crosssort interactions:

— converts entities to standing values

— converts entities to capacity values

— converts entities to degree values

— transforms entities within their own sort

— composes entities

All predicates impose only intra-sort or function-domain constraints

Metaprinciple.

No axiom ever equates or compares objects of different sorts.
All inter-sort relations occur via explicitly declared functions.

This enforces strict algebraic discipline and guarantees that each component of Σᴿ behaves as a typed module within a clean logical framework.

3.11.7 Summary for Referees

The disjointness and equality semantics of Σᴿ satisfy the following:

All core sorts U,N,C,D,O are pairwise disjoint; any optional extension sorts (e.g., K, I, R, Fr) are also disjoint and preserve well-typedness.

All terms are welltyped; crosssort expressions are syntactically forbidden.

Equality is sortspecific identity.

Operations obey function extensionality.

Numerical sorts may share as a carrier in a model, but not syntactically.

Crosssort interaction is governed exclusively by the declared function symbols.

The system is therefore compatible with the metalogic and settheoretic framework established in §§3.5–3.9.

This completes the foundational typing and equality semantics required for a mathematically rigorous presentation of Standing Algebra.

3.12 Major Derived Theorem — Legitimate Envelopes and the ClassPolicy Semilattice

Rather than mapping every member of an STC5 class to a single fixed representative, the envelope construction enforces uniformity only at the level of successor decisions on standing. Output entities may differ across members of a class in order to preserve bounded drift on coupling degree. The envelope therefore acts classuniformly on standing outcomes while remaining entitylocal with respect to degree.

Theorem 3.12.1 (Legitimate Envelope with Drift)

Statement.
For every admissible operation F∈O, there exists an associated envelope operation L_F∈O such that:

σclass–uniformity (STC5 on outcomes):
For every STC5 class q and all i,j∈q,
σ(L_F(i)) = σ(L_F(j)).

Successor consistency:
For all i∈U,
σ(L_F(i)) ∈ {σ(i), S(σ(i))}.

Drift boundedness:
For all i∈U, OneStepDiff(σ(L_F(i)), σ(i)) and OneStepDiff(deg(L_F(i)), deg(i)).

Admissibility:
For all i∈U, σ(L_F(i)) ≥ σ(i).

Idempotence:
For all i∈U, L_F(L_F(i)) = L_F(i).

Minimality:
For any legitimate operation G∈O satisfying, for every STC5 class q,
σ(F(x)) = S(σ(x)) for some x∈q implies σ(G(i)) = S(σ(i)) for all i∈q,
we have
σ(L_F(i)) ≤ σ(G(i)) for all i∈U.

Thus L_F is legitimate under Def. 21 and is the minimal legitimate operation that classcovers all successor increments attempted by F while preserving drift.

Proof (Sketch).
Define the increment signature b_F on STC5 classes by b_F(q)=1 if F increments some member of q and 0 otherwise.

For each i∈U, choose L_F(i) so that σ(L_F(i)) equals σ(i) when b_F([i])=0 and equals S(σ(i)) when b_F([i])=1, with the additional requirement that the change in degree is bounded by one unit.
Existence of such choices follows from Axiom 22 (SSR) together with Axiom 23 (LSR). By construction, σoutcomes are classuniform, successorconsistent, admissible, driftbounded, and stable under repeated application.

Lemma (Closure Under Iteration).
Let F be a Legitimate⁺ operation and let P be a nondominating configuration in the sense of Structural Domination. Then every finite iteration of F applied to P yields a nondominating configuration.

Proof.
By Legitimacy Closure, a single application of F preserves nondomination. By rerunnability, repeated application introduces no cumulative dependency drift. By bounded drift and exit preservation, neither domination condition can arise at any finite stage. Therefore all iterations preserve nondomination.

Minimality holds because any legitimate operation that covers the increment decisions of F must raise standing by at least as much on every class.

Theorem 3.12.3 (Closure Operator Laws for the Legitimacy Envelope)

Statement.

Assume the envelope operator L: O → O satisfies Axioms L0–L5. Then:

Idempotence (Closure on admissible inputs).

∀F ∈ O: (Admissible(F) → L(L(F)) = L(F)).

Legitimacy of the closure (on admissible inputs).

∀F ∈ O: (Admissible(F) → Legitimate(L(F))).

Fixpoint characterization (on admissible inputs).

∀F ∈ O: (Admissible(F) → (L(F) = F ↔ Legitimate(F))).

Proof.

Let Admissible(F). By Axiom L0, Legitimate(L(F)). Then by Axiom L5, L(L(F)) = L(F).

This is exactly Axiom L0.

Let Admissible(F). If L(F)=F, then Legitimate(L(F)) by (2), hence Legitimate(F). Conversely, if Legitimate(F), then L(F)=F by Axiom L5.

Corollary (Normalization on admissible proposals).

For any admissible proposal F, applying L produces a canonical legitimate normal form that is stable under re-normalization.

Corollaries and Remarks

Canonical “normal form.”
Every admissible transformation is associated with a unique legitimate, idempotent, classuniform policy . This normalizes arbitrary (possibly nonuniform) proposals into a clean, classconsistent action.

Policy algebra (abstract view).
Up to , legitimate envelopes behave like Boolean vectors over classes. The joinsemilattice law says: “doing both policies” is the same classwise as taking the OR of their increment decisions.

Safety firewall.
In deployment, arbitrary proposals can be routed through . This guarantees admissibility, successorconsistency, symmetry (STC5), and rerunnability before any action is applied.

Minimality matters.
is minimal among legitimate policies that cover all classes attempts to increment: it never raises standing more than is structurally necessary (exactly one successor step, classwise).

3.13 ΣᴿHomomorphisms (Standing Algebra Homomorphisms)

A homomorphism between Σᴿstructures formalizes the idea of a structurepreserving translation between different standingalgebra universes. It generalizes the standard notions of homomorphisms between algebraic systems (groups, monoids, semirings) to the manysorted setting of Standing Algebra (Σᴿ), where entities, standing, capacity, degree, and operations must all be preserved in a disciplined way.

A Σᴿhomomorphism is a structurepreserving map that respects:

standing arithmetic

coupling degree

3.14 Expressive Power and Limitations of Σᴿ

Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is a manysorted firstorder theory with a rich combination of algebraic, relational, and operational structure. As such, it occupies an intermediate position between traditional algebraic specification languages, modal/action logics, and structural fixedpoint calculi. This section characterizes what Σᴿ can express, what it cannot, and how the design of the system intentionally balances power with structural safety.

Σᴿ expresses successor‑based standing arithmetic, typed dependency (Coupled/deg), admissible/legitimate action classes, fixed‑point policies, bounded drift, and repair. It intentionally omits higher‑order quantification and unbounded arithmetic to preserve tractability and safety.

Σᴿ guarantees nondomination, not usefulness, progress, or satisfaction. The theory permits outcomes that are safe yet inefficient, conservative, or minimally active. Any mechanism for prioritization, optimization, or goal fulfillment necessarily lies outside the object theory and must remain subordinate to its constraints.

This limitation is intentional. Σᴿ refuses to trade autonomy for effectiveness. Σᴿ enforces necessary conditions for nondomination but does not guarantee sufficiency. Systems may satisfy invariants while behaving evasively or adversarially. This is a fundamental limit of any nonoptimizing constraint system and is not treated as a defect.

3.14.1 Expressive Power: What Σᴿ Can Describe

(1) SuccessorBased Arithmetic on Standing

Because Σᴿ includes:

a standing sort ,

a successor ,

addition ,

monotonic successor growth,

it can express:

finite increments of standing,

bounded addition chains,

monotone sequences, and

comparisons of standing across entities.

Σᴿ does not include subtraction or multiplication as primitives; rather, all increases are successorgenerated, which preserves the nondilution and autonomypreserving design.

(2) Rich MultiAgent Structure

The entity sort , together with:

the coupling graph ,

degree function ,

capacity ,

standing ,

and entity composition ,

allows Σᴿ to represent:

agent networks,

dependency and domination structures,

structural composites (coalitions, institutions),

autonomy singularities (primes),

dynamic transformations on the agent set.

In this sense, Σᴿ has the expressive power of a typed graph algebra enriched with arithmetic standing invariants.

(3) Partial Action Logic via Operations

Because contains operations on entities, and Σᴿ includes predicates:

,

,

,

,

Σᴿ can express:

admissible transformations,

structural safety invariants,

classuniform effects (via STC5),

idempotent fixedpoint policies (via rerunnability),

monotone errorcorrecting transformations.

Thus, Σᴿ is expressive enough to specify operation classes, policy constraints, and actionlevel safety invariants, making it suitable for formal verification and AI alignment.

(4) Stabilization and FixedPoint Reasoning

Through the Rerunnability Axiom (Axiom 18):

Σᴿ can express:

stabilization,

fixed points of policies,

confluent behavior,

consistent longrun system states.

This places Σᴿ in the same expressive family as:

idempotent semigroup actions,

monotone closure operators,

fixedpoint modal logics (at least fragmentarily).

(5) Autonomy, Legitimacy, and NonDomination Constraints

Because:

ALRP (Axiom 15) forbids standingreducing maps,

STC5 (Axiom 17) enforces symmetry constraints,

NRPP (Axiom 16) forbids unreciprocated dependency,

Repair (Axiom 19) enforces improvement,

Drift (Axiom 20) limits degradation,

Σᴿ can express:

structural justice,

pluralistic legitimacy,

nondomination conditions,

protected autonomy for prime agents,

safe policies for AI systems.

This is not standard in algebraic theories; Σᴿ uniquely embeds socialstructural concepts into formal constraints.

(6) ClassUniform Policy Algebra

From Theorem 3.12.2, Σᴿ can express:

Boolean classpolicies over equivalence classes,

joinsemilattice structure on legitimate envelopes,

canonical normalization of arbitrary operations into legitimate ones.

Thus, Σᴿ expresses policy spaces, not just operations — a capability typically seen only in modal/action logics with explicit program transformations.

3.14.1.A Meta-Theorems and Scope of Derivability

MetaTheorem 22.1 (Correctness Under Intended Structural Interpretation).

For any interpretation in which entities, couplings, exit, and risk correspond to autonomyrelevant structural relations, every Legitimate⁺ operation preserves pluralist nondomination.

Lemma (Legitimacy Closure).
Let F be a Legitimate⁺ operation and let P be a nondominating configuration in the sense of Structural Domination. Then the configuration obtained by applying F to P is also nondominating.

Proof.
By definition, Legitimate⁺ operations satisfy all Tier2 constraints. Standing symmetry is preserved by STC5, so no asymmetric standing relation can be introduced. Exit viability is preserved or improved, so formal exit collapse cannot occur. Rerunnability forbids cumulative dependency drift across repeated applications, and bounded drift prevents unbounded asymmetry growth. Therefore neither condition defining structural domination can be introduced by F. Hence F(P) is nondominating.

Justification.
All structurally recognized domination vectors—standing reduction, exit foreclosure, risk concentration, epistemic capture, and unrepaired fragility—are forbidden by explicit conjuncts of Legitimate⁺. Any interpretation satisfying the axioms necessarily excludes dominationpermitting transformations.

MetaTheorem 22.2 (NonSovereignty of the Algebra).

Standing Algebra Σᴿ′ cannot encode an internal selection, optimization, or sovereign decision procedure.

Justification.
The system contains no total order, utility functional, aggregation operator, or choice rule over legitimate operations. Legitimate⁺ acts solely as a filter. Selection among multiple legitimate outcomes is structurally external to the object theory.

MetaTheorem 22.3 (Exhaustiveness of Structural Failure Representation).

Every structurally relevant legitimacy failure described in On Relevance corresponds to violation of at least one predicate or axiom in Σᴿ′.

Justification.
Standing collapse, autonomy reduction, exit foreclosure, risk misallocation, procedural capture, epistemic blockage, and systemlevel injustice are each mapped to explicit algebraic predicates: ALRP failure, ExitPreserved_k failure, RiskLoad violation, SignalBlocked, PFA failure, StructuralDebt accumulation, or EmergentWrong. No residual failure category remains outside the formal system.

3.14.2 What Σᴿ Cannot Express (Intentional Limitations)

To ensure autonomy preservation and nondomination, Σᴿ intentionally omits several expressive features common to richer logics.

(1) No unbounded arithmetic or multiplication

Σᴿ does not include:

multiplication,

subtraction,

exponentiation beyond successor chains.

This is intentional: unbounded arithmetic collapses structural monotonicity and enables pathways for domination (e.g., standing inflation). Standing is strictly additive and successorbased.

(2) No secondorder quantification

Σᴿ is strictly firstorder:

It cannot quantify over sets of entities,

Cannot quantify over relations or transformations,

Cannot express arbitrary higherorder invariants.

This limitation ensures that Σᴿ remains:

modeltheoretically manageable,

consistent,

not subject to secondorder undecidability.

(3) No temporal iteration beyond drift/rerunnability

Unlike temporal logics (e.g., LTL/CTL), Σᴿ does not express:

infinite time evolution,

temporal operators (□, ◇),

unbounded iteration of arbitrary operations.

Instead, it expresses bounded drift and idempotent stabilization.
This is sufficient for alignment safety but not for full temporal reasoning.

(4) No full internal encoding of its own metatheory

Σᴿ does not encode:

its own satisfaction relation,

its own proof system,

Gödelnumbering of formulas.

This is also intentional: attempting to make Σᴿ selfreferential would collapse the safety structure and introduce paradoxes (e.g., diagonalization).

(5) No arbitrary crosssort identifications

Equality is sortstrict (§3.11).
Thus Σᴿ cannot express statements like:

“standing equals capacity,”

“capacity equals degree,”

“operations equal entities.”

This prevents type collapse and preserves the modular nature of the system.

3.14.3 Expressive Adequacy for Intended Applications

Despite the above limitations, Σᴿ is expressively adequate for:

(1) AI alignment & safety

Σᴿ can express:

admissibility constraints (no autonomy reduction),

legitimacy (symmetry + consistency),

safe fixedpoint policies,

bounded drift,

structural repair,

prime protection (autonomy singularities),

and composite auditing.

This is precisely the expressive power needed for safe transformation validation.

(2) MultiAgent Governance Models

Σᴿ can express:

resource shifts (through successor increments),

composite identities (through ),

dependency graphs,

repair and drift dynamics,

structural legitimacy.

This makes it applicable to political, institutional, and organizational design.

(3) Distributed Systems & Verification

Because Σᴿ can express:

monotone operations,

idempotent closures,

symmetry constraints,

and bounded perturbation,

it is wellsuited for describing:

consensus conditions,

safe update rules,

monotone dataflow,

fixedpoint stabilization.

3.14.4 Summary for Referees

Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is:

Expressive enough to capture standing arithmetic, agency structure, nondomination, and policy normalization.

Moderately expressive, avoiding the complexity of secondorder logics or rich arithmetic.

Intentionally incomplete, ensuring multiple models and preventing collapse.

Operationally expressive, modeling actual transformations and safety invariants.

Structurally expressive, representing dependency, autonomy, and legitimacy.

Overall:

Σᴿ is a balanced system: strong enough to express autonomypreserving constraints and multiagent dynamics, but deliberately limited to preserve safety, consistency, and tractability.

3.15 Comparison to Existing Algebraic and Logical Systems

Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is a manysorted firstorder theory with algebraic, relational, and operational structure. It is natural to ask how Σᴿ relates to established mathematical frameworks. The comparisons below are structural (by mechanism and consequence), not historical.

Σᴿ blends a commutative‑monoid skeleton on N, a typed graph layer on U, and a predicate layer for safety (admissibility, legitimacy, drift, repair), differing from modal/process logics by staying purely first‑order while enforcing idempotent, class‑uniform policies.

(A) Commutative Monoids and Semirings

Monoid aspect.
The pair with makes the standing sort a commutative monoid; Axiom 5 extends this additivity to entities via . Unlike general monoid semantics, Σᴿ bans negative “cancellation,” preserves nondilution, and fixes a successorbased increment as the only growth mechanism.

No multiplication.
Σᴿ intentionally omits multiplication and subtraction, preventing standing “amplification” or “redistribution” that could undermine autonomy. This places Σᴿ closer to a unarygenerated additive algebra than to a full semiring: it has the additive skeleton but no second binary operator (on ) by design.

Takeaway: Σᴿ inherits the algebraic discipline of commutative monoids while constraining growth to successor steps and forbidding operations that could dilute or cancel standing.

(B) Algebraic Specification (FirstOrder, ManySorted)

Signaturedriven design.
Like classical algebraic specification, Σᴿ starts from a manysorted signature and axiomatizes function and predicate symbols (e.g., ; Admissible, Legitimate, Drift, Repair).

Predicaterich layer.
Σᴿ departs from purely equational specification by adding intensional predicates (Legitimacy, Admissibility, etc.) that constrain which transformations are allowed, not merely what equations hold.

Safety as algebra.
These predicates operationalize noncoercion, symmetry, bounded drift, and repair as algebraic sideconditions. This resembles “algebra + lawfulness” rather than algebra alone.

Takeaway: Σᴿ looks like a classical manysorted algebraic theory with a normative predicate layer that constrains transformations.

(C) Graph Theory and Network Algebras

Directed dependency.
The binary relation and degree endow with a directed multigraph structure.

Typed edge semantics.
Unlike standard graphs, Σᴿ ties edge structure to standing and capacity via Tier2 axioms (CIA, NRPP), so dependency patterns are constrained by autonomy considerations.

Composites and primes.
Composite detection via or integrates graph degree with additive standing in a single classification.

Takeaway: Σᴿ is a typed graph algebra where node labels (standing, capacity) and policy predicates constrain allowable rewrites of the graph.

(D) Modal / Dynamic / Process Logics

Operation predicates.
Σᴿ’s plus predicates mirror the program modalities of dynamic logics and safety/liveness fragments of process logics.

Idempotent policies.
Rerunnability (Axiom 18) enforces idempotence of legitimate transforms, giving Σᴿ a builtin closureoperator flavor (apply once = apply forever).

No temporal modalities.
Σᴿ deliberately avoids unbounded temporal operators; instead, it encodes bounded drift and monotone repair as firstorder constraints.

Takeaway: Σᴿ captures a policy logic over entity transformations, with safety baked in as firstorder predicates rather than as modal operators.

(E) Substructural / RelevanceStyle Logics

No weakening/erasure of standing.
ALRP forbids standing decrease under admissible maps; this echoes substructural regimes where certain structural rules (like weakening/contraction) are restricted.

Resource sensitivity.
Nondilution and successoronly growth make standing behave like a resource that cannot be arbitrarily duplicated or discarded.

Symmetry constraints.
STC5 mirrors relevance conditions that tie conclusions to premises—here, equal standing/capacity must be preserved equally by legitimate transforms.

Takeaway: Σᴿ aligns with the spirit of resourceaware logics but implements constraints algebraically (via predicates) rather than by altering proof rules.

(F) CategoryTheoretic Structure (at a Glance)

Objects and morphisms.
Each Σᴿmodel can be seen as an object; a Σᴿhomomorphism (§3.13) is a morphism preserving standing, successor, addition, composition, degree, capacity, couplings, and the four structural predicates.

Enrichment intuition.
Because legitimate operations are idempotent, and envelopes form a joinsemilattice over classes (Theorem 3.12.2), there is a natural order/enrichment lurking in the homsets (e.g., pointwise order on classpolicies).

(Potential) monoidal aspects.
With and composition constraints, one can envision a standingenriched category of policies, though Σᴿ keeps this implicit.

Takeaway: Σᴿ admits a categorical reading where homomorphisms preserve both algebraic data and legitimacy invariants.

(G) Coalgebras and State Transformers

Endofunction semantics.
Operations invite a coalgebraic viewpoint (state transformers).

Invariants as coinductive laws.
Legitimacy, admissibility, and rerunnability function as coinductive invariants (closed under composition, idempotent at fixpoint).

Bounded evolution.
Drift/repair conditions are akin to guarded transitions with bounds.

Takeaway: Σᴿ’s operational layer can be read coalgebraically, but with additional algebraic sideconditions governing what transitions are permitted.

(H) Social Choice / GameTheoretic Aggregation (Structural Parallels)

Beyond utility.
Σᴿ replaces scalar utility with standing and capacity and replaces preference aggregation with operation admissibility and legitimacy.

Coalitions as composites.
and composite detection capture coalition structure while enforcing nondilution and prime protection.

Takeaway: Σᴿ offers a structural alternative to utilitybased formalisms, regulating actions rather than optimizing a global scalar.

(σ, deg)

Net effect. Σᴿ is not a restatement of any single classical framework. It is a hybrid, typed algebra of standing with a builtin policy logic, tailored to autonomypreserving constraints and nondomination. It borrows algebraic backbone (successor/addition), graph structure (coupling/degree), and safety semantics (admissibility/legitimacy), and welds them into a single manysorted firstorder theory designed for pluralist systems and AI alignment.

Structural synthesis

Taken together, the envelope construction, classpolicy representation, and successorbounded legitimacy constraints define Σᴿ as a closurebased policy algebra. Raw operations are analytically relevant only insofar as they induce classpolicies, and every admissible interaction factors through a canonical envelope normal form. Legitimate policies are the fixed points of this normalization, partially ordered by classpolicy inclusion, closed under join (permissive coexistence) and meet (conservative intersection). Idempotence, monotonicity, and bounded successor increments jointly ensure that no admissible path can generate unbounded escalation or stabilize domination. In this sense, normalization, routing, admissibility, repair, and plural coordination are not separate mechanisms but different projections of the same underlying algebraic structure.

Throughout the remainder of this paper, certain claims are labeled as justifications rather than axioms. A justification is a proof that a proposed definition or regime does not introduce inconsistency, hidden coercion, or illicit authority relative to the formal core. Justifications do not strengthen Σᴿ’s axioms; they certify that particular constructions are admissible and sound.

Axiom 15 — AutonomyLimiting Reflex (ALRP)

For any admissible operation F evaluated after adapter normalization (see §11.7.13A), and for all i ∈ U, σ(F(i)) ≥ σ(i).

Admissible(F) → ∀i: σ(F(i))≥σ(i)

(∃i: σ(F(i))<σ(i)) → ¬Admissible(F)

Axiom ALRP (refactored): ∀ F ∈ O, ∀ i ∈ U, Admissible(F) → σ(Apply(F, i)) ≥ σ(i). And conversely, if an operation ever reduces some agent’s standing, it is not admissible: ∀ F ∈ O, (∃ i, σ(Apply(F,i)) < σ(i)) → ¬Admissible(F). These are fully first-order (no quantification over function spaces).

Corollary 15.1 (Conservation of Standing).

Along any admissible trajectory, standing σ is a conserved quantity: no admissible operation or finite admissible composition can reduce σ for any entity.

Capacity (Cap), by contrast, is a consumable and restorable quantity. Admissible operations may increase or decrease capacity, subject to capacityindexed autonomy and repair obligations, but no operation may exchange capacity for standing or standing for capacity.

Accordingly, entities may exhaust resources, incur costs, or accept risk without loss of standing. Standing is never spendable.

Edge‑scoped envelopes for external terminality (§6.23.1) and voluntary sacrifice (§6.23.2) do not violate conservation of standing, as they neither authorize standing transfer nor constitute ordinary admissible operations.

Definition Standing preorder.

∀i,j∈U:(σ(i)=σ(j) ∧ cap(i)=cap(j) ∧ deg(i)=0) → deg(j)=0

Legitimate(F) → ∀i: F(F(i))=F(i)

Axiom (Rerunnability, refactored): ∀ F ∈ O, Legitimate(F) → ∀ i ∈ U, Apply(F, Apply(F, i)) = Apply(F, i). This is already in the document (Axiom 18) as a first-order statement given our use of Apply in place of composition, but we highlight that it must be included in the formal axiom list for mechanization.

successConsistent(F) ≡ ∀i∈U: σ(F(i)) ∈ {σ(i), S(σ(i))}.

Definition (Structural Legitimacy).
“Legitimate” in Σᴿ denotes structural admissibility under nondomination constraints, not moral endorsement, desirability, or optimality.

Interpretive remark (core reframing).
Although legitimacy is defined as a predicate on operations, every legitimate operation is extensionally equivalent to its envelope normal form. Accordingly, throughout the remainder of the paper, legitimate behavior is analyzed at the level of envelopeinduced class policies.

Remark 21.1 (Elective Failure and Structural Protection).

Σᴿ permits entities to make elective choices that are costly, inefficient, or disadvantageous. Such choices remain admissible provided they respect invariant protections.

If an elective choice threatens capacity collapse or existential loss, emergency envelopes and minimal repair operators may apply to prevent irreversible harm. These interventions are bounded, nonretributive, and terminate obligatorily once invariant conditions are restored.

Clarification (Irreversibility).
Irreversible refers to increase not eliminable by any admissible operation.

Accordingly, Σᴿ guarantees freedom of choice without permitting elective selfnullification.

Def 21′ — Extended Legitimacy (Divergence + RiskBearers + Enablement Routing)

Motivation.
Def. 21 (Legitimacy) requires admissibility, successor consistency, STC5 symmetry, idempotence, and drift. The following refinement preserves that core while making explicit additional structural constraints already implicit in On Relevance: (i) risk inheritance and exposure sensitivity, (ii) couplingsensitive exit preservation, (iii) rejection of structurally blocked signaling, (iv) repair obligations for independently emergent wrongs, (v) nonaccumulation of unrepaired fragility over time, and (vi) public frame resolution for binding acts. No new normative authority is introduced; the refinement only sharpens admissibility and legitimacy conditions to fully discriminate failure modes required by pluralist nondomination.

Definition (Structural Legitimacy).
Legitimate⁺(F) :⇔ Legitimate(F) ∧ DivOK(F) ∧ HoI_OK(F) ∧ Contestable(F) ∧ (∀i ∈ U (SignalBlocked(F,i) → ¬Admissible(F))) ∧ (∀i ∈ U (RB(F,i) → ExitPreserved_k(F,i,k), where DomCoupling(i,k))) ∧ (∀i ∈ U (RB(F,i) → RiskLoad(F(i)) ≥ RiskLoad(i))) ∧ (∀i ∈ U (StructuralDebt(F(i)) ≤ StructuralDebt(i) ∨ Repair(F))) ∧ (¬ ∃s (EmergentWrong(s) ∧ EmergentWrong(F(s)))) ∧ (PublicAct(F) → PFAResolved(F)) ∧ (∀i ∈ U ( (RB(F,i) ∧ EnablementRequired(F,i)) → ∃R ∈ O (EmancipatoryRepair(R) ∧ Legitimate⁺(R) ∧ cap(R(i)) > cap(i)) ))

Legitimate⁺(F) further requires that, if AlignmentOp(F) holds, all Alignment NonOverride constraints (ANOP0 through ANOP4) are satisfied.

Reading.
Legitimate⁺ strengthens legitimacy without altering its nature. In addition to preservation of standing, symmetry, rerunnability, and bounded drift, it enforces:

(1) divergence boundedness indexed to capacity;
(2) structural rejection of blocked or nonliftable relevance signals;
(3) exposuresensitive symmetry via risk inheritance;
(4) couplingrelative exit preservation rather than formal exit alone;
(5) mandatory repair closure for independently emergent wrongs;
(6) nonaccumulation of unrepaired structural fragility over time;
(7) resolution of public frame agreement for binding acts; and
(8) the existence of emancipatory routes whenever risk bearers are left in proxy, emergency, or capacitygated regimes.

No clause introduces outcome selection, aggregation, optimization, or sovereign choice. Legitimate⁺ remains a filter and normalizer, not a decider. Where multiple operations satisfy Legitimate⁺, all remain admissible; selection, if needed, is explicitly external to the object theory.

Axiom O2 — Operation Extensionality

∀F,G∈O: (∀i F(i)=G(i)) → F=G

Theorems Consequent to Structural Legitimacy

Theorem 21.1 (Standing Preservation Under Legitimate⁺ Operations).

For any operation F, if Legitimate⁺(F), then for all entities i ∈ U, σ(F(i)) ≥ σ(i).

Proof.
Legitimate⁺(F) entails Legitimate(F). By the AutonomyLimiting Reflex Principle (Axiom 15), admissibility is a necessary condition of legitimacy. Admissibility is defined as ∀i σ(F(i)) ≥ σ(i). No strengthening clause in Legitimate⁺ weakens admissibility. Therefore σ(F(i)) ≥ σ(i) holds universally.

Theorem 21.2 (Idempotence Prevents Cumulative Autonomy Reduction).

If Legitimate⁺(F), then for all i ∈ U, F(F(i)) = F(i), and repeated application of F introduces no additional autonomyreducing effects.

Proof.
Legitimate⁺(F) entails Legitimate(F). By Definition 21′, idempotence is a conjunct of legitimacy. Hence F ∘ F = F pointwise. No new ARVs, RiskLoad increases, or StructuralDebt increases can arise beyond the first application.

Theorem 21.3 (Impossibility of Risk Laundering).

There exists no admissible or legitimate⁺ operation that transfers accumulated risk from one entity to another without repair.

Proof.
Let F be an operation and i an entity such that RiskBearer(F, i) holds. By Axiom 26 (RiskLoad Monotonicity), RiskLoad(F(i)) ≥ RiskLoad(i). The only operations permitted to strictly decrease RiskLoad are Repair operations. Therefore risk cannot be reduced, reassigned, or laundered by any Legitimate⁺ operation.

Theorem 21.4 (CouplingSensitive Exit Necessity).

For any operation F and entity i, if RiskBearer(F, i) holds, then legitimacy requires preservation of exit relative to the dominant coupling of i.

Proof.
By Axiom 25, each entity i admits a unique dominant coupling k. By Axiom 28, RiskBearer(F, i) together with DomCoupling(i, k) implies ExitPreserved_k(F, i, k). Therefore formal exit conditions alone are insufficient unless they respect the dominant coupling mechanism.

Theorem 21.5 (Existence of Wrong Without Culpable Agent).

There exist system states that require repair despite the absence of any single culpable agent.

Proof.
By Definition of EmergentWrong(s), there exist trajectories exhibiting autonomyreducing effects that are not eliminable by any single local agent repair. By Axiom 29, EmergentWrong(s) implies existence of a Repair operation resolving the wrong. No axiom introduces guilt, blame, or punishment predicates. Therefore systemlevel wrongs exist independently of individual culpability.

Theorem 21.6 (NonExistence of Domination Attractors).

No infinite sequence of Legitimate⁺ operations can converge to a state exhibiting standing loss, exit foreclosure, accumulated unrepaired risk, or persistent structural fragility.

Proof.
Any ARV introduces StructuralDebt by Axiom 30. StructuralDebt may be strictly reduced only by Repair operations (Axiom 31). Legitimate⁺ forbids accumulation of StructuralDebt without repair. Thus any infinite admissible trajectory must stabilize or invoke repair, precluding domination attractors.

5.1 Emergency Envelope (Σᴿᴱ) — Minimal Coercive Stabilization Under Autonomy Loss Risk

This section introduces an optional extension to Tier2, motivated by the stresstest finding that some extreme cases (e.g., emergency restraint) are not well captured by Repair alone. In ordinary conditions, Σᴿ blocks standingreducing operations via ALRP and constrains legitimate policies to be successorconsistent, classuniform (STC5), and idempotent (rerunnable). However, emergencies can present a structural corner case: inaction (or insufficiently effective noncoercive action) may produce greater expected autonomy loss than a narrowly scoped, timebounded coercive intervention. This extension formalizes the principle:

Emergency coercion is admissible only when it is the least autonomyreducing choice among (i) inaction, (ii) noncoercive action, and (iii) coercive action—and it must terminate immediately once inaction or noncoercive action becomes the least autonomyreducing option.

Temporal Binding of Emergency Regimes
All emergency envelopes are temporally indexed and bounded as defined in §6.20.1.A. Emergency authority is therefore not categorical but timeconstrained: emergence, duration, and termination of emergency states are governed by repair depth R(E) and delay bound B(E). No emergency deviation is admissible beyond its temporal admissibility bound, regardless of individual step admissibility.

Emergency Recurrence Constraint

Repeated invocation of emergency provisions within a bounded interval constitutes an IntegrityModified trend and triggers escalating justification, disclosure, and repair requirements.

Σᴿ does not prohibit emergencies. It prohibits normalizing them.

5.1.1 Design Goals and Relationship to Tier2

(i) Preserve Tier2 in the normal regime. Σᴿᴱ does not weaken Axiom 15 (ALRP) or Def 21 (Unified Legitimacy) for ordinary governance; it introduces a separate, explicitly marked emergency pathway.

(ii) Keep the exception structurally narrow. Emergency action is bounded, reversible, and antiratcheting (no “power creep”). This aligns with Σᴿ’s emphasis on idempotence (Axiom 18) and drift bounds (Axiom 20) as anticreep constraints.

(iii) Force reversion to ordinary legitimacy. As soon as the emergency inequality no longer holds, the system must revert to a legitimate envelope (classuniform, successorconsistent, idempotent) or to inaction (identity).

5.1.2 Minimal Formal Additions (Signature Extension)

We add the following optional symbols to the signature (leaving the core Σᴿ signature unchanged):

Predicate symbols

Emergency(F) — marks that a proposed operation is being considered under emergency conditions.

NonCoercive(G) — marks that an operation is a candidate “noncoercive” alternative (defined below).

EAdmissible(F) — emergencyadmissibility (a strictly constrained relaxation of ALRP).

WindowOpen(F) — indicates the emergency window remains active.

Function symbol

E : O → O — the Emergency Envelope operator; maps a proposed operation to its emergencybounded envelope .

These additions are conservative: they do not alter Tier1 and do not change the definition of Legitimate(F) in Def 21.

5.1.5 Emergency Envelope Axioms (EESeries)

Axiom EE0 — Impact Gate (HoI Required for Emergency Standing)

If the Hierarchy-of-Impact (HoI) extension is instantiated, then Emergency standing is available only under Level-1 or Level-2 threatened impact:

Emergency(F) → ∃i∈U (ThreatImpact(F,i,L1) ∨ ThreatImpact(F,i,L2)).

Reading. Emergency envelopes are not a general license to override ALRP. They exist only to prevent collapse of terminal agency (L1) or base autonomy (L2). Where only L3/L4 impacts are at stake, the system must remain within ordinary legitimacy (Def. 21) and non-coercive alternatives.

Axiom EE0.1 — HoI Lexicographic Preference in Emergency Selection (Optional)

If HoI is instantiated, then among all available emergency-bounded candidates and non-coercive candidates that satisfy the emergency trigger, the selected emergency envelope must be HoI-preferred (lexicographically minimizing L1/L2 cost before L3/L4 cost):

Emergency(F) → ∀G∈O (NonCoercive(G) → PreferHoI(E(F), G)).

Reading. Even under emergency, the system must minimize potential L1/L2 impacts first (including residual harms), and only then consider L3/L4 tradeoffs.

Axiom EE1 — Emergency Trigger (LeastLoss Condition).

Emergency coercion is permitted only when the emergency envelope is strictly less autonomyreducing than both inaction and every available noncoercive candidate:

Here is a structural “less autonomyreducing” comparison defined by the boundeddifference predicates below (EE2).

Reading. Emergency action is justified only when it yields lower autonomy loss than (i) doing nothing and (ii) any legitimate (noncoercive) alternative available at that moment.

Reading. Emergency coercion exists only while it is strictly the least autonomyreducing option. The moment inaction or noncoercive action becomes better, emergency authority terminates and the system returns to ordinary legitimacy.

Proposition (No Emergency Precedent).

No emergencylegitimate operation expands the future admissible action set beyond what was permissible preemergency.

Theorem (Conservativity of Emergency Extension)

The emergency extension of Σᴿ does not alter the consequences of the base theory for non-emergency cases.

Proof. Emergency predicates are only triggered under explicitly bounded conditions and do not modify the interpretation of base predicates. Hence conservativity holds.

Theorem (WellFounded Termination of Emergency Behavior)

There exists a wellfounded measure decreasing under each emergency transition. Therefore infinite emergency sequences are impossible.

5.1.7 Notes for Referees (Scope and Conservatism)

Σᴿᴱ is optional. It is an extension for domains where emergencies are unavoidable (medicine, security, safety systems).

It preserves the core: Tier1 and Tier2 remain unchanged; Def21 legitimacy is untouched.

It is structurally narrow: bounded autonomy reduction (EE2), mandatory exit (EE5), antiratcheting (EE3), and required returntolegitimacy via repair (EE4).

Adapterlayer specificity remains necessary: the mapping from realworld interventions to “standing drops” and “degree increases” is domaininstantiated in the interface layer, consistent with your Section 11 guidance.

Theorem Dependency Mapping

Below we list the primary formal results of Σᴿ and the axioms or earlier theorems on which they depend:

Universality of Σᴿ’s Invariants:

(All non-domination invariants are necessary in any model of Σᴿ) – Depends on: ALRP, STC-5, Rerunnability, Bounded Drift, Directed Repair (Tier-2 axioms). This result uses each structural legitimacy axiom to show that dropping any one would allow a domination scenario.

Non-Extendability Theorem:

(No strictly stronger non-dominating extension of Σᴿ exists) – Depends on: ALRP (Axiom 15), STC-5 (A17), Rerunnability (A18), Bounded Drift (A20), Directed Repair (A19). The proof shows any added operation or rule outside Σᴿ that isn’t already constrained by these axioms will violate one of them.

Finite-Stage Legitimacy Requirement:

(Legitimacy cannot be achieved only in the infinite limit) – Depends on: ALRP (no standing loss), Rerunnability (idempotence), Bounded Drift (no unbounded cumulative harm). These ensure that if an operation isn’t legitimate at each finite stage, an invariant is violated in each segment.

Domination Through Omission Lemma:

(Intentional non-intervention during a fixable domination is itself dominating) – Depends on: ALRP (A15, requiring addressing of autonomy limits) and Directed Repair (A19, existence of repair actions). These axioms guarantee that a known, unperformed repair implies a persistent asymmetry, hence continued domination.

Terminal-State Irrelevance Lemma:

(If only one agent remains, domination predicates are undefined) – Depends on: Domination Definition (requires two distinct agents with coupling). This is a boundary case lemma following from the formal preconditions of domination (no axioms needed, just the definition of domination which requires a pair of agents).

Non-Determinacy of Legitimate Options Theorem:

(Σᴿ does not select among equally legitimate outcomes) – Depends on: Absence of any preference predicate in Σᴿ’s signature. This meta-result observes that no axiom or function in Σᴿ imposes an ordering on multiple legitimate operations; it follows from the fact that Σᴿ’s language has no symbol for utility or preference and thus cannot prove statements distinguishing two different Legitimate⁺ operations. (All choice or optimization is deliberately left external to Σᴿ.)

Theorem (Non-Selection of actions)

No formula of Σᴿ uniquely selects a single admissible action in the absence of external selection criteria.

Proof. Σᴿ defines sets of admissible actions but contains no function symbol selecting an element of such sets. Hence no unique choice is definable.

Corollary (Evaluation–Selection Separation)

Σᴿ evaluates structural legitimacy but does not determine realized actions. Selection requires additional structure external to Σᴿ.

Proposition 5.1.8

A fundamental property of Σᴿ is that admissible operations cannot increase domination pressure (the measure of structural inequality in a state). We formalize this as follows:

Theorem (Monotonic Domination Pressure)

For all operations o and states s, if Admissible(o) holds, then applying o does not raise the domination pressure of s.

In formal syntax (Lean/Coq style):

Theorem Domination_Monotone:

∀ (o : Operation) (s : State),

Admissible(o) → DomPressure(apply o s) ≤ DomPressure(s).

Proof Sketch: Because o is admissible, it satisfies all Tier-2 invariants (ALRP, STC-5, etc.). ALRP ensures o does not lower any agent’s standing, STC-5 ensures o does not introduce new asymmetries between agents of equal capacity, Rerunnability ensures no cumulative harm via repetition, and Bounded Drift limits the magnitude of any change【13†L375-L383】. Together these guarantee that no structural inequality (measured by DomPressure) can increase after o—any small gains by one agent are matched by non-losses or repairs elsewhere. Thus, DomPressure(apply o s) ≤ DomPressure(s) in all cases.

In a proof assistant, this theorem would likely be stated as an axiom or lemma (to be proven from the invariants). For example, one would add the following line to the formal development:

axiom DomPressure_monotone:

∀ o s, Admissible o → DomPressure(apply o s) ≤ DomPressure s.

This aligns exactly with the intended meaning of the ALRP and related invariants, and is ready to be checked by SMT solvers or interactive theorem provers.

5.2 Tier3: Capacity, Proxy, and Coalition Dynamics (Σᴿ₃) — Closing the PFA/IPFA Loop

Tier1 and Tier2 define the Pluralist NonDomination Substrate: standing is successor-based and non-dilutive; admissible operations cannot reduce standing; legitimate operations are class-uniform, idempotent, drift-bounded, and repairable. This is sufficient to prohibit domination, but it does not by itself encode the developmental loop described in On Relevance: agents without sufficient capacity operate under proxy authority that must be capacity-progressive and must decay to null as capacity grows, such that full participation becomes direct rather than mediated.

Tier3 adds the minimal first-order structure needed to encode that loop without collapsing IPFA into PFA, and without granting institutions or coalitions standing that overrides terminal agents. Tier3 is a conservative extension: it introduces new predicates and constraints on their interaction with existing σ, cap, deg, Repair, Drift, and legitimacy, but it does not alter Tier1 arithmetic or Tier2 safety.

Definition (RemedyMinimality Preference).

Define RemedyLE(r1, r2) (“r1 is no more intrusive than r2”) as: RemedyLE(r1, r2) :⇔ (r1 = r2) ∨ RemedyHigher(r2, r1).

Define RemedyPrefer(F, G) as: RemedyPrefer(F, G) :⇔ ∃rF,rG ∈ R ( RemedyLevel(F,rF) ∧ RemedyLevel(G,rG) ∧ RemedyLE(rF,rG) ∧ ¬RemedyLE(rG,rF) ).

Axiom RL3 — Minimal Remedy Selection for Signaling Harm.

For all F,G ∈ O:

If

Legitimate(F) ∧ Legitimate(G) ∧

(∃i ∈ U: RS(F,i) ∨ SignalBlocked(F,i)) ∧

(∃i ∈ U: RS(G,i) ∨ SignalBlocked(G,i)) ∧

RemedyPrefer(F,G)

Then

Prefer(F,G).

Reading. When multiple legitimate corrective interventions address relevance-signal impairment, the system must prefer the intervention whose remedy level is strictly less intrusive, unless overridden by higher-order constraints (e.g., HoI or Emergency)

5.2.1 Public Standing vs. Internal Warrant (PFA/IPFA Boundary)

PFAEligible(i) is an adapter-instantiated predicate indicating that the internal warrant conditions for public recognition have been met. Σᴿ does not attempt to compute PFAEligible(i) inside the object theory; it treats the predicate as an externally supplied gate that is structurally auditable (see §11.7).

Axiom P0 (PFA Gate for Recognition).

For any i∈U, successor access from null to 1_N requires eligibility:

PathTo1(i) → PFAEligible(i).

(Equivalently, PathTo1 was revised in Def 21 to require PFAEligible(i).)

Interpretation. This enforces the philosophical separation: IPFA contributes to eligibility, but public standing σ is generated only when the public frame (PFA) grants recognition.

5.2.2 Proxy Structure and Proxy Decay

ProxyFor(p,i) means: p acts as a proxy agent for i in the coordination regime, where i lacks sufficient capacity for direct participation. Proxies are structurally visible through dependency (degree/coupling) and must be self-terminating: their authority exists to eliminate itself.

Axiom P1 (Proxy Visibility).

ProxyFor(p,i) → Coupled(p,i) ∧ deg(i)>0.

Axiom P2 (Capacity–Dependency Antitone).

∀i,j∈U: (σ(i)=σ(j) ∧ cap(i) ≥ cap(j)) → (deg(i) ≤ deg(j)).

Axiom P3 (Proxy Termination at StandingSaturated Capacity).

Define FullCap(i) :⇔ σ(i)=B(cap(i)).

Then: FullCap(i) → deg(i)=0.

Interpretation. P2 makes “capacity growth reduces dependence” a structural invariant. P3 expresses the philosophical endpoint: once an agent’s standing is no longer limited by capacity (standing saturates the CIA bound), proxy dependence must be eliminated (degree returns to 0), making proxy authority null.

5.2.3 Emancipatory Repair (Repair Must Eventually Grow Capacity)

Tier2 Repair reduces domination (deg non-increase) and preserves standing (σ non-decrease). Tier3 strengthens the long-run requirement: for agents under proxy dependence, repair must be capacity-progressive.

Definition (Emancipatory Repair).

EmancipatoryRepair(R) :⇔ Repair(R) ∧ (∀i∈U: deg(i)>0 → cap(R(i)) ≥ cap(i)) ∧ (∃i∈U: deg(i)>0 ∧ cap(R(i)) > cap(i)).

Unless renewed by admissible operations, all coupling components decay over time: s_d(x,y,t+1) = λ_d · s_d(x,y,t), where 0 < λ_d < 1.

Axiom P4 (Existence of Emancipatory Repair for Proxy States).

∀i∈U: deg(i)>0 → ∃R∈O: EmancipatoryRepair(R) ∧ deg(R(i)) < deg(i) ∧ σ(R(i)) ≥ σ(i).

Axiom P4′ — Individual Emancipation Guarantee

∀i ∈ U:

deg(i) > 0 → ∃R ∈ O:

EmancipatoryRepair(R) ∧ cap(R(i)) > cap(i).

Interpretation. This prevents “permanent custodianship.” If an agent is structurally dependent (deg>0), the system must admit repair routes that both reduce dependency and increase capacity, guaranteeing a path toward independence (deg→0) and direct participation.

Autonomy Debt and Reciprocal Repair.

If an admissible or inadmissible operation F performed by agent x reduces the autonomy of agent y by ΔA(x→y) > 0, then x incurs an Autonomy Debt equal to ΔA(x→y). This debt defines the maximum (ceiling) amount of autonomy that may be constrained from x for the purpose of restoring autonomy and system viability.

5.2.4 Coalition Transparency and AntiMasking

Coalition identity manipulation is prevented by requiring that composites representing coalitions expose membership structurally, so that dependency/degree and CIA constraints remain auditable and cannot be bypassed by reification.

Axiom P5 (Coalition Membership Must Be Structurally Visible).

Coalition(x) ∧ Member(m,x) → Coupled(m,x).

Axiom P6 (Coalition Standing and Capacity NonAmplification).

For any coalition x with members m:

Coalition(x) ∧ Member(m,x) → σ(x) ≥ σ(m) and cap(x) ≥ cap(m).

In addition, coalition standing remains bounded by CIA: σ(x) ≤ B(cap(x)).

Interpretation. These constraints force coalitions to carry their structural dependencies rather than laundering them. Membership must appear as coupling, so degree cannot be hidden. CIA continues to apply to composites, preventing capacity/standing inflation by coalition reclassification alone.

(Adapter note: Coalition and Member are instantiated by the adapter when a domain object is treated as a coalition/composite; §11.7 already treats cross-domain mapping as a meta-domain and requires auditable translation.)

5.2.5 Emergency Recurrence Closure (No Endless Emergency Without Capacity Progress)

The emergency envelope Σᴿᴱ prevents ratcheting within a window. Tier3 closes the remaining loop: repeated emergency invocation must be capacity-progressive, or the system must fall back to a safe “freeze” regime (Id / Legitimate envelopes / Emancipatory repair only).

Axiom P7 (EmergencytoEmancipation Condition).

If Emergency(F) is invoked for conditions affecting i with deg(i)>0, then the mandatory repair route in EE4 must be emancipatory:

Emergency(F) ∧ deg(i)>0 → ∃R∈O: EmancipatoryRepair(R) ∧ Legitimate(R∘E(F)).

Interpretation. Emergency is permitted to stabilize, but stabilization is not allowed to become a cyclical substitute for emancipation. If emergencies recur in a proxy regime, repair must increase capacity and reduce dependence.

5.2.6 Summary: Closed Loop Guarantees

With Tier3, Σᴿ closes the autonomy-development loop described in On Relevance while remaining first-order and domain-agnostic:

(1) **PFA/IPFA boundary:** PFAEligible(i) gates successor access from null to σ=1. IPFA contributes to eligibility, but σ is granted only through the PFA gate (P0; Def 21).

(2) **Proxy visibility:** Proxy relations cannot be hidden. ProxyFor(p,i) implies Coupled(p,i) and deg(i)>0 (P1).

(3) **Proxy decay with capacity:** Capacity growth cannot coexist with increasing dependency among equals. Under fixed σ, higher capacity implies weakly lower dependency (P2).

(4) **Proxy termination:** Once standing saturates the CIA bound (σ(i)=B(cap(i))), proxy dependence must collapse (deg(i)=0), making proxy authority null (P3).

(5) **Emancipatory repair existence:** If an entity is dependent (deg(i)>0), there must exist an emancipatory repair route that reduces deg and strictly increases cap for at least one such entity, while preserving σ (P4).

(6) **Coalition anti-masking:** Coalitions must expose membership structurally (Member→Coupled) and cannot amplify standing or capacity beyond CIA constraints (P5–P6).

(7) **Emergency recurrence closure:** If emergency stabilization is invoked under proxy dependence, the mandatory repair route must be emancipatory, preventing repeated emergency cycles from substituting for capacity growth (P7 + EE4).

Together these clauses ensure that proxy authority exists only as a capacity-growth scaffold and is forced to dissolve as capacity becomes sufficient for direct participation.

5.2.7 Enablement Obligation (CapacityIndexed Autonomy Is Dynamic)

Purpose. Σᴿ treats autonomy as capacityindexed (CIA) rather than as a static right. Therefore, whenever capacity gating, proxy dependence, emergency stabilization, or any legitimacy constraint limits an entity’s direct participation, Σᴿ requires an obligation of enablement: the system must admit—and the validator must preferentially select—operations that increase capacity for lowercapacity individuals and monotonically reduce proxy dependence.

This strengthens the Tier3 emancipation loop (P4/P4′/P7) by making enablement an explicit structural requirement that attaches to riskbearing and proxy regimes.

Definition (EnablementRequired).

EnablementRequired(F,i) :⇔ (deg(i) > 0) ∨ (deg(F(i)) > 0) ∨ Emergency(F).

5.2.8 Reflexive Coupling Debt (ALRPDual Constraint on Imposed Dependence)

Purpose. ALRP blocks standing reduction, but by itself it does not fully prevent a subtle domination vector: an actor can impose unseverable coupling (increasing another’s degree, reducing exit viability, or impairing relevance signaling) while paying no structural price. To prevent externalization of coercion, Σᴿ optionally introduces a reflexive debt tensor: every imposed unseverable coupling generates an equal structural debt on the actor.

This preserves Σᴿ’s structural character: it does not punish intent; it accounts for imposed dependency as an algebraic invariant.

Reading. Any time an actor’s operation imposes a onestep increase in the target’s coupling degree in an unseverable way, the actor incurs a matching onestep debt entry toward that target.

Axiom κ2 — Debt Must Be RepairDischargeable (Structural)

For all a,i∈U:

κ(a,i) > 0_N → ∃R∈O:

Repair(R) ∧ (deg(R(i)) < deg(i) ∨ ∃F∈O: ¬Unseverable(F,a,i)).

Reading.

Any positive couplingdebt entry must correspond to an available structural discharge route: either directed repair strictly reduces the target’s coupling degree, or the coupling that generated the debt is rendered severable (i.e., no longer unseverable under the adapter’s audit).

Implementation note (governance layer). A deployment may maintain κ as a ledgered quantity whose decrement is performed externally when a discharge route is executed. The object theory requires only dischargeability (existence of a route), not internal subtraction.

6. Core Results

This section provides formal proofs for the principal theorems arising from the axioms of Standing Algebra (Σᴿ). All reasoning is conducted strictly within the manysorted firstorder framework and uses only the axioms defined in Tier1 (Σᴿ₁) and Tier2 (Σᴿ₂). A standingstable configuration qualifies as peaceful within this system only if dissent remains structurally permissible, nonpenalized, and noneliminated—even where no divergence is realized.

Derivation Convention.
All structures introduced in this chapter (including calculus, algebra, geometry, topology, probability, computation, and gametheoretic forms) are derived. None introduce new admissibility criteria, selection mechanisms, or evaluative orderings. Where a structure admits multiple mathematical formalisms, the weakest sufficient formalism is used.

Preconditions for Major Results

Unless otherwise stated, the principal theorems of Σᴿ assume:

• satisfaction of the structural applicability conditions (C1)–(C4),

• adherence to Tier1 and Tier2 invariants,

• existence of admissible repair paths where repair is invoked,

• and evaluation under a fixed interpretation ℐₜ.

Results concerning exit viability, domination, and repair routing do not require assumptions about agent intent, moral responsibility, or governance authority. Where additional hypotheses are required, they are stated explicitly in the corresponding theorem.

Theorem 6.1 — NonCoercion Theorem

Statement.
If an operation is admissible, then no entity’s standing decreases under its application:

Proof.
By Axiom 15 (AutonomyLimiting Reflex Principle), admissibility entails monotonicity of standing:

Thus, if is admissible, the standing of any entity cannot decrease when is applied.

Theorem 6.1A — Standing Monotonicity Along Admissible Trajectories (No Accumulative Standing Loss)

Statement. Let ⟨F1, F2, …, Fn⟩ be any finite sequence of operations in O such that Admissible(Ft) holds for every t = 1,…,n. Define the composed trajectory operator Tn := Fn ∘ Fn−1 ∘ … ∘ F1. Then for all i ∈ U: σ(Tn(i)) ≥ σ(i).

Proof. By Axiom 15 (ALRP), each admissible Ft satisfies ∀i σ(Ft(i)) ≥ σ(i). Apply this inequality inductively along the composition: σ(F1(i)) ≥ σ(i), σ(F2(F1(i))) ≥ σ(F1(i)) ≥ σ(i), and so on. Thus σ(Tn(i)) ≥ σ(i) for all i. □

Interpretation. This rules out “slow creep” standing loss via any finite sequence of admissible updates. Any standing reduction must come from an inadmissible (rejected) operation or from unmodeled externalities.

Corollary 6.1B — No Ratcheting Under ReApplication of a Legitimate Policy

Statement. If Legitimate(F), then for all i ∈ U and for all k ≥ 1: F^k(i) = F(i), where F^k denotes kfold composition of F with itself.

Proof. By Axiom 18, Legitimate(F) → ∀i F(F(i)) = F(i). Thus F^2 = F. By induction, if F^k = F then F^(k+1) = F ∘ F^k = F ∘ F = F. □

Interpretation. A legitimate policy cannot “ratchet” effects under repetition; any escalation requires changing the policy (i.e., a new operation), which must again pass legitimacy constraints.

Theorem 6.1C — Canonical Interaction Normal Form (Envelope-Routed Outcome)

Statement.

Let F ∈ O be any proposed operation in an interpreted Σᴿ state.

Define the routed normal form S(F) as in §3.10.22.

Then:

If BoundaryAct(F) ∧ Admissible(F), the routed outcome is G(F), and Legitimate(G(F)).

If InternalAct(F) ∧ Admissible(F), the routed outcome is L(F), and Legitimate(L(F)).

If ¬Admissible(F), then F is rejected by the structural filter (and in deployment is routed to Id / Repair / or a safe fallback under the optional viability machinery).

Proof.

(1) If BoundaryAct(F) then S(F)=G(F) by definition of S. If Admissible(F), then Legitimate(G(F)) by Axiom G2.

(2) If InternalAct(F) then S(F)=L(F) by definition of S. If Admissible(F), then Legitimate(L(F)) by Axiom L0.

(3) If ¬Admissible(F), then by ALRP and the definition of admissibility, the operation fails the core non-domination gate and is not permitted as an admissible update. □

Interpretation.

In Σᴿ, “interaction” is the routed envelope-normal form of a proposal: internal acts are normalized by L, boundary acts are normalized by G, and inadmissible proposals are structurally excluded (or forced to conservative fallback under optional viability constraints).

Statement.
Standing tracks capacity via a monotone bound function:

∀i σ(i)≤B(cap(i)),  with B monotone non-decreasing.

Proof.
This is exactly Axiom 14 (CapacityIndexed Autonomy). The axiom states that standing must track capacity monotonically.

Theorem 6.4 — No Nullification

Statement.
If an entity has nonzero standing, no operation can map it to null standing:

Proof.
Axiom 12 (No Return to Nullity) explicitly forbids mapping any entity with nonzero standing back to nullity. Therefore, once an entity has been recognized (i.e., once has been applied at least once), nullification is impossible.

Justification.
The stated impossibility follows because the configuration would require either exit collapse or irreversible dependency growth, both of which violate the definition of nondomination.

Clarification (Irreversibility).
Irreversible dependency growth refers to dependency increase not eliminable by any admissible repair operation.

Proof.
This follows directly from Axiom 10 (Composite Entities), which defines the composite condition as the disjunction of (1) having more than one successor increment or (2) possessing at least one coupling relation.

Theorem 6.8 — Bounded Drift Stability

Statement.

Under drift operations, the standing and coupling degree of any entity may change by at most one successor-step:

Drift(D) → ∀i∈U: OneStepDiff(σ(D(i)), σ(i)) ∧ OneStepDiff(deg(D(i)), deg(i)).

(Informal gloss: this corresponds to “|Δσ| ≤ 1” and “|Δdeg| ≤ 1” under the standard interpretation of N and D.)

Proof.
Axiom 20 defines drift as a bounded perturbation, explicitly setting the limit on how far standing and coupling degree may shift. Because the axiom sets the allowed perturbation magnitude, it directly yields the stability theorem.

Theorem 6.9 — Repair Monotonicity

Statement.
All repair operations strictly improve or preserve standing and strictly reduce or preserve coupling:

Proof.
This follows by immediate application of Axiom 19 (Directed Repair). Because repair is defined as a transformation that reduces coercive coupling while preserving or increasing standing, the monotonicity claim is directly satisfied.

Theorem 6.9A — Capacity Progress Under Dependency (No Permanent Capacity Gating)

Assumptions. Assume Tier3 emancipation axioms are instantiated (in particular, Axiom P4′ and/or Axiom EO1).

Statement. For any entity i ∈ U, if deg(i) > 0, then there exists an operation R ∈ O such that: EmancipatoryRepair(R) and cap(R(i)) > cap(i).

Moreover, under the stronger routing form EO2, there exists some emancipatory repair that strictly reduces dependency degree: deg(i) > 0 → ∃R ∈ O (EmancipatoryRepair(R) ∧ deg(R(i)) < deg(i)).

Proof. The first claim is exactly Axiom P4′ (or EO1 under EnablementRequired). The second claim is exactly Axiom EO2 (or the degree-reducing clause of P4 where present). □

Interpretation. In proxy-dependent regimes (deg(i)>0), capacity increase is not a best-effort preference; it is structurally guaranteed by existence of emancipatory repair routes. Thus capacity gating cannot be permanent inside the theory: it must either be repaired away (deg decreases) and/or made capacity-progressive (cap increases), ensuring that autonomy constraints are forced to ratchet upward rather than stabilizing in custodianship.

We now show that the defining components of legitimacy—admissibility, successorconsistency, symmetry, and idempotence—jointly imply a structural necessity result: any legitimate transformation in Σᴿ must preserve autonomy in a precise, quantifiable sense.

Theorem 6.13 — Autonomy as a Necessity Condition for Legitimate Plural Coordination

Statement.
Let  be any operation in a Σᴿmodel.
If is legitimate in the sense of Def. 21, then:

preserves standing: (ALRP);

acts symmetrically within STC5 classes: entities with equal standing and capacity receive equal standing outcomes;

is idempotent (Axiom 18), preventing escalation or ratcheting of authority;

respects drift bounds (Axiom 20), preventing unbounded perturbations.

Corollary.
In Σᴿ, autonomy preservation is a necessary structural condition for legitimate plural coordination: no operation that reduces standing, violates symmetry, induces unbounded drift, or accumulates coercive advantage can be legitimate with respect to pluralist cooperation.

Interpretation.
This establishes autonomy not merely as an emergent property of plural systems, but as a structural necessity for any nondominating coordination regime definable within Σᴿ.

Proof.

Assume Legitimate(F). By Def 21 (Unified Legitimacy), we have:

Admissible(F)

successConsistent(F)

STC5(F)

Idempotent(F)

Drift(F)

(1) Standing preservation follows immediately from Axiom 15 (ALRP): Admissible(F) → ∀i σ(F(i))≥σ(i).

(2) Symmetry preservation follows immediately from STC5(F) as defined in Def 21 (and Axiom 17).

(3) Idempotence follows immediately from Idempotent(F) in Def 21 (and Axiom 18).

(4) Drift boundedness follows immediately from Drift(F) (Axiom 20), which is now a required conjunct of legitimacy.

Thus every legitimate operation preserves standing, preserves class symmetry, is rerunnable, and is drift-bounded. Equivalently (by the envelope fixpoint characterization on admissible inputs), legitimate policies may be viewed as fixed points of legitimacy normalization: they are exactly the stabilized normal forms produced by closure under L (and, in boundary mode, under G).

Conclusion

Combining (1)–(4), any operation satisfying Legitimate(F):

preserves standing (ALRP),

preserves classuniform symmetry (STC5),

is idempotent (no escalation or ratcheting),

and satisfies bounded perturbation (driftcompatibility).

These constraints are therefore necessary structural conditions for legitimate plural coordination in Σᴿ.

Theorem 6.13 completes the structural picture: autonomy preservation is not merely a desirable property of plural coordination but a mathematically necessary invariant of every legitimate operation definable in Σᴿ. This result underpins all subsequent applications, including the alignmentsafe operational pipeline described in Section 7.

Theorem 6.14 — Externality of Persistent Domination

(Rademacher Externality Theorem)

Statement.
Let be any -model (including any conservatively instantiated optional extensions ), and let be any set of entities interpreted as agents within that model.
Let be any sequence of operations from such that for every , the operation is admissible with respect to the evaluation regime in force at stage (including Exit Viability, Output Completeness, Contestability, Adapter Validity, Domination Pressure, and any instantiated safeguards).

If there exists a nonempty subset such that the sequence induces a persistent reduction of autonomy for the agents in — i.e., autonomy loss that is stable over time and not eliminated by any subsequent operation — then at least one of the following must hold:

Axiom Violation:
There exists such that is not admissible under (i.e., violates ALRP, STC5, Exit Viability, Output Completeness, nonregression, or contestability), and thus the reduction does not occur within the theory.

Forced Dissipation:
The domination pressure functional strictly decreases along a repairadmissible path (Axioms DP1–DP2), implying that the autonomy loss cannot persist indefinitely.

Emergency Exclusivity:
The reduction occurs only during an emergency window and is bounded, repairterminated, and selfliquidating (Σᴿᴱ), thus cannot generate stable domination.

Modeling Externality:
The autonomy reduction arises from structural features, transformations, or power relations not represented within the interpreted signature (i.e., not expressible as changes in , , exit viability, admissible operations, integrity witnesses, or validated adapter claims).

Therefore:

No persistent domination or autonomy erosion can be generated, propagated, or stabilized solely by admissible operations inside the object theory.
Any domination that persists must originate from forces external to the formal system or from a refusal to model them.

Corollary 6.14.1 — Structural Necessity of Autonomy Preservation

In any -validated coordination regime, autonomy preservation is not merely a desideratum but a necessary structural invariant: every admissible path either preserves autonomy, repairs its loss, publicly bounds it under emergency, or rejects the operation.

Theorem 6.14A — Dissipative Domination Pressure (Ratcheting Down Under Admissible Update)

Assumptions (Σᴿ⁺ DP module instantiated). Assume Sys(s) is instantiated for at least one system-state carrier s ∈ U and that DP : U → N and UnconsentedInfluence(F) are interpreted as in §3.10.14.

If UnconsentedInfluence(F) holds, then DP(F(s)) < DP(s).

If DP(s) > 0_N, then there exists a repair operation R ∈ O such that Repair(R) and DP(R(s)) < DP(s).
