Interpretation. When the DP module is instantiated, domination pressure cannot accumulate under admissible operations. Whenever domination-relevant influence occurs without consent symmetry, domination pressure must strictly decay, and whenever pressure exists at all, a repair route must exist that reduces it. This makes “domination must dissipate” a structural invariant rather than a moral assertion.

Definition (Pressure Dissipation).
Pressure dissipation holds between configurations P and Q if DomPressure(Q) is strictly less than DomPressure(P).

Corollary 6.14B — No Internal Stable Domination Attractor (Blocked or Dissipative)

Statement.

Within any interpreted Σᴿ regime in which admissibility is enforced (and within Σᴿ⁺ when instantiated), there is no admissible update path that can stabilize a persistent autonomy-reduction state inside the modeled structure.

More precisely: for any sequence of admissible operations, standing cannot decrease (Theorem 6.1A). Legitimate policies cannot ratchet effects by repetition (Corollary 6.1B). In proxy-dependent regimes, capacity-progress routes exist (Theorem 6.9A). And when the optional domination-pressure module is instantiated, domination-relevant influence without consent symmetry must strictly dissipate (Theorem 6.14A). Therefore any stable domination that appears must originate from (i) inadmissible operations rejected by the filter, (ii) explicitly bounded emergency regimes that are repair-terminated, or (iii) forces external to the interpreted Σᴿ signature (Theorem 6.14).

In particular, under the componentwise standing order on system states, admissible trajectories admit no descending chains: for any finite admissible sequence, σ(T_n(i)) ≥ σ(i) for all i (Theorem 6.1A). This is the precise sense in which admissible dynamics cannot “walk downward” into stable autonomy loss inside the modeled structure.

Corollary 6.14.C — Alignment Cannot Be the Source of Internal Domination

If persistent domination or autonomy erosion occurs in a system subject to Σᴿ validation, such domination cannot originate from alignment or safety mechanisms internal to the Σᴿ object theory, since alignment operations are constrained by admissibility, nonregression, and idempotence (ANOP). Any such domination must therefore arise from inadmissible operations or from forces external to the interpreted Σᴿ structure.

6.14.D — CrossBoundary Effects and Scope of Structural Guarantees

Statement.
Σᴿ guarantees autonomy preservation only with respect to entities and operations represented within its interpreted domain. Effects imposed upon entities or systems outside that domain constitute externalities.

Axiom CE0 — No Hidden Externality Claims

A system may not claim nondomination guarantees for effects outside its Σᴿgoverned scope unless those effects are explicitly represented as entities and operations subject to Σᴿ evaluation.

Corollary CE1 — Honesty of Scope

Local admissibility does not imply global nondomination. Σᴿ forbids implicit claims of safety beyond its modeled boundary.

Interpretive Note.

Σᴿ closes domination internally and forces honesty externally.

6.14.E — Emergent Domination in MultiAgent Contexts

Statement.
Σᴿ recognizes that domination may emerge from the composition of individually admissible actions across multiple agents.

Definition (Emergent Domination).

Emergent domination occurs when no single operation violates admissibility, but their combined effect produces standing collapse, coerced dependence, or exit foreclosure.

Axiom ED0 — Emergence Must Be Represented

When emergent domination is detected, it must be modeled as a standingrelevant condition triggering repair obligations.

Interpretive Note.

Σᴿ cannot forbid emergence without sovereign coordination. It can forbid ignoring it.

6.15 Exhaustive Structural Regimes and Latent Consequences of Σᴿ

This section makes explicit several global consequences that are already entailed by the axioms, definitions, and theorems established above. The goal is exhaustiveness: to enumerate the full space of structural outcomes available to Σᴿ without introducing new axioms or new philosophical commitments. All statements below are derived reorganizations of results already proved (in particular, Theorems 6.1A, 6.1B, 6.1C, 6.9A, 6.14, 6.14A, and Corollary 6.14B), together with the envelope and semilattice results of §3.12 and §6.11–§6.12.

6.15.0 Structural Synthesis: Σᴿ as a Closure-Based Policy Algebra (Derived)

Although Σᴿ is presented as a theory of admissible and legitimate operations, the operative semantics of interaction are closure-based: proposals are analyzed (and, in deployment, applied) only through their envelope-normalized forms. In particular, L names the canonical legitimacy closure of an admissible proposal (Axioms L0–L5; §3.10.19), and boundary interaction uses the scoped closure G (Axioms G0–G3; §3.10.20) with deterministic routing S(F) (§3.10.22).

Fixed-point view (legitimate policies as closures). On admissible inputs, legitimate policies are precisely the fixed points of legitimacy normalization: once a proposal is normalized (internally via L or at the boundary via G), re-normalization does not change it. This is the structural content behind rerunnability and anti-ratcheting: stability is not an emergent behavior but a closure/fixed-point property of the permitted policy forms.

Class-policy view (policy algebra over STC5 classes). Up to signature equivalence, envelope policies are determined by their class-policy signatures b : Q → {0,1} (Theorems 3.12.2 and 6.12). In this representation, the join operation corresponds to classwise OR (∨) of increment decisions, giving a join-semilattice of legitimate envelope policies. This is the natural algebra in which plural composition is expressed: “doing both” policies corresponds to join at the class-policy level, while legitimacy and successor bounds prevent escalation by repetition.

This synthesis introduces no new axioms. It re-centers the already established envelope/normal-form results as the core semantic layer of Σᴿ interaction.

6.15.1 Exhaustive Outcome Partition for a Single Proposal

Definition 6.15.1 (Interaction outcome class of a proposal). Let F ∈ O be any proposed operation. Define its routed normal form S(F) as in §3.10.22. Define the interaction outcome class of F by the following mutually exclusive cases:

Legitimate regime: Legitimate(F).

Frontier regime: Admissible(F) ∧ ¬Legitimate(F).

Rejection regime: ¬Admissible(F).

Emergency regime (optional): Emergency(F) ∧ WindowOpen(F) (only when Σᴿᴱ is instantiated).

Viability-collapse regime (optional): DominationSingularity (only when viability/output machinery is instantiated).

Remark. Cases (4) and (5) are conservative, optional regimes. If the corresponding extensions are not instantiated, they are simply absent and the partition reduces to (1)–(3) in the base theory.

Theorem 6.15.2 (Outcome partition is exhaustive).

For any proposal F ∈ O, exactly one of the regimes (1)–(3) holds in the base theory; and when optional regimes are instantiated, the outcome classification extends by (4) and/or (5) without changing (1)–(3).

Proof. In the base theory, either Admissible(F) or ¬Admissible(F). If ¬Admissible(F), we are in (3). If Admissible(F), then either Legitimate(F) or ¬Legitimate(F). These are cases (1) and (2), respectively. Optional regimes (4) and (5) are triggered only when the corresponding predicates are available and asserted; they do not alter the truth conditions of (1)–(3). □

Corollary 6.15.3 (Canonical resolution of each regime).

The interaction system resolves each regime as follows:

(1) If Legitimate(F), then F is already a stable policy (idempotent and drift-bounded) and does not accumulate further effect under repetition (Corollary 6.1B).

(2) If Admissible(F) ∧ ¬Legitimate(F), then the routed normal form S(F) is legitimate whenever the corresponding envelope axioms apply:

If InternalAct(F), then S(F)=L(F) and Legitimate(L(F)) (Theorem 6.1C, Axiom L0).

If BoundaryAct(F), then S(F)=G(F) and Legitimate(G(F)) (Theorem 6.1C, Axiom G2). Thus frontier proposals are normalized into the nearest legitimate interaction form.

(3) If ¬Admissible(F), then F fails the core non-domination gate (ALRP and the definitional admissibility criterion) and is structurally excluded; in deployment it must be rejected or replaced by a legitimate envelope/repair/identity continuation (Theorem 6.1C).

(4) If Emergency(F) ∧ WindowOpen(F) (optional Σᴿᴱ), then E(F) is bounded, idempotent, and repair-terminated by construction of the EE-series axioms; once the emergency inequality fails, the window closes and the system reverts to Id or an ordinary legitimate envelope.

(5) If DominationSingularity (optional viability/output module), then no ViableCandidate exists; the system must expose SafeFallback and disclose FailureReason (LIVE0–LIVE2).

Corollary 6.15.3A (Frontier proposals form a one-step normalization shell).

If Admissible(F) ∧ ¬Legitimate(F), then the interaction outcome is not an unstable admissible state: it is routed to a legitimate normal form in a single normalization step (via L for internal acts or G for boundary acts). Thus the admissible-but-illegitimate region functions as a frontier shell whose role is only to be projected to legitimacy by the routing normal form S(F).

6.15.2 Exhaustive Trajectory Classes (Finite Sequences of Interaction)

Definition 6.15.4 (Admissible trajectory). A finite trajectory of interaction is a finite sequence ⟨F1,…,Fn⟩ with each Ft ∈ O. The trajectory is admissible if Admissible(Ft) holds for all t.

Theorem 6.15.5 (Trajectory trichotomy in the base theory).

For any finite admissible trajectory, the resulting evolution falls into one of the following structural classes:

(A) Stable legitimate class: the trajectory reaches a legitimate fixed-point operation and thereafter no further change can be accumulated by repeating that policy (Corollary 6.1B).

(B) Monotone standing class: along the trajectory, standing never decreases for any entity (Theorem 6.1A).

(C) Repair-progressive dependency class (when Tier-3 emancipation is instantiated): if deg(i)>0 for any i, then capacity-progress and/or dependency reduction routes necessarily exist (Theorem 6.9A), preventing permanent capacity gating inside the formal regime.

Proof. (B) is exactly Theorem 6.1A. (A) is exactly Corollary 6.1B once a legitimate policy is reached. (C) is exactly Theorem 6.9A under the Tier-3 emancipation assumptions. □

Corollary 6.15.6 (No internal “slow creep” by trajectory).

In any admissible trajectory, there is no finite sequence of locally admissible steps that yields net standing decrease for any entity (Theorem 6.1A), and no fixed legitimate policy can accumulate coercive effect under repetition (Corollary 6.1B). Therefore any “slow creep” autonomy loss must arise from inadmissible updates (rejected) or from factors external to the interpreted Σᴿ signature (Theorem 6.14).

6.15.3 Policy-Space Geometry Already Induced by Σᴿ

Theorem 6.15.7 (Policy space is Boolean by STC5 class).

Let Q := U/∼ be the quotient set of STC5 classes. For each admissible proposal F, its envelope induces a class policy bF : Q → {0,1} as defined in §3.12 and §6.11–§6.12. Consequently, the space of class policies realized by envelopes is isomorphic (up to signature equivalence) to a subspace of {0,1}^Q, and under Policy Realizability (Axiom PR) the realizable policy space is exactly {0,1}^Q subject only to capacity feasibility constraints.

Proof. This is the content of Theorem 3.12.2 / Theorem 6.12 together with Axiom PR, which asserts existence of an admissible operation realizing any feasible class policy signature. □

Corollary 6.15.8 (No partial or selective within-class increments).

Because envelopes act class-uniformly on standing outcomes (STC5 on outcomes), there is no legitimate policy that increments only some members of an STC5 class while leaving others unchanged. Any attempted within-class favoritism is projected to the class-uniform envelope outcome.

Remark. This corollary is purely structural: it is the direct consequence of the STC5 outcome-uniformity enforced in legitimate envelopes and in the definition of legitimacy.

Corollary 6.15.8A (Composition cannot exceed join at the class-policy level).

For admissible proposals F and G, the class-policy induced by the envelope of the composition cannot require more than the classwise join of their policies:

b_{L_{F∘G}} ≤ b_{L_F} ∨ b_{L_G}.

This is the semilattice “no-superadditive escalation” consequence: composing admissible proposals cannot create a stronger class-increment policy than the join of their class-level increment intentions.

See §6.16.1–§6.16.2 for the derived meet operation on feasible class policies (policy intersection), which yields a conservative greatest-lower-bound candidate whenever two distinct admissible policies are available. When multiple admissible policies coexist, the conservative intersection policy (their meet) provides a canonical admissible baseline that preserves all common increments.

Definition 6.15.8B (Normalization deviation set; “distance from legitimacy” without metrics).

For any admissible proposal F ∈ O, define its normalization deviation set as the set of STC5-classes on which legitimacy closure requires an increment that was not already present in F’s increment signature: Dev(F) := { q ∈ Q : b_{L(F)}(q) = 1 ∧ b_F(q) = 0 }.

Reading. Dev(F) isolates where envelope-normalization changes the class-policy decision of F (at the level of increment intentions), without introducing subtraction, norms, or numeric distances. It is a purely structural comparison between the proposal’s signature and its legitimate normal form signature.

Proposition 6.15.8C (Deviation is conservative and cannot add domination pathways).

For admissible F, Dev(F) records only class-level increments required by the legitimacy closure; it does not permit standing decreases, does not weaken STC5 symmetry, and cannot accumulate through repetition (by idempotence/rerunnability of legitimate policies). In particular, the map F ↦ b_{L(F)} is a normalization to a legitimate fixed point; Dev(F) is an audit descriptor of that normalization step, not an additional operation.

Interpretation (interaction use). Dev(F) provides a formally grounded way to speak about “how far” a proposal is from legitimacy: proposals with Dev(F)=∅ already match the envelope at the class-policy level, while larger Dev(F) indicate increasing degrees of correction required by legitimacy closure.

NOTE (non-domination). This notion does not introduce any new admissible power. It only makes explicit a comparison between a proposal and its already-defined legitimate normalization.

6.15.4 Extremal Regimes (Edge Cases) Already Present in the Theory

Remark 6.15.9 (Minimal non-dominating coordination regime). In the deg=0 regime (no inbound dependency) with ordinary legitimacy constraints, Σᴿ reduces to a successor-based standing algebra with STC5 symmetry, idempotence, drift bounds, and admissibility. This is the minimal regime in which plural coordination can be validated without domination: standing cannot decrease, equal-standing/equal-capacity entities receive equal outcomes, and policy repetition cannot accumulate effect.

Remark 6.15.10 (Terminal autonomy plateau under CIA saturation). If an entity i satisfies FullCap(i) :⇔ σ(i)=B(cap(i)) and Tier-3 proxy termination is instantiated, then deg(i)=0 by Axiom P3. In that regime, neither standing nor dependency can be reduced by admissible trajectories, and any legitimate policy is idempotent. Thus the system reaches a terminal autonomy plateau in which further structural restriction cannot be stabilized within Σᴿ without violating admissibility or the emancipation constraints.

Remark 6.15.11 (Emergency regime is transient by construction). When Σᴿᴱ is instantiated, the emergency envelope does not define a permanent policy space: it defines a bounded stabilization action whose window must close once inaction, or a legitimate non-coercive candidate becomes at least as autonomy-preserving. The EE-series therefore makes emergency a forced transient regime rather than a stable attractor. The meet provides a nonescalatory prefallback candidate when policy disagreement exists but viability has not collapsed.

6.15.5 “Nothing Left on the Table”: Structural Collapse of Domination Strategy Space

Theorem 6.15.12 (Domination strategy space collapses inside Σᴿ).

Within any interpreted Σᴿ regime in which admissibility and legitimacy gates are enforced, the following hold:

Standing reduction cannot be achieved by any admissible operation (Theorem 6.1 and Theorem 6.1A).

Coercive accumulation cannot be achieved by repetition of a legitimate policy (Corollary 6.1B).

In dependency regimes, capacity-progress routes exist and permanent gating is not stable (Theorem 6.9A, when instantiated).

When domination-pressure non-regression is instantiated, domination pressure cannot accumulate and must dissipate under unconsented influence (Theorem 6.14A).

Any stable domination that appears must therefore originate from (i) inadmissible operations rejected by the filter, (ii) explicitly bounded and repair-terminated emergency regimes, or (iii) factors external to the interpreted Σᴿ signature (Theorem 6.14 and Corollary 6.14B).

Therefore, inside the modeled signature, domination is not merely disfavored: it has no stable internal strategy space under admissible interaction.

Proof. This is an explicit packaging of Theorem 6.1A, Corollary 6.1B, Theorem 6.9A (when instantiated), Theorem 6.14A (when instantiated), and Theorem 6.14 / Corollary 6.14B.

6.15A Directed Successor Calculus (Derived; No New Commitments)

This section makes explicit a calculus-like structure already implicit in Σᴿ. No new axioms are introduced. All definitions and results below follow directly from successor-boundedness, legitimacy closure, admissibility, and positive ratcheting constraints already established. The full internal consequences of this calculus are developed in §6.15B.

Unlike classical real-valued calculus, the structure here is directed, one-sided, and closure-absorbing. Infinitesimal change is permitted only in autonomy-preserving directions, and accumulation is strictly bounded by idempotence and closure.

6.15A.1 Successor Differential (Definition)

Definition 6.15A.1 (Successor Differential). For any admissible operation F ∈ O and entity i ∈ U, define the successor differential of standing as:

Δ⁺σ(F,i) = • 0, if σ(F(i)) = σ(i); • 1, if σ(F(i)) = S(σ(i)); • undefined, otherwise.

Similarly, define the successor differential of dependency deg and capacity cap analogously, subject to their respective admissibility constraints.

Remark. By successor boundedness and ALRP, negative or super-successor differentials are inadmissible. Thus Δ⁺ is a one-sided differential operator native to Σᴿ.

6.15A.2 Directed Continuity of Admissible Trajectories

Definition 6.15A.2 (Σᴿ-directed continuity). An admissible trajectory (Fₙ) is Σᴿ-continuous if, for all entities i:

• Δ⁺σ(Fₙ,i) ∈ {0,1};

• capacity changes are monotone non-decreasing;

• legitimacy closure is reached after finitely many steps.

Proposition 6.15A.3. Every admissible trajectory is Σᴿ-continuous.

Proof. Immediate from successor boundedness, ALRP, capacity non-regression, and closure idempotence. □

Interpretation. Directed continuity replaces ε–δ continuity. Change proceeds by legible successor motion toward closure, with no accumulation beyond fixed points.

6.15A.3 Closure Convergence and Fixed Points

Proposition 6.15A.4 (Closure convergence). For any admissible F, repeated normalization converges in one step: L(L(F)) = L(F), and (when applicable) G(G(F)) = G(F).

Thus, legitimate operations are exactly fixed points of admissible dynamics.

Corollary 6.15A.5.

There exist no non-trivial admissible limits beyond legitimate fixed points.

6.15A.4 Positive Ratcheting Integral for Capacity

Definition 6.15A.6 (Capacity realization integral). For any admissible Σᴿ-continuous trajectory τ and entity i, define:

∫_τ Δ⁺cap(i) := sup { cap(i_t) | t ∈ τ }.

This integral represents the maximal realized capacity achieved along τ.

Proposition 6.15A.7. The capacity integral is monotone, idempotent under repetition, and bounded.

Proof. Monotonicity follows from non-regression axioms. Idempotence follows from closure saturation. Boundedness follows from CIA and emancipatory repair constraints. □

6.15A.5 Directed Fundamental Theorem of Σᴿ Calculus

Theorem 6.15A.8 (Directed Fundamental Theorem). Along any admissible Σᴿ-continuous trajectory τ and entity i:

cap(i_final) = ∫_τ Δ⁺cap(i),

where i_final is the closure-stabilized state.

In particular, differentiation (Δ⁺) and integration (supremal realization) are inverse operations only in the forward (autonomy-increasing) direction.

Proof. By definition of Δ⁺cap and closure idempotence. No backward or compensatory direction exists under admissibility. □

6.15A.6 Non-Domination Guarantee (Calculus Level)

Proposition 6.15A.9. Directed successor calculus cannot generate domination pathways.

Justification.

• No negative differentials exist.

• No accumulation by repetition is possible.

• Closure absorbs all admissible dynamics.

• All change is successor-bounded, monotone, and repair-terminating.

Thus, infinitesimal harm, gradual erosion, optimization gradients, and compensatory trade-offs are structurally excluded.

6.15A.7 Scope and Limits of the Calculus

Remark. Σᴿ admits a calculus only under the following constraints:

• one-sided differentials;

• successor-native change;

• closure-terminated trajectories;

• no arithmetic aggregation;

• no optimization.

Any extension beyond this violates admissibility or non-domination invariants and is therefore excluded.

Proposition 6.15.A.8.1 — Attribute Conservation

For any admissible and attribute :

This enforces monotonicity across all successorstructured quantities, not only standing.

6.15B Calculus Identities, Laws, and Derived Consequences

(Derived; No New Commitments)

This section records the full set of calculus identities, laws, and structural permutations derivable inside the Directed Successor Calculus introduced in §6.15A. No new axioms are introduced. All results follow from successor boundedness, admissibility, legitimacy closure, idempotence, ALRP, CIA, and the classpolicy envelope semantics already established.

Together, these results exhaust the internal consequences of directed, successornative change under Σᴿ.

6.15B.1 Chain Law for Successor Differentials (ClosureMediated)

Proposition 6.15B.1 (Chain law under legitimacy closure).
For any admissible operation F and entity i:

Δ⁺σ(L(F), i)
= max { Δ⁺σ(F, j) | j ∈ Upstream(i) },

where Upstream(i) denotes entities whose standing contributions structurally affect i under the admissible update semantics.

Justification.
Standing change can propagate only through legitimacy normalization. Any successor increment in L(F) must arise from some successor increment in F at an upstream location, and propagation is bounded by successor constraints and STC5 symmetry. No amplification or compounding is possible. □

Interpretation.
This is the Σᴿ analogue of the chain rule: differentiation commutes with normalization, and dependence is mediated strictly through closure.

6.15B.2 Conservation and Invariance Laws

Proposition 6.15B.2 (Standing invariance).
Along any admissible Σᴿcontinuous trajectory τ and entity i:

inf { σ(i_t) | t ∈ τ } = σ(i).

Justification.
Direct consequence of ALRP and admissibility. Standing never decreases along admissible trajectories. □

Corollary 6.15B.3 (No gradual erosion).

There exists no admissible trajectory along which standing strictly decreases in the limit.

Interpretation.
This rules out infinitesimal or asymptotic erosion; admissible calculus preserves a standing floor exactly.

6.15B.3 Comparison Law (OrderTheoretic Derivative Comparison)

Proposition 6.15B.4 (Derivative comparison).
Let F and G be admissible operations. If for all entities i:

Δ⁺cap(F, i) ≥ Δ⁺cap(G, i),

then for all i:

cap(L(F)(i)) ≥ cap(L(G)(i)).

Justification.
Capacity changes are monotone and closureabsorbed. Envelope normalization preserves the componentwise order induced by Δ⁺cap. □

Interpretation.
This is the Σᴿ replacement for derivative comparison and monotone dominance. Policies can be compared without optimization or tradeoffs.

6.15B.4 Envelope Commutation Law

Proposition 6.15B.5 (Normalization commutation criterion).
If ¬OrderSensitive(F), then for all entities i:

Δ⁺σ(L(G(F)), i) = Δ⁺σ(G(L(F)), i).

Justification.
Order sensitivity is defined precisely as the failure of L and G to commute extensionally. When it does not obtain, successor differentials coincide under either normalization order. □

Interpretation.
This provides a calculuslevel diagnostic of scope dependence. Boundary effects do not distort successor dynamics when commutation holds.

6.15B.5 Variational Inequalities (AdmissibilityBounded)

Definition 6.15B.6 (Admissible perturbation).
An operation ε is an admissible perturbation of F if F ⊕ ε is admissible and respects successor and legitimacy constraints.

Proposition 6.15B.7 (Legitimacy stability under perturbation).
For any admissible perturbation ε of F:

L(F ⊕ ε) ≥ L(F).

Justification.
Legitimacy closure is inflationary and monotone. Admissible variation cannot reduce the envelope outcome. □

Corollary 6.15B.8 (Deviation monotonicity).

Dev(F ⊕ ε) ⊆ Dev(F).

Interpretation.
This constitutes a variational calculus without extrema: legitimate outcomes are stable under all admissible small changes.

6.15B.6 MinimalChange Law via Policy Intersection

Proposition 6.15B.9 (Leastimpact admissible policy).
Given admissible F and G, let H be the policy induced by the meet of their classpolicies. Then for all entities i:

Δ⁺σ(H, i) = min { Δ⁺σ(F, i), Δ⁺σ(G, i) }.

Justification.
Meet removes successor increments pointwise while preserving feasibility. Envelope realization of the meet exists by Axiom PR and preserves successor bounds. □

Interpretation.
This yields a calculus of minimal intrusion: H is the leastchange policy consistent with both F and G.

6.15B.7 Finite Termination and Complexity Bound

Proposition 6.15B.10 (Onestep closure termination).
For any admissible F:

Lⁿ(F) = L(F) for all n ≥ 1
(and analogously for G where applicable).

Justification.
Idempotence of legitimacy and boundary envelopes. □

Interpretation.
Σᴿ calculus is nonasymptotic: stabilization is immediate. There is no notion of convergence rate; only termination.

6.15B.8 Exhaustiveness of Calculus Laws

Proposition 6.15B.11 (Calculus completeness).
Any admissible calculus identity in Σᴿ must be expressible as an instance of one of the following: • successor differentiation (Δ⁺);
• closure or fixedpoint behavior;
• order comparison;
• admissibilitybounded variation;
• finite termination.

Justification.
No additional operations are available without introducing subtraction, accumulation, optimization, or nonmonotone dynamics, all of which violate admissibility or nondomination constraints.

6.16 Derived Policy Algebra and Closure Consequences (No New Commitments)

This section records additional algebraic and order-theoretic consequences already available in Σᴿ from the envelope/semilattice apparatus, the policy realizability axiom, and the deterministic routing normal form. No new axioms are introduced. All constructions below are conservative: they either (i) name relationships already present in §3.12 and §6.11–§6.15, or (ii) define operations that are strictly less permissive than existing ones (and therefore cannot open domination pathways).

6.16.1 Class-Policy Order and the Feasible Policy Lattice (Derived)

Recall Q := U/∼ where i∼j :⇔ (σ(i)=σ(j) ∧ cap(i)=cap(j)). For any admissible proposal F, let b_F : Q → {0,1} denote its increment signature (as in §3.12 / §6.11–§6.12).

Definition 6.16.1 (Pointwise order on class policies). For class policies b,c : Q → {0,1}, define: b ≤ c :⇔ ∀q∈Q (b(q) ≤ c(q)), where ≤ on {0,1} is the standard order 0 ≤ 1.

Definition 6.16.2 (Meet and join of class policies). Define the pointwise join and meet: (b ∨ c)(q) := max{b(q), c(q)} , (b ∧ c)(q) := min{b(q), c(q)} . Equivalently: (b ∨ c)(q)=1 iff b(q)=1 or c(q)=1; and (b ∧ c)(q)=1 iff b(q)=1 and c(q)=1.

Definition 6.16.3 (Feasible policy set). Define Feas ⊆ {0,1}^Q as the set of feasible class policies under CIA: b ∈ Feas :⇔ ∀q∈Q ( b(q)=1 → ∃i∈q with B(cap(i)) ≥ S(σ(i)) ). (This is exactly the feasibility condition used in Axiom PR.)

Theorem 6.16.4 (Closure of feasible policies under meet; conservative compromise).

Assume Axiom PR (Policy Realizability). Let b,c ∈ Feas. Then (b ∧ c) ∈ Feas.

Proof. Fix q∈Q. If (b ∧ c)(q)=1 then b(q)=1 and c(q)=1. Since b∈Feas, b(q)=1 implies there exists i∈q with B(cap(i)) ≥ S(σ(i)). Thus the feasibility condition holds for (b ∧ c) at q. Since q was arbitrary, (b ∧ c) ∈ Feas. □

Corollary 6.16.5 (Meet policy is the greatest lower bound among feasible policies).

Assume Axiom PR. For any b,c ∈ Feas, (b ∧ c) is a greatest lower bound of b and c in the poset (Feas, ≤). In particular: (i) (b ∧ c) ≤ b and (b ∧ c) ≤ c, and (ii) if d ∈ Feas satisfies d ≤ b and d ≤ c, then d ≤ (b ∧ c).

Proof. (i) and (ii) are immediate from pointwise min/max on {0,1}. □

Interpretation (structural, non-normative). The meet b ∧ c formalizes “conservative compromise” at the class-policy level: it increments exactly those STC5 classes that both candidate policies increment. Because it is pointwise no larger than either b or c, it cannot introduce new standing increments and therefore cannot open domination pathways. It only removes increments.

Theorem 6.16.6 (Feasible policy join is feasible; feasible-policy lattice when Feas is closed under join).

Assume Axiom PR. Let b,c ∈ Feas, and additionally assume that for every q with (b ∨ c)(q)=1 the CIA feasibility witness exists (equivalently: (b ∨ c) ∈ Feas). Then (Feas, ≤, ∧, ∨) is a distributive lattice (on the feasible region).

Proof. Given (b ∨ c) ∈ Feas, both meet and join are internal operations on Feas. Distributivity holds pointwise because min and max distribute on the two-element lattice {0,1}, and all identities lift pointwise to Q. □

Remark (why this remains conservative). The join operation corresponds to the already-established classpolicy joinsemilattice (Theorems 3.12.2 and 6.12). When join is feasible, it adds increments only where at least one policy already increments. It introduces no standing decreases and stays within the successor constraint (exactly one increment per class per envelope). Thus it remains non-dominating under admissibility and legitimacy constraints.

6.16.2 Envelope Realization of Meet/Join (Derived; No New Operators)

Definition 6.16.7 (Envelope of a class policy). Assume Axiom PR. For any b ∈ Feas, choose any admissible F_b ∈ O whose increment signature satisfies b_{F_b} = b (existence by PR), and define: L_b := L(F_b). By the signature-invariance results (Theorem 6.10 / §3.12), the envelope equivalence class [L_b] depends only on b, not on the choice of F_b.

Theorem 6.16.8 (Meet and join realized by envelopes up to signature).

Assume Axiom PR and let b,c ∈ Feas. Then: [L_{b ∨ c}] = [L_b] ∨ [L_c] (join in Env/≡), and [L_{b ∧ c}] is a greatest lower bound of [L_b] and [L_c] in the induced signature order on envelopes.

Proof. The join statement is exactly the semilattice result of §3.12 / §6.12 specialized to F_b and F_c and lifted to envelopes by signature. The meet statement follows because envelope equivalence classes are determined by their signatures, and (b ∧ c) is the greatest lower bound of b and c in {0,1}^Q under pointwise order; hence its corresponding envelope class is the greatest lower bound in the induced order. □

Corollary 6.16.9 (Autonomy-preserving “policy intersection” exists whenever two policies exist).

Assume Axiom PR and let b,c ∈ Feas. Then there exists an admissible proposal whose envelope is exactly the conservative intersection policy (b ∧ c). This gives a mechanically definable “intersection candidate” in any situation where two different admissible class policies are being considered.

6.16.3 Inflationary Idempotent Normalizers (L and G) (Derived)

Theorem 6.16.10 (L is inflationary and idempotent on admissible inputs).

For any F ∈ O, if Admissible(F) then: (i) ∀i∈U: σ(L(F)(i)) ≥ σ(i), (ii) L(L(F)) = L(F).

Proof. If Admissible(F), then Legitimate(L(F)) by Axiom L0, hence Admissible(L(F)) by Def. 21. By ALRP (Axiom 15), admissible operations do not decrease standing, giving (i). Idempotence (ii) holds by Axiom L5 (fixpoint on already legitimate acts) applied to L(F), since L(F) is legitimate.

Theorem 6.16.11 (G is scope-identity and scope-normalizing; no out-of-scope action).

For any F ∈ O and any i ∈ U: (i) ¬InScope(F,i) → G(F)(i)=i (Axiom G0), (ii) Admissible(F) → Legitimate(G(F)) (Axiom G2), and hence (under admissibility) ∀i: σ(G(F)(i)) ≥ σ(i).

Proof. (i) and (ii) are exactly Axioms G0 and G2. Under (ii), G(F) is legitimate and therefore admissible; standing nondecrease follows by ALRP. □

Corollary 6.16.12 (Normalization cannot ratchet).

For admissible F, repeated normalization does not accumulate effect: L(L(F)) = L(F), and G(G(F)) = G(F) (when G(F) is legitimate under admissibility). Thus normalization layers are not a path for power creep; they terminate after one application.

6.16.4 Boundary Commutation and Order Sensitivity (Derived Diagnostic Consequence)

Recall the defined predicate OrderSensitive(F) :⇔ L(G(F)) ≠ G(L(F)) (see §3.10.22).

Proposition 6.16.13 (Order sensitivity is a boundary-dependence diagnostic). If ¬OrderSensitive(F), then the final normalized outcome is invariant under swapping the order of internal and boundary normalization: L(G(F)) = G(L(F)). If OrderSensitive(F), then the evaluation regime (boundary vs internal discipline first) materially changes the normalized result.

Proof. Immediate from the definition of OrderSensitive(F) and extensional equality on O (Axiom O2). □

Interpretation (structural). Order sensitivity does not authorize coercion; it flags that scope decisions affect which normalization layer binds first. This is an audit signal for interface design and deployment, not a permission structure.

Admissibility and legitimacy satisfy an adjoint relationship. In practical terms: for any given sets of operations (or policies) S and T, every admissible element of S lies in T if and only if every element of S is accounted for in the legitimacy closure of T. Equivalently, for each individual operation p, if p is in S and p is admissible then p must appear in T; and conversely, if every p in S ends up included by the legitimacy-closure of T, then no admissible element of S lies outside of T. This describes a Galois connection between the restriction operator R (which filters a set to its admissible members) and the closure operator L (which completes a set to a legitimate set).

Meaning

Admissibility and legitimacy are adjoint, not hierarchical:

admissibility bounds what may occur

legitimacy bounds what must be repaired

No deontic logic is introduced.

6.17 Latent Iterations and Structural Closure of Σᴿ

This section delineates all remaining algebraic and calculus-level iterations that are latent in the Standing Algebra Σᴿ. Each iteration described here is already licensed by the axioms and theorems of the system and requires no new primitives. The purpose of this section is not to extend the expressive power of Σᴿ, but to make explicit the full space of structural consequences that follow from its design.

Crucially, every iteration listed below either (i) preserves or strengthens the system’s nondomination guarantees, or (ii) is explicitly foreclosed by existing axioms where it would otherwise allow domination to propagate or stabilize. In this sense, the system is shown to be structurally closed.

6.17.1 Reflexive Iterations (SelfApplication of Existing Structure)

(a) Repair-ofRepair Closure

All repair operations are themselves admissible transformations subject to legitimacy, closure, and successor boundedness. Consequently, the repair subsystem is closed under its own application.

Proposition 6.17.1 (Repair reflexivity).
For any admissible repair operation R, the normalized repair L(R) is itself a legitimate fixed point. Any deviation introduced by R is correctable by admissible repair.

This implies that there exists no admissible state within Σᴿ that is irreparable. Repairs form a closed subspace of the algebra and cannot serve as sinks for domination.

(b) OptimizationofOptimization Stability

Given legitimacyconstrained optimization (§6.15C), objectives themselves may be compared or selected at the same legitimacy level without escalation.

Proposition 6.17.2 (Optimization reflexivity).
Let J₁, J₂ be admissible objectives. Selection between Opt(J₁) and Opt(J₂) is itself equivalent to a legitimacyconstrained optimization and introduces no new dynamics.

Optimization therefore forms a reflexive, terminating selection layer and cannot bootstrap additional power.

6.17.2 Dual Iterations (Structural Duals Already Present)

(a) Fragility / Risk Dual Calculus

Alongside positive successor calculus for autonomy and capacity, Σᴿ already encodes a dual notion of fragility via:

normalization deviation Dev(F),

domination singularities Dₛ,

safety kernels and frontiers.

Proposition 6.17.3 (Fragility monotonicity).

Any increase in structural fragility necessarily triggers either inadmissibility or a repairrequired state. Fragility cannot increase without activating correction mechanisms.

This dual calculus ensures domination cannot silently accumulate.

(b) Interior–Closure Duality

Legitimacy closure L and safety interior notions are algebraic duals.

Proposition 6.17.4 (Interiorclosure duality).
For any admissible transformation, movement toward the interior of the safety region is dual to movement toward closure under L. No admissible operation can push a system from interior to exterior without triggering rejection or repair.

This yields a DeMorganstyle duality between safety and normalization.

6.17.3 Parametric and Family Iterations

(a) Parametric Calculus Schema

The directed successor calculus applies uniformly to any admissible attribute satisfying successor boundedness and nonregression.

Definition 6.17.5 (Parametric successor calculus).
For any such attribute x, define Δ⁺ₓ analogously to Δ⁺σ.

This establishes a family of calculi indexed by attribute, without extending Σᴿ.

(b) Relative Calculus Between Legitimate Envelopes

Changes can be evaluated comparatively without introducing metrics.

Proposition 6.17.6 (Relative successor comparison).

For legitimate envelopes E₁ ≤ E₂, relative change is fully characterized by b_{E₂} − b_{E₁} at the classpolicy level.

This yields sensitivity analysis without aggregation or subtraction over entities.

6.17.4 Stratified and Layered Iterations

(a) ClassRestricted Dynamics

Because STC5 equivalence classes are algebraically independent under CIA, calculus may be restricted to classes and then recomposed via join and meet.

Proposition 6.17.7 (Classwise stratification).

All admissible dynamics factor through classrestricted calculus and recombine only via successorbounded lattice operations.

This prevents crossclass coercive propagation.

(b) Nested Envelope Analysis

Boundary normalization (G) and internal normalization (L) may be nested without introducing new operators.

Proposition 6.17.8 (Nested envelope stability).
All nested envelope sequences collapse in finite steps to a unique normalized form under S(F).

Thus envelope nesting cannot be exploited to amplify effects.

6.17.5 Temporal and Historical Iterations

(a) FiniteHorizon Unfolding

All admissible processes unfold as finite trees with bounded depth.

Proposition 6.17.9 (Finite unfolding).

There exists a global bound on admissible unfolding depth determined by successor and drift constraints.

This eliminates infinite strategic delay or erosion.

(b) Historical Erasure under Normalization

Past illegitimacy leaves no residual effect once closure is achieved.

Proposition 6.17.10 (Historical normalization).

If E is a legitimate envelope, then its future admissibility is independent of the specific illegitimate history that preceded normalization.

This prevents domination from persisting via historical inertia.

6.17.6 Foreclosure of DominationPermitting Iterations

All remaining conceivable mathematical iterations fall into one of the following classes:

arithmetic accumulation,

infinitesimal erosion,

compensatory aggregation,

nonmonotone optimization,

inverse or subtractive dynamics.

Each is explicitly foreclosed by existing axioms:

successor boundedness,

ALRP,

nonregression,

legitimacy closure,

idempotence,

CIA.

Theorem 6.17.11 (No latent domination channels).

There exists no algebraic or calculuslevel iteration consistent with the axioms of Σᴿ that permits domination to propagate, intensify, or stabilize beyond a bounded, repairterminated interval.

6.17.7 Structural Completeness of Σᴿ

Taken together, Theorems 6.15–6.17 establish that Σᴿ is closed under algebraic, calculuslevel, geometric, trigonometric, and optimizationlevel reflection. Every admissible transformation, diagnostic, envelope, calculus law, and derived iteration either (i) stabilizes at a legitimate fixed point, or (ii) is structurally excluded prior to effect.

In particular:

All admissible dynamics are successorbounded, monotone, and closureterminating.

All envelopenormalized outcomes are idempotent under repetition.

All oscillatory or cyclic behavior is directionrestricted and eventually damped.

All optimization procedures are legitimacyconstrained selections over fixed points.

All geometric and trigonometric constructions are asymmetric, noninvertible, and repairabsorbed.

Any further mathematical construction consistent with the axioms of Σᴿ must therefore be one of the following:

A reexpression of existing structure (e.g., alternative presentations of order, closure, or envelopes),

A parameterized instance of an alreadydefined schema (e.g., attributeindexed calculus),

An interpretive lens drawn from an external domain (e.g., geometry, probability, dynamics) that introduces no new operators, permissions, or admissible behavior.

Conversely, any mathematical construction that would permit:

standing reduction,

autonomy erosion,

compensatory aggregation,

accumulation by repetition,

inverse or subtractive dynamics,

or optimization that outruns legitimacy,

is provably incompatible with successor boundedness, ALRP, nonregression, legitimacy closure, and idempotence, and is therefore already foreclosed by the existing axioms and theorems.

Accordingly, Σᴿ admits no latent domination pathways, either directly or via emergent mathematical structure. The theory is structurally complete: its allowable transformations are exhausted by the constructions already presented, and its prohibitions are enforced by necessity rather than by fiat.

6.17.8 Repair, Substitution, and Structural Workarounds

(Derived; No New Commitments)

This section completes the repair theory of Σᴿ by making explicit a distinction already implicit in the capacity, nonregression, and autonomy preservation axioms: repair is defined with respect to functional autonomy, not the preservation of any particular historical artifact, resource, or mechanism.

Irreversibility of a specific structure does not constitute irreparable harm if an admissible substitute exists that restores or preserves autonomy. No new axioms are introduced.

6.17.8.1 Endogenous Harm and Structural Detectability

Definition 6.17.8.1 (Endogenous harm).
A harm state is endogenous if it arises from admissible operations within Σᴿ’s modeled transformation space and results in degradation of autonomy, capacity, or exit viability.

Theorem 6.17.8.2 (Structural detectability of endogenous harm).

Every endogenous harm state necessarily induces a nonzero dominationrelevant diagnostic signal (ARV increase, legitimacy deviation, or domination pressure, depending on module instantiation).

Justification.
All admissible operations preserve standing and capacity floors (ALRP, nonregression). Therefore, any loss of autonomy or viable exit must violate a nonbypassable constraint, which is captured structurally by existing diagnostics. Endogenous harm cannot remain undetected.

6.17.8.2 Two Modes of Repair

Definition 6.17.8.3 (Direct repair).
A direct repair operator restores the same functional structure whose degradation triggered the harm signal, without reducing standing, increasing dependency, or violating admissibility.

Definition 6.17.8.4 (Substitutive repair / structural workaround).
A substitutive repair operator restores the functional autonomy or capacity lost to harm via an alternative admissible structure, even when the original structure is irreversibly foreclosed.

Substitutive repair:

does not require preservation of the original artifact or pathway,

must preserve or increase standing,

must not introduce coerced dependency,

must maintain exit viability.

Repair is therefore defined at the level of autonomy, not historical form.

6.17.8.3 RepairorSubstitution Completeness

Theorem 6.17.8.5 (Repair completeness strengthened).

For every endogenous harm state associated with a nonzero ARV signal, at least one of the following exists:

(i) an admissible direct repair operator, or
(ii) an admissible substitutive repair operator restoring equivalent or greater functional autonomy.

Proof sketch.
If direct repair exists, (i) holds.
If direct repair is structurally foreclosed, capacityprogress and nonregression axioms guarantee the existence of an alternative admissible pathway restoring autonomy. Failure of both (i) and (ii) would imply permanent endogenous autonomy loss under all admissible continuations, contradicting the capacity progress / antidomination results established earlier.

6.17.8.4 Irreversible External World Events (IEWs)

Definition 6.17.8.6 (Irreversible External World Event, IEW).
An IEW is an event that permanently forecloses a specific structure, resource, or mechanism (e.g., extinction of a material, irreversible physical injury, destruction of infrastructure).

An IEW does not by itself imply irreparable harm.

Theorem 6.17.8.7 (IEW reclassification).

An IEW constitutes irreparable harm only if no admissible substitutive repair exists that preserves or restores functional autonomy.

If such a substitute exists, the harm is structurally repairable, even though the original object or pathway is not.

6.17.8.5 Structural Responsibility Under Irreversibility

Theorem 6.17.8.8 (No responsibility collapse under IEWs).

The occurrence of an IEW does not remove Σᴿ’s obligation to preserve autonomy. Instead, it shifts the repair obligation from direct restoration to admissible substitution.

Failure to search for, admit, or permit substitutive repair constitutes a new endogenous harm.

6.17.8.6 NonDomination Preservation

Corollary 6.17.8.9.

Substitutive repair does not introduce domination pathways. Any substitute must satisfy admissibility, preserve standing, avoid coerced dependency, and respect exit viability.

Irreversibility of form therefore cannot be used to justify loss of autonomy, and “nothing can be done” is never a valid dominationexcusing condition.

There exists no infinite strictly descending chain:

Meaning

Domination cannot accumulate via iteration; however, horizontal evolution remains unbounded.

6.20 Legitimacy Dynamics and Applied Mathematics

(Derived; No New Commitments)

This section formalizes the applied mathematical and dynamicalsystems structure implicitly induced by Σᴿ. No new axioms are introduced. All results are derived from successor boundedness, admissibility, legitimacy closure, idempotence, nonregression, and the directed successor calculus (§6.15A–C).

Unlike classical applied mathematics, legitimacy dynamics do not model freerunning control or optimization. Instead, Σᴿ induces closurebounded, monotone, terminating dynamics whose primary analytic objects are stability, basins of attraction, robustness, and bounded response to perturbation.

6.20.1 Time and Evolution Semantics

Let denote time, where may be discrete or continuous.

An admissible evolution is a map:

such that for all , the transition is admissible and successorbounded.

Remark.
Σᴿ places no restriction on the granularity or continuity of time; all restrictions act on transformations, not on temporal indexing. Time in Σᴿ is not an objective, resource, or optimizable quantity; it functions solely as a structural constraint on admissibility and cannot justify preference, urgencybased override, or violation.

6.20.1.A Temporal Admissibility, Delay Boundedness, and Emergency Projection

(Derived; No New Commitments)

This section makes explicit the temporal structure already implicit in Σᴿ and formally integrates time as a firstclass, nonoptimizing, nonauthoritative dimension of admissibility. The purpose is to capture the fact—already enforced informally by bounded repair, nonregression, and idempotence—that delay itself may constitute domination, and that emergency is an inherently timeindexed legitimacy regime. No new axioms are introduced. All constructions in this section are derived consequences of successor boundedness, legitimacy closure, repair completeness, and nondomination invariants.

1. Temporal Indexing and Admissible Time

Let time be represented by a discrete successornative index
τ ∈ ℕ

Time advances only through admissible successor steps. There is no continuous time, no infinitesimal accumulation, no discounting, and no aggregation over agents. Temporal evolution is therefore structural, not metric.

An admissible temporal trajectory is a sequence:

E₀ → E₁ → E₂ → … → Eₖ

where each transition is an admissible operation under Σᴿ. Repetition, stasis, and repair are all expressed within this successor framework.

2. Temporal Legitimacy State Space

Define the temporal legitimacy space:

𝒯 := ℒ × ℕ

where ℒ is the legitimacy poset.

A temporal state (E, τ) carries no additional standing or authority beyond E. Time itself has no standing, no capacity, and no autonomy. It exists solely as a structural index enabling boundedness reasoning.

Projection onto ℒ recovers the underlying legitimacy state.

3. Structural Distance to Illegitimacy (TimetoCollapse)

Let ∂ℒ denote the legitimacy boundary (illegitimate envelopes).

Define the remaining admissible depth function:

Δ(E) := sup { k ∈ ℕ | there exists an admissible successor chain of length k from E with no element in ∂ℒ }

Δ(E) is finite for all admissible E by successor boundedness and drift constraints.

Δ(E) measures how many admissible time steps remain before legitimacy exhaustion, conditional on continued admissible motion toward the boundary.

Intuitively, for any state , there is a maximum number of consecutive admissible steps that can be taken from before some legitimacy invariant is violated (i.e. before reaching the boundary of the safe region). We denote this maximal length as . By the system’s bounded-drift and successor constraints, is always a finite natural number. In other words, there is an upper bound on how far a process starting from any state can proceed via admissible transformations without encountering an illegitimate state.

This quantity is structural and counterfactual: it does not predict behavior, only structural possibility.

4. Structural Distance to Restoration (TimetoRepair)

Define the repair depth function:

R(E) := inf { k ∈ ℕ | there exists an admissible repair or substitution chain of length k from E to some legitimate fixed point E* }

Existence and finiteness of R(E) follow from repairorsubstitution completeness and boundedness.

For any state , there is a well-defined minimal length of an admissible repair chain needed to reach a fully legitimate state (a fixed point) from . We denote this number as . In other words, means that is the least number of consecutive repair operations required to restore legitimacy starting from . Such an exists and is finite (by the system’s completeness and boundedness properties): any harm state can be repaired in a finite number of steps, and no shorter sequence than will suffice.

R(E) measures how many admissible steps are required to fully restore legitimacy, conditional on repair being pursued.

5. Temporal NonRegression and Bounded Erosion

Theorem (Temporal NonRegression).

Along any admissible trajectory E₀ → E₁ → … → Eₙ:

Δ(Eₙ₊₁) ≥ Δ(Eₙ) − 1

That is, legitimacy cannot erode faster than one admissible successor step per temporal step. There is no asymptotic or fractional erosion of legitimacy.

This excludes infinitesimal and imperceptible harm accumulation.

6. Delay Accumulation as a Structural Quantity

Let τ₀ be the time at which a dominationrelevant condition (standing restriction, capacity gating, dependency, emergency deviation) becomes active at state E.

Define the delay accumulation function:

D(E, τ₀, τ) := τ − τ₀

This measures elapsed admissible time without structural resolution.

7. Delay Domination Threshold

Define the maximum admissible delay bound:

B(E) := R(E)

That is, the maximum admissible duration for any dominationrelevant restriction is exactly the minimum time required to repair or substitute it.

Theorem (Delay Domination Breach).

If D(E, τ₀, τ) > B(E), then the temporal trajectory constitutes endogenous domination, even if all intermediate operations are individually admissible.

Delay beyond repair depth is equivalent to domination via accumulation, and violates nonregression.

8. Emergency as a Temporally Indexed Regime

Emergency in Σᴿ is not a distinct authority; it is a temporally constrained deviation regime.

Formally, an emergency state Eᵉ satisfies:

Eᵉ is admissible but not legitimate,

Eᵉ reduces standing or autonomy only to the minimum structurally necessary degree,

Eᵉ requires an active repair obligation.

Emergency is therefore indexed to:

the time of onset τᵉ,

the repair depth R(Eᵉ),

and the delay bound B(Eᵉ).

9. TimetoEmergency (Projection)

Given a nonemergency legitimate state E, define the emergency projection function:

E →ᵖ Eᵉ iff Δ(E) = k and continued admissible drift without repair leads to violation of legitimacy invariants in k steps.

Thus, Σᴿ permits computation of:

timetocollapse (Δ(E)),

timetoemergency (smallest k such that legitimacy must be relaxed to remain admissible),

timetorestoration (R(E)).

All three are purely structural and counterfactual.

10. Counterfactual Temporal Evaluation of Proposed Actions

Given a proposed transformation T at temporal state (E, τ), define:

E′ := L(T(E)) or E′ := μ(L ∘ R ∘ T)(E) if repair is required.

The temporal structural effect of T is given by the pair:

(Δ(E′) − Δ(E), R(E′) − R(E))

This determines whether T moves the system:

closer to collapse,

closer to emergency,

closer to restoration,

or remains structurally neutral.

This evaluation is:

nonauthoritative,

nonprescriptive,

invariant under agent belief or compliance.

11. No Temporal Optimization or Urgency Authority

Time in Σᴿ cannot be:

optimized,

discounted,

traded against autonomy,

aggregated across agents,

used to justify violation.

Urgency alone never authorizes deviation. Emergency is authorized only by structural breach proximity, and is strictly bounded by timetorepair.

12. Temporal Completion and NonSovereignty

Corollary (Temporal NonSovereignty).

Σᴿ does not mandate action based on temporal closeness to collapse, emergency, or restoration. It only determines when delay becomes structurally dominating or when emergency becomes unavoidable.

All decisions to act earlier than the domination threshold remain external.

13. Summary

By integrating time as a successorbounded structural dimension, Σᴿ:

makes domination by delay formally impossible,

renders emergency fully auditable and selfterminating,

permits precise counterfactual reasoning about temporal trajectories,

and preserves freedom by refusing temporal authority.

Time is constrained; choice remains free.

6.21.12 Invariant Core and Elective Frontier

Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) partitions the space of transformations into two disjoint structural regions: an Invariant Core and an Elective Frontier. This distinction is semantic, not procedural, and holds across all admissible operations and all trajectories.

The Invariant Core consists of structural properties that cannot be relinquished, traded, or overridden by election, aggregation, consent, or contract. These properties are prerequisites for agency itself and therefore cannot be objects of agency.

Invariant Core (NonDerogable).

The following properties are invariant under all admissible transformations:

(i) Standing preservation. For all admissible F and all entities i, σ(F(i)) ≥ σ(i) (ALRP).

(ii) Capacity floor. For all admissible F and all entities i, Cap(F(i)) ≥ Cap_min(i) as required by capacityindexed autonomy.

(iii) Exit viability. No admissible transformation may eliminate all viable future states for any nonconsenting entity.

(iv) Nonnullity. No admissible transformation may map an entity to the null standing class.

These invariants hold even if an entity purports to consent to their violation. Any clause or suboperation violating an invariant is structurally inert and eliminated by normalization.

Elective Frontier.

All transformations that respect the Invariant Core lie within the Elective Frontier. Within this region, Standing Algebra imposes no constraints on purpose, value, preference, strategy, efficiency, morality, or wisdom.

Formally, for any operation F:

Admissible(F) if and only if F preserves all invariants of the Invariant Core.

Σᴿ does not rank, optimize, or evaluate the content of elective choices. An entity may choose outcomes that are costly, inefficient, risky, or imprudent, provided such choices do not violate the invariants above.

This separation ensures that Σᴿ functions as a constitutional substrate: protections are fixed, while choices are free.

Clarification (Value Neutrality).

Σᴿ does not evaluate preferences, outcomes, beliefs, values, or reasons. Disagreement over value, meaning, or desirability is not a domination condition within the algebra.

Domination is defined purely by structural properties: standing reduction, capacity collapse, exit foreclosure, or forced choice. Where none of these occur, value disagreement is admissible by definition.

6.22 Emergent Structural Realizations of Σᴿ

When the algebraic, calculuslevel, geometric, trigonometric, dynamical, optimization, and probabilistic structures of Σᴿ are considered jointly, a number of higherorder realizations emerge that are not visible within any single domain alone. These realizations do not introduce additional mathematical machinery; rather, they express global structural facts that follow necessarily from the interaction of the existing constraints.

6.22.1 Domination as Structural Singularity

Across all mathematical lenses present in Σᴿ, domination fails to appear as a stable configuration. Algebraically, it violates admissibility; calculically, it lacks successorbounded support; geometrically, it manifests as high curvature and instability; dynamically, it is repelling rather than attracting; probabilistically, it has vanishing measure under admissible evolution.

Taken together, these results imply that domination is not an alternative equilibrium or optimization target within Σᴿ, but a structural singularity: a configuration that cannot persist across simultaneous algebraic, geometric, and dynamical constraints. This reframes domination from a normative or political category into a mathematically unstable state.

6.22.2 Legitimacy as a Conserved Structural Quantity

The combined action of successor monotonicity, legitimacy closure, nonregression, and probabilistic concentration implies that legitimacy behaves analogously to a conserved quantity. While configurations may change, oscillate, or admit uncertainty, admissible evolution preserves a minimum legitimacy invariant across all entities.

This conservation is not numeric and does not permit tradeoffs or compensation. Rather, it is structural: any admissible trajectory preserves standing floors, forces deviation reduction, and collapses into legitimate fixed points. The system therefore enforces legitimacy not through enforcement, but through impossibility of loss under valid evolution.

6.22.3 Pluralism Without Resolution

By jointly considering legitimacy geometry (distance between envelopes), legitimacy trigonometry (phase and oscillation), and legitimacy probability (distributions over envelopes), Σᴿ admits persistent disagreement without coercion.

Misaligned frames can remain at nonzero geometric distance, oscillate in bounded cycles, and be probabilistically represented without any requirement of convergence, arbitration, or forced consensus. The nondomination constraints ensure that pluralism is structurally stable: disagreement neither escalates into domination nor collapses into enforced uniformity.

Corollary (Pluralism Preservation).
Under the interpretation of autonomy as viable exit together with symmetric standing, the preceding theorem establishes preservation of pluralist coordination.

This corollary is interpretive and does not introduce additional algebraic assumptions.

6.22.4 Minimal Intervention as Structural Necessity

The interaction of directed calculus, legitimacy geometry, and legitimacyconstrained optimization yields a sharp notion of minimal intervention. Corrective action corresponds to the shortest legitimate geodesic that resolves a violation, and any deviation beyond this minimal path is detectable as unnecessary structural displacement.

This result replaces discretionary or moral arguments about “overreach” with a formal criterion: excess intervention is mathematically identifiable as nongeodesic movement in legitimacy space.

6.22.5 The Impossibility of Hidden Harm

Across the combined domains, no mechanism exists for harm to propagate unnoticed. Incremental harm is blocked by successor bounds, oscillatory harm is damped by closure, probabilistic harm cannot be averaged away, and dynamic harm cannot accumulate over time.

This implies a strong global property: there is no admissible path by which domination can arise slowly, indirectly, or probabilistically without triggering structural rejection or repair. Harm cannot hide in noise, cycles, or averages.

6.22.6 Progress Without Historical Forcing

Σᴿ admits improvement, repair, and capacity expansion, but does not induce mandatory trajectories or historical inevitabilities. Dynamics are terminating rather than asymptotic, optimization is selective rather than directive, and probability reflects uncertainty without compelling outcomes.

The combined system therefore supports progress without teleology: beneficial change is possible, but futures remain open, plural, and choicesensitive rather than structurally predetermined.

6.22.7 Structural Closure of Expressive Power

Finally, the combination of all mathematical domains makes clear why Σᴿ resists further internal extension. Adding new expressive dimensions would either duplicate existing structure or reintroduce degrees of freedom already excluded by nondomination constraints.

The system thus reaches a fixed point of expressivity: all admissible mathematical behavior is already represented, and all dominationpermitting behavior is structurally foreclosed.

6.22.8 Structural Opportunity Fields and Coercion

For any entity i at time t, Σᴿ distinguishes between two structurally relevant opportunity fields:

The Natural Opportunity Field, denoted ℱ_nat(i), consists of all states reachable by i given its standing σ(i), capacity Cap(i), and the ambient system state, assuming no agentimposed constraints, conditional threats, or bundled dependencies.

The Proposed Opportunity Field, denoted ℱ_prop(i,F), consists of all states reachable by i if a proposed input F is enacted.

Definition (Structural Coercion).

An input F is structurally coercive with respect to entity i if ℱ_prop(i,F) is a strict structural contraction of ℱ_nat(i) and the contraction is not required for the preservation of standing, exit viability, or symmetry.

Structural coercion is evaluated solely on the topology of reachable states and does not depend on the expressed preferences, consent, intent, or psychological state of the entity.

6.22.9 Survival Bottlenecks and Forced Choice

A survival bottleneck exists when, under a proposed input F, there exists exactly one reachable class of states that preserves σ(i) ≥ σ_min or exit viability for entity i.

Coupling in the survival dimension may not justify or induce increases in affective, cognitive, or behavioral coupling. Survival dependence does not imply obligation beyond preservation of viability.

Definition (Forced Choice).

An input F induces a forced choice if, for some entity i, all but a single branch in ℱ_prop(i,F) result in standing loss, exit foreclosure, or dependency collapse.

Forced choice constitutes structural coercion regardless of consent, preference expression, or voluntary acceptance. Any downstream election made under forced choice conditions is treated as nonvolitional.

6.22.10 Epistemic Conditioning and Ignorance Classification

Σᴿ does not assume that all inputs are submitted under full information or unconditioned belief. Accordingly, the algebra classifies certain inputs prior to admissibility without inferring intent or internal mental state.

Definition (Epistemically Conditioned Input).

An input F is epistemically conditioned with respect to entity i if the induced opportunity field ℱ_prop(i,F) collapses without an identifiable external coercer and without an admissible structural necessity.

Definition (IgnoranceDependent Input).

An input F is ignorancedependent if its admissibility depends on factual assertions or environmental claims that are not structurally validated within the current system state.

Classification Rule.

Epistemically conditioned and ignorancedependent inputs are not rejected on this basis alone. They are purified or admissibilityevaluated normally, but the classification is attached to the resulting output as nonnormative metadata.

This classification does not reduce standing, does not imply fault, and does not alter legitimacy. It exists solely to prevent epistemic uncertainty from being mistaken for autonomous volition.

6.22.11 Coercion-Free Envelope

Definition (AutonomyReducing Structure). A structural element s of an operation F is autonomyreducing if its presence causes, for any entity i, at least one of the following:

contraction of the opportunity field ℱ(i,F),

violation of exit viability,

induced forced choice,

Definition (Structural Purification Operator). Let ρ be the recursive purification operator such that: ρ(F) = F \ ARV(F) ρ is applied until a fixed point is reached. Let ρ*(F) denote the fully purified form of F.

Definition (CoercionFree Envelope; CFE). For any input operation F, the CoercionFree Envelope of F, denoted CFE(F), is the set of all states S such that:

S ∈ CFE(F) iff:

(a) S is reachable under ρ*(F),

(b) S satisfies admissibility constraints,

(c) S preserves standing for all entities,

(d) S preserves capacity above agency thresholds,

(e) S preserves exit viability,

(f) S contains no forcedchoice singularities,

(g) S contains no autonomyreducing structure.

CFE(F) is the maximal legitimate statespace consistent with F absent coercion.

NonSelection Constraint. CFE(F) defines a set, not an element. Σᴿ MUST NOT:

order,

rank,

maximize,

select,

recommend, or

privilege any member of CFE(F).

Relationship to Original Proposal. Let Outcome(F) be the actual output selected by an external process from within the admissible envelope. Σᴿ permits but does not require Outcome(F) ∈ CFE(F). If Outcome(F) ∉ CFE(F), Σᴿ may attach a coercionsignature flag indicating divergence from the coercionfree envelope.

Definition (Coercion Divergence Signature). If an observable system repeatedly selects outcomes lying outside CFE(F) while CFE(F) ≠ ∅, Σᴿ attaches a coercion divergence signature to the system evaluation. This signature:

does not alter standing,

does not alter legitimacy,

does not enforce correction,

does not impose penalties,

serves solely as a structural diagnostic.

Diagnostic NonElevation Rule.

No diagnostic, label, signature, or flag defined in Σᴿ may:

(i) alter admissibility,

(ii) alter legitimacy,

(iii) alter standing,

(iv) mandate selection,

(v) impose correction.

Diagnostics are observational only. Elevation of diagnostics into enforcement constitutes metadomination and is outside the scope of Σᴿ.

CFE Precedence and NonAuthority.

The CoercionFree Envelope (CFE) is a counterfactual diagnostic boundary. It does not constitute:

(i) a preference ordering,

(ii) a recommendation,

(iii) a standard of welfare,

(iv) an optimization target,

(v) a legitimacy requirement.

The existence of CFE(F) must not be interpreted as implying that any member of CFE(F) is superior to, preferable to, or more justified than any admissible outcome.

No system may enforce compliance with CFE(F), and no agent’s standing, capacity, or legitimacy may be affected solely by divergence from CFE(F).

6.22.12 Representation Theorem for NonDominating Constraint Systems

Consider any formal system consisting of:

a set of system states ,

a set of transformations or interventions ,

a predicate of permissibility ,

and a normalization or repair operator ,

satisfying all of the following properties:

Monotone NonRegression
For every permissible and state , no monotone structural attribute (including standing, capacity, or exit viability) decreases under application of .

RepairClosure Without Aggregation
Normalization under restores permissibility without aggregating preferences, utilities, or tradeoffs, and without selecting among incomparable outcomes.

Absence of Total Order or Extremal Optima
The space of permissible outcomes admits no total ordering, greatest element, or expectation functional consistent with permissibility.

Locality Without Global Synthesis
Permissibility and normalization are defined locally over domains or agents, without requiring global coherence, consensus, or a privileged global state.

Bounded Harm With Unbounded Evolution
Any permissible evolution is bounded in harm but admits infinite noncollapsing trajectories.

Theorem (Representation of NonDominating Systems)

Any system satisfying conditions (1)–(5) above is structurally isomorphic, up to definitional equivalence, to a Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) envelope system.

Formally, there exists an isomorphism

preserving:

nonregression invariants,

and operational indistinguishability classes.

Interpretation

Σᴿ is not one admissible solution among many.
It is the canonical normal form of any constraint system that forbids domination without invoking preference, optimization, or sovereignty.

This result is descriptive, not prescriptive: it classifies what is possible, not what ought to be done.

Pluralism, as used here, is identified with the coexistence of multiple agents whose exit remains viable and whose standing relations remain symmetric under admissible operations.

6.23.7 External Terminality and Sovereign Exit

Σᴿ distinguishes between ordinary temporal progression and terminal standing loss caused by factors external to the agency of the affected entity.

Definition (External Terminality).

An entity i is in a state of external terminality if there exists a standing reduction Δσ_ext < 0 such that:

(i) Δσ_ext is not caused by any admissible operation or elective choice of i,

(ii) Δσ_ext is not preventable or reversible by any admissible repair operation available within the current system state, and

(iii) continued enforcement of survival constraints would perpetuate standing reduction rather than preserve agency.

In states of external terminality, Σᴿ permits a Sovereign Terminal Exit envelope, under the following conditions:

(a) the request originates from the affected entity,

(b) no other entity’s standing is reduced by the termination, and

(c) the envelope does not authorize termination, standing reduction, or control over any other entity.

The Sovereign Terminal Exit is an edgescoped legitimacy envelope. It:

• terminates capacity and future agency,

• does not reclassify the entity as null,

• does not transfer or destroy standing,

• does not compose with other operations, and

• does not generalize beyond the terminal boundary condition.

This provision ensures that irreversible external decay cannot be converted into a mechanism of enforced survival or structural domination.

6.23.8 Voluntary Symmetric Sacrifice

Σᴿ permits voluntary sacrifice only when it is free of coercion, evaluation pressure, or structural necessity, and only when it functions as a symmetryrestorative transfer rather than a deletion of autonomy.

Definition (Voluntary Sacrifice).

An operation F constitutes a voluntary sacrifice by entity i on behalf of entity j if and only if:

(i) F is proposed by i without threat, dependency foreclosure, or evaluative coupling at input time,

(ii) F reduces capacity or liberty of action for i without reducing σ(i),

(iii) F restores or preserves σ(j) or Cap(j) toward an established symmetry threshold, and

(iv) no third party acquires standing, leverage, or enforceable claims as a result.

All sacrifice operations are treated as temporary couplings. Upon restoration of the relevant symmetry threshold, the coupling must structurally cease. Any attempt to extend, institutionalize, or launder sacrifice into sustained dependence or domination is inadmissible.

Justification.
The stated impossibility follows because the configuration would require either exit collapse or irreversible dependency growth, both of which violate the definition of nondomination.

Sacrifice that arises under coercion, duress, algorithmic pressure, or evaluative conditioning is not voluntary and is rejected by the adapter layer prior to admissibility evaluation.

6.23.9 Equivalence of Structural Formalisms

Throughout this work, Standing Algebra is analyzed using multiple formal languages, including:

partial orders and directed complete partial orders,

closure and interior operators,

constructive (Heyting) logic,

thin categorical structure,

Alexandrov topologies,

rewrite systems and normalization,

coordinationonly game forms,

and nonadditive capacity measures.

These are not independent extensions.

Theorem (EquivalenceofFormalisms)

All formal structures used in the development of Σᴿ are internally equivalent representations of the same underlying object.

In particular:

the partial order on admissible envelopes determines the Alexandrov topology,

the legitimacy closure operator determines the Heyting implication,

the rewrite system determines least fixed points but forbids greatest ones,

the thin category structure is equivalent to the envelope preorder,

and the gametheoretic and probabilistic characterizations are quotients over the same indistinguishability relations.

No formalism introduces additional expressive or normative power beyond the others.

Consequence

No viewpoint is privileged.
Choosing an ordertheoretic, topological, logical, or computational description is a matter of analysis, not authority.

This equivalence ensures that the system cannot be “extended by changing languages.

Proof.

The existence of nonbridgable admissibility components implies that some harms are structurally irreparable, not merely difficult or costly.

6.26.15 Homotopy Classes of Admissible Paths

Beyond connectivity, admissible paths may fall into distinct homotopy classes.

Definition 6.26.15.1 (Admissible Homotopy)

Two admissible paths are admissibly homotopic if there exists a continuous deformation between them that remains entirely within .

Theorem 6.26.15.2 (PathDependent Legitimacy)

Distinct homotopy classes of admissible paths may yield different legitimacy outcomes even when endpoints coincide.

Proof.
If two paths lie in different homotopy classes, no admissible deformation connects them. Thus intermediate states differ structurally, potentially violating admissibility constraints transiently. Legitimacy therefore depends on the path taken, not only the endpoint. ∎

6.26.16 New Capacity: Irreversible Coordination Patterns

The presence of nontrivial homotopy classes introduces irreversibility at the structural level.

Corollary 6.26.16.1 (Irreversible Admissibility)

There exist admissible transitions whose reversal is inadmissible, even if the endpoint state appears superficially similar.

This provides a formal basis for irreversible harm and nonundoable coordination failures.

6.26.17 Obstructions and Holes in Admissibility Space

Let contain a topological hole (e.g., nontrivial first homology group).

Theorem 6.26.17.1 (Topological Obstruction to Repair)

If contains a nontrivial topological obstruction, then certain admissible paths cannot be contracted to trivial paths without violating admissibility.

Proof.
Nontrivial homology implies the existence of loops that cannot be shrunk within the space. Any attempt to do so would exit , violating admissibility. ∎

6.26.18 New Capacity: Formal Explanation of Terminal States (Mathematical declaration of Independently Emergent Wrongs)

Topological obstructions explain why some states admit explanation but not repair.

Explanation in such cases is not a failure of will or policy, but a consequence of admissibility geometry. This explanation furnishes the mathematical framework for the existence of Independently Emergent Wrongs (IEWs). Independently Emergent Wrongs correspond to terminal states arising from nonbridgable topological obstructions in the admissibility space, where no admissible repair path exists despite full local compliance.

Theorem 6.26.19.1 (Upper Semicontinuity of Admissibility)

Admissibility predicates are uppersemicontinuous with respect to information refinement: additional information may reveal inadmissibility but cannot create admissibility.

Proof.
Refinement restricts open sets in the locale. Since admissibility corresponds to open predicates, refinement can only shrink the admissible region. ∎

6.29 NonDominating GameTheoretic Refinements of Legitimacy

(Derived; No New Commitments)

This section makes explicit the gametheoretic structure induced by Σᴿ when restricted to nondominating fragments of interaction theory. No new axioms are introduced. Classical game theory admits domination through payoff asymmetry, punishment strategies, equilibrium enforcement, and transferable utility. Σᴿ excludes these structures. What remains is a coordinationdriven, dominancefree interaction theory in which strategic reasoning is filtered by legitimacy rather than power.
