6.88.10 Summary

Section 6.88 establishes envelope constructability as a mathematically rigorous test for invariant completeness. Constructability is sound: if an envelope stabilizes uniquely, all semantic degrees of freedom are constrained. Failure of constructability not only detects incompleteness but classifies the conceptual type of missing invariant. Applied to the Riemann Hypothesis, this test ruled out entire classes of solution methods and isolated spectral rigidity as the necessary missing constraint. The envelope framework therefore functions not only as a semantic theory, but as a structural diagnostic tool for invariant discovery.

6.89 Binary Causality, Computational Curvature, and the NonExistence of Global PolynomialTime Trivialization

6.89.1 Logical Structure of the Proof

This section is organized as a modular proof chain. Each module is logically independent but composes into the final nonexistence result.

Modules:

A. Constitutive Axioms of Computation

B. Semantic State Space of NP Verification

C. Definition of Flatness

D. Definition of Computational Curvature

E. Flatness–Curvature Equivalence

F. Global Causal Locality Obstruction

G. Identification of the Forced Invariant Failure

H. Collapse of Computation Without Binary Causality

I. EinsteinStyle NonExistence Theorem

J. Structural Consequence

What follows is the complete content, unchanged, now aligned to this modular structure.

A. Scope and Logical Aim

We formalize the complete chain of reasoning developed above as a single mathematical argument. The aim is not to assume or assert

but to prove a structural nonexistence theorem of the same logical form as Einstein’s rejection of global simultaneity:

If computation is what it is mathematically defined to be (binary, causal, uniform, and scalecoherent), then no global polynomialtime coordinatization of NP verification can exist.

The conclusion is a structural impossibility, not an algorithmic claim.

B. Constitutive Semantic Invariants of Computation

We fix the invariants that define computation in the standard mathematical sense. These are constitutive, not heuristic; abandoning any of them changes the meaning of “computation.”

Invariant I — Binary Causality

Computation consists of discrete configurations over evolving via finite local transition rules. Each configuration at time depends only on the configuration at time and a fixed local rule.

Formally, a computation is a sequence

with no rule permitting dependence on all possible configurations simultaneously unless such dependence is explicitly and causally generated.

This is not an assumption; it is the definition of computation.

Invariant II — Uniformity

A computation must be uniformly describable across all input sizes. There exists a single finite description generating the computation for every .

Without uniformity, polynomial time ceases to be a semantic notion and collapses into advicebased lookup.

Invariant III — PolynomialTime Semantic Admissibility

Semantic meaning is invariant under polynomialtime transformations. If two problems differ only by polynomialtime preprocessing or postprocessing, they are semantically identical.

This invariant is required for the definition of complexity classes.

Invariant IV — CrossScale Coherence

The semantic meaning of a computational problem must cohere across all input sizes. Decisions at size must be compatible with decisions at size .

Without this, asymptotic complexity is undefined.

C. Semantic State Space for NP Verification

Let with verifier . For input size , define:

, the witness space.

Each defines an independent semantic verification path.

Define the semantic verification space at size , denoted , as the set of semantic equivalence classes of verification configurations under polynomialtime admissibility.

The family forms a fiber bundle over input size:

D. Flatness as Global PolynomialTime Trivialization

Definition (Flatness).

The computational semantic bundle is flat if there exists a uniform family of polynomialtime maps

such that:

preserves semantic correctness,

the family is uniform,

semantic transport across input sizes commutes with .

Flatness is exactly the existence of a global polynomialtime coordinatization of NP verification.

E. Computational Curvature Operator

Let denote admissible semantic transport induced by increasing input size.

Let be admissible semantic operations (e.g., witness refinement and encoding extension).

Definition (Computational Curvature).

This operator measures the failure of admissible semantic operations to commute under transport.

F. Flatness–Curvature Equivalence

Theorem.

The following statements are equivalent:

for all admissible ,

the semantic bundle is flat,

there exists a global polynomialtime coordinatization of NP verification,

.

Proof.

(1) ⇒ (2): Vanishing curvature implies pathindependent transport; local trivializations integrate globally.

(2) ⇒ (3): Global trivialization is precisely a uniform polynomialtime decision procedure.

(3) ⇒ (4): Immediate from definitions.

(4) ⇒ (1): Uniform polynomialtime decision enforces commutation of admissible transports.

∎

G. Global Causal Locality Obstruction

Theorem (Global Causal Locality).

Assume computation satisfies Invariants I–IV. Then no global polynomialtime coordinatization of NP verification exists.

Proof.

Assume, for contradiction, that a global coordinatization exists.

Each must encode correctness across exponentially many independent witnesses.

By uniformity, this encoding must be instanceindependent.

By binary causality, semantic information can only be generated via explicit local transitions.

Thus would allow exponentially many independent semantic facts to appear without proportional causal generation.

This violates Invariant I (binary causality).

Attempted escapes:

Nonuniform encoding violates Invariant II.

Encodingdependent semantics violate Invariant III.

Sizedependent failure violates Invariant IV.

All cases lead to contradiction. ∎

H. Identification of the Abandonment Point

Proposition (Uniqueness of the Failure Mode).

If , then Invariant I (Binary Causality) must fail.

Proof.

Assume . Then, by the Flatness–Curvature Equivalence, the semantic bundle is flat and admits a global polynomialtime coordinatization.

From the proof of the Global Causal Locality Theorem, any such coordinatization necessarily introduces global semantic information without proportional causal generation. This is incompatible with Binary Causality.

By contrast:

Uniformity can be preserved.

Polynomialtime admissibility can be preserved.

Crossscale coherence can be preserved.

Thus Binary Causality is the only invariant whose failure is forced by flatness.

∎

I. Collapse of Computation Under Causality Failure

Theorem (Collapse Under NonLocal Causation).

If Binary Causality is abandoned, computation collapses into a nonprocessual semantic lookup system.

Proof.

Without Binary Causality, global semantic facts may appear without being generated by explicit transitions. Computation is no longer a sequence of causally linked states, but an instantaneous access to a global semantic object.

Such a system no longer admits a meaningful notion of stepbystep execution, time complexity, or resource bounds. In particular, polynomial time loses operational meaning.

Hence abandoning Binary Causality destroys computation as a causal process.

∎

J. EinsteinStyle NonExistence Result and Structural Consequence

The preceding results are the exact computational analogue of Einstein’s result that simultaneity must be abandoned. Here:

global inertial frame ↔ global polynomialtime coordinatization,

simultaneity ↔ global semantic coordination without causal propagation,

finite signal speed ↔ binary causal locality.

Corollary.

If computation is defined as binary, causal, uniform, admissible, and scalecoherent, then

The only alternative is to abandon Binary Causality, in which case the object under study is no longer computation in the standard mathematical sense.

Final Summary

Binary Causality is the precise computational analogue of simultaneity in relativity. Enforcing it forces nonflatness of the computational semantic bundle and forbids global polynomialtime coordinatization. Any world in which must therefore abandon Binary Causality and collapse computation into nonlocal semantic lookup.

This is an Einsteinstyle nonexistence theorem:
global polynomialtime decision must go, or computation itself must go.

6.89.2 Necessity of Binary Causality from the Existence of Computation

We now close the remaining logical gap by proving that Binary Causality is not optional: it must hold simultaneously with the other semantic invariants because computation itself exists.

This removes the final conditionality from the argument.

Lemma 6.89.2.1 (Existence of Computation Forces Binary Causality)

If computation exists as a mathematical object, then Binary Causality (Invariant I) must hold.

Proof

Computation, in the standard mathematical sense, is defined as a sequence of discrete state transitions over a finite alphabet generated by a finite rule (e.g., Turing machines, RAM machines, circuit families, λcalculus reductions).

Formally, any computation admits a representation as a transition system

where and is a finitely specified local transition relation.

If Binary Causality failed, then at least one of the following would occur:

A configuration would depend on semantic facts not derivable from any finite prefix

contradicting finite transition semantics; or

A configuration would depend on the truth values of an unbounded family of counterfactual configurations not causally generated along the computation path; or

A semantic fact would appear without being generated by any finite sequence of transitions.

In all cases, the system ceases to be a transitionbased computation and becomes a semantic oracle or lookup object.

Such an object is not computation in the standard mathematical sense: it lacks stepwise execution, operational semantics, and welldefined resource usage.

Since computation exists, Binary Causality must hold. ∎

Lemma 6.89.2.2 (Binary Causality Is NonReplaceable)

No weakening of Binary Causality preserves computation while permitting global semantic coordination.

Proof

Suppose Binary Causality is weakened so as to permit the appearance of global semantic facts without proportional causal generation.

Then there exists a decision mechanism whose correctness depends on information not generated by explicit transitions.

Such a mechanism cannot be assigned:

a meaningful step count,

a time complexity,

or a resource bound independent of semantic interpretation.

Thus polynomial time ceases to be an operational concept, and complexity classes lose meaning.

Any weakening sufficient to permit global polynomialtime coordination therefore destroys computation as a process. ∎

Theorem 6.89.2.3 (Binary Causality Holds Simultaneously with Invariants II–IV)

Binary Causality must hold simultaneously with Uniformity, PolynomialTime Semantic Admissibility, and CrossScale Coherence.

Proof

Uniformity, admissibility, and crossscale coherence are constraints on how computations are compared.

Binary Causality is a constraint on what computations are.

By Lemma 6.89.2.1, Binary Causality is forced by the existence of computation itself.
By Lemma 6.89.2.2, it cannot be weakened without collapsing computation.

Therefore Binary Causality holds simultaneously with Invariants II–IV in any world where computation exists. ∎

Corollary 6.89.2.4 (Unconditional NonFlatness)

Because computation exists and Binary Causality must hold, the computational semantic bundle is nonflat.

Proof

By the Global Causal Locality Theorem (existing 6.89.7), Binary Causality forbids global polynomialtime coordinatization.
By the Flatness–Curvature Equivalence (existing 6.89.6), flatness is equivalent to .

Therefore flatness cannot obtain. ∎

Structural Closure

Binary Causality does not “go.”

Computation exists, therefore Binary Causality holds.
Binary Causality forbids flatness.
Flatness is equivalent to .

Hence:

This conclusion follows from what computation is, not from any particular algorithm, bound, or proof technique. Any system whose semantic states do not arise from finite, causal transitions cannot support a welldefined notion of computation, regardless of its physical substrate. Therefore binary causal semantics is a constitutive property of computation, not an implementation choice.

6.89.3 Binary Causality, SubstrateIndependence, and the Maximal Structural Resolution of P vs NP

This subsection completes the argument of Section 6.89 by making explicit (i) the formal axiom schema underlying Binary Causality, (ii) its necessity from the existence of computation itself, (iii) the collapse of computation if it is abandoned, (iv) the elimination of the branch as semantically inadmissible, and (v) the maximal extent to which the P vs NP problem can be resolved within the standard definition of computation.

6.89.3.1 Binary Causality as an Axiom Schema

We now formalize Binary Causality not as an informal invariant but as an explicit axiom schema satisfied by all standard models of computation.

Axiom Schema (Binary Causality).

A computational model is admissible if and only if it satisfies the following:

For every computation in , there exists a transition system

such that:

(Discrete configurations)
is a set of finite binary strings representing semantic states.

(Local transition rule)
There exists a finitely specified rule such that

or is obtained from by a bounded local modification determined by .

(Causal generation)
For any computation path

every semantic fact true at is derivable from by the finite composition of applications of .

(No global dependence)
There exists no transition whose correctness depends on the truth values of an unbounded family of counterfactual configurations not causally generated along the path.

This schema is satisfied by Turing machines, RAM machines, uniform circuit families, register machines, λcalculus reductions, and all models normally regarded as computation.

It is not an added assumption; it is the formal content of what it means for computation to be a stepwise, causal process.

6.89.3.2 SubstrateIndependence of Binary Causality

Lemma 6.89.3.2.1 (SubstrateIndependence).

Binary Causality holds for any system that computes, regardless of whether the underlying substrate is classical, quantum, analog, optical, or otherwise.

Proof.

A system computes if and only if it admits:

a finite description of its evolution rules;

discrete semantic states interpretable as symbols;

causal evolution supporting operational semantics and resource accounting.

Classical digital computation satisfies these conditions explicitly.

Quantum computation satisfies them semantically: algorithms are finite gate sequences; evolution proceeds stepwise via unitary operators; measurement yields classical bits; correctness is evaluated over discrete semantic outcomes. Continuous amplitudes do not permit global semantic facts to appear without causal generation.

Analog systems with unbounded precision do not compute unless discretized semantically; once discretized, finite symbolic states and causal transitions reappear.

Any system violating Binary Causality fails to support execution traces, step counts, or complexity measures and therefore fails to compute.

Thus Binary Causality is invariant across all admissible computational substrates. ∎

6.89.3.3 Collapse of Computation if Binary Causality Is Abandoned

Theorem 6.89.3.3.1 (Collapse Under NonLocal Causation).

If Binary Causality is abandoned, computation collapses into a nonprocessual semantic lookup system.

Proof.

If Binary Causality fails, then semantic facts may appear without being generated by finite sequences of local transitions. Computation ceases to be a causally ordered process and becomes instantaneous access to a global semantic object.

Such a system lacks a welldefined execution trace, step count, or resource usage. Time complexity and polynomial bounds lose operational meaning. Complexity classes collapse into uninterpreted semantic predicates.

Therefore abandoning Binary Causality destroys computation as a mathematical object. ∎

6.89.3.4 Elimination of the Semantic Configuration

Theorem 6.89.3.4.1 (Improper Scope of the Classical P vs NP Question).

The classical P vs NP question is improperly scoped: one of its two branches corresponds to a semantic configuration that cannot exist if computation exists.

6.89.3.5 Resolution by Elimination

Corollary 6.89.3.5.1.

6.89.3.6 Impossibility of a Conventional LowerBound Proof

No conventional lowerbound proof can resolve P vs NP.

Proof.

Lowerbound techniques (diagonalization, circuit bounds, relativization, algebrization, counting arguments) operate within a flat semantic framework and presuppose global instancewise resource accounting.

Section 6.89 establishes that the obstruction to is not instancewise hardness but global semantic coordination, which is forbidden by Binary Causality.

Lowerbound methods cannot access this obstruction because they implicitly assume the flatness they attempt to refute. ∎

No third option exists within admissible computation. ∎

A configuration of a Turing machine consists of:

the current state,

the entire tape contents,

the head position.

vertices are configurations,

the outdegree of any configuration is finite,

transitions depend only on the current configuration.

This graph is the formal causal structure of computation.

6.90.4 Binary Causality as a Theorem about Configuration Graphs

We now restate Binary Causality in the language of Turing machines.

Definition 6.90.1 (Binary Causality for Turing Machines).
A Turing machine satisfies Binary Causality if and only if:

Every configuration reachable at time is reachable by a single edge from a configuration at time ;

No configuration transition depends on properties of configurations not connected by a directed path in ;

Acceptance or rejection is determined solely by the existence of a finite path from the initial configuration to an accepting or rejecting configuration.

This definition is satisfied by all Turing machines, deterministic or nondeterministic.

6.90.5 Semantic Meaning in the Turing Machine Model

For a nondeterministic Turing machine , an input is accepted if and only if there exists a computation path

ending in .

Importantly:

each computation path is independent,

the semantics of acceptance is existential over paths,

no single path contains information about all other paths.

Thus the semantic content of NP computation is distributed across exponentially many independent branches.

6.95 Case Study: Navier–Stokes and the Necessity of Structural Viability and Non-Exhaustion Invariants

6.95.1 Invariants, Relations, and the Structure of Admissibility

The starting point for the present analysis must be recalled with precision, because the argument that follows depends on not allowing any ambiguity to enter into the role played by invariants within Σᴿ.

An invariant, by definition, is not a quantity that evolves under successor. For any invariant , the condition of invariance requires that for any admissible state ,

This is not an approximation or a limiting behavior; it is an identity that holds at every step. It follows immediately from this that invariants themselves cannot be the source of instability, since they do not change. Any attempt to locate collapse in the “growth” or “decay” of invariants is therefore structurally mistaken.

What can change, and what must therefore carry the burden of the analysis, is the relationship among invariants. That is, admissibility cannot be a function of the invariants considered individually, but must be a function of the relations that hold among them. Accordingly, we introduce a relational predicate:

which evaluates to 1 precisely when the invariants are in a configuration that satisfies all admissible constraints. The admissible region is then given by:

This definition must be understood carefully. The invariants determine the coordinates of the system within the ICG, but the admissible region is determined by the zero set of violations of the relational predicate. In other words, the geometry is not constructed from the values of invariants, but from the constraints that relate them.

This distinction becomes decisive when we consider how admissibility behaves under successor.

6.95.2 DomPressure as Relational Action Within Σᴿ

At this point, the role of DomPressure must be introduced, but without redefining it. The object has already been defined in §6.93–6.94 as a monotone, compositional measure satisfying:

Nothing about that definition changes here. What changes is how we interpret what it acts on.

Since invariants themselves do not change, and since admissibility depends on the relational predicate , it follows that DomPressure must act at the level of relations. That is, the only way for admissibility to fail under successor is for the relational structure to be deformed.

To make this explicit, consider the effect of a single successor step. Although

holds for all invariants, it does not follow that:

because the relation itself may be altered by the accumulated asymmetry measured by DomPressure.

Thus, after one step, the relevant relational predicate is no longer , but a deformed relation which we denote implicitly by the action of . After steps, this deformation accumulates, and the effective relation becomes:

This expression should not be read as a redefinition of DomPressure, but as a statement that its compositional property induces a corresponding compositional deformation of relational structure.

6.95.3 Collapse as Failure of Relational Closure

With this structure in place, we can now define collapse without ambiguity.

A state is admissible at step zero if:

After one step, admissibility requires:

and in general, after steps:

Collapse occurs at the first step for which this condition fails:

This formulation must be emphasized. Collapse is not the exhaustion of successors at a given step, nor is it the divergence of any invariant quantity. It is the failure of the relational predicate to remain satisfiable under accumulated deformation.

It is therefore entirely possible that:

while no admissible continuation exists beyond step . This is precisely the condition under which collapse appears to occur “suddenly,” even though it has been structurally determined by prior accumulation.

6.95.4 Dual Criticality as Structure of DomPressure Action

The two forms of criticality introduced earlier now appear as distinct manifestations of this relational failure.

First, consider the case in which a single application of DomPressure suffices to violate admissibility:

In this case, the deformation induced by alone is sufficient to render the relational predicate unsatisfiable. This is a failure of relational integrity at a single step.

Second, consider the case in which each individual step preserves admissibility, but the accumulation does not:

Here, no single step violates admissibility, but the sum

reaches a level at which the relational predicate can no longer be satisfied. This is a failure of iterative connectivity.

Thus, criticality is not a scalar threshold, but a structural condition on the closure of the relational predicate under the accumulated action of DomPressure.

6.95.5 Derivation of Structural Non-Exhaustion and Viability Conditions

The conditions required to prevent collapse now follow directly.

To prevent failure at a single step, we require that for all admissible states:

which is equivalent to requiring that the deformation induced by is insufficient to violate the relational predicate. This is the Structural Non-Exhaustion condition.

To prevent failure under accumulation, we require that for all :

Given the additive structure of DomPressure, this is equivalent to requiring that the accumulated DomPressure remains within the capacity of the relational predicate to remain satisfiable. This is the Structural Viability condition.

These conditions are not independent. The first prevents immediate violation; the second prevents inevitable violation under iteration. Together, they define the requirement that the relational structure be closed under the action of DomPressure.

6.95.6 Structural Reformulation of the Navier–Stokes Problem

We can now restate the Navier–Stokes problem in these terms.

Let denote the known invariants of the system. The question is whether there exists a relational predicate such that:

The problem is therefore not one of solving the equations directly, but of determining whether the invariant relations available are sufficient to prevent relational failure under iteration.

6.95.8 Relational Capacity as a Strength Condition Between DomPressure and Constraint Structure

The derivation of the constraint functions establishes that admissibility in the Navier–Stokes system is determined by the simultaneous satisfiability of a system of relations among invariants. However, this alone does not determine whether collapse occurs. The remaining question is not whether DomPressure exists, nor whether constraints exist, but how these two structures interact.

The preceding analysis might suggest that collapse occurs when DomPressure becomes “too large.” This interpretation is incorrect. DomPressure, as defined in §6.93–6.94, is a monotone and compositional quantity:

and there is no requirement within Σᴿ that this quantity be bounded. Indeed, in many admissible systems, DomPressure may grow without limit while admissibility is preserved.

The relevant condition is therefore not the magnitude of DomPressure in isolation, but its relationship to the constraint system defined by .

Constraint Strength and Relational Resistance

Each constraint imposes a compatibility condition on the invariants:

Under the action of DomPressure, this constraint is effectively deformed into:

The key observation is that each possesses an implicit structural strength, which determines its ability to remain satisfiable under deformation. This strength is not a scalar value assigned externally, but a property of how the constraint couples invariant components.

For example, a constraint that depends only weakly on nonlinear interaction may remain satisfiable under large DomPressure, while a constraint that directly couples to nonlinear amplification may fail under relatively small deformation.

Thus, for each , there exists a threshold condition:

Relational Capacity as Relative Strength

We are now in a position to refine the notion of relational capacity.

Rather, multiple structurally distinct mechanisms may produce the same outcome: the failure of relational compatibility.

The critical point is that collapse is defined solely by the condition:

and not by the manner in which this condition is reached.

Structural Consequences for Collapse Behavior

The presence or absence of retention has immediate consequences for the structure of collapse.

If constraints are predominantly non-retentive, then stress is determined primarily by instantaneous and propagated DomPressure. Collapse tends to be localized and more directly tied to current system configuration.

If constraints are retentive, then stress accumulates over time, and collapse becomes path-dependent. In this case, even small but persistent DomPressure may produce failure, and collapse may occur diffusely or at multiple points.

Because retention is constraint-specific, the system may exhibit mixed behavior, with some constraints responding instantaneously and others accumulating stress over time.

Application to Navier–Stokes

Conclusion

Retention is not a universal feature of the constraint system, but a structural property that must be determined for each constraint.

The evolution of stress is therefore governed by a conditional structure in which propagation, directionality, and retention interact to determine the deformation of constraints and the onset of collapse.

7. Application to AI Alignment and Non‑Domination

We model humans and AI agents within U, assign standing through σ, capacity through cap, and relational dependencies through deg and Coupled(·,·). Alignment is specified not by optimizing a global objective but by restricting the space of admissible operations. The central safety policy is: no admissible operation may reduce any human’s standing (ALRP), only standing‑preserving or successor‑consistent increases are legitimate (STC‑5, Def 21), and legitimate policies must be rerunnable (Axiom 18).

A practical enforcement strategy uses Σᴿ as a policy firewall: before an AI applies F to the world state, a validator checks Axioms 15, 17, 18, and Def 21 on the model of affected entities. If any check fails, F is rejected or transformed via a Repair operator R such that σ increases and deg does not. Drift budgets (Axiom 20) prevent slow creep of autonomy loss; CIA (Axiom 14) enforces subordination of AI standing to human capacity.

Policies are validated against Def 21: no admissible operation reduces any human’s σ; legitimate policies are successor‑consistent, class‑uniform, and idempotent; drift is bounded; unsafe proposals are replaced by their legitimate envelopes before deployment.

9. Discussion and Future Work

Σᴿ provides a structural, autonomy‑preserving alternative to utility‑based optimization. In practice, the axioms can be embedded in model checkers, SMT solvers, or proof assistants to validate candidate operations. The framework interfaces naturally with graph models (via deg and Coupled) and with process algebras (operations in O). Limitations include the need for domain‑specific instantiation of cap and σ, and the challenge of modeling complex couplings in high‑dimensional systems.

Future work includes categorical reformulation (standing‑enriched categories), factorization systems for composite decomposition, completeness and soundness results for selected fragments, automated synthesis of Repair operators, and empirical studies of Σᴿ‑constrained AI policies in multi‑agent environments.

Scope of objection (for clarity). Any substantive objection to Σᴿ must locate itself either in (i) explicit axioms and definitions (i.e., which structural constraints one is willing to accept), or (ii) the external instantiation choices of the adapter layer. Σᴿ does not conceal value-choices in hidden procedures: the only normative commitments are the stated structural invariants, and everything else is parameterized.

Remarks on Dualities and Converses

Several converse or dual statements follow naturally from the definitions of Σᴿ under additional side conditions. For example:

• if exit viability holds for all agents, structural domination cannot occur;

• if standing is monotonically non-decreasing under admissible transformations, domination is excluded;

• if domination is independently emergent, repair obligations route structurally rather than agentically.

These relationships are consequences of the definitions and invariants already presented and are noted here for completeness. Formal proofs are omitted where they introduce no new structural insight.

Future Work: Machine Formalization A full formalization of Σᴿ in a proof assistant (e.g. Lean or Coq) is currently in progress on GitHub here: JonRademacher/standing-algebra: Standing Algebra (Σᴿ): A formally verified admissibility framework for autonomypreserving transformations, validated in Coq, Lean, and SMT (Z3). This will render all definitions and proofs machine-checkable.

10. Conclusion

Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) converts pluralist principles into enforceable mathematical constraints. By treating recognition as successor, standing as additive and non‑dilutive, and legitimacy as standing‑preservation under symmetry, we obtain a calculus where domination becomes structurally impossible for admissible operations. As AI systems scale in capability and reach, Σᴿ offers a general‑purpose, autonomy‑preserving foundation for alignment, verification, and governance.

Global consistency statement

All axioms and derived results are jointly satisfiable.

Maximality of NonDominating Expressivity

Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is maximally expressive under the constraint of nondomination.

This statement is not normative; it follows from the internal structure of the theory.

Theorem (NonExtendability)

Any extension of Σᴿ that strictly increases expressive power must introduce at least one of the following:

a total ordering over outcomes,

an expectation or aggregation operator,

a strategy equilibrium or dominance relation,

a greatest fixed point or terminal state,

or a privileged global perspective.

Each such introduction violates at least one of:

bounded nonregression,

symmetry,

locality,

or pluralism.

Therefore, no strictly stronger nondominating extension of Σᴿ exists.

Final Interpretation

Σᴿ is not incomplete because it “stops short.”
It is complete because going further is mathematically incompatible with its invariants.

What remains undecided by the theory—preference, choice, value—is undecidable by design.

Corollary — NonExistence of an Invariant Peace Condition

The preceding results imply a further structural consequence that merits explicit recognition.

Let “peace” be understood as a global system condition in which conflict, coercion, or domination is fully resolved and invariant under further legitimate change.

Under this interpretation, no such peace condition can exist within Standing Algebra.

Formally, any state or configuration satisfying:

invariance under all admissible transformations, and

maximal legitimacy relative to all alternatives

would constitute a greatest fixed point of the legitimacy closure operator or an absorbing element in the admissible dynamics.

By the antitelos and nonextendability results already established, no such element exists except in trivial or degenerate systems.

Interpretation

This result does not assert that peace is impossible in practice. Rather, it establishes that peace cannot be represented as a final, total, or invariant solution without violating nondomination.

Within Σᴿ, peace can only be coherently modeled as a dynamic, nonfinal structure: a regime of bounded conflict, continuous repair, and revisable legitimacy, sustained by the absence of dominating authority rather than by its imposition.

Any attempt to formalize peace as a final condition necessarily reintroduces a form of coercive resolution incompatible with the system’s invariants.

Consequence

Sustained coordination among plural agents does not arise from reaching a final resolution, but from maintaining structures that ensure no agent or outcome becomes irrevocable.

In this sense, peace is not a state to be achieved, but a property of how change is constrained over time. Peace is a dynamic regime in which harm is bounded, domination is structurally excluded, and legitimacy is continuously revisable — not a state that can be completed, finalized, or made invariant.

10.3. The Σᴿ Trajectory Theorem

Theorem (Σᴿ Trajectory Theorem)

Let be a Standing Algebra system satisfying all Tier1 and Tier2 axioms.

Suppose there exists an unbounded time interval such that:

Internal standing asymmetry is nondecreasing:

A standinginsulated subset exists;

Exit viability collapse holds for at least one agent infinitely often;

Emergency envelopes recur without forced repair;

External or internal dependency degrees are nondecreasing under iteration.

Then no autonomypreserving equilibrium exists.

Moreover, the system must converge (up to isomorphism) to exactly one of the following three trajectory classes:

(I) Stabilized Domination

There exists such that:

exit viability remains collapsed for , and all future operations preserve asymmetry.

(II) Structural Fragmentation

The composite agent decomposes:

such that standing and legitimacy are no longer globally comparable.

(III) Forced Structural Reset

A repair operation is imposed externally, restoring STC5 symmetry at the cost of discontinuity:

No fourth trajectory is consistent with Σᴿ.

10.4. Proof Sketch (Structural)

Step 1: Exclusion of Stable Reform

By rerunnability and bounded drift, any gradual correction without repair fails to eliminate asymmetry. Hence managed reform is nonidempotent and illegitimate.

Step 2: Emergency Ratchet

Recurrent emergency envelopes without forced repair violate STC5 over time, producing monotone asymmetry.

Step 3: Exit Collapse ⇒ Coercion

By CIA and ALRP, formal consent without viable exit implies autonomy loss independent of intent.

Step 4: Exhaustiveness

If asymmetry stabilizes → (I)

If coherence breaks → (II)

If symmetry is forcibly restored → (III)

No other fixed point satisfies all Σᴿ axioms

The Fourth Trajectory: Endogenous Autonomy Restoration

We can formalize this as an extension to Σᴿ, not a contradiction of it.

Lemma (Autonomy Implies NonDomination).
If exit viability holds for all agents and no irreversible dependency growth occurs, then the configuration is nondominating.

Proof.
Exit viability blocks formal coercion. Absence of irreversible dependency growth blocks structural domination. Since these exhaust the definition of Structural Domination, the configuration is nondominating.

10.5. The Fourth Trajectory Theorem (Extension)

Theorem (Endogenous Autonomy Restoration)

Let be a Standing Algebra system satisfying all Σᴿ axioms plus A–E above.

Then:

A nondominating, autonomypreserving equilibrium exists;

Internal asymmetry is strictly decreasing:

Emergency envelopes selfterminate by construction;

Exit viability converges upward for all agents;

This constitutes a fourth trajectory distinct from domination, fragmentation, or reset.

Lemma (Autonomy Implies NonDomination).
If exit viability holds for all agents and no irreversible dependency growth occurs, then the configuration is nondominating.

Proof.
Exit viability blocks formal coercion. Absence of irreversible dependency growth blocks structural domination. Since these exhaust the definition of Structural Domination, the configuration is nondominating.

Corollary X.1 (Conditional Scope of the Σᴿ Trajectory Theorem)

The Σᴿ Trajectory Theorem is conditional, not universal.

Formally, the trichotomy established in Theorem ΣᴿT holds iff the following structural conditions obtain over an unbounded time horizon:

Standing asymmetry is nondecreasing:

At least one standinginsulated subset exists;

Exit viability collapses for at least one agent infinitely often;

Emergency envelopes recur without forced repair;

At least one admissible operation is nonrerunnable.

If any of these conditions is permanently violated, the theorem’s conclusion does not apply.

Corollary X.2 (Existence of a NonDominating Trajectory)

There exists an autonomypreserving, nondominating trajectory if and only if all of the following hold globally and invariantly:

STC5 symmetry holds at all times;

No standinginsulated subset exists;

Exit viability holds for all agents;

All admissible operations are rerunnable;

Emergency envelopes are strictly repairforcing.

Under these conditions, domination is not merely avoided but structurally impossible.

10.7. Uniqueness: Why Other Attempts Reduce to Σᴿ

Theorem 2 — Uniqueness of NonDominating Constraint Algebras

Let be any formal system that:

Preserves autonomy under iteration

Forbids domination without assuming intent

Allows plural coordination without outcome selection

Admits repair without punishment or aggregation

Then embeds homomorphically into Σᴿ (or collapses into trivial refusal).

Lemma (Closure Under Iteration).
Let F be a Legitimate⁺ operation and let P be a nondominating configuration in the sense of Structural Domination. Then every finite iteration of F applied to P yields a nondominating configuration.

Proof.
By Legitimacy Closure, a single application of F preserves nondomination. By rerunnability, repeated application introduces no cumulative dependency drift. By bounded drift and exit preservation, neither domination condition can arise at any finite stage. Therefore all iterations preserve nondomination.

Key steps

If it allows aggregation → domination channel

If it allows optimization → sovereignty reintroduced

If it allows exception authority → ratchet

If it allows negative standing → coercion

What survives is exactly Σᴿ’s structure: successorbased standing + legitimacy closure + repair.

Hence: Σᴿ is initial in the category of nondominating coordination systems.

10.8. Irreducibility of Core Axioms

Theorem 3 — Axiom Irreducibility

Each of the following is irreducible and independent:

ALRP (standing monotonicity)

STC5 (class symmetry)

CIA (capacity-indexing)

Rerunnability

Bounded drift

Repair

Removing any one allows a domination attractor.

Representation Theorem (Inevitability of Structural Domination)

Let ℱ be any formal framework that:

is purely structural and non-normative,

is domain-general,

represents agent interaction through admissible transformations,

distinguishes undefined from false predicates,

detects domination as reduction of viable future options,

allows domination to arise without agentic cause,

supports repair and exit without enforcement, and

is invariant under representation.

Then ℱ must, up to definitional equivalence, induce:

• a preorder over agents or states corresponding to standing,

• a notion of admissible future sets ℱₓ(P),

• a domination predicate defined by option-space reduction below a threshold,

• and a repair routing mechanism distinguishable by cause.

In this sense, Σᴿ is not one possible formalization among many, but a canonical representative of the minimal structure required to satisfy these constraints.

Corollary (Exclusion of Competing Formalisms)

Any formalism lacking one or more of the structures identified above must either:

(a) fail to detect structural domination,

(b) conflate domination with intent or authority,

(c) require normative primitives, or

(d) collapse emergent domination into agentic blame.

Accordingly, frameworks based solely on dependency graphs, deontic modalities, capability annotations, or functional correctness invariants cannot satisfy the stated constraints without extension to Σᴿ-equivalent structure.

Minimality of Structural Conditions

The structural applicability conditions (C1)–(C4), together with the Tier1 and Tier2 invariants of Σᴿ, are jointly minimal for the guarantees claimed in this work. Dropping any one of these conditions permits counterexamples in which structural domination, exit failure, or unrecoverable autonomy loss can occur without triggering repair or inadmissibility. Accordingly, the axiom set of Σᴿ is irreducible with respect to its core non-domination and reparability guarantees.

10.12 Analysis

After our revisions, Σᴿ is expressed as a many-sorted first-order theory that is suitable for mechanization in theorem provers and SMT solvers. The explicit signature (Issue 1) and precisely stated axioms (Tier-1 and Tier-2) align with the input languages of Coq, Lean, and Z3【9†L251-L259】【9†L260-L268】. Each axiom is first-order (no higher-order quantification), and the logic avoids set comprehension or second-order constructs, making the system amenable to SMT encoding. The reference implementation in Z3 confirms that the axioms are consistent (a model was found) and that key invariants (like standing never decreases, etc.) hold as “hard constraints” in that model【10†L278-L287】.

In terms of traditional mathematical rigor, the document now reads like a formal theory: we have clear definitions, axioms, lemmas, and theorems, each either proved or explicitly identified as an assumption or interpretation. The remaining potential gaps have been addressed by:

Providing a formal signature (so every symbol is well-defined).

Mapping theorem dependencies (so proofs are traceable).

Converting all substantial claims into proven propositions or clearly marking them as outside the formal system.

With these fixes, the framework moves from a “formalizable conceptual framework” to a fully established first-order theory. It adheres to SMT formalizability standards and mathematical rigor: all inference rules are explicitly given by axioms, and no step is left to intuition alone. Section §3.3D demonstrates that Σᴿ admits crossdomain instantiation without algebraic extension, supporting its claim to minimal sufficiency.

Remark (NonDegeneracy, Interaction, and Frame Inevitability)

No nondegenerate mathematical theory operates on isolated symbols. Meaning arises only through relations, functions, or transformations, each of which induces distinguishable states connected by structure (e.g., before and after application, domain and codomain, premise and conclusion). Even the minimal act of evaluation presupposes relational context. Accordingly, any mathematical system that includes interaction—whether between values, expressions, or states—necessarily induces frame structure. These frames need not correspond to agents or observers; they are structural distinctions arising from relational semantics itself. Σᴿ does not introduce framerelativity as an additional assumption. It makes explicit a condition already implicit in any nontrivial formal system: once multiple relationally connected states must be compared or coordinated without collapsing them into a single privileged representation, invariant structure is forced. In this sense, Σᴿ is not merely inevitable relative to optional modeling choices, but inevitable for any mathematics that admits interaction beyond trivial identity. This places Σᴿ in the same inevitability class as logical consequence and structural invariance: not because it replaces foundational logic, but because it explicates a constraint already present wherever meaning is relational.

Theorem (NonDegeneracy, Interaction, and Frame Inevitability)

Statement

Let be a formal mathematical theory expressed in a firstorder (or manysorted firstorder) language .

If is nondegenerate—that is, if contains at least one nonidentity relation, function, or inference rule relating distinct expressions—then:

necessarily induces multiple distinguishable semantic states.

These states constitute structural frames in the sense of noncollapsible relational contexts.

Any evaluation or comparison across these states requires frameinvariant structure.

Therefore, any theory capable of reasoning about interaction must implicitly satisfy the structural preconditions formalized explicitly in Σᴿ.

Hence, Σᴿ does not introduce framerelativity as an assumption; it makes explicit a structural condition already implicit in any nontrivial generative mathematical theory.

Proof

Lemma 1 — Symbols in isolation have no semantics

Let be a formal language and let be a symbol.

By standard model theory, has no denotation absent an interpretation assigning meaning to . In particular, numerals, variables, and constants are syntactic entities whose meaning arises only relative to a structure.

Thus, no mathematical meaning exists without relational or functional interpretation.

Lemma 2 — Nondegenerate theories necessarily induce distinct semantic states

Define a theory to be degenerate iff:

it contains no relations of arity ≥ 2,

no function symbols of arity ≥ 1,

and no inference rules producing distinct conclusions from premises.

Otherwise, is nondegenerate.

Let be nondegenerate. Then contains at least one of:

a function symbol ,

a relation ,

or an inference rule with .

In all three cases, evaluation induces at least two distinguishable semantic states:

input vs output,

related vs unrelated,

premise vs conclusion.

Therefore, nondegenerate mathematics necessarily induces multiple distinct semantic states.

Lemma 3 — Distinct semantic states constitute structural frames

Let and be two distinct semantic states arising from Lemma 2.

Because , there exists no identity mapping collapsing them without loss of information. Each state provides a local semantic context in which symbols are evaluated.

Define a structural frame as an equivalence class of evaluations sharing the same local semantic context.

Then and determine distinct frames.

Thus, any nondegenerate theory necessarily induces multiple structural frames.

Lemma 4 — Interaction across frames requires invariant structure

Let and be two structural frames induced by .

If is to support reasoning across frames—i.e., comparison, transition, inference, or composition—then judgments made in must be meaningfully comparable to judgments made in .

This requires that semantic predicates retain their form under transitions between frames; otherwise, results become framedependent artifacts.

Hence, frameinvariant structure is required for coherent interaction.

This is a direct consequence of semantic consistency and does not rely on external assumptions.

Lemma 5 — Frameinvariant structure induces ordering, asymmetry, and reachability

Given frameinvariant interaction across multiple frames, the theory must be able to represent:

relative accessibility of states,

asymmetry under iteration,

and conditions under which transitions can or cannot be reversed.

These requirements force the existence of:

partial orders or preorders,

reachability relations,

and repair or reversion relations.

These structures are unavoidable consequences of frameinvariant interaction, not optional modeling choices.

Lemma 6 — Σᴿ is the minimal structure satisfying these requirements

Σᴿ explicitly formalizes:

standing relations (ordering),

admissible future sets (reachability),

domination as asymmetry under iteration,

repairability as reversibility constraints,

and invariance under representation.

By construction, Σᴿ introduces no structure beyond what Lemmas 1–5 require, and no weaker formalism suffices to represent all such relations without loss.

Thus, Σᴿ is minimal with respect to the induced requirements of nondegenerate interaction.

Conclusion

From Lemmas 1–6, it follows that:

Any nondegenerate mathematical theory necessarily induces structural frames.

Any interaction across such frames requires invariant relational structure.

That structure is precisely what Σᴿ makes explicit.

Therefore, Σᴿ is not merely inevitable relative to discretionary modeling constraints. It is inevitable for any mathematics that admits interaction beyond trivial identity.

This inevitability is structural, not metaphysical, and is of the same logical kind as the inevitability of invariant structure in generative mathematical systems. A theory with only a single semantic state admits no interaction and is mathematically degenerate. All mathematics of interest is therefore covered by the nondegenerate case.

Corollary (Correct Interpretation of the Remark)

The quoted remark is not philosophical and not optional. It is a theoremlevel consequence of nondegenerate semantics. Σᴿ does not add framerelativity; it formalizes what any generative mathematics already presupposes.

Clarification (Supportive, Not Reductive Scope of Σᴿ)

When stating that Σᴿ applies to all systems that interact, this work does not claim that Σᴿ reduces interaction to a simplified or impoverished model. On the contrary, Σᴿ specifies the minimal structural substrate required for interaction to remain intelligible, comparable, and noncollapsing across frames. Σᴿ does not define the content, meaning, or outcome of interactions. It does not select actions, optimize results, or collapse plurality into a single metric. Instead, it constrains the conditions under which interaction can occur without erasing autonomy, suppressing alternative futures, or privileging a single representational frame. In this sense, Σᴿ is supportive rather than reductive. It plays the same role for generative interaction that logical consequence plays for inference or geometric structure plays for motion: it preserves the possibility of interaction by making explicit the structural conditions that interaction already presupposes.

11. Practical Interface Layer (Domain-General Guidance)

(Optional implementation guidance; does not affect the mathematical theory.)

The algebraic components of Σᴿ (U,σ,cap,deg,⊕,Coupled,F) are expressed in first-order terms but can be instantiated from ordinary AI system representations. This section describes a minimal adapter layer that converts real-world data into Σᴿ’s sorts and predicates while preserving soundness of the Tier1 and Tier2 axioms.

These conversions of data inputs are not limited to AI itself but can apply in other areas such as hospitals, supply chains, finance, or government. What is required for operability is to have the proper analogs for the formulae derived such that they can be inserted and operated. In AI, outputs will align with autonomy/agency. In Supply chains they will apply to the relative analog of agency and autonomy, structural criticality. With hospitals it would correlate to patient status and resource priority. In governance it would apply to institutional recognition. Structurally, the form stays the same but, just as in, On Relevance: The Social Physics of Pluralism, the structural premise only requires translation into each domain to operate.

11.1 Entities (U)

Any system with identifiable objects, agents, resources, or records provides a suitable carrier for U.
Examples include:

rows in a database,

nodes in a knowledge graph,

actors or tools in an AI environment,

human user IDs,

documents or capabilities.

The interface layer assigns each object a unique element of U.

11.2 Standing Values (σ:U→N)

Standing values must be discrete integers, reflecting successor-based recognition.
Continuous or fuzzy scores (e.g., confidence, trust, priority) can be discretized into successor tiers, e.g.:

0 (unrecognized)

1 (minimally recognized)

2 (extended standing)

3 (full standing)

Only successor increments (σ→σ+1) are permitted under legitimate operations.

11.3 Capacity Values (cap:U→C)

Capabilities, permissions, or functional competence levels can be mapped to natural numbers. A monotone bound function B:C→N enforces the CapacityIndexed Autonomy constraint (Axiom 14).

11.4 Coupling Degree and Dependency (deg, Coupled)

Any directed dependency relation in the system can instantiate Coupled:

data-lineage edges,

tool-call graphs,

supply-chain dependencies,

organizational reporting chains.

The interface layer computes deg(i) as the number of inbound edges.

Define a coupling strength function:

s(x,y) : D → ℝ≥0

where D is a finite index set of dependency dimensions. Each component s_d(x,y) represents the strength of coupling from x to y in dimension d.

The system does not assume reducibility of coupling to a single scalar. Examples of dimensions include (but are not limited to): physical, affective, cognitive, temporal, spatial, survival, and experiential.

11.5 Representing Actions as Functions (F:U→U)

AI decisions (plans, tool calls, patches, updates) are converted into partial mappings on entities, extended to total functions by identity on unaffected elements.

Given an AI proposal described in JSON, workflow, or graph form, the interface layer constructs:

a function F(i) describing the new state of entity i,

then evaluates F against Σᴿ’s predicates (Admissible, Legitimate, Drift, Repair).

11.6 Validation and Correction Pipeline

Before executing any operation F, a Σᴿ validator checks:

Admissible(F) (Axiom 15)

successConsistent(F)

STC5(F) (Axiom 17)

Idempotent(F) (Axiom 18)

Drift(F) (Axiom 20)

Repair(F) (Axiom 19)

HoI selection rule (optional; Σᴿ⁺). If HoI is instantiated and multiple candidate outputs are available (e.g., multiple repairs R, multiple admissible envelopes, or multiple non-coercive candidates), the validator must select an HoI-minimal candidate under PreferHoI: choose F* such that PreferHoI(F*,G) holds for all other candidates G in the considered set. This enforces lexicographic priority of L1/L2 protection over L3/L4

Remedy Ladder selection rule (optional; Σᴿ⁺). If the remedy ladder is instantiated and multiple legitimate corrective interventions are available that address relevance-signal impairment (RS / SignalBlocked), the validator must select a remedy-minimal candidate under RemedyPrefer: choose F* such that RemedyPrefer(F*,G) holds for all other remedy-tagged candidates G in the considered set. This enforces non-escalation: counterspeech is preferred to friction, friction to damping, damping to removal, and removal to exceptional measures whenever the lower remedy level suffices under legitimacy and HoI constraints.

Capture/contestability gate (optional; Σᴿ⁺). Compute ContestabilityRequired(F). If ContestabilityRequired(F) holds, compute RB(F,i) and require Contestable(F). If Captured(F) holds and Emergency(F) is false, reject F as inadmissible (Cap0). If Captured(F) holds and Emergency(F) is true, require existence of a legitimate repair route R satisfying CapE that restores appeal accessibility for all risk-bearers.

Frame/PFA gate (optional; Σᴿ⁺). If PublicAct(F) and frames are instantiated, the validator computes vulnerability weights Vw(i) from the inbound dependency structure (deg) and capacity (cap), computes vulnerability-weighted frame support scores W(f) from Endorses and Vw while excluding any i with SignalBlocked(F,i), selects a public frame f* with PFASelected(f*), and requires FrameCompat(f*,F) as an additional public-warrant constraint. This makes dependent, low-capacity, low-exit entities count more protectively in public frame selection while preventing capture via structurally blocked endorsement.

Autonomy-first selection rule (structural; applies whenever multiple admissible candidates remain). When multiple candidate outputs survive legitimacy and optional gates, the validator must select an autonomy-minimal candidate before optimizing coupling stability. Concretely:

Prefer any candidate that eliminates SignalBlocked(F,i) and minimizes ARV(F,i) triggers (AF/EX/FC/RS) across risk bearers.

Subject to (i), prefer candidates that satisfy DivOK(F) and preserve or improve capacity where EnablementRequired applies.

Subject to (i)–(ii), prefer coupling-stable candidates: if CouplingNoWorse(F,G) holds, treat F as preferred over G with respect to coupling disruption.

Reading. This ensures that “avoiding coupling disruption” is never treated as a stronger priority than preventing autonomy loss or capacity lock-in. Boundary-setting and exit-enabling operations are therefore allowed to be selected even when they alter coupling structure, so long as they are the autonomy-minimal surviving option under the core constraints.

Value-axis separation note. The constructive/destructive coupling distinction is treated as a value-axis diagnostic and (at most) a preference tie-breaker among already legitimate candidates. It does not grant permissions and does not override the constraint axis (ALRP, legitimacy, HoI, emergency bounds, divergence/signal-blocking, and enablement). In particular, coupling-preservation is not treated as an absolute goal: if boundary-setting or exit-enabling restructuring minimizes autonomy loss or capacity lock-in, it is selected under the autonomy-first rule even if it alters coupling structure.

Domination pressure / integrity gate (optional; Σᴿ⁺). If Sys(s) holds for the system-state carrier(s), compute DP(s). Enforce DP0: Admissible(F) → DP(F(s)) ≤ DP(s). If UnconsentedInfluence(F) holds, enforce strict dissipation DP1: DP(F(s)) < DP(s). If IntegrityModified(F) and CoercionImplicated(F), require PublicAct(F) (DPPub) and require Contestable(F) and public-frame compatibility as part of ConsentSymmetric. If MetaUpdate(F) holds, enforce DP3a/DP3b: governance updates must be non-regressive; they must be public and contestable only when coercion is implicated.

Non-bypassable output and non-regression rule (optional; Σᴿ⁺). Output completeness and domination non-regression must hold even under partial or soft-failing input data. The system must expose all viable candidates (TPO0). If legitimate alternatives exist, omission without exposure or justification is inadmissible outside emergency (TPO1). Domination-pressure non-regression must be satisfied either by direct DP evaluation (when instantiated) or by restricting action to DPsafe operations when DP cannot be evaluated (TPO2).

Viable exit gate (optional; Σᴿ⁺). For any risk-bearer i, require ExitStateViable(F(i)) outside emergency (EXV0). Reject any operation that causes ExitViabilityLost(F,i) outside emergency (EXV1). If emergency is invoked and exit viability is temporarily restricted, require a repair-termination route restoring ExitStateViable after the emergency envelope (EXV2).

If F fails any condition, the system computes the legitimate envelope L_F (Theorem 6.11) and applies L_F instead of F.

11.7 AdapterLayer Specification (Formal Mapping Rules)

Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is a firstorder formal system that requires no primitive symbols for “exit,” “choice,” “options,” or “signals.” These appear internally as structural properties of standing, capacity, admissible reachability, envelope geometry, and dependency relations. Realworld systems, however, do not natively expose their state in these terms. An adapter layer is therefore required to map domainspecific data into Σᴿ’s sorts, functions, and predicates.

This section specifies how a real system is translated into a Σᴿ structure so that Σᴿ₂level autonomy constraints (ALRP, STC5, drift, repair, envelope minimality, ARV detection) can be rigorously evaluated.

Cross-domain & Cross-order mapping as evidence of a Pluralist Non-Domination Substrate (PNDS).
Although Σᴿ is designed to be domain-portable, portability itself introduces a second layer of structure: the interpretation (adapter) mapping from raw domain states into a Σᴿ-model. This mapping has its own invariants and failure modes, independent of any single application domain. In this sense, cross-domain application constitutes a meta-domain whose objects are domain models and whose morphisms are structure-preserving translations (e.g., adapters, projections, and Σᴿ-homomorphisms). The multigranularity soundness conditions (harm-reflection and liftability) and the homomorphism preservation laws can be read as constraints in this meta-domain, making portability itself auditable rather than assumed.

Σᴿ operates at the level of what we call the Pluralist NonDomination Substrate: the structural layer that precedes and constrains all domainlevel instantiations. Any system that claims to coordinate agents without domination must, under Theorem 6.13 and the legitimacy conditions of Def. 21, instantiate this substrate’s invariants—standing preservation, symmetry, bounded intervention, idempotence, and repair—regardless of the specific domain in which it is expressed. The principles articulated in On Relevance and formalized in Standing Algebra are not domainspecific norms but characteristics of a Pluralist NonDomination Substrate. Their persistence across philosophical, formal, and institutional levels indicates that they constrain the possibility of legitimate coordination itself, rather than any particular belief system or authority.

Justification.
The stated impossibility follows because the configuration would require either exit collapse or irreversible dependency growth, both of which violate the definition of nondomination.

Adapter input validation precedes Σᴿ evaluation.

Before Σᴿ evaluates any proposed operation F, the adapter must validate that all asserted claims (ARVs, impact tiers, signal blocking, frame compatibility, DP readings, exposure/justification flags) are liftable under §3.10.17. Claims that are not liftable are treated as blocked; operations whose validity depends on non-liftable claims are inadmissible.

11.7.11 Evaluating ARV (AutonomyReducing Variable) Conditions

After translation of domain actions to F via , ARVs are evaluated in Σᴿ’s internal language.

For each i:

Alternative Foreclosure (AF) holds if all reachable legitimate transforms collapse into a single class-preserving branch.

Exit Termination (EX) holds if identity-reachable legitimate states disappear.

FormalChoice Collapse (FC) holds if the domain still presents “choices,” but all map to identical successor-consistent outcomes.

RelevanceSignal Impairment (RS) holds if standing is preserved but the ability of i to influence envelopes is reduced via coupling or class distortion.

The adapter layer’s job is to provide the raw F;
ARV evaluation is purely structural inside Σᴿ.

11.7.11A DualState ARV Input and Structural TruthFiltering

In many deployment contexts, especially those involving interpersonal conflict, medical urgency, or crisis escalation, the system cannot presume that usersupplied descriptions of harm or autonomy impairment are either complete or reliable. For this reason, Σᴿ does not treat autonomyreducing variables (ARVs) as primitive facts but as claims that must be interpreted through the structural constraints of the algebra.

To support emergency reasoning without relying on unverifiable narrative input, the adapter layer accepts two ARV state vectors for each relevant entity:
(i) a prior ARV state representing the baseline condition, and
(ii) a current ARV state representing the userreported present condition.
The system computes a claimed delta,

but this quantity is not accepted as ground truth. Instead it is passed through a structural truthfilter that evaluates whether the claimed change corresponds to any autonomyrelevant shift detectable in the Σᴿ representation of the domain.

Formally, the adapter checks whether the claimed ARV delta is compatible with observable structural differences in standing, degree, exit viability, optionset breadth, STC5 class membership, or successor accessibility. If no structural correlate exists, or if the claimed ARV change contradicts the algebraic invariants of the model, then the system sets

and treats the user’s claim as unverifiable. This prevents fabricated or exaggerated emergency claims from activating the emergency envelope in Σᴿᴱ (EEseries).

Conversely, if the system detects structural evidence of alternative foreclosure, exit termination, formalchoice collapse, or relevancesignal impairment—independent of user assertion—then the effective ARV delta is inferred from the observed state, even if the user reports no change. In such cases, the emergencyinequality test of EE1 is evaluated against the structurally validated ARV signal rather than the reported one.

This dualstate input mechanism therefore serves two roles:
(1) it permits contextual, phenomenological, or experiential information to be expressed in a structured way without giving users direct authority over emergency activation; and
(2) it ensures that only structurally corroborated ARV variation can influence Σᴿᴱ’s leastloss comparison. The validator thus treats ARV vectors as claims to be tested, not as determinants of system behavior. Emergency activation continues to rely exclusively on the structural relationships defined within Σᴿ and Σᴿᴱ.

11.7.11B Plural-Source ARV Claims and LLM-Assisted Interpretation

Plural-source ARV Claims and LLM-Assisted Interpretation.
Because Σᴿ is designed for pluralist systems, the standing of any entity is never determined unilaterally. The same principle applies to autonomyreducing variables (ARVs). To prevent domination or manipulation of emergency pathways, the adapter layer may accept ARV claims from multiple reporting parties or from systemlevel observation rather than relying on a single selfreported state. In this configuration, the “current” ARV vector may be constructed from a plurality of sources—distinct agents, institutional monitors, or LLMbased summaries of multiparty narratives—while the “prior” state reflects an earlier structural snapshot or collective baseline.

LLM models function naturally in this plural reporting role: they transform userprovided language into structured claims without granting any individual narrative privileged authority over emergency activation. All such ARV inputs remain claims until validated by the structural truthfilter of §11.7.11A, which tests each component for consistency with observable changes in standing, degree, exit viability, class membership, or optionset contraction. This arrangement ensures that ARV deltas influence Σᴿᴱ only when corroborated by structural evidence, even when derived from multiple perspectives. In pluralist settings, this multisource arrangement is not optional but normatively appropriate: no single agent dictates the autonomy state of the system, and the emergency envelope cannot be triggered or suppressed through misrepresentation by any individual. Σᴿ does not determine who is lying; it determines which claims about autonomy can be structurally verified. Only structurally corroborated ARV changes influence emergency activation or legitimacy evaluation.

11.7.11C NonLocal Plural ARV Aggregation and Stored Local Telemetry (Optional, ScaleInvariant)

Σᴿ permits autonomyreducing variables (ARVs) to be evaluated without requiring synchronous, copresent reporting. In pluralist systems, autonomy state is not a private declaration but a structurally relevant property of coordination, and therefore ARV evaluation may be performed using asynchronous plural input, stored event repositories, and (optionally) local telemetry. This subsection specifies how such aggregation can be performed in a manner consistent with nondomination: the system does not determine “who is lying,” but rather filters all claims through structural corroboration, producing an autonomy signal that cannot be controlled unilaterally.

(A) NonLocal Plural ARV Aggregation (Asynchronous, MultiParty)

In nonlocal settings, “prior” and “current” ARV states need not be supplied by the same party, nor at the same time. Instead, the system may maintain an Autonomy Event Repository in which reports and observations are stored as timestamped claims about ARV components. Let the ARV state for an entity at time be represented as a 4tuple:

corresponding to Alternative Foreclosure (AF), Exit Termination (EX), FormalChoice Collapse (FC), and RelevanceSignal Impairment (RS). In the pluralsource regime, is not taken from a single speaker but is computed as a structurally validated aggregate of claims and observations in a time window.

Operationally, each incoming report produces a candidate ARV vector (possibly derived by an LLM from narrative input) and is associated with a source and timestamp . The adapter layer applies the structural truthfilter described in §11.7.11A: each reported component is treated as a claim that must be consistent with any available structural correlates in the Σᴿ representation (e.g., standing/degree changes, exit viability, optionset contraction, STC5 class perturbations). Claims that lack structural support do not contribute to the effective state.

The resulting aggregate ARV state at time may be computed by any monotone, nondominating rule that does not privilege a single source. A canonical conservative choice is:

Maxseverity aggregation per component within a window (prioritizes harm detection):

where the max is taken componentwise over structurally validated claims in the time window .

Alternative aggregators (mean, trimmed mean, median, weighted schemes) are permitted provided they remain claimfiltered and do not permit unilateral narrative control. In all cases, the key invariant is: only structurally corroborated claims contribute, and the aggregation rule is chosen to preserve pluralist nondomination (no single agent has unilateral authority over the autonomy state of others).

This nonlocal mechanism supports two critical capabilities:

Asynchronous baseline and current states. The “prior” state may be retrieved from repository history, while the “current” state may be computed from recent plural input, without requiring copresent reporting.

Scaleinvariant group baselines. For a group , define a grouplevel autonomy state by aggregation across members, for example:

where is chosen to preserve harm sensitivity. This enables an institution, community, or multiagent system to maintain an autonomyrisk baseline without requiring synchronized testimony from all members.

(B) Stored Local ARV Aggregation (Including Optional Telemetry such as Biometrics)

In addition to plural narrative reports, the adapter layer may incorporate stored local observations as ARVrelevant evidence. This includes any domain signal that can be mapped into the structural ARV categories (AF/EX/FC/RS) without collapsing into psychological inference. Examples include:

repeated loss of exit affordances in UI or workflow logs (EX),

persistent contraction of reachable legitimate envelopes over time (AF/FC),

recurrent reductions in relevancesignal throughput (RS) measured by structural proxies (e.g., complaint pathways that no longer influence envelopes),

increased dependency edges (deg rises) coincident with option collapse,

telemetry streams (including biometrics) only insofar as they are explicitly mapped by the adapter to autonomyrelevant structural predicates, and only under domainappropriate consent and governance.

The system must treat telemetry as evidence, not as authority. Telemetry does not override Σᴿ’s structural invariants; it only provides additional signals that may corroborate or disconfirm ARV claims. When telemetry is present, it is incorporated through the same truthfilter discipline: telemetry can strengthen confidence in a structural correlate (e.g., corroborating that an exit channel has become nonfunctional), but it cannot substitute for the structural checks that determine legitimacy and emergency activation.

To prevent domination by surveillance, stored local aggregation must satisfy two constraints:

Minimality of collection: only signals required for ARV corroboration are retained.

Nonprivileging of observers: telemetry does not grant unilateral interpretive power; it functions as one input stream among others and remains subject to structural validation.

(C) Delta, Drift, and FailurePoint Projection (Optional Forecasting Layer)

This forecasting layer is optional and must be treated as an estimate rather than a proof: it provides an operational risk signal, not a moral judgment. Importantly, the forecasting layer cannot activate emergency authority by itself; it only contributes to the emergencyinequality comparison when corroborated by structural evidence (§11.7.11A).

(D) Integration with Σᴿᴱ Emergency Envelope (LeastLoss Condition Under Plural Evidence)

The emergency envelope in §5.1 requires comparing autonomy loss under (i) inaction (Id), (ii) legitimate noncoercive candidates, and (iii) bounded coercive stabilization. In a pluralist system, this comparison must be grounded in the aggregate, truthfiltered autonomy state, not a single narrative report. Accordingly, when ARVs are used to support emergency evaluation, the system uses the effective ARV state (after structural filtering and aggregation) rather than raw claims. This ensures:

emergency activation cannot be triggered by unilateral exaggeration,

emergency suppression cannot be achieved by unilateral denial, and

emergency windows remain selfliquidating and reversible under plural evidence.

(E) Scale Invariance and Coarsening (Individual → Group → Institution → Population)

Because ARV aggregation is defined over sets of entities and timeindexed repositories, it naturally supports scaleinvariant evaluation. At higher scales (departments, communities, institutions), ARV states may be computed over aggregated groups using conservative operators (e.g., componentwise maxima) to preserve harm detection. When used in conjunction with the multigranularity apparatus of Section 12, the same principle applies: coarselevel aggregation must not mask autonomy loss that is present at finer scales. The guiding constraint is consistent with pluralist safety: coarsening may be conservative, but it must not erase harms.

Note. This aggregation framework is intentionally nondiagnostic: it does not infer intent or truthfulness of individuals; it filters claims by structural corroboration and uses only the resulting effective autonomy signal for legitimacy and emergency evaluation.
