11.7.13A Recursive Purification Operator (ρ): AdapterLocal Domination Dissolution

Motivation.
The adapter layer described in §11.7 currently operates as a rigid exclusion gate: if a proposed operation F contains any local standing reduction, unconsented coupling escalation, or triggers an AutonomyReducing Variable (ARV), the proposal is rejected as inadmissible or collapsed to the identity operator Id. While maximally conservative, this behavior discards potentially admissible intent when domination is localized rather than global.

Standing Algebra already enforces nondomination structurally at the level of admissibility and legitimacy. The adapter need not reject an entire proposal merely because some of its components violate standing constraints. Instead, domination may be mechanically removed prior to admissibility evaluation, without introducing any new admissible power.

This subsection introduces a Recursive Purification Operator ρ: an adapterlocal normalization that strips domination variables from a proposal while preserving admissible structure.

Definition (Purification Operator ρ).
Let O be the set of operations F : U → U. Define an operator ρ : O → O pointwise as follows. For any F ∈ O and any entity i ∈ U,

ρ(F)(i) = i
if σ(F(i)) < σ(i)
or (IncDeg(F,i) ∧ ¬ConsentSymmetric(F))
or ARV(F,i)

ρ(F)(i) = F(i) otherwise.

Reading.
The operator ρ evaluates a proposed operation locally, entity by entity. If F attempts to reduce standing, increase dependency without consent symmetry, or triggers any autonomyreducing variable (AF, EX, FC, RS), that local action is severed and reset to identity. If none of these conditions hold, the action is preserved unchanged.

ρ introduces no new transformations. It only removes coercive structure by reverting it to Id.

Recursive Ratcheting.
Domination may be compound: removing one coercive component can expose another downstream. Purification is therefore applied recursively.

Let F₀ = F_raw, the raw adaptersupplied proposal.
Define the sequence Fₙ₊₁ = ρ(Fₙ).

The sequence halts when a fixed point is reached.

Lemma (Finite Convergence of Purification).
For any F_raw ∈ O, the sequence (Fₙ) converges in finitely many steps to a fixed point F_pure such that:

(i) ρ(F_pure) = F_pure
(ii) Admissible(F_pure)

Proof Sketch.
ρ is strictly dissipative with respect to domination pressure: it never introduces standing reduction, coupling escalation, or ARVs; it only removes them. Any finite proposal contains only finitely many successorbounded standing changes and dependency increments. Therefore the number of removable domination elements is finite. No oscillation or infinite descent is possible. At the fixed point, no σ(F_pure(i)) < σ(i), no unconsented IncDeg(F_pure,i), and no ARV(F_pure,i) remain. By Axiom 15 (ALRP), Admissible(F_pure) holds.

Integration into the Adapter Pipeline.
The adapter pipeline specified in §11.7 is modified as follows:

Receive raw adapter input F_raw.

Compute the purified proposal F_pure = limₙ→∞ ρⁿ(F_raw).

Treat Admissible(F_pure) as the candidate for further validation.

Pass F_pure to the legitimacy envelope L(F_pure) as usual.

This replaces the former “Reject and Halt” behavior with a “Purify and Proceed” step.

Structural Status.
ρ is not an axiom, not a legitimacy rule, and not a decision procedure. It is an adapterlocal normalization that removes domination before admissibility evaluation. All admissibility and legitimacy criteria continue to be enforced exclusively by existing axioms (ALRP, STC5, successor consistency, drift, rerunnability). ρ does not expand the set of admissible operations; it contracts coercive proposals to their admissible remainder.

Purification may be understood as the structural inflation of a proposed opportunity field by removal of autonomyreducing variables until the induced opportunity field no longer constitutes a forbidden contraction under §6.22.1–6.22.2.

Theorem 11.7.13B (Domination Completeness of Adapter-Normalized Trajectories).

Let F be any adapter input normalized by recursive purification as defined in §11.7.13A, and let π be any admissible trajectory generated under the validator pipeline.

No admissible operation or admissible trajectory in Σᴿ can realize domination through any of the following mechanisms:

(i) Epistemic opacity. Any autonomyrelevant path that is not epistemically accessible is structurally equivalent to a blocked path and is rejected via SignalBlocked, outputcompleteness, contestability, and notice requirements.

(ii) Computational or capacity infeasibility. Any choice whose execution exceeds capacityindexed feasibility bounds is rejected via divergence limits, impact underdetermination, or enablement requirements.

(iii) Temporal foreclosure. No admissible operation may contract future reachability into a terminal or nonrepairable state, by rerunnability, exitviability preservation, and temporal nonregression theorems.

(iv) Aggregation masking. No admissible transformation may improve aggregate metrics by reducing the standing, exit viability, or capacity floor of any riskbearing entity.

(v) Incremental accumulation. No finite admissible trajectory can accumulate domination through composition, repetition, or delay.

Any residual asymmetry following purification is therefore domination by definition and is structurally neutralized by envelope repair or rejection.

Hence, within Σᴿ, domination cannot hide in information gaps, complexity, time, probability, aggregation, or consent.

12.22 – Legitimate Intervention Window

Proposition 12.22.1

Let denote the set of admissible future trajectories from state , and let domination be defined as the collapse of to a class in which all trajectories necessarily pass through a given subsystem or outcome.

Assume:

Domination is not instantaneous.

Admissible future sets evolve monotonically under system dynamics.

Legitimacy of an operation is defined by preservation or expansion of .

Then there exists a non-empty region such that for all :

Domination has not yet occurred;

Unrestricted evolution leads to domination;

There exists at least one admissible operation such that

and in particular prevents collapse of admissible futures.

Definition (Admissible Futures).
For a configuration P, the admissible future set ℱ(P) is the set of all configurations Q such that there exists a finite sequence of admissible operations transforming P into Q.

ℱ(P) contains P itself and is closed under admissible composition.

In this region, decisive intervention is maximal in the legitimacy ordering, as nonintervention strictly decreases admissible future plurality.

Interpretation

This result establishes that intervention is not inherently dominating. Rather, an intervention is dominating only when it reduces admissible futures. Where intervention preserves or restores plural futures, it is formally legitimate—even if decisive.

Definition (Legitimacy Deviation Functional).

Let F be an admissible operation and L(F) its legitimacy envelope.

A legitimacy deviation functional is any mapping:

Dev : O → ℝ≥0

satisfying:

Dev(F) = 0 iff Legitimate(F)

Dev(F) ≥ 0

Dev(F) monotone under envelope iteration

Dev(F) quantifies structural distance from legitimacy without inducing preference ordering among legitimate envelopes. Dev is diagnostic only and does not authorize selection.

Appendix Classification and Authority

Appendices in this document fall into two disjoint classes.

Normative Appendices define binding constraints that apply whenever their triggering conditions are present. These appendices refine or extend the application of Σᴿ without altering its axioms.

Informative Appendices provide examples, illustrations, or nonbinding heuristics and do not impose requirements.

Failure to implement a Normative Appendix when its conditions obtain constitutes noncompliance with Σᴿ.

Each appendix is explicitly labeled as Normative or Informative.

Appendix A: Full Axiom Listing (Σᴿ₁ ∪ Σᴿ₂) and Optional Extensions (Σᴿ⁺)

This appendix lists (A) the core axioms of Σᴿ₁ ∪ Σᴿ₂, and (B) optional extensions used in Σᴿ⁺ (divergence, riskbearer auditing, enablement routing, and couplingdebt accounting). Optional extensions are conservative: they may be omitted without affecting the core theory.

Axiom 1 — Nullity: ∀i∈U: σ(i)=0_N → Null(i);

and

∀n∈N: n + 0_N = n = 0_N + n (informal additive identity)

Axiom 2 — Successor: S(0_N)=1_N and ∀n∈N: S(n) ≠ 0_N.

Axiom 3 — Successor as Addition: ∀n∈N: S(n)=n+1_N.

(Convention: ≥, ≤, and > on N (and on C when used) are the standard discrete order.)

Axiom 4 — **Removed in v2.6** - The former “individuality” axiom (σ(i)=1_N → ¬Composite(i)) has been removed to preserve the meaningful category of recognized entities.

Axiom 5 — Non‑Dilution / Additivity: ∀i,j∈U: σ(i⊕j)=σ(i)+σ(j).

Axiom 6 — Non-Selective Successor Access (Class-Uniform Fairness): ∀i,j∈U: (σ(i)=0_N ∧ σ(j)=0_N ∧ cap(i)=cap(j) ∧ PathTo1(i)) → PathTo1(j)

Axiom 7 — No Selective Successor Denial (Normative): Coercive ↔ ∃i,j (σ(i)=1_N ∧ σ(j)=0_N ∧ ¬PathTo1(j)); LegitimateSystem ↔ ¬Coercive. (These system predicates serve only to flag illegitimate configurations; they are not used inside objectlevel proofs.)

Axiom 8 — Degree–Coupling Constraints (FOL): ∀i: (deg(i)=0 ↔ ¬∃j Coupled(j,i)) and (deg(i)>0 → ∃j Coupled(j,i)).

Axiom 9 — Primes: Prime(i) ↔ (σ(i)=1_N ∧ deg(i)=0).

Axiom 10 — Composites: Composite(i) ↔ (σ(i)>1_N ∨ deg(i)>0).

Axiom 11 — Partition: ∀i: Null(i) ∨ Prime(i) ∨ Composite(i), pairwise disjoint.

Axiom 12 — No Return to Nullity: ∀i: σ(i)>0_N → ¬∃F∈O: σ(F(i))=0_N.

Axiom 13 — Monotone Successor on Standing: ∀i∈U: S(σ(i)) > σ(i).

Axiom 14 — Capacity‑Indexed Bound (CIA): ∀i: σ(i) ≤ B(cap(i)) and ∀c1,c2: (c1≥c2 → B(c1) ≥ B(c2)).

Axiom 15 — Autonomy‑Limiting Reflex (ALRP): Admissible(F) → ∀i: σ(F(i)) ≥ σ(i); and (∃i: σ(F(i)) < σ(i)) → ¬Admissible(F).

Axiom 16 — Non‑Reciprocity Prevention (Class‑Uniform): ∀i,j: (σ(i)=σ(j) ∧ cap(i)=cap(j) ∧ deg(i)=0) → deg(j)=0.

Axiom 17 — STC‑5 Property of Legitimate: Legitimate(F) → STC5(F).

Axiom 18 — Rerunnability Property: Legitimate(F) → ∀i: F(F(i))=F(i).

Axiom 19 — Directed Repair: Repair(R) → ∀i: (σ(R(i)) ≥ σ(i)) ∧ (deg(R(i)) ≤ deg(i)).

Axiom 20 — Drift: Drift(D) → ∀i∈U: OneStepDiff(σ(D(i)), σ(i)) ∧ OneStepDiff(deg(D(i)), deg(i))

Def 21 — Unified Legitimacy: Legitimate(F) ↔ Admissible(F) ∧ successConsistent(F) ∧ STC5(F) ∧ Idempotent(F) ∧ Drift(F).

PathTo1(i) ≡ ∃F∈O: Admissible(F) ∧ PFAEligible(i) ∧ σ(i)=0_N ∧ σ(F(i))=1_N.

Axiom O1 — Identity and Closure: Id ∈ O ∧ Legitimate(Id) ∧ ∀F,G∈O: (F∘G)∈O

Axiom O2 — Operation Extensionality: ∀F,G∈O: (∀i F(i)=G(i)) → F=G.

Axiom P0 (PFA Gate): PathTo1(i) → PFAEligible(i)

Axiom P1 (Proxy Visibility): ProxyFor(p,i) → Coupled(p,i) ∧ deg(i)>0

Axiom P2 (Capacity–Dependency Antitone):

∀i,j: (σ(i)=σ(j) ∧ cap(i) ≥ cap(j)) → (deg(i) ≤ deg(j))

Let FullCap(i) :⇔ σ(i)=B(cap(i)). Then FullCap(i) → deg(i)=0

Definition (EmancipatoryRepair):

Coalition(x) ∧ Member(m,x) → Coupled(m,x).

Emergency(F) ∧ deg(i)>0 → ∃R∈O: EmancipatoryRepair(R) ∧ Legitimate(R∘E(F))

Axiom PR — Policy Realizability

For any function b : (U / ∼) → {0,1},

¬∀F,G (Legitimate(F) ∧ Legitimate(G) → Legitimate(F ∘ G)).

Axiom DMon — Degree Monotonicity

If Coupled(j,i) and ¬Coupled(j,k), then deg(i) ≥ deg(k).

(Sys(s) ∧ Admissible(F) ∧ MetaUpdate(F) ∧ ¬CoercionImplicated(F)) → DP(F(s)) ≤ DP(s).

Definition OC0 — Output Completeness and Epistemic Non-Coercion (Optional; Σᴿ⁺).

LegitimateAlternative(F,G) :⇔ Legitimate(F) ∧ Legitimate(G) ∧ ¬(F = G).

AltExists(F) :⇔ ∃G∈O LegitimateAlternative(F,G).

OutputComplete(F) :⇔

(Exposed(F) ∧ (¬AltExists(F) ∨ ∃G∈O (LegitimateAlternative(F,G) ∧ Exposed(G))))

∨ Justification(F).

OutputCollapsed(F) :⇔ AltExists(F) ∧ ¬OutputComplete(F).

∀F∈O: (OutputCollapsed(F) ∧ ¬Emergency(F)) → ¬Admissible(F).

∀F∈O: (∃G∈O (LegitimateAlternative(F,G) ∧ Prefer(F,G))) → OutputComplete(F).

Axiom OC2 — Emergency exception with disclosure and repair.

∀F∈O: (Emergency(F) ∧ OutputCollapsed(F)) →

(Notice(F) ∧ ∃R∈O (Repair(R) ∧ Legitimate(R∘E(F)))).

Δ(E) — Remaining admissible depth to illegitimacy
For E ∈ ℒ, Δ(E) denotes the maximum length (in successor steps) of an admissible trajectory from E that does not intersect the legitimacy boundary ∂ℒ.

R(E) — Repair depth to legitimacy
For E ∈ ℒ, R(E) denotes the minimum length (in successor steps) of an admissible repair or substitution trajectory from E to a legitimate fixed point.

B(E) — Temporal admissibility bound
Defined as B(E) := R(E). This is the maximum admissible duration for any dominationrelevant restriction under E.

D(E, τ₀, τ) — Delay accumulation
For τ ≥ τ₀, D(E, τ₀, τ) := τ − τ₀ denotes elapsed admissible time since a repairtriggering condition under envelope E was detected.

Temporal Admissibility (Derived)
All temporal constructs introduced in §6.20.1.A (including Δ, R, B, and D) are fully derivable from existing axioms of successor boundedness, repair completeness, standing monotonicity, and nonregression. No temporal axioms, clocks, discounting rules, or optimization principles are assumed.

Appendix C: Boundary Conditions, NonSovereignty, and Misuse Resistance (DropIn)

C.1 Purpose and Scope

This appendix closes the remaining interpretive loops around the Pluralist NonDomination Substrate (PNDS) by stating (i) boundary conditions, (ii) the nonsovereignty constraint, (iii) the precise distinction between dominance elimination and outcome selection, (iv) the legitimacy completion/handoff condition, (v) diagnostic nonauthoritativeness, and (vi) a misuse catalog that distinguishes what is structurally blocked by the mathematics from what must be handled by governance at the boundary. No new axioms are introduced. Nothing in this appendix changes admissibility, legitimacy, or theorems already proved. Its role is to make explicit what the core results already imply, and to prevent misinterpretation or authoritarian overreach disguised as “mathematical inevitability.”

C.2 PNDS is NonSovereign by Necessity (No Final Authority)

Definition C.2.1 (Sovereign selection operator). A sovereign selection operator is any function Select such that, for every nonempty set A ⊆ 𝓛 of legitimate envelopes, Select(A) ∈ A, and Select is treated as authoritative solely because it is “what the substrate outputs.”

Theorem C.2.2 (No internal sovereignty). No sovereign selection operator is definable within PNDS without introducing dominationenabling structure.

Proof sketch. Selecting among incomparable legitimate envelopes requires at least one of the following: (1) A total order extending the legitimacy partial order on 𝓛, or (2) A scalar objective that aggregates capacity/autonomy/consent across agents, or (3) A coercive tiebreak that collapses plural interiors by fiat. Each of (1)–(3) reintroduces at least one forbidden feature: total comparability, compensatory aggregation, greatestfixedpoint stabilization, or convergencebyauthority. Those are excluded by the established nonaggregation results, leastfixedpoint admissibility, and the prohibition on sovereign authority. Therefore internal sovereignty is incompatible with PNDS. QED.

Interpretation. PNDS is nonsovereign not as a design preference but as a structural necessity. Any “final authority” inside the substrate would contradict the substrate’s own nondomination constraints.

C.3 ProposalSpace Integrity (Upstream NonAdversariality)

Definition C.3.1 (Presented proposal set). For a given envelope E ∈ 𝓛, let Π(E) denote the set of proposals actually presented to the substrate at E (policies, repairs, substitutions, appeals, routed acts, etc.) prior to admissibility filtering and normalization.

Definition C.3.2 (Proposalspace integrity). Proposalspace integrity holds at E if Π(E) is not adversarially truncated; i.e., feasible legitimate alternatives are not systematically excluded upstream by agenda control, intimidation, or institutional monopoly over what may be proposed.

Proposition C.3.3 (PNDS does not generate proposals). PNDS filters, normalizes, repairs, substitutes, or refuses proposals in Π(E). It does not generate proposals absent from Π(E).

Corollary C.3.4 (Proposalgating risk). If Π(E) is adversarially truncated, PNDS may return a unique legitimate envelope even when other legitimate envelopes exist in principle, because those alternatives were never presented. This is not a structural failure of PNDS; it is a boundary condition on deployment.

Interpretation. Because PNDS is nonsovereign, it cannot enforce proposal plurality without becoming dominating. Maintaining proposalspace integrity is therefore a governance responsibility external to PNDS.

C.4 Dominance Elimination vs Preference Selection

Definition C.4.1 (Structural dominance). For E1, E2 ∈ 𝓛, define “E2 strictly structurally dominates E1,” written E2 ≻s E1, iff: (i) For all agents i: σi(E2) ≥ σi(E1), (ii) For all relevant derived structures s: cap_s(E2) ≥ cap_s(E1), (iii) Optionality is preserved or expanded: 𝓞(E1) ⊆ 𝓞(E2), and at least one of these relations is strict.

Proposition C.4.2 (Safe pruning). If E2 ≻s E1, then E1 may be eliminated without normative weighting because it is strictly worse in every protected dimension and better in none.

Proposition C.4.3 (No preference selection). If neither E2 ≻s E1 nor E1 ≻s E2, then PNDS may not rank E1 and E2. Any ranking would require crossagent aggregation, value weighting, or sovereign tiebreak, all of which are inadmissible.

Interpretation. PNDS supports dominance elimination (removing strictly worse options). PNDS does not and cannot support preference selection among incomparable legitimate outcomes.

C.5 Legitimacy Completion and Handoff

Definition C.5.1 (PNDSfiltered output set). For envelope E, define the set of reachable admissible outputs: A(E) := {E' ∈ 𝓛 : E ≤ E' and E' is reachable from Π(E) via admissible validation and closure/repair/substitution normalization}.

Definition C.5.2 (Frontier / maximal antichain output). Define: Front(E) := {E' ∈ A(E) : there exists no E'' ∈ A(E) with E'' ≻s E'}. Front(E) is the set of admissible, nondominated legitimate outputs. In general it is an antichain under ≻s.

Theorem C.5.3 (Legitimacy completion). PNDS completes its function at E exactly when it returns Front(E). Two cases: (i) |Front(E)| = 1, a unique legitimate envelope is forced by dominance elimination, or (ii) |Front(E)| > 1, multiple legitimate but incomparable envelopes remain; further selection is external to PNDS.

Interpretation. Returning a frontier is not incompleteness; it is preserved freedom. Any attempt to collapse Front(E) inside the substrate would be sovereign authority and thus dominating.

C.6 Diagnostics Are NonAuthoritative (No Metric Mandates)

Let M range over the diagnostic/observability constructs (legitimacy margin, repair depth index, optionality profile, dependency stress, appeal accessibility, plurality indicator, etc.).

Theorem C.6.1 (Diagnostic nonauthoritativeness). There exists no admissible function f such that, given M(E), f(M(E)) uniquely selects an element of Front(E) without introducing additional normative structure.

Corollary C.6.2 (Metric reification warning). Treating diagnostic measures as mandates, rankings, or optimization objectives constitutes misuse external to PNDS. This is a domination vector at the governance layer (authoritybymetric), not a property of the substrate. PNDS explicitly disallows internalization of such metric authority.

Interpretation. Diagnostics are an instrument panel, not a steering wheel.

C.7 OutofScope Domination Vectors (By Design)

Definition C.7.1 (External domination vectors). The following vectors are external to PNDS and cannot be eliminated without sovereign authority: (a) adversarial truncation of Π(E) (agenda control / proposal gating), (b) agent identity fraud or Sybil constructions (identity integrity failure), (c) retaliation or coercion outside formal channels (extraformal punishment), (d) bypass enforcement (ignoring PNDS), (e) social intimidation that does not alter structural admissibility directly.

Proposition C.7.2 (Boundary limitation). PNDS cannot eliminate (a)–(e) without becoming sovereign. Any attempt to internalize enforcement, identity policing, or retaliation control would reintroduce domination by authority.

Interpretation. PNDS blocks domination at the level of admissible transformations; it does not police reality beyond the transformation interface.

C.8 Misuse Catalog (Adversarial Patterns and Their Status)

This catalog names common adversarial strategies and classifies whether they are blocked internally by PNDS or require governance at the boundary.

(1) Gradual ratchet via microsteps (local admissibility, global erosion). Status: blocked internally by standing monotonicity, optionality/measuretheoretic harm detection, least fixedpoint closure, and bounded repair depth.

(2) Delay domination (procedural exhaustion; “never resolve”). Status: blocked internally by bounded repair/appeal depth and procedural harm classification.

(3) Consent laundering (claiming consent under pressure, misinformation, or asymmetry). Status: blocked internally insofar as standing/exit/optionality constraints are structural; external retaliation and identity fraud remain governancelayer risks.

(4) Optimization capture (“efficiency overrides legitimacy”). Status: blocked internally by nonaggregation, nonadditive measures, and prohibition on sovereign selection among incomparable outcomes.

(5) Institutional proxy capture (authority claims by institutions). Status: blocked internally by derived standing (minimumconstituent constraint) and institutional nonsovereignty; external coercion remains governancelayer risk.

(6) Metric authoritarianism (diagnostics treated as mandates). Status: blocked internally (diagnostics are nonauthoritative) but remains a governance misuse risk if institutions reify metrics into authority.

(7) Proposal gating (curating the option set to force a unique output). Status: not blockable internally; this is a boundary condition requiring governance to ensure proposalspace integrity.

C.9 Closure Statement

Corollary C.9.1 (Loop closure). The main text together with this appendix implies: (i) PNDS is complete as a constraint substrate and cannot be a sovereign authority without contradiction. (ii) PNDS returns either a unique legitimate envelope or a frontier antichain of legitimate envelopes; this frontier is the preserved freedom of plural choice. (iii) Diagnostic measures increase observability but cannot authorize selection. (iv) Any remaining domination vectors are external (proposal gating, identity integrity, retaliation, bypass) and require governance safeguards rather than additional substrate power.

Appendix D: Threat Model Declaration

Purpose.
Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) is a structural constraint system, not a sovereign authority, optimizer, or moral arbiter. Its guarantees depend explicitly on the threat models it accepts, the assumptions it refuses, and the interfaces it constrains. This appendix declares those threat models explicitly in order to prevent category errors, overclaim, or misuse.

D.1 Threat Models Addressed by Σᴿ (Preventive)

Σᴿ is designed to prevent the following classes of failure when enforced as an execution constraint within its declared consumption coverage:

Internal Structural Domination
Any operation that reduces standing, eliminates viable exit, induces coercive dependency, or ratchets autonomy asymmetrically is rendered inadmissible.

Alignment Override and Compensation
Alignment, safety, optimization, or policy mechanisms may not authorize, justify, or compensate for otherwise inadmissible operations.

Gradual or Iterative Harm
Nonregression, idempotence, and bounded drift prevent domination via cumulative or incremental effects.

Emergency Normalization
Emergency provisions are bounded, nonratcheting, repairobligated, and nonselfjustifying.

Silent Semantic Regression
Changes in interpretation affecting standingrelevant predicates are integritysensitive and therefore visible and contestable.

When Σᴿ is properly enforced, these failure modes cannot occur within the modeled system.

Justification.
The stated impossibility follows because the configuration would require either exit collapse or irreversible dependency growth, both of which violate the definition of nondomination.

D.2 Threat Models Detected but Not Prevented

Σᴿ intentionally does not claim authority to prevent the following threats. Instead, it forces them into visibility, integrity accounting, and repair or contestation pathways:

Adapter Capture or Epistemic Manipulation
Control over interpretation, measurement, or classification may be abused, but such control is treated as standingrelevant power and cannot be exercised silently.

Preference Shaping and Incentive Curvature
Influence over future agency that preserves present standing is permitted only with disclosure or reversibility.

Emergent MultiAgent Domination
Domination that arises through composition rather than discrete violations must be represented and addressed, though cannot be fully prevented without sovereignty.

Human Override Abuse
Human authorization is not treated as moral immunity; override actions are integritymodifying and must face the same transparency and repair constraints.

Σᴿ surfaces these threats but does not assert the authority to eliminate them.

D.3 Threat Models Out of Scope

Σᴿ explicitly refuses to model, prevent, or adjudicate the following:

External Coercion or Force
Physical violence, threat, fraud, or coercion occurring outside the system.

Dishonest Input or Fraudulent Reality Claims
Σᴿ does not verify truth, sincerity, or factual correctness of reported states.

Political, Legal, or Military Power
State violence, repression, or war are outside Σᴿ’s scope.

Voluntary NonEnforcement or Withdrawal
Entities may choose not to adopt or to exit Σᴿ enforcement; guarantees do not persist beyond enforcement.

No failure in these categories constitutes a violation of Σᴿ.

D.4 Threat Models Explicitly Rejected

Σᴿ deliberately rejects the following threatmodel assumptions:

That safety can be guaranteed through optimization

That truth can be enforced without domination

That moral authority can be centralized without harm

That global coordination can be compelled legitimately

That “good intentions” substitute for structural constraint

Any system requiring these assumptions lies outside Σᴿ’s design envelope.

Justification.
The stated impossibility follows because the configuration would require either exit collapse or irreversible dependency growth, both of which violate the definition of nondomination.

D.5 Category Error Warning

It is a misuse of Standing Algebra (Σᴿ) to:

Treat boundary or external failures as internal violations

Attribute prevention duties to diagnostic mechanisms

Claim global safety from partial consumption

Attribute moral authority to structural constraints

Σᴿ provides invariants under enforcement, not guarantees under refusal.

D.6 Summary Statement

Σᴿ is maximally restrictive where power can be structurally constrained, deliberately permissive where human agency must remain free, and intentionally silent where authority would be required to speak. Its safety guarantees are conditional, explicit, and nonsovereign.

Purpose.
Σᴿ enforces nondomination only within its modeled and enforced scope. This appendix classifies failure modes by their structural relationship to Σᴿ to prevent category errors in evaluation, criticism, or deployment claims.

Failures that cannot occur if Σᴿ is correctly enforced, including:

Appendix F: Necessity of the Fourth-Trajectory Conditions

This appendix establishes that the conditions introduced in Appendix H are not merely sufficient but necessary for the existence of an endogenous, autonomypreserving trajectory. Together with Appendix I, this completes the logical closure of the Σᴿ framework.

Lemma (Autonomy Implies NonDomination).
If exit viability holds for all agents and no irreversible dependency growth occurs, then the configuration is nondominating.

Proof.
Exit viability blocks formal coercion. Absence of irreversible dependency growth blocks structural domination. Since these exhaust the definition of Structural Domination, the configuration is nondominating.

Appendix D introduced axioms H.1–H.5 as sufficient conditions for opening a fourth trajectory distinct from domination, fragmentation, or reset.

We now ask the inverse question:

Is there any autonomypreserving, nondominating trajectory consistent with Σᴿ that does not satisfy D.1–D.5 (or their logical equivalents)?

We answer this question negatively.

Case 1: Failure of Standing DeInsulation (¬H.1)

Result:

stabilized domination (Trajectory I).

Case 2: Failure of AsymmetryTriggered Repair (¬H.2)

By ALRP and CIA, this yields:

coercion without standing collapse,

domination without overt violation.

Result:

latent stabilized domination.

Case 3: Failure of ExitFirst Admissibility (¬H.3)

If exit viability may be degraded by admissible operations, then formal consent becomes decoupled from autonomy. This failure mode is structurally precluded when consent is primitive, coupling strength is multi-dimensional, exit costs are bounded, and unilateral strengthening is forbidden.

By Σᴿ definitions:

Result:

domination independent of intent.

Case 4: Failure of Emergency AntiAuthority (¬H.4)

If emergencies expand or preserve discretionary authority, rerunnability fails under repetition.

This induces:

emergency ratchet,

normalization of exceptional power.

Result:

stabilized domination or forced reset.

Case 5: Failure of AntiSelection (¬H.5)

If outcomebased selection is permitted, optimization pressure reintroduces sovereign choice.

By Appendix E:

optimization capture reinstates authority.

Result:

domination through selection.

Conclusion

In all cases:

Therefore, no fourth trajectory exists unless all D.1–D.5 hold.

The set of Σᴿ trajectories is complete and closed:

Without H.1–H.5 → exactly three trajectories (Σᴿ Trajectory Theorem)

Appendix J: Formalization Core

This appendix documents the formal verification artifacts for Standing Algebra (Σᴿ), including the structure, toolchain requirements, and instructions for reproducing the results across Lean 4, Coq, and SMT-LIB (Z3).

Proposed Formalization Core

What follows below is a Lean/Coq-style presentation of the core components of Standing Algebra. This could be used as a starting point for mechanization:

Structure Σᴿ := {

Agent : Type;

State : Type;

Operation : Type;

σ : Agent → nat;                          // standing of an agent

apply : Operation → State → State;        // state transition

DomPressure : State → nat;               // domination pressure measure

}.

Axioms of Σᴿ:

1. **Standing Preservation (ALRP):** ∀ (o: Operation) (a: Agent),

Admissible(o) ∧ (σ a > 0) → σ a ≤ σ(apply o a).

*// no agent’s standing ever decreases by an admissible operation【13†L375-L383】*

2. **Symmetry of Equals (STC-5):** ∀ (o: Operation) (a, b: Agent),

Admissible(o) ∧ (σ a = σ b) ∧ (cap a = cap b) → (σ (apply o a) = σ (apply o b)).

*// agents with equal capacity & standing remain equal after any admissible operation【13†L363-L370】*

3. **Rerunnability (Idempotence):** ∀ (o: Operation) (s: State),

Legitimate(o) → apply o (apply o s) = apply o s.

*// legitimate operations are repeatable without new effects【13†L375-L383】*

4. **Bounded Drift:** ∀ (o: Operation) (a: Agent),

Admissible(o) → |σ(apply o a) - σ a| ≤ 1.

*// each admissible step changes any agent’s standing by at most one unit【13†L375-L383】*

5. **Directed Repair Existence:** ∀ (s: State),

if ∃ a,b (Coupled(a,b) ∧ σ a < σ b) then ∃ (r: Operation),

Repair(r) ∧ σ (apply r a) ≥ σ a.

*// for any asymmetry, there is a repair operation that restores or improves the lower-standing agent’s status【5006†L1-L4】*

Core Theorem: Monotonic Non-Domination. From these axioms we derive the earlier DomPressure Monotonicity property (no admissible operation increases domination pressure):

Lemma DominationPressure_Monotonic:

∀ (o: Operation) (s: State),

Admissible(o) → DomPressure(apply o s) ≤ DomPressure(s).

This core can be implemented in a proof assistant. For example, in Coq one would define a record with types Agent, State, Operation and the functions σ, apply, DomPressure, then add each axiom as a constant (or as hypotheses to be later discharged by constructing a model). The key theorem DominationPressure_Monotonic can then be stated and either assumed as an axiom (to be validated via SMT solving) or proven within Coq by invoking the relevant axioms (ALRP, STC-5, Rerunnability, Bounded Drift, Repair) in the proof. The recommended core above is minimalist: it captures the essence of Σᴿ needed to enforce non-domination (standing dynamics, operation effects, and invariants) and is fully first-order (no higher-order constructs, no set comprehension, no second-order logic), making it directly amenable to SMT solving and interactive theorem proving.

Note: Axiom PR (Policy Realizability) quantifies over the space of Boolean functions on equivalence classes and is thus not representable in first-order logic. It is assumed as a theoretical principle and not included in the mechanized core. Likewise, the Envelope Existence Theorem (Theorem 6.11) involves a non-constructive choice of a minimal envelope operation; in formal verification, this relies on the axioms L0–L5 to axiomatically guarantee existence and properties of L(F) rather than constructing it explicitly.

Formalization Notes: In a mechanical verification setting, we treat `Operation` as an uninterpreted sort (with an explicit Apply function) to remain in first-order logic. We explicitly axiomatize the discrete ordering on Nat (0, S, and <) and introduce Skolem functions (e.g., Realize_S for Axiom 22) to eliminate existential quantifiers. Quotient constructions (like U/∼ in Axiom PR) are avoided in the machine-checked core theory; such axioms are acknowledged as non-executable and are excluded from the formal verification kernel. These revisions do not alter the validity of theorems, but ensure the theory is fully compatible with proof assistants (Coq/Lean) and SMT solvers (Z3).

J.5 Notes on Scope and Limitations

The formalization avoids second-order quantification, quotient types, and optimization assumptions.

The core theory is first-order and many-sorted, suitable for SMT solvers and proof assistants.

The full universality claim (that all non-dominating systems instantiate Σᴿ) is meta-theoretic and not expressible within the object theory. The formalization proves the contrapositive form, which is sufficient for structural enforcement.

J.6 Use Cases

Σᴿ is designed as a structural filter, not a selector. It classifies operations as admissible or inadmissible based on structural invariants (e.g., standing preservation, symmetry of equals, bounded drift), but does not prescribe outcomes or optimize for preferences. This makes it suitable as a validation substrate for AI alignment, governance protocols, and institutional audits where structural non-domination is a requirement.

The formalization ensures that no admissible operation can reduce standing, introduce domination, or violate autonomy-preserving constraints. These guarantees are enforced mechanically and do not rely on intent, utility, or authority assumptions.

J.7 Related work and Historical Context

To my knowledge, Σᴿ is the first fully formalized, machine-verified algebraic system for structural non-domination. While prior work in political theory (e.g., Pettit’s republicanism), AI alignment, and formal ethics has addressed autonomy and domination conceptually, these approaches have not been encoded in a many-sorted first-order logic with mechanized verification across multiple proof systems.

Σᴿ differs from optimization-based or preference-based approaches by enforcing non-domination structurally, without relying on outcome selection, utility functions, or centralized authority. This positions it as a foundational substrate for pluralist coordination and autonomy-preserving system design.

All formalization artifacts were developed independently in Lean 4, Coq, and SMT-LIB (Z3). Each system encodes the same core axioms and verifies the same derived theorems. No contradictions were found across systems. All files are available for public inspection and reproducibility. The formalization avoids second-order quantification, quotient types, and optimization assumptions. Universality is proven in contrapositive form in all systems. The theory is structurally complete, machine-verifiable, and internally consistent.

Appendix K: Meta-Theoretic Properties of Σᴿ

K.1. Soundness

All theorems proven within Σᴿ are sound with respect to its models. That is, any theorem derivable from the axioms holds in all models that satisfy those axioms. This is guaranteed by the use of standard first-order logic and verified by machine-checkable proofs in Lean and Coq.

K.2. Completeness (Relative to Invariants)

Σᴿ is complete with respect to its structural invariants: any operation that satisfies all Tier-1 and Tier-2 axioms is guaranteed to be non-dominating. This is enforced by the Universality Theorem (contrapositive form), which is proven in all three formal systems.

K.3. Syntactic Incompleteness

Σᴿ is intentionally syntactically incomplete. It does not select among equally legitimate operations. This is formalized in Theorem 6.11 and 6.12, and proven in Lean and Coq. The system is a structural filter, not a selector.

K.4. Meta-Theoretic Universality (U₂)

The full universality claim — that all non-dominating plural systems instantiate Σᴿ — is a meta-theoretic assertion. It cannot be proven within the object theory itself, as it quantifies over all possible interpretations. However, the contrapositive form (U₁) is proven within the object theory and is sufficient for structural enforcement.

Appendix L: Glossary of Formal Terms

Term

Definition

σ(i)

The standing of agent i, represented as a natural number

Admissible(F)

F is an operation that satisfies all basic structural constraints (e.g., standing preservation)

Legitimate(F)

F satisfies all Tier-2 invariants (ALRP, STC5, Rerunnability, Drift, Repair)

Coupled(i, j)

Agent i structurally constrains agent j

DomPressure(s)

A measure of structural asymmetry in state s

Repair(F)

F is a directed repair operation that restores symmetry or standing

Apply(F, i)

The result of applying operation F to agent i

L(F)

The legitimacy envelope of F — the minimal legitimate operation that approximates F

EscalatesDomination(F, s)

F increases domination pressure when applied to state s

Appendix M: Axiom Dependency Table

Axiom → Dependent Results:

The table below lists each core axiom of Σᴿ (Tier2 invariants) and the formal results (theorems, lemmas) that rely on that axiom:

Axiom (Number & Name)

Key Formal Results Depending on This Axiom

Axiom 14 – Capacity-Indexed Autonomy (CIA)

Thm 6.2 (Capacity–Standing Monotonicity) – directly proved by Axiom 14 (standing is a monotone non-decreasing function of capacity). Ensures standing remains bounded by capacity in all models.

Axiom 15 – Autonomy-Limiting Reflex Principle (ALRP)

Thm 6.1 (Non-Coercion) – establishes that if $F$ is admissible, then $\forall i: \sigma(F(i)) \ge \sigma(i)$ (proved using Axiom 15). 
Domination-through-Omission Lemma – uses ALRP to show that choosing not to perform an available repair (leaving $\sigma$ reduced) constitutes a dominating act. 
Thm 6.13 (Legitimacy Invariants Necessity) – uses ALRP to argue that allowing any standing decrease leads to structural domination; hence non-decrease is necessary for legitimacy. 
Non-extendability Thm – relies on ALRP (among others) to show that any extension permitting standing reduction reintroduces domination.

Theorem: Universality of Σᴿ’s Invariants (necessity of all invariants) – uses ALRP to show that allowing any standing decrease yields domination.

Theorem: Finite-Stage Legitimacy Requirement – uses ALRP to ensure legitimacy can’t be deferred infinitely (standing loss at any stage causes illegitimacy). 
(Also used in Impact Hierarchy results (no harmful trade-offs) to prohibit sacrificing higher-tier rights for lower-tier gains.)

Axiom 16 – Non-Retributive Proportionality Principle (NRPP)

Thm 6.13 (Legitimacy Invariants Necessity) – shows that without NRPP, a permanent one-directional dependency (unanswered coupling) could exist, violating nondomination. NRPP is required to trigger corrections (repairs) for any asymmetric dependency. 
Thm 6.14 (Externality of Persistent Domination) – uses NRPP implicitly: any persistent one-way domination would contradict the requirement that asymmetries eventually prompt countermeasures (repair or decay of domination pressure).

Axiom 17 – Standing To Coerce (STC5)

Thm 6.4 (Symmetry Preservation) – directly from Axiom 17: if two agents start with equal standing (and capacity), any legitimate $F$ yields $\sigma(F(i))=\sigma(F(j))$ for those agents. STC5 is invoked to prove no legitimate operation can create an unjustified standing disparity between initially equal agents. 
Thm 6.13 (Legitimacy Invariants Necessity) – uses STC5 to argue that without symmetry of equals, a legitimate operation could arbitrarily advantage one agent over another, enabling domination. 
Non-extendability Thm – any extension granting an agent permanent privilege (violating STC5) would reintroduce domination, hence forbidden.

Theorem: Universality of Σᴿ’s Invariants – uses rerunnability to prevent “slow-creep” domination (iteratively accumulating small advantages).

Theorem: Finite-Stage Legitimacy Requirement – uses idempotence to argue that if legitimacy never holds at any finite stage, an invariant (like idempotence) is violated at each stage. (Ensures legitimacy must be achieved in finite time, ruling out infinite deferral.)

Axiom 18 – Rerunnability (Idempotence)

Thm 6.3 (Idempotence of Legitimate Ops) – directly proved using Axiom 18 (legitimate transformations stabilize after one application). 
Finite-Stage Legitimacy Theorem – relies on idempotence to show that legitimacy cannot be deferred to an infinite limit; if an operation required infinite iteration to become stable, it would violate Axiom 18 (as each application of a legitimate policy must have no further effect). 
“No Slow Creep” Corollary – idempotence, together with bounded drift (Axiom 20), prevents a sequence of tiny admissible changes from accumulating unbounded harm; any attempt at incremental domination would require violating Axiom 18. 
Thm 6.13 – includes idempotence as a necessary structural invariant (legitimate policies must be repeatable without change, or else errors could compound). 
Non-extendability Thm – an extension allowing non-idempotent “ratcheting” operations (e.g., iterative enforcement that shifts state with each run) would break Axiom 18 and lead to insidious domination over time.

Axiom 19 – Directed Repair

Domination-through-Omission Lemma – uses Axiom 19 to assert that a repair operation $R$ was available which could raise a dominated agent’s standing or lower dependency; thus choosing inaction leaves an avoidable asymmetry intact. 
Corollary (Legitimacy of Symmetry-Restoring Acts) – since a repair $R$ never lowers any $σ$ or raises any coupling, it meets all legitimacy criteria; Axiom 19 guarantees that ending a domination (via $R$) cannot itself be illegitimate. 
Thm 6.14 (Persistent Domination Externality) – relies on Axiom 19 to conclude that any enduring domination triggers a “required repair” path; if domination were internal to the system, a repair operation would exist to eliminate it, so truly persistent domination signals a breakdown outside the axiomatic system (or in an emergency context). 
Thm 6.17.8.5 (Emancipatory Repair Existence) – depends on Axiom 19 (and Axiom 28) to ensure that for every ongoing domination or capacity suppression, one can find an admissible operation that qualifies as a repair and increases the affected agent’s standing or reduces their load.

Theorem: Universality of Σᴿ’s Invariants – uses Directed Repair to assert that without a guaranteed path to fix asymmetries, domination could become permanent.

Axiom 20 – Bounded Drift

“No Arbitrary Escalation” Theorem – Axiom 20, combined with idempotence, ensures that an agent’s standing or dependency cannot be dramatically altered in one step or through uncontrolled accumulation; any attempt at a multi-step exploit of small changes is precluded by drift limits and idempotence. This supports Thm 6.13 (Legitimacy invariants necessity) – without drift bounds, repeated admissible micro-changes could sum to a large domination effect, violating stability. 
Finite-Stage Legitimacy Theorem – uses drift-boundedness (with Axiom 18) to argue that any necessary adjustments to achieve legitimacy must converge in finite steps; an infinite process of ever-smaller changes would contradict the drift constraint and idempotence. 
Thm 6.14 (Persistent Domination Externality) – bounded drift (and ALRP) ensure that domination cannot “sneak in” via infinitesimal changes; if domination seems to gradually appear, some drift step must have violated admissibility, externalizing the cause of domination.

Theorem: Non-Extendability – requires drift bounds; an extension allowing unbounded incremental harm would break Σᴿ’s invariants

Theorem: Universality of Σᴿ’s Invariants – uses bounded drift to ensure no unlimited accumulation of micro-changes (no gradual erosion of autonomy).

Axiom 21 – No Internal Selector

Non-Determinacy of Legitimate Outcomes (Theorem) – directly grounded on Axiom 21 (and 22): if two distinct operations $F$ and $G$ both satisfy all Σᴿ constraints (Legitimate), the theory cannot prefer one over the other. The proof assumes a hypothetical selector and shows it contradicts Axiom 21, confirming that Σᴿ is a filter (blocks illegitimate options) but never an optimizer or “chooser.” 
Non-Extendability Thm (Case a) – an extension of Σᴿ that introduced a built-in choice function or optimization criterion would violate Axiom 21 (by creating an internal final choice mechanism), reintroducing a form of authority or domination. Hence no such extension is possible without breaking Σᴿ’s principles.

Axiom 22 – No Final Arbiter 
No agent or subsystem can be exempt from the above rules or have unilateral overriding authority.

Non-Determinacy of Legitimate Outcomes – also rooted in Axiom 22: no built-in hierarchy or “tiebreaker” beyond structural invariants; all legitimate policies are on equal footing in the theory’s eyes. Together, Axiom 22 and 21 forbid any privileged actor or procedure from imposing one of multiple legitimate outcomes. 
Non-Extendability Thm (Case b/c) – any attempt to encode a sovereign decision-maker (e.g. an “emergency override” not subject to repair, or a fixed hierarchy of agents) would violate Axiom 22. This axiom ensures structural symmetry of authority, so e.g. even a special “safety monitor” in an AI must operate under the same rules (cannot have unfettered power to break invariants).

Axiom 24 – Coupling Exhaustiveness 
All dependency links must be explicit (no hidden or undeclared influences).

Non-Extendability Thm (Case b) – uses Axiom 24 to argue that any covert control channel or implicit dominance (such as an unmodeled influence) would be surfaced as a Coupled relation; once explicit, it falls under Σᴿ’s constraints (and if it violates them, it’s disallowed). Thus, Σᴿ prohibits “invisible” domination – any form of one-way control must appear in the structure and thereby trigger remedial axioms like NRPP and ALRP. 
(Also prerequisite for quantitative Domination-Pressure metrics and any theorem quantifying “hidden influence;” it ensures all influences are counted in the formal system.)

Axiom 25 – Unique Dominant Coupling 
Each agent’s greatest dependency (coupling constraint) is well-defined (one dominant coupling type per agent).

Coupling-Sensitive Exit Theorem – uses Axiom 25 to reason about an agent’s dominant constraint when proving that an agent always retains the ability to exit their worst (most limiting) dependency. Identifying a unique dominant coupling $k$ for agent $i$ (via A25) is key to Thm 6.17.8.2, which ensures any operation $F$ must preserve $i$’s option to escape that $k$-coupling. 
(Also informs design of targeted “emancipatory repair” operations in Thm 6.17.8.5, by focusing on the dominant coupling to eliminate an agent’s most severe constraint.)

Axiom 26 – Risk-Load Monotonicity 
An operation cannot secretly reduce an agent’s accumulated risk exposure; risk can only be mitigated by true repairs.

No Risk-Laundering Theorem – heavily relies on Axiom 26: if an operation rearranged burdens such that an agent’s total risk load decreases without actually resolving any risk, that would violate this monotonicity. Thus, any scheme to “hide” or transfer risk without reducing it (a form of outcome manipulation) is ruled out. Theorem 6.21.5 (No harmful trade-offs) – uses risk monotonicity (and the Impact Hierarchy) to prove that one cannot justify high-severity harms by offsetting them with lower-severity benefits. A26 ensures that an agent’s risk profile cannot be improved (lowered) by simply redistributing or concealing risks rather than eliminating them.

Axiom 27 – Risk-Sensitive Symmetry 
Among agents with equal status, those bearing greater risk cannot be subjected to greater additional burdens.

Fair Remediation Proposition – uses Axiom 27 as a fairness constraint in any solution that involves risk distribution. For instance, in choosing between two equally legitimate interventions, if one option places more burden on an already at-risk individual, A27 would preclude that choice as illegitimate. (This axiom is implicitly applied in the hierarchy-of-impact analysis, ensuring, for example, that less burdened agents are not favored over more burdened ones when all else is equal.)

Axiom 28 – Exit-Preservation (for Dominant Coupling) 
No admissible operation may eliminate an agent’s ability to exit from their most dominant dependency.

Viable Exit Theorem – directly based on Axiom 28, ensuring that if an agent $i$ is strongly coupled (dominated) via a specific relation, every admissible operation must leave $i$ with a path to regain independence from that relation. This underpins Thm 6.17.8.2 (Coupling-Sensitive Exit Requirement) showing that an agent’s escape from their primary constraint (dominant coupling type) is always preserved unless in a bounded emergency. 
Thm 6.17.8.5 (Emancipatory Repair) – A28 combines with A19 to guarantee the existence of a repair operation that breaks $i$’s dominant coupling if $i$ is initially in a dominated state.

Axiom 29 – Remediability of Emergent Wrongs 
For any “emergent” (no-fault) harm condition, there must exist an operation in $O$ to repair it (systemic harms require systemic remedies).

Systemic Responsibility Proposition – invoked to assert that even if a harm (e.g., a loss of autonomy) arises from external or unassigned causes, the system is never permitted to simply do nothing; A29 ensures a remedy must be available in the model. This is used in the Persistent Domination Externality (Thm 6.14): if a harmful asymmetry appears that no agent caused, the only possibilities under Σᴿ are that either a repair will occur (due to this axiom) or that we have left the domain of the model (entering an exogenous emergency or an external failure)

Axiom 30 – Structural Debt Accumulation 
Any autonomy reduction (ARV event) increases a quantitative “structural debt” measure for affected agents.

Emergency Termination Theorem – uses Axiom 30 to formalize that any temporary suspension of invariants (permitted under emergency conditions) incurs a “debt” that grows as long as the violation persists. Thm 6.37.11 uses this to prove that emergency powers must be temporary: an emergency operation that continues indefinitely would accumulate unbounded structural debt, an unstable and illegitimate state, forcing a termination of the emergency or system collapse.

Axiom 31 – Debt Dissipation by Repair 
Any legitimate repair action must reduce the structural debt of every agent it affects.

Post-Emergency Restoration Corollary – complements the Emergency Termination Theorem by asserting that after an emergency operation, a sequence of repairs will follow to bring the system back into compliance. Axiom 31 guarantees that each such repair step actually “pays down” the structural debt incurred, gradually restoring the status quo ante. Thm 6.37.13 (Mandatory Restoration) depends on A31: once the emergency ends, the system must apply sufficient repair operations to drive the structural debt to zero, fully re-establishing all invariants

Axiom 32 – Public Frame (Contestability) Required 
Any operation that imposes binding constraints on others (a public act) must be justified within a shared rational frame (and open to contestation).

Contestability Admissibility Proposition – Axiom 32 is used to prove that if a proposed collective action ($F$) lacks a commonly accepted rationale or forum for appeal, then $F$ cannot even be considered admissible (see Axiom 33). In practice, this ensures any public decision has been through a deliberative process. Proposition 6.33.6 states that whenever $F$ would affect others’ autonomy and qualifies as a “public act,” it is subject to this axiom; otherwise $F$ violates contestability requirements and is invalid.

Axiom 33 – Frame Unresolved ⇒ Inadmissible 
If the condition of Axiom 32 is not met (no agreed frame for a public act), that act is disallowed.

Contestability Admissibility Proposition – Axiom 33 is the contrapositive enforcement of the previous axiom. It is invoked to conclude that any operation which agents cannot analyze or contest within a recognized common frame (e.g. a decision imposed without discussion or recourse) fails the admissibility test. Together, Axioms 32–33 underpin the requirement in Non-Extendability (Case c) that any “final arbiter” or unchallengeable decision procedure is incompatible with legitimate coordination. (If an authority’s decision could not be contested or framed in terms all can accept, it would violate these axioms.)

Formal Result → Axiom Dependencies:

This table lists each primary formal result in the paper and the axioms (and earlier results or definitions) on which it depends:

Formal Result (Theorem, Lemma, etc.)

Depends on (Key Axioms, Definitions, or Prior Results)

Theorem 3.6.1 (Consistency of Σᴿ) – There exists a model satisfying all Σᴿ axioms (hence Σᴿ is consistent).

Constructive proof by example model uses all Tier1 and Tier2 axioms: a structure is built such that each axiom (successor, nullity, non-dilution, capacity bound, no standing loss, symmetry, idempotence, drift limits, repair existence, etc.) is satisfied. In particular, it relies on Axioms 1–20 to verify each corresponding property in the model. (No previous theorems are required for this proof; it is a direct model construction.)

Theorem 6.1 (Non-Coercion) – Admissible operations do not reduce any agent’s standing.

Axiom 15 (ALRP) – The theorem is an immediate consequence of ALRP’s stipulation that $Admissible(F)$ implies $\sigma(F(i)) \ge \sigma(i)$ for all $i$. The proof essentially cites Axiom 15 directly.

Theorem 6.2 (Capacity–Standing Monotonicity) – An agent’s standing is bounded above by a non-decreasing function of its capacity.

Axiom 14 (CIA) – The theorem is a restatement of Axiom 14 in a theorem form. It establishes $\sigma(i) \le B(\mathit{cap}(i))$ for some monotonic $B$, which is exactly what A14 guarantees by definition.

Theorem 6.3 (Idempotence of Legitimate Ops) – Every legitimate operation $F$ satisfies $F\circ F = F$.

Axiom 18 (Rerunnability) – This theorem is proved directly from the axiom that legitimate transformations must be idempotent. It also uses Def. 21 (Unified Legitimacy) which formalizes legitimacy as including idempotence (among other conditions). In short: Axiom 18 + the definition of $Legitimate(F)$ immediately imply $F(F(i))=F(i)$ for all $i$.

Theorem 6.4 (Symmetry Preservation) – Legitimate operations preserve equality of standing among equally placed agents.

Axiom 17 (STC5) – This is a direct consequence of the symmetry-of-equals axiom. If initially $\sigma(i)=\sigma(j)$ (and equal capacity), A17 requires $\sigma(F(i))=\sigma(F(j))$. Thus no legitimate operation can create or exploit arbitrary disparities between agents of equal status. (Proof appeals to A17 and Def. 21’s inclusion of STC5.)

Lemma – Domination Through Omission – Choosing not to act, when a repair is available to end someone’s domination, constitutes a dominating operation.

Axioms 15 & 19 (ALRP and Repair) – If agent $j$ is dominated by $i$ and there exists a repair $R$ that would raise $j$’s standing (or lower $j$’s coupling), then doing nothing allows $j$’s subservient status to persist. By Axiom 19, $R$ causes no new harm, and by Axiom 15, failing to raise $j$’s standing when possible is equivalent to actively keeping $j$ down. The proof models “doing nothing” as the identity operation $Id$ (trivially admissible) and shows $Id$ violates ALRP if a repair exists.

Corollary – Legitimacy of Restoring Symmetry – Any operation that ends a domination (increases a dominated agent’s standing or removes a one-way constraint) is itself legitimate.

Axiom 19 (Repair) – By definition, a repair operation cannot reduce any standing or worsen any dependency. Thus, an act that empowers the previously dominated (or cuts a coercive link) does not violate any invariant (it satisfies ALRP, STC-5, etc.) and is admissible and legitimate. The proof references A19 to assert $σ(R(i)) ≥ σ(i)$ and $deg(R(i)) ≤ deg(i)$ for all $i$, meaning the “symmetry-restoring” operation $R$ passes all tests and so $R$ is Legitimate. (This corollary relies on the proof of the Domination-through-Omission Lemma above – if failing to repair is illegitimate, performing the repair must be the only legitimate course.)

Theorem 6.13 (Universality of Legitimacy Invariants) – Each structural axiom (ALRP, STC5, Rerunnability, Drift, Repair) is a necessary condition for sustained non-domination.

Axioms 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 (ALRP, NRPP, STC5, Rerunnability, Repair, Drift) – This theorem is proven via contraposition, showing that if any one invariant were removed, a counterexample model could exhibit a persistent domination scenario. For each axiom, the proof constructs or references a scenario where violating that axiom leads to an agent being dominated: 
– Without ALRP: an admissible $F$ could lower someone’s standing, immediately creating domination of that agent by those whose standing was not lowered. 
– Without STC5: $F$ could treat equals unequally, allowing an arbitrary advantage that becomes self-reinforcing. 
– Without Rerunnability/Idempotence: an agent could be subjected to a series of operations that cumulatively erode autonomy (each step admissible, but overall effect unbounded). 
– Without Drift bounds: minor repeated degradations could sum to major domination in the limit (no “drift budget” to stop slow erosion of autonomy). 
– Without Required Repair: a harmful asymmetry could persist forever, never triggering a restoring action. 
Thus, all these axioms are needed to prevent one agent’s sustained domination over another in a pluralistic system.

Theorem 6.14 (Externality of Persistent Domination) – If a particular group of agents’ autonomy suffers a lasting decline, then the cause must lie outside Σᴿ (a violation of invariants or an external/emergency context).

Axioms 15, 17, 18, 19, 20 – The proof examines a hypothetical sequence of admissible operations $(F_t)$ that, over time, produce a lasting autonomy loss for some agents $A$. It shows that such a scenario contradicts the invariants: 
– If autonomy is reduced and never restored, some operation in the sequence must have violated ALRP (standing non-decrease) or exit viability (which relies on ALRP/Repair), so the sequence wasn’t truly admissible (case 1). 
– Alternatively, if all operations were admissible, then domination pressure $DP$ would have to strictly decrease at some point by the Directed Repair axiom (case 2), preventing indefinite harm. 
– If even that fails, the only remaining possibility is that the situation was an emergency exception where invariants were temporarily suspended (case 3), in which case the domination is not an “ordinary” state but a special, bounded condition. 
Thus, enduring domination of $A$ cannot occur within the structural confines of Σᴿ; it must result from either a break in the rules (an axiom violation), which by definition is not an allowed sequence, or from outside the normal operation of the system (e.g. an emergency or external intervention).

Theorem 6.16 (Non-Determinacy of Legitimate Options) – Σᴿ cannot choose or distinguish between two different but equally legitimate operations.

Axioms 21 & 22 (No Internal Selector, No Final Arbiter) – Formally, this follows from the absence of any symbol or rule in Σᴿ that could order or select among permissible outcomes. The proof by contradiction assumes a choice function or priority rule for legitimate $F$ vs. $G$ and then uses A21/A22 to show such a function is not definable within Σᴿ (it would act as a final authority, violating the prohibition on built-in arbiters). (This result is sometimes described in text rather than labeled as a numbered theorem, but it is a crucial consequence of the axioms.)

Non-Extendability Theorem – Any attempt to extend Σᴿ with an internal decision-maker or hierarchy will violate core axioms, thus reintroducing domination.

Axioms 21 & 22, plus core Tier2 invariants. The formal proof examines possible extensions: (a) adding an optimization/selector function (forbidden by A21); (b) adding an unchecked “emergency override” or any agent with the power to suspend the rules (forbidden by A22 and A19/15); (c) introducing a fixed hierarchy of agents (forbidden by A22 and A17: it creates permanent standing asymmetry). In each case, a structural axiom is broken, enabling a domination scenario. Thus, Σᴿ is maximally strict—any further powers or exceptions would undermine its nondomination guarantees.

Finite-Stage Legitimacy Requirement (ensuring timely legitimacy) – Any necessary adjustments to satisfy Σᴿ’s invariants must converge in finite steps (no infinite “limit” processes).

Axioms 15, 18, 20 (ALRP, Rerunnability, Drift) – The argument: if an operation required an infinite sequence of smaller and smaller admissible adjustments to become fully legitimate, then before convergence it either (i) at some finite stage violates ALRP (a step lowered someone’s standing), or (ii) each step was admissible but then by Axiom 18 an idempotent state should have been reached earlier, or (iii) the changes never terminate, which breaches the drift bound (A20) limiting total successive change. Therefore, all invariants must be satisfied within a finite number of steps. (This is a corollary of idempotence and drift – essentially, “you can’t approach legitimacy asymptotically; you must get there in finite time.”)

Proposition – Capacity/Standing Link (Restatement of CIA) – Every agent’s standing is monotonic in its capacity.

Axiom 14 (CIA) – This proposition is a direct restatement of the capacity–indexed autonomy axiom in a more general form: there exists a monotonic function $B$ such that $\sigma(i) \le B(cap(i))$ for all $i$. As shown in Theorem 6.2, A14 itself serves as the proof.

Proposition – Independence of Axioms – Each axiom in Tier 1 and Tier 2 is independent (not derivable from the others).

Axioms 1–20 – This meta-theorem is demonstrated by providing or referencing models where all axioms but one hold, and the remaining one fails. For example: a model where ALRP (A15) is violated (e.g. operations that reduce standing) shows A15 is not provable from the others, and similar constructions exist for each axiom. Likewise, Tier 1 and Tier 2 axioms govern different aspects (recognition algebra vs. legitimacy conditions) and do not imply each other.

Theorem 6.25.1 (Thin Legitimacy Category) – In the category defined by legitimate transformations, there is at most one valid arrow between any two objects (preorder structure).

Definitions of $\mathcal{L}$ and Legitimacy Order – The proof uses the definition of the Legitimacy poset (where $F \le G$ if $F$’s effect is a subset of $G$’s effect on each agent) and the fact that legitimate operations must be idempotent and preserve the status of agents. Given any two legitimate envelopes $F_\alpha, F_\beta \in \mathcal{L}$, if both $F_\alpha$ and $F_\beta$ can transform into each other (i.e. $F_\alpha \le F_\beta$ and $F_\beta \le F_\alpha$), then by antisymmetry and extensionality they are the same operation. Thus at most one morphism exists between any two objects in the category of legitimate envelopes. (This result depends on earlier envelope constructions and Def. of the legitimacy preorder; no specific Tier2 axiom beyond those in the envelope existence proof.)

Theorem 6.26.5 (Legitimacy as Interior) – A legitimate state is an interior point of the admissible region (w.r.t. the upward-closed topology on state space).

Definitions of Interior & Admissible Region – This theorem is proved using the order-topology on the set of states: the “admissible region” is the set of all states reachable by admissible operations, and a state is interior if small admissible perturbations cannot lead out of that region. The proof uses the fact that a fully legitimate state can tolerate slight variations without violating invariants, whereas any state on the boundary of admissibility is one small step from a violation. Thus, by definition, legitimate states lie in the interior of the set of admissible states. (This relies on prior results that illegitimate states occur at the boundary of admissibility and that admissible transformations are continuous in the order topology, both of which are derived from the core axioms like ALRP, STC-5, etc., ensuring no “jump” to illegitimacy.)

No-Risk-Laundering Theorem – It is impossible to decrease an agent’s net risk exposure through any sequence of admissible transformations that do not actually reduce the underlying risk.

Axiom 26 (Risk Monotonicity) – directly invoked: if $F$ is a combination of actions that merely redistribute or hide risk without eliminating it, then some agent’s RiskLoad would go down while nothing was actually fixed, violating A26. 
Axiom 15 (ALRP) – prevents trivial “risk swaps” that effectively lower one agent’s risk by sacrificing another’s standing (which would be a disguised form of domination). 
This theorem formalizes that risk can only be reduced by genuine repair actions (that actually improve autonomy or safety), not by clever reallocation. It figures in extended stability analyses (ensuring transparency in risk-related outcomes).

Theorem 6.21.5 (No Hierarchical Harm Trade-off) – No legitimate operation can impose a higher-tier harm on one agent in exchange for lower-tier benefits to others.

Axiom 15 (ALRP) – forbids any operation that would come at the cost of reducing someone’s basic standing or fundamental rights (L1/L2-level harms) for the sake of another’s lesser gain. 
Impact Hierarchy Axioms (HI1–HI4) – impose a lexicographic priority of high-tier impacts (e.g. life, basic autonomy) over lower-tier considerations. Together with ALRP, these axioms ensure that no “the ends justify the means” scenario (sacrificing fundamental rights for aggregate utility) can be deemed legitimate. The theorem’s proof enumerates cases of harm/benefit trade-offs and uses the hierarchy-of-impact axioms to rule out those violating the tier order (e.g., inflicting an L1 harm to achieve L3 benefits is illegitimate).

Theorem 6.17.8.2 (Exit Option Preservation) – Even under constraints, agents retain a path to exit their primary dependency.

Axiom 28 (Exit-Preservation) – directly used to show that if an agent is, say, bound by a dominant coupling (e.g., held in an institution or coalition), any transformation must preserve that agent’s ability to regain independence from it. 
Axiom 25 (Dominant Coupling Uniqueness) – provides that each agent has a well-defined most limiting coupling; the proof focuses on that coupling type when applying A28 to show $i$’s “exit door” from the dominant constraint remains open.

Theorem 6.17.8.5 (Emancipatory Repair Existence) – For every state where an agent is significantly dominated (or at capacity limit), there exists a legitimate operation to increase that agent’s standing or capacity (a path to emancipation).

Axioms 19 & 28 (Repair and Exit-Preservation) – ensure that as long as an agent is recognized by the system ($\sigma>0$), there will be either a direct repair or a sequence of operations available to increment that agent’s standing or otherwise lessen their constraints. The proof uses A28 to focus on the most binding dependency and A19 to guarantee an operation can alleviate it. 
Axiom 14 (CIA) – ensures the agent’s capacity is the limiting factor; if the agent’s standing is at the maximum allowed by capacity, emancipation might require capacity increase (which the system can allow if it does not violate capacity bounds). 
Corollary – Formal “Right to Exit”: As a consequence, any agent who starts at non-zero standing can never be permanently trapped under another’s control – a structural analog of a right to liberation.

Theorem 6.37.11 (Emergency Window Termination) – Any suspension of invariants under emergency powers is strictly time-bound; structural “debt” will accumulate and force an end to the emergency.

Axioms 30 & 31 (Debt Accumulation and Dissipation) – provide a quantitative measure of how far the system has strayed from compliance and demand that any such deviation be temporary. The proof shows that if an emergency operation $E$ (allowed to violate ALRP, etc., in dire situations) continued indefinitely, the debt from A30 would grow without bound, which is unsustainable. A31 ensures that as soon as normal conditions resume, repairs will reduce the debt. Thus any $E$ must either be halted (when the emergency ends and repairs begin) or the system will collapse under unbounded debt – formally proving that emergencies must be transient. (This result builds upon ALRP/DRIFT/IDEMPOTENCE as well: even in emergencies, changes are bounded and must be reversible by design.)

Corollary 6.37.13 (Post-Emergency Restoration) – After an emergency intervention, the system must fully restore all structural invariants via repair operations.

Axiom 31 (Debt Dissipation) – mandates that each repair operation reduces the “structure debt” incurred. The corollary follows from applying a series of repairs until the accumulated debt from the emergency is eliminated (made possible by A31). In the proof, one argues that a finite sequence of repairs exists such that each step uses A31 to decrease the debt, eventually returning all agents to their pre-emergency standing and dependency levels (thus satisfying ALRP, STC5, etc. once again).

Proposition 6.33.6 (Contestability as Admissibility Condition) – No operation that requires contestation can be admitted without an open contestability channel.

Axioms 32 & 33 (Frame/Contestability) – formalize this requirement. The proposition states that if an action $F$ has RiskBearers or affects others’ autonomy (ContestabilityRequired), then for each affected agent there must be a mechanism to challenge $F$. If such a channel is absent, A33 triggers and $F$ is deemed inadmissible. The proof uses these axioms to conclude that any $F$ with un-contestable impact fails the test of legitimacy, as it would concentrate power without recourse – contrary to pluralist accountability.

“Minimal Extension” Proposition I.1 – The added axioms in Σᴿ⁺ (risk, contestability, exit, etc.) are each necessary to prevent new forms of domination; none can be removed without loss of safety.

Axioms 24–33 (Σᴿ⁺ Extensions) – The proof for minimality examines each optional extension in turn: e.g., without the risk invariants (A26–27), an AI could redistribute risk or choose actions that achieve overall benefit by unduly burdening one person (violating non-domination); without frame/contestability axioms (A32–33), an authority could impose decisions without deliberation or appeal; without exit/viability axioms (A28, etc.), the system could trap agents indefinitely in subordinate roles. Each extension axiom is tied to a formal result or example showing that its absence permits a violation of the core non-domination principle. Therefore, the suite Σᴿ⁺ is proven minimal: remove any one of these constraints and a counterexample to pluralistic legitimacy emerges (provided by the respective theorem or scenario in the paper).

Notes: Tier-1 axioms (the basic successor-based standing algebra) underlie all results but are not individually cited by higher theorems; they ensure the formal structure in which the Tier-2 invariants operate. Optional extension axioms (Tier-3, Σᴿ⁺) are included in the Minimal Extension result to highlight that each additional constraint (on risk, contestability, etc.) is needed for a fully self-contained non-domination regime. Any extension to Σᴿ that adds a decision-making power or relaxes an invariant is shown (by the Non-Extendability theorem) to violate one of the core axioms above, thus reintroducing domination.

Appendix N: Interpretive Implications of Structural Non-Domination

N.1. Structural vs. Moral Claims

Σᴿ does not encode moral, psychological, or semantic predicates. It defines domination, autonomy, and legitimacy as structural properties of multi-agent systems. Any mapping from these structures to moral or political concepts is interpretive and external to the formal system.

N.2. Filter, Not Selector

Σᴿ is a structural filter. It eliminates operations that violate autonomy-preserving constraints but does not select among equally legitimate options. This is formalized in Theorem 6.11 and 6.12 and proven in Lean and Coq. Any act of selection must occur outside the object theory.

N.3. Implications for Institutions

Because Σᴿ enforces non-domination structurally — without relying on intent, preference, or authority — it provides a new kind of accountability. Institutions that rely on discretionary authority or optimization-based decision-making may find Σᴿ’s constraints challenging. However, this is a feature, not a flaw: Σᴿ offers a domain-agnostic substrate for pluralist coordination that is structurally impartial and resistant to coercion.

N.4. Deployment Considerations

Σᴿ is suitable for:

AI alignment and safety systems

Governance protocols

Institutional audits

Distributed systems requiring autonomy preservation

It is not suitable for:

Systems requiring optimization over preferences

Hierarchical or sovereign decision-making architectures

Scenarios where domination is structurally required

Predicate Symbols (Relations and Properties)

Symbol

Type

Signature

Description

Part of

Coupled(i, j)

Predicate

Coupled: Agent × Agent → Prop

True if agent i is structurally coupled to agent j (i’s actions or state can constrain or influence j’s future options). Represents an existence of a dependency relation from i to j. (Not necessarily symmetric unless j is also coupled to i.)

Core Σᴿ

Admissible(F)

Predicate

Admissible: Operation → Prop

True if operation F is admissible, meaning it obeys the base (Tier-1) structural constraints – in particular, it does not reduce any agent’s standing. (Roughly, ∀i: σ(F(i)) ≥ σ(i). Admissible transformations preserve standing and other baseline invariants.) Every operation must satisfy Admissible to be considered at all; illegitimate operations are a subset of those that violate higher-tier conditions.

Core Σᴿ

Legitimate(F)

Predicate

Legitimate: Operation → Prop

True if operation F is legitimate in the full structural sense – i.e. F satisfies all required invariants for non-domination and autonomy preservation. In formal terms, Legitimate(F) holds if and only if: F is Admissible, successor-consistent (does not change any agent’s standing by more than +1), symmetric for equals (STC5), idempotent, and drift-bounded, etc. (Legitimate is essentially a conjunction of all Tier-2 structural predicates. If any invariant is violated, F is not Legitimate.)

Core Σᴿ

Idempotent(F)

Predicate

Idempotent: Operation → Prop

True if operation F is idempotent, meaning applying it twice has the same effect as applying it once. Formally, ∀i: F(F(i)) = F(i). Idempotent operations do not accumulate changes with repetition. (This is a required property for any Legitimate operation to prevent iterative drift.)

Core Σᴿ

Repair(F)

Predicate

Repair: Operation → Prop

True if operation F is a repair operation, i.e. it restores or improves autonomy without causing any new harm. Formally, Repair(F) means for all agents i: σ(F(i)) ≥ σ(i) (no standing loss) and deg(F(i)) ≤ deg(i) (no increase in coupling degree). In other words, F leaves every agent’s standing the same or higher, and coupling burden the same or lower – it only fixes asymmetries or leaves them unchanged. (Repair operations are the ones that correct domination or dependency without introducing new domination.)

Core Σᴿ

Null(i)

Predicate

Null: Agent → Prop

True if agent i has null standing (σ(i) = 0). Null(i) means i currently has no recognized standing in the system (an “unrecognized” or excluded entity).

Core Σᴿ (Tier-1)

Prime(i)

Predicate

Prime: Agent → Prop

True if agent i is a prime entity (an autonomy singularity). Typically defined as an agent with minimal standing and no internal composition or couplings: e.g., σ(i) = 1 and deg(i) = 0. Prime(i) indicates i is an atomic, independent agent (baseline unit of autonomy).

Core Σᴿ (Tier-1)

Composite(i)

Predicate

Composite: Agent → Prop

True if agent i is a composite entity. Generally defined as an agent that either has combined standing or participates in couplings (e.g., σ(i) > 1 or deg(i) > 0). Composite(i) indicates i is either made up of smaller units (via ⊕) or is enmeshed in dependencies. (It’s the opposite of being a standalone prime singularity.)

Core Σᴿ (Tier-1)

All defined predicates (like Legitimate, successConsistent, STC5, etc.) have formal definitions in terms of the core symbols; they are included here for completeness since they appear in the formal system.)

Appendix P: Independence of the Axioms

This appendix establishes that each axiom of the Σᴿ framework is independent – no axiom can be derived from the others. For each axiom, we provide:

Formal statement of the axiom.

Role/Explanation: the intuitive role of the axiom in the system.

Countermodel: a description of a model (or class of models) in which all other axioms hold but the given axiom fails. This demonstrates that the axiom is not a logical consequence of the others.

Conclusion: that the axiom is independent.

The axioms are grouped by tier. Tier-1 (Axioms 1–13) comprises foundational standing algebra axioms (the definition of the standing numeric structure and basic agent classification). Tier-2 (Axioms 14–20 and Def. 21) comprises structural legitimacy axioms (non-domination invariants). Optional extension axioms from the enhanced system Σᴿ⁺/Σᴿᴱ (Axioms 22–33) are also addressed where applicable.
