All axioms are stated in first-order logic over the many-sorted domain of Σᴿ (with sorts: $U$ for agents, $N$ for natural-number standing values, etc.).

Tier-1 (Σᴿ₁) – Foundational Standing Algebra Axioms

Axiom 1 (Nullity / Pluralistic Inclusion):

Formal: There exists at least one agent with zero standing:

Role: Guarantees the existence of null-standing entities (agents with no initial standing). This ensures the system acknowledges the possibility of a completely unrecognized agent and provides a “starting point” for inclusion. Intuitively, Axiom 1 prevents trivializing the concept of null standing by forbidding models in which every agent already has positive standing.

Countermodel: Consider a model where every agent has $\sigma(i)\ge 1_N$ (no agent is ever in state $\sigma=0_N$). All other Tier-1 axioms can be satisfied in this model (the arithmetic and structural conditions on standing and coupling can be upheld even if the minimum standing value in use is 1 rather than 0). However, Axiom 1 is violated, since there is no agent with $\sigma=0_N$ (the Nullity predicate is empty).

Conclusion: Axiom 1 is independent – it cannot be derived from the other axioms. Without it, one can construct a valid Σᴿ model in which no agent ever starts at zero standing, contrary to the intended principle of universal includability (that every agent could be initially excluded and then gain standing).

Axiom 2 (Successor Definition – Non-Identity of $S$):

Formal: The successor function is not the identity on $N$ (and has no fixed point): (Equivalently, $S$ is a function with no value $n$ such that $S(n)=n$.)

Role: This axiom ensures that the successor operator $S$ genuinely produces a “next” standing value, rather than leaving a number unchanged. In other words, it guarantees that advancing an agent’s standing via $S$ constitutes a real increase to a new value. This prevents degenerate interpretations of $S$ that would undermine the meaning of “successor” (for example, disallowing a model in which $S(n)=n$ for all $n$, which would make $S$ trivial).

Countermodel: Define a variant model in which the successor function is interpreted as the identity on $N$: $S(n)=n$ for all $n \in N$. In this model, an agent’s “successor standing” is always the same as its current standing. All other Tier-1 axioms can still be satisfied under this interpretation: one can maintain a coherent standing ordering, non-dilutive addition, and the prime/composite classification without requiring $S$ to change a value. (For example, standing values can be the natural numbers, but $S$ is interpreted as the identity function on those numbers, and $+$ is interpreted in a way that remains consistent with other axioms.) This model violates Axiom 2 because $S$ does nothing (for some or all $n$, $S(n)=n$), but it does not necessarily conflict with any other axiom directly.

Conclusion: Axiom 2 is independent. The ability to redefine $S$ as a do-nothing (identity) function without violating the rest of the axioms shows that the non-triviality of $S$ is not enforced by other axioms. Only Axiom 2 excludes such pathological definitions of $S$.

Axiom 3 (Successor as Addition – Successor Increments Standing by 1):

Formal: The successor of a standing value equals its sum with $1_N$:

Role: This axiom fixes the interpretation of the successor operator $S$ to be the “+1” function on standing values. It is the algebraic statement that each agent’s standing can only increase in discrete one-unit increments (no jumps larger than one, and no other strange behavior of $S$). It anchors the meaning of $S$ so that $S(n)$ truly represents “one step higher than $n$.”

Countermodel: Consider a model where the standing domain $N$ is the natural numbers (as usual), but define the successor function in a non-standard way; for example, let $S(n)=2n$ (doubling instead of adding 1). All other Tier-1 axioms can still be satisfied in such a model: there is still a null element ($0_N$ which yields $0$ under doubling, so $S(0)=0$ in this specific example, but we could adjust by defining $S(0)=2\cdot 0=0$ or $S(0)=0$ separately without affecting others), addition can be defined appropriately (one could define the “$+$” operation to coincide with this $S$ in an appropriate way), non-dilution and the prime/composite conditions can be interpreted in terms of this new $S$, etc. Notably, the axioms do not explicitly require that $S$ add exactly one. Thus the “successor” could behave, say, multiplicatively or in some non-linear fashion. This violates Axiom 3, which demands $S(n)=n+1$, but does not violate, for instance, the requirement that composite standing is the sum of parts (one can still define $\oplus$ consistently) or that standing increases monotonically (a doubling successor is still monotonic and non-identity).

Conclusion: Axiom 3 is independent. Were it omitted, $S$ need not coincide with the “+1” operation; the other axioms alone cannot enforce the specific additive nature of successor. Only Axiom 3 fixes the successor function to ensure it represents a unit increment in standing.

Axiom 4 (Initial Element “0” and Injectivity of $S$):

Formal: (a) $0_N$ is not the successor of any number, and (b) $S$ is injective. In formal terms:

Role: These conditions (familiar from Peano arithmetic) ensure the standing algebra has a well-founded “zero” element and that the successor function doesn’t identify distinct values. (a) says there is a unique minimal standing value $0_N$ with no predecessor – i.e. null standing is a “bottom” element that no one can reach from a higher standing via $S$. (b) says the successor mapping produces unique new values (no two different inputs share the same successor), which guarantees a well-defined stepwise hierarchy of standing without cycles or merges. These are needed for the integrity of the standing scale.

Countermodel: (a) Without the “no predecessor of $0_N$” clause, one could posit a model where $0_N$ itself is the successor of some other number. For example, let the standing values be integers mod 5 (a cyclic structure rather than the naturals) and interpret $0_N$ as having a predecessor (say $S(4)=0$ in this mod-5 arithmetic). Such a model could satisfy non-dilution (if composition still adds values mod 5), prime/composite definitions, etc., but it violates the intended well-foundedness of $0_N$. (b) Without injectivity of $S$, one could define a model where $S$ is not one-to-one. For instance, let $N={0,1,2}$ with $S(0)=S(1)=2$ (so $2$ is the successor of both $0$ and $1$). One can adjust $\oplus$ and classifications in $U$ to avoid contradicting other axioms: e.g., define $\sigma$ and $\oplus$ in a trivial way such that standing addition doesn’t reveal the non-injectivity (perhaps by making all agents have standing 0 or 2 only). This model breaks the injectivity requirement but does not automatically force a breach of ALRP or other Tier-2 invariants, since those focus on comparisons of standing, not the internal uniqueness of $S$ values.

Conclusion: Axiom 4 is independent. The other axioms do not ensure the existence of a unique minimal standing or the one-to-one nature of the successor step. Only Axiom 4 enforces these foundational properties (which ensure that “zero standing” is a proper base element and that $S$ generates an endless ascending chain of new values rather than cycling or collapsing values).

Axiom 5 (Non-Dilution – Additivity of Composite Standing):

Formal: The standing of a composite agent is the sum of the standings of its components:

Role: Also called the non-dilution of standing axiom, this ensures that combining entities (forming a coalition or composite entity $i\oplus j$) preserves the total “amount” of standing. No standing is lost or gained in the composition: the composite’s standing is exactly the arithmetic sum of the parts’ standings. This is crucial for preventing dilution of standing (where combining agents could reduce their influence) or amplification (where combining could unfairly boost influence). Axiom 5 guarantees a linear, additive measure of collective standing.

Countermodel: Define a model in which the composition operator $\oplus$ does not respect standing additivity. For example, interpret $i \oplus j$ as some fixed agent (or in some arbitrary way) without tying its standing to $\sigma(i)+\sigma(j)$. One could even define $\sigma(i \oplus j) = \sigma(i)$ (ignoring $j$ entirely), or some other function (like the maximum or a constant) rather than the sum. As long as this operation satisfies basic requirements (one can ensure other axioms hold by carefully defining $\oplus$’s effect on prime/composite status, etc.), the rest of the Tier-1 axioms are not violated. For instance, one can maintain a consistent successor function and classification of primes/composites in such a model while breaking additivity: say, let $\sigma(i \oplus j) = \max{\sigma(i),\sigma(j)}$. This model violates Axiom 5 (it is dilutive or at least non-additive) but does not inherently violate, e.g., the successor axioms or capacity constraints (since it doesn’t involve capacity yet), nor the definitions of prime or composite (as long as those definitions are adjusted to some consistent criteria).

Conclusion: Axiom 5 is independent. The other axioms of Σᴿ do not force the $\oplus$ operator to be additive. Without Axiom 5, standing could be combined in non-additive ways (potentially allowing collusion to “hide” standing by forming a coalition, or conversely to double-count standing), defeating the intended invariance of total standing. Only Axiom 5 prohibits such behavior.

Axiom 6 (Standing Value Non-Triviality):

Formal: There exists at least one agent with minimal non-zero standing:

Role: This axiom ensures that the system actually exhibits the first unit of standing as a realized value (and not all agents are either null or extremely high in standing). In other words, there is at least one agent who has exactly one “unit” of standing (the successor of 0). This is a technical axiom to guarantee that the standing scale is properly populated and that the system is not degenerate (e.g. with all agents null or all agents having huge standing). It complements Axiom 1 by ensuring not only that null standing is possible, but that the next level of standing (1) is also instantiated.

Countermodel: A trivial model that violates this could have all agents either null or with standing greater than 1 (for instance, every agent might have $\sigma(i)=0$ or $\sigma(i)\ge 2$, but no agent with exactly $1$). Such a scenario does not violate any arithmetic or structural constraints directly – one could have a universe in which standing values are, say, all even numbers or all zeros, and define $S$, $+$, etc., in a way consistent with those values. All other axioms (additivity, ALRP, etc.) could still be satisfied in such a restricted model, but Axiom 6 fails because no entity ever attains the standing value $1_N$.

Conclusion: Axiom 6 is independent. The other axioms do not stipulate that an agent actually have a standing of 1; they only constrain how standing behaves if it exists. Axiom 6 explicitly requires the non-zero minimum standing to be realized by at least one agent, a condition not enforceable by any other axiom alone.

Axiom 7 (No Permanent Nullification / Successor Availability):

Formal: In an equivalent form, “no legitimate system keeps an agent forever at zero standing.” In the model, this can be captured by saying that if some agent is at $\sigma=0$ while another is at $\sigma\ge 1$, then there must be an admissible operation that gives the null agent a successor standing of 1. Equivalently, one can define a predicate $PathTo1(i)$ meaning “there exists an admissible transformation that raises $i$’s standing from 0 to 1”. The axiom can then be stated as:

(I.e. it is forbidden for an agent $j$ to be stuck at zero while another $i$ has standing 1; at least the opportunity for $j$ to be included must exist.) In practice this axiom is often framed as: “In a legitimate system, no agent who is eligible for inclusion remains at zero standing”.

Role: This axiom (sometimes called the Autonomy of Inclusion or no selective successor denial) formalizes a core non-domination principle: every agent must be afforded the chance to be recognized (gain the first unit of standing) if the conditions for inclusion are met. It prohibits a system in which one agent is “locked out” at $\sigma=0$ while others hold power, with no possible transition for the excluded agent. In other words, it bans permanent underclass scenarios by requiring that a successor step to 1 is structurally available to any null agent (assuming any external eligibility criteria are satisfied—see Tier-3).

Countermodel: Remove Axiom 7 and consider a model with two agents: agent $a$ has $\sigma(a)=1_N$, agent $b$ has $\sigma(b)=0_N$. Modify the rules so that no operation can raise $b$’s standing to 1 (violating inclusion). For example, imagine that $b$ is simply declared ineligible for any inclusion operation (no $F$ exists with $\sigma(F(b))=1$). This does not contradict any Tier-1 arithmetic axiom or most Tier-2 axioms: we can still have ALRP (no one’s standing is decreased by any operation; here $b$ is just stuck at 0), symmetry axioms don’t apply because $a$ and $b$ are not equal in standing to start with, etc. Thus all other axioms can hold true in this scenario. Yet, intuitively, this model is coercive: $b$ is structurally excluded with no recourse. This is precisely what Axiom 7 rules out.

Conclusion: Axiom 7 is independent. It encodes a normative inclusion requirement that is not a logical consequence of the other structural axioms. Without Axiom 7 (and the associated “successor availability” principle), one can have a system where a subset of agents are permanently excluded (zero standing) while others have standing — a situation not prevented by the rest of Tier-1 or Tier-2 alone.

Axiom 8 (Degree–Coupling Consistency):

Formal: The coupling-degree relation (the function $deg:U \to D$ counting an agent’s incoming couplings) must agree with the coupling predicate. Formally: and moreover if $deg(i)>0$ then $\exists j$ such that $Coupled(j,i)$. Equivalently, $deg(i)$ must equal the number (possibly finite number) of agents $j$ for which $Coupled(j,i)$ holds.

Role: This axiom ensures that the numeric coupling degree $deg(i)$ (which represents how many distinct other agents have structural power over $i$) accurately reflects the reality of the coupling relation. If no one is coupled to $i$, then $deg(i)=0$; if $deg(i)>0$ there must be at least one coupler. In short, it prohibits inconsistency such as claiming an agent has a nonzero “dependency count” without any actual source, or vice versa. This is essentially a well-formedness condition connecting two primitives ($deg$ and $Coupled$) so that dependency count = number of dependency relations.

Countermodel: Take a structure in which we drop the coupling-degree consistency. For example, let $U={x,y}$ with $Coupled(x,y)$ (so $y$ has one incoming coupling from $x$), but assign $deg(y)=0$ (indicating zero dependencies) while still having $Coupled(x,y)$ true. All other axioms can be interpreted in this structure: we can satisfy standing axioms (assign $\sigma(x),\sigma(y)$ arbitrarily, etc.), and enforce ALRP, STC5, etc., since those pertain to changes in standing and symmetry, not directly to the integrity of $deg$. None of the other axioms will catch the mismatch that $y$ is in fact coupled but has $deg(y)=0$. Conversely, we could have a model where $deg(i)$ is nonzero but no actual $Coupled(j,i)$ links exist (an “imaginary dependency” that never materializes). The rest of Σᴿ’s axioms impose no direct check on that scenario.

Conclusion: Axiom 8 is independent. It is the only axiom tying the numeric $deg$ values to the existence of coupling relations, and removing it permits models where the coupling graph and the recorded dependence counts diverge. Only Axiom 8 guarantees the correctness of the dependency count.

Axiom 9 (Definition of Prime):

Formal:

Axiom 10 (Definition of Composite):

Formal:

Role: These axioms formally define the categories of prime entities (autonomy singularities with minimal nonzero standing and no dependencies) and composite entities (entities that either have higher-than-unit standing or are involved in dependency relations). They partition the set of non-null agents into “atomic” ones vs. those that are composed or dependent. These definitions are stipulated as axioms to incorporate the concepts into the theory’s formal vocabulary. They do not directly constrain the behavior of the system beyond providing the terminology, but they are used in other axioms (like Axiom 11, the Partition axiom).

Independence Consideration: Because Axioms 9 and 10 are definitions, their “independence” means that each provides a classification that cannot be derived from the other axioms. If one omitted the definition of, say, Prime, one could still have a model of the remaining axioms (with no predicate identifying “prime” agents). For example, a countermodel for Axiom 9 (Prime) is simply any model in which the predicate $\textit{Prime}(i)$ is not interpreted as $\sigma(i)=1 \wedge deg(i)=0$ (one could interpret $\textit{Prime}(i)$ as always false or always true, or some unrelated condition) while keeping all other axioms true. The other axioms (including the standing algebra and legitimacy constraints) do not force the specific identification of $\textit{Prime}(i)$ with $(\sigma(i)=1 \land deg(i)=0)$ — they use the concept of Prime in Axiom 11, but if one removed Axiom 9, the $\textit{Prime}$ predicate could be interpreted arbitrarily without immediate contradiction of others. Similarly, dropping Axiom 10 allows an arbitrary interpretation of $\textit{Composite}(i)$ independent of standing and coupling. For instance, one could declare every agent to be “composite” regardless of its standing or degree, and still satisfy all other axioms by appropriately weakening the meaning of Axiom 11 (or if Axiom 11 is also removed).

Conclusion: The prime and composite definitions (Axioms 9 and 10) are independent of each other and of the rest of the system. They provide necessary classification schemes that are not consequences of the other axioms. Removing either one allows models where the notion of “prime” or “composite” agents is unmoored from standing and coupling (or even empty/trivially true), without conflicting with the rest of Σᴿ’s requirements.

Axiom 11 (Prime/Composite Partition):

Formal: and these three predicates are mutually exclusive for any given $i$.

Role: This axiom states that every non-null agent falls into exactly one of the categories: Prime or Composite (and agents with $\sigma(i)=0$ are classified as Null). It is a completeness and disjointness condition on the classification introduced by Axioms 9–10. Essentially, if an agent is not null, it must be accounted for as either a standalone (prime) agent or a composite (dependent or higher-standing) agent, but not both. This axiom prevents any ambiguity or overlap in the classification.

Countermodel: Consider a model in which the classification is not exhaustive or is overlapping. For example, take an agent $u$ with $\sigma(u)=1_N$ and $deg(u)>0$ (so $u$ has minimal standing but is coupled to someone). In such a model, $u$ could be (according to Axioms 9–10) simultaneously Prime (because $\sigma(u)=1$) and Composite (because $deg(u)>0$), violating the mutual exclusivity required by Axiom 11. Alternatively, one could construct a scenario where an agent is non-null but designated as neither Prime nor Composite (for instance, interpret $\textit{Prime}(i)$ and $\textit{Composite}(i)$ both as false for some $i$ with $\sigma(i)>0$). Such a model can satisfy the technical side of other axioms: the arithmetic and coupling constraints can still hold, ALRP, STC5, etc., are about transformations of standing and are indifferent to how we label agents as prime/composite. Thus, nothing outside Axiom 11 itself forces the classification to cover all cases without overlap.

Conclusion: Axiom 11 is independent. It is the only axiom that asserts a complete and disjoint categorization of agents into Null/Prime/Composite. The other axioms do not preclude an agent from being mis-classified or un-classified if Axiom 11 is dropped. Only with Axiom 11 do we ensure a clean partition of agents into the intended categories.

Axiom 12 (No Return to Nullity):

Formal:

Role: This axiom forbids any operation from nullifying an agent that has positive standing. In plain terms, once an agent has a non-zero standing in the system (once they have been recognized and “counted”), no admissible or legitimate transformation may drive them back to zero standing. It encodes the idea that inclusion is irrevocable: an agent cannot be completely un-recognized or “erased” by any allowed process (except perhaps by exiting the system entirely, which is outside the normal operations on standing). This protects against operations that would strip an agent of all standing (e.g., expulsion or elimination from the system’s perspective) after they have attained personhood in the system.

Countermodel: Suppose we remove Axiom 12. Consider a model where there exists an operation $F$ (perhaps performed by some powerful agent or an authority) that can take an agent with $\sigma(i)=1_N$ and “reset” them to $\sigma(F(i))=0_N$. For example, imagine a system with an operation $F$ that, without decreasing anyone else’s standing, simply sets a particular agent’s standing to zero (essentially expelling them from recognition). This does not inherently violate ALRP (since ALRP prohibits standing decreases by admissible operations, but if we allow such an operation we are effectively saying this operation is admissible once Axiom 12 is gone). None of the other Tier-2 axioms explicitly forbids this scenario: one can satisfy STC5, idempotence, drift, repair, etc., in other respects, while permitting a “nullification” operation as long as we do not count it as illegitimate. Indeed, if Axiom 12 is removed, a powerful agent or system function could reduce another’s standing to zero; ALRP (Axiom 15) would classify that operation as inadmissible, but we could simply consider that operation exogenous or outside the admissible set, or bypass ALRP by claiming it’s an exceptional case. The key is that without A12, there is no absolute prohibition in the theory’s universe of discourse on a transition to zero standing.

Conclusion: Axiom 12 is independent. No other axiom guarantees that an agent’s standing, once non-zero, remains non-zero. Only Axiom 12 enshrines the irreversibility of inclusion. Dropping it allows models in which “undoing” an agent’s standing (turning someone back into a null agent) is possible, a scenario not prevented by the remaining axioms.

Axiom 13 (Monotonic Successor Growth):

Formal: Equivalently (as a statement about $N$), $\forall n \in N: S(n) > n$.

Role: This axiom asserts that the successor operation strictly increases the standing value. It is a monotonicity requirement ensuring that $S(n)$ is always “one step higher” than $n$ in the well-ordering of $N$. In combination with Axiom 3, this essentially means $S(n)=n+1$ and $n+1>n$, which aligns with the arithmetic of natural numbers. The purpose is to guarantee that each successive increment of standing truly represents a gain in standing—no stagnation or negative cycles are possible. It prevents pathological cases where, for example, $S(n)$ might equal $n$ (ruled out by Axiom 2) or be smaller than $n$. Together, Axiom 13 and the earlier successor axioms build the standard Peano-like behavior of the standing metric (0 is the least element, and $S$ produces an ascending sequence $0,1,2,\dots$ without loops).

Countermodel: If Axiom 13 is omitted, one could conceive a model where the successor function does not guarantee an increase. For instance, consider an ordered standing set that is not well-founded or where the “successor” sometimes returns a value that is not actually greater. A simple illustration: let $N={0,1,2, \dots}$ as usual, but redefine $S(n)$ so that for some $n_0$ we set $S(n_0) = n_0$ or $S(n_0) = n_0 - 1$ (violating monotonicity while perhaps still satisfying other conditions in a contrived way). Or a more drastic example: let $N$ be the integers (allowing negative values) and let $S(n) = n$ for $n \le 0$ and $S(n)=n+1$ for $n>0$. In such a model, $0$ is a minimum (no predecessor) and $S$ is injective (except on the negative side) and not identity on positive side, etc., but $S(0)=0$ fails the monotonic increase (and violates Axiom 2 as well in this particular construction). To focus on A13 specifically: one can use a non-standard model of arithmetic permitted by the other axioms to have a successor that does not increase value (e.g., mapping some $n$ to itself or to a smaller value, while carefully adjusting other functions). None of the other axioms directly prevent this: ALRP and other Tier-2 axioms don’t concern the internal ordering of $N$ except insofar as one-step changes, and Axiom 2 prevents equality but not the possibility of, say, $S(n) < n$. Thus, without A13, the standing scale could in theory have a decreasing or non-increasing segment.

Conclusion: Axiom 13 is independent. The strict growth property of $S$ is not implied by the rest of Σᴿ. Only with Axiom 13 do we enforce that each application of $S$ moves an agent to a strictly higher standing than before, reflecting the intuitive notion of “advancement” in standing.

Tier-2 (Σᴿ₂) – Structural Legitimacy Axioms

Axiom 14 (Capacity-Indexed Autonomy, CIA):

Formal: with $B: C \to N$ a non-decreasing function of capacity (i.e. if $c_1 \ge c_2$ then $B(c_1) \ge B(c_2)$).

Role: This axiom establishes an upper bound on an agent’s standing based on its capacity $cap(i)$. It encodes the idea that an agent’s recognized standing or influence should not exceed its functional capacity or competence. In other words, one cannot grant an agent more “standing power” than its intrinsic capabilities (for example, an AI or proxy cannot be given more authority than its measured capacity warrants). CIA is crucial for preventing scenarios where a low-capability entity wields excessive influence, which could lead to structural instability or domination by incompetence. This axiom ties together the quantity of standing with an agent’s capacity (often interpreted as ability, maturity, or resilience), ensuring proportionality between them.

Countermodel: Remove Axiom 14 and consider a model where capacity plays no limiting role on standing. For instance, imagine a system with two agents $x$ and $y$ that both satisfy all Tier-1 axioms. Give $x$ a very low capacity $cap(x)$ and $y$ a higher capacity $cap(y)$, but assign both agents a high standing (or even let $x$ have higher $\sigma$ than a more capable $y$). If we simply don’t enforce any relationship between $\sigma$ and $cap$, all other structural axioms can still hold: ALRP (A15) is about not lowering standing, STC-5 (A17) is about treating equals equally (which can still be done regardless of capacity values), etc. In this model, $cap(i)$ could even be a dummy variable with no influence on any other predicate. For example, set $cap(i)$ constant for all agents (so $B(cap(i))$ is the same for everyone, effectively removing any capacity-based stratification). Then obviously one can give an agent standing beyond what its capacity would normally allow without conflicting with ALRP or other axioms – because those axioms don’t reference capacity. This violates Axiom 14, but no other axiom notices the violation, since capacity was not constrained by any of them except CIA.

Conclusion: Axiom 14 is independent. The other axioms of Σᴿ do not by themselves ensure any connection between capacity and standing. Only Axiom 14 imposes that foundational link. Without CIA, an agent’s standing could be arbitrarily high regardless of its capacity, which is precisely what this axiom is meant to forbid.

Axiom 15 (Autonomy-Limiting Reflex Principle, ALRP):

Formal: No admissible operation may ever reduce an agent’s standing. In logical form: Equivalently, if there exists any $i$ such that $\sigma(F(i)) < \sigma(i)$, then $F$ is not admissible.

Role: ALRP is the fundamental non-coercion axiom: it declares that any operation which lowers someone’s standing is forbidden (in the sense that such an operation cannot be considered admissible in the system). This is the core safeguard against unilateral domination: no agent or mechanism is allowed to directly strip away an agent’s recognized standing or rights. ALRP ensures that standing is a non-decreasing quantity along any allowed trajectory: agents can maintain or increase their standing, but never lose it due to an admissible transformation. This principle prevents coercive power removal or demotion and is key to guaranteeing that once agents have standing, it cannot be arbitrarily taken away by the system’s own dynamics. (Any standing reduction would classify the operation as inadmissible/illegitimate, thereby disallowed.)

Countermodel: Suppose we drop Axiom 15. Construct a scenario with an operation $F$ that does reduce some agent’s standing, while satisfying all other Tier-2 axioms. For example, imagine an operation $F$ where $\sigma(F(p)) = \sigma(p) - 1$ for some agent $p$ (so $p$ loses one unit of standing), but for all other agents $q \neq p$, $\sigma(F(q)) = \sigma(q)$ (no one else is affected). We can further stipulate that $F$ leaves coupling degrees unchanged (so STC-5 symmetry can still be respected among agents of equal standing except $p$, and if $p$ was unique in standing or capacity this might not violate STC-5), and $F$ can be idempotent (apply it twice and $p$’s standing doesn’t go below the first decrement if we design $F$ to only remove one unit once), and does not introduce any new couplings (satisfying drift or NRPP conditions vacuously) – in other words, we try to violate ALRP in the smallest way possible while obeying other invariants. Without ALRP, nothing in STC-5, idempotence, drift, or repair explicitly forbids this one-step standing reduction for $p$. Indeed, one can craft a model where $F$ is considered admissible (since we removed the rule that it isn’t) and none of the other axioms catch the violation: STC-5 might not trigger if $p$ was unique in its class or if capacities differ, Rerunnability (A18) is not violated if $F$ has no further effect after the first application, etc. Thus $F$ could be “admissible” in the weakened system. This scenario demonstrates how a dominated outcome (agent $p$ loses standing relative to others) can occur if ALRP is not in place.

Conclusion: Axiom 15 is independent. It is the sole axiom banning standing reductions by system operations. The other axioms (symmetry, drift limits, etc.) do not inherently prevent an operation from lowering someone’s standing if ALRP is removed. ALRP’s necessity is evidenced by the ease of constructing a model (and an operation) where standing is lost without violating any other invariant.

Axiom 16 (Non-Retributive Proportionality Principle, NRPP):

Formal: Standing dependencies cannot remain one-sided among equals. One way to state this axiom is: for any two agents $i,j$ with equal standing and equal capacity, if one of them has no dependencies ($deg(i)=0$), then the other must also have none ($deg(j)=0$). Symbolically:

Role: NRPP is a symmetry-of-dependence requirement ensuring that among peers, no agent is unilaterally dependent on another. If two agents are in the same position (same standing and capacity), it cannot be that one is free of dependencies while the other is burdened by a dependency. In effect, this axiom forces structural reciprocity: any asymmetry in which one equal-status agent is subjugated to another equally-endowed agent violates legitimacy unless it is addressed (by increasing the subjugated agent’s status or removing the dependency). NRPP thus prohibits a subtle form of domination: an agent $j$ having the same standing and capacity as $i$, yet being under $i$’s power (coupled) while $i$ is free. It is a formal way to say “peers cannot have non-mutual power relations; if $j$ is constrained by $i$, then if $i$ had exactly the same status as $j$, $i$ must also be constrained in some way (hence, if $i$ has no constraints, $j$ can’t either).”

Countermodel: Without Axiom 16, one can have a configuration where two agents are equal in status initially, yet an operation introduces an unreciprocated dependency of one on the other. For example, let agents $a$ and $b$ both have $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=1_N$ and $cap(a)=cap(b)$ initially. Now consider a transformation $F$ after which $deg(a)=0$ (no one constrains $a$) but $deg(b)=1$ (now $b$ is coupled to $a$, say). If ALRP (A15) is respected, neither $a$ nor $b$ loses standing in this transformation; if STC-5 (A17) is not violated, we must be careful: here $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)$ and $cap(a)=cap(b)$, but after $F$, $\sigma(F(a))=\sigma(a)$, $\sigma(F(b))=\sigma(b)$ so their standings remain equal – STC-5’s condition is satisfied as long as $σ$ didn’t change, even though the dependency relation broke the symmetry. Rerunnability (A18) can be satisfied if applying $F$ again doesn’t further change anything (we can make $F$ idempotent by having it simply create that single coupling). Bounded drift (A20) is satisfied because the coupling increase for $b$ was only one step. Directed repair (A19) isn’t immediately violated by the scenario (it says any Repair operation must reduce asymmetry, but if we haven’t required a repair, it’s fine). In short, without NRPP, nothing in the remaining axioms forces $a$ and $b$ to have reciprocal coupling if they start symmetric. We have a persistent asymmetric coupling (one free agent, one dependent) among equals – a clear domination scenario that all other axioms allow when NRPP is absent.

Conclusion: Axiom 16 is independent. It addresses a specific pattern of domination (persistent non-reciprocal dependence among equals) that is not ruled out by any other single axiom. Only NRPP closes this loophole. Removing it permits at least conceptually the existence of models where two agents are equal in every respect except that one is subject to the other’s unchecked influence.

Axiom 17 (Standing To Coerce – STC5 – Symmetry of Equals):

Formal: Any legitimate operation must treat equal agents equally: if two agents have the same standing and capacity, they must end up with the same standing after the operation. In logical form:

Role: Often referred to as STC-5, this axiom is a formal equality/symmetry requirement: it forbids arbitrarily discriminating among agents who were initially at the same status. If two agents are identical in terms of their structural status (same standing and capacity), a legitimate transformation cannot raise one and not the other, or otherwise treat them differently, because that would create an unjustified asymmetry. STC-5 is crucial for non-domination because it prevents emergence of new asymmetries out of nowhere – differences in treatment must be justified by differences in the agents’ states (like differences in standing or capacity). It captures a formal notion of fairness or symmetry: “equals should be treated equally by the structure.”

Countermodel: Without Axiom 17, a transformation could create inequalities from equality. For example, consider a transformation $F$ acting on two agents $i$ and $j$ who start with $\sigma(i)=\sigma(j)$ and $cap(i)=cap(j)$. Imagine $F$ leaves $i$’s standing unchanged but increases $j$’s standing by one (or vice versa). This immediately gives $j$ an edge over $i$ that did not exist before. If we remove STC-5, nothing in ALRP (A15) forbids this (no one’s standing went down – one went up by +1, the other stayed the same), nothing in CIA (A14) is necessarily violated if both had similar capacities (or even if $j$ had a slightly higher capacity, but $i$ and $j$ were equal in standing, $F$ could choose to favor $j$), idempotence (A18) and drift (A20) can still hold (this could be a one-time +1 change, with no further effect), and directed repair (A19) does not force a repair because no one’s standing decreased or coupling increased – only a new asymmetry was created in standing. In short, $F$ could be admissible (it didn’t reduce anyone’s $\sigma$) and might satisfy all other legitimacy criteria except symmetry. Yet the result is that two agents who were equal are now unequal – a clear case of structural favoritism or domination potential. No other axiom prohibits this scenario (as long as the favored agent’s increase is within capacity bounds and no other invariant is broken).

Conclusion: Axiom 17 is independent. It addresses discrimination between initially equal agents, a condition not covered by the other axioms. Only STC-5 stops a system from, say, arbitrarily picking one of two identical agents and elevating their standing (which could be exploited to create dominance). Without A17, as the countermodel shows, the framework would permit the spontaneous generation of hierarchy from symmetry, undermining the spirit of nondomination.

Axiom 18 (Rerunnability – Idempotence of Legitimate Operations):

Formal: Any legitimate operation is idempotent, meaning applying it twice in succession has the same effect as applying it once. In formal terms:

Role: This axiom captures the idea that legitimate transformations should not accumulate further changes when repeated. If an operation is truly structurally fair and justified, doing it a second time in a row (with no changes in between) should not yield any new effect. Stated differently, any legitimate change is a minimal adjustment to the structure that “self-terminates” – once done, re-applying it doesn’t continue to change anything. Rerunnability is a safeguard against incremental creeping domination: it prevents a situation where an operation individually seems innocuous but can be repeated to gradually degrade someone’s autonomy. If $F$ is legitimate, $F \circ F$ must do nothing more than $F$ alone, ensuring that $F$’s effect can’t be compounded through iteration. (This also implies legitimate operations are reversible in a sense – since $F(F(i))=F(i)$, applying $F$ again doesn’t push things further.)

Countermodel: Remove Axiom 18 and consider an operation $F$ that, each time it’s applied, imposes a small additional burden on some agent (or increases some asymmetry slightly), while perhaps preserving standing and satisfying other invariants for each single step. For example, let $F$ be an operation that introduces a new dependency link from agent $a$ to agent $b$ each time it’s executed (increasing $deg(b)$ by 1) while leaving all standings the same (so ALRP is satisfied). If $F$ is not idempotent, then $F(F(b))$ will increase $deg(b)$ again. Without A18, nothing prevents repeated application of $F$ from continuously increasing $b$’s dependence on $a$ (or on multiple agents) as long as each individual application of $F$ is admissible (which it is, since no standing is decreased, STC5 can be arranged not to trigger if $a$ and $b$ started with different standing or capacity, etc.). Over an unbounded number of iterations, $b$’s autonomy can be arbitrarily curtailed (as $deg(b)$ grows without bound), creating a domination scenario – but one “step at a time” so that no single step was illegitimate. All other Tier-2 axioms could hold in each step of this process: ALRP is respected (standing never drops), STC5 might not apply if $a$ and $b$ differ initially, drift (A20) is respected in each step (each coupling increment is only one step), and so on. Thus, in the absence of A18, we can have a sequence of individually admissible operations whose composition has a highly domination-inducing effect.

Conclusion: Axiom 18 is independent. No other single axiom stops cumulative exploitation via sequential application. Only the Rerunnability axiom ensures that an operation cannot be used to “chip away” at autonomy through repetition – a protection that is not guaranteed by ALRP, STC5, or others if taken alone. Without A18, it’s possible to imagine a slowly worsening domination that escapes detection because it occurs through many small, individually allowed steps.

Axiom 19 (Directed Repair):

Formal: Any repair operation (an operation $R$ flagged as $Repair(R)$) must only restore autonomy and never cause new harms:

Role: This axiom defines what it means to be a repair operation: it can only increase or preserve every agent’s standing, and decrease or preserve every agent’s dependency degree. In short, a repair action may fix problems (raise someone’s standing, or remove/decrease couplings) but never create new ones (it cannot knock anyone’s standing down or introduce new dependencies). This ensures that repairs are safe and truly corrective – they don’t cause side-effects that harm someone else’s autonomy. Directed Repair is fundamental for guaranteeing that if an agent is in a dominated position, there exists a legitimate operation to improve that position without hurting others.

Countermodel: If we remove the constraints on what constitutes a repair, one could have an operation $R$ that is labeled a “repair” while actually causing harm. For instance, consider a model where we declare some operation $R$ as Repair(R) even though $\sigma(R(x)) < \sigma(x)$ for some agent $x$ (it lowers $x$’s standing or increases $x$’s $deg$). Without Axiom 19, the mere label “Repair” has no teeth; nothing in ALRP or other axioms automatically restricts an operation’s effects unless that operation is declared admissible or legitimate. We could simply say this harmful $R$ is not admissible (so ALRP doesn’t apply to it) but still call it a “repair” action in name. In the absence of Axiom 19, there is no requirement that a Repair-designated operation must obey any particular inequalities. Thus one could conceive of a structure where a so-called repair operation actually reduces someone’s standing or increases dependency (for example, an authoritarian “solution” to a crisis that in fact centralizes power, couched in terms of being a corrective measure). All other axioms could remain intact (the harmful “repair” might never be used in an admissible sequence or would be considered an emergency measure outside ordinary admissibility, etc.), so no immediate contradiction arises. For instance, we could have an operation $R$ that sets $\sigma(R(v)) = 0$ for some $v$ (a clear reduction) but still call it a repair – this violates A19 but if we drop A19, nothing else forbids misusing the Repair label this way. Even more simply, we can take a fully developed Σᴿ model and just relabel some non-repair operation as Repair; without A19, this causes no axiom violation except the one we removed.

Conclusion: Axiom 19 is independent. It is the sole guarantee that a “repair” truly repairs. The rest of Σᴿ’s axioms do not force an operation labeled as repair to be benign – only Axiom 19 ties the repair predicate to the condition of non-harm (standing non-decrease, degree non-increase). Therefore, dropping A19 would allow logically consistent models in which an operation is deemed a “repair” while in fact it causes harm (no other axiom would disqualify it just by the name).

Axiom 20 (Bounded Drift):

Formal: Any operation labeled as a drift $D$ can only make at most one-step changes in standing or coupling for each agent: Here $OneStepDiff(x,y)$ means that $x$ equals either $y$ or $S(y)$ or (in general, when defined) the predecessor of $y$ – in practice, since ALRP forbids decreases, $OneStepDiff$ reduces to “either no change or an increase of one” for standing, and similarly for coupling degree.

Role: This axiom limits the magnitude of change any single drift operation can induce. In effect, it requires that any admissible transformation (since any admissible transformation can be seen as a drift under some conditions) may increase an agent’s standing by at most +1 and an agent’s dependency count by at most +1 (and of course not decrease them due to ALRP). Bounded Drift is a safeguard against large, sudden structural changes: it stops an operation from imposing a drastic increase in someone’s power or dependencies in one step. It also works with Rerunnability (A18) to prevent a series of small allowed changes from adding up to a large change (since idempotence stops unlimited repetition). In summary, A20 ensures that changes to status or dependence happen gradually and in small increments, giving the system (and potentially the affected agents) opportunities to react or invoke repairs before a situation gets out of control.

Countermodel: If Axiom 20 is removed, an operation could cause an arbitrary jump in standing or coupling degree in a single application, while still satisfying other invariants. For example, consider an operation $F$ that increases a certain agent $p$’s standing by 5 (from $\sigma(p)=1$ to $\sigma(p)=6$) in one go, without lowering anyone else’s standing (so ALRP is satisfied for others and only positive jumps occur) and without introducing any symmetry violations among equals (perhaps no one else had $\sigma=1$ to begin with, so $p$ was unique). This $F$ could even be made idempotent by stipulating that any further applications of $F$ have no effect beyond the first jump (preventing cumulative changes beyond the 5-point increase). In this scenario, $F$ breaks the one-step drift rule by giving $p$ an outsized boost in one step, but we have removed that rule. None of the remaining axioms would catch this: ALRP allows increases in standing (it forbids only decreases, and here we increased $p$’s standing), STC5 only cares about how equals are treated (if $p$ was in a class by itself or if $p$’s capacity was higher, STC5 is not triggered), idempotence can be satisfied by our construction, and repair isn’t relevant since no one’s autonomy was reduced. Thus $F$ could be admissible and legitimate in the absence of A20, yet it enables a kind of sneaky domination: $p$ leapt far ahead of its peers in one move.

Conclusion: Axiom 20 is independent. The other axioms do not inherently limit the step-size of changes in standing or coupling. Only A20 does. Without bounded drift, a system could allow “jump conditions” or gradual but unbounded erosion of autonomy (if Rerunnability were also absent) that individually respect non-decrease and symmetry but collectively result in domination.

Definition 21 (Legitimacy, unified conditions):

Formal: An operation $F$ is Legitimate (i.e., satisfies all structural legitimacy conditions) if and only if it is admissible and satisfies successor-consistency, symmetry of equals (STC5), idempotence, and drift-boundedness:

(The predicates on the right are defined as: $successConsistent(F) \equiv \forall i:, \sigma(F(i)) \in {\sigma(i), S(\sigma(i))}$; $STC5(F)$ and $Idempotent(F)$ are as in Axiom 17 and Axiom 18; $Drift(F)$ as in Axiom 20.)

Role: Def. 21 is a conjunctive definition that collects the Tier-2 invariants into a single condition for convenience. It is essentially a summary of Axioms 14–20 applied to a single operation. It does not introduce a fundamentally new constraint beyond Axioms 14–20, but ensures we can speak of “Legitimate(F)” within the logic. In some versions of the framework, this definition is treated as an axiom or axiom schema (to allow using it in proofs). While it is not an independent axiom per se (it’s a derived definition from axioms 15, 17, 18, 20 and parts of 14, 16, 19), we address it for completeness.

Independence: Since Def. 21 is a logical combination of separate axioms, it is not independent in the same way as a fundamental axiom; it is derivable from Axioms 14–20. If any of the constituent axioms were removed, the definition of $Legitimate(F)$ would change (or the concept would need redefinition), but the consistency of the system would not be broken by the absence of the definition itself – one could simply not define $Legitimate(F)$ as the conjunction. However, if we treat “Legitimate” as an axiomatically constrained predicate (as some formalizations do), then to show its independence we argue: if the legitimacy predicate were not defined as the conjunction of those properties, one could imagine a theory where “Legitimate(F)” is either undefined or defined differently (even inconsistently or arbitrarily) while still satisfying each of Axioms 14–20 separately. For instance, without Def. 21 one could add a new predicate $Legitimate'(F)$ that does not require all those conditions, or simply have no single predicate capturing them, and no other axiom would force $Legitimate$ to have the intended meaning. In particular, it is possible to conceive of a model where $Admissible, successConsistent, STC5, Idempotent, Drift$ are all defined and hold as needed, but the predicate $Legitimate(F)$ (if it exists at all) is interpreted in a way unrelated to those (or only requires some of them but not all). This would violate the intended coherence of the term “legitimate.”

Conclusion: The unified Legitimacy definition is not provable from the other axioms – it is essentially a definition. If it (or any part of it) is omitted or altered, the theory does not enforce that the missing component is automatically satisfied. Each element (ALRP, STC5, etc.) is needed as a separate axiom; their conjunction as “Legitimate” is a matter of definition and convenience, not a theorem of the remaining axioms alone. (If one of the constituent axioms is removed, the equivalence in Def. 21 can no longer hold; thus the definition is also independent in the sense that it relies on each part.)

Extension Axioms (Σᴿ⁺ and Σᴿᴱ) – Optional Modules

(The following axioms belong to optional extensions (Σᴿ⁺ for pluralist safeguards and Σᴿᴱ for emergency constraints). While not every model includes these, when they are included they function as additional axioms. Each, if assumed, is independent of the others and of the core axioms. We outline their content and independence arguments for completeness.)

Axiom 22 (Standing Successor Realizability, “SSR”):

Formal: For every agent, a successor-standing entity exists: (Equivalently, the sort $U$ is closed under the operation of “someone having the next higher standing.”)

Role: This axiom, sometimes called the Standing Successor Realizer, ensures that for every level of standing an agent might have, there is some agent (possibly a hypothetical or actual one) that has the next level of standing. It’s a technical axiom guaranteeing no “dead end” in the standing hierarchy: informally, it says for every agent of standing $n$, there is (or could be) an agent with standing $n+1$ in the system. This prevents pathological models where, for example, agents can have a certain standing but no agent can exist with one level higher, which might break the interpretation of what it means to add one to a standing. SSR is related to the idea of the successor axiom in Peano arithmetic and ensures the richness of the standing domain. (In practical terms, it also means the system always considers it possible to imagine an agent with one more unit of standing – an important property in ensuring the system’s rules scale uniformly at all levels.)

Countermodel: Without Axiom 22, one could have a model where the standing domain $N$ has a “top element” or simply where $U$ does not contain any agent for some attainable standing value. For instance, consider a system with a fixed maximum standing $M$ (no agent can have $\sigma > M$), or a system where $N$ is infinite but we only populate $U$ with agents of standing $\le M$. All other core axioms might hold in such a system: ALRP, STC5, etc., don’t demand the existence of agents at every standing level, they just constrain how operations work on whatever agents do exist. As a concrete example, let $N = \mathbb{N}$ and interpret $S(n)=n+1$ normally, but restrict $U$ to contain only agents with standing in ${0,1,2,\dots,M}$ for some finite $M$. This violates Axiom 22 because there is no agent with standing $M+1$ even though $M+1$ is a valid standing value (the structure “stops” at $M$ in terms of actual agents). Yet none of the other axioms are violated: $0$ exists, $S$ works fine up to $M$ (except no instantiation at $M+1$), capacity and other constraints can be satisfied. Thus a model without SSR is possible and does not inherently contradict other axioms.

Conclusion: Axiom 22 is independent. It is the only axiom that ensures the standing ladder is complete in the sense of having a “next rung” for every rung occupied. Omitting it allows models where the standing of agents has a maximum or where some levels are simply unoccupied by any agent, which the rest of the theory does not prevent.

Axiom 23 (Local Successor Realizer, LSR):

Formal: For every agent $i$ there exists an agent $j$ that has the next standing and is not dramatically more coupled than $i$. In formula:

Role: This extension of the successor realizability axiom (A22) adds a condition about coupling degrees. It ensures that not only does some agent have the next level of standing above $i$, but one can be found at the next level without a huge jump in dependency count. In other words, any “next higher-standing” agent can be chosen so that its dependency burden is within one increment of $i$’s dependency. This prevents pathological cases where the only available agent at standing $n+1$ is, say, an all-powerful overseer with vastly higher dependencies (or none at all) – instead, one can always realize the next standing step in a way that is structurally continuous in terms of dependency as well. LSR helps guarantee a smooth gradation in both standing and dependency when moving up the hierarchy.

Countermodel: Without A23, one could imagine a model where whenever an agent increases in standing, the only available agents at that higher standing have dramatically different dependency profiles. For instance, suppose an agent $i$ has $\sigma(i)=n$ and $deg(i)=d$. If we drop LSR, it might be that the only agent with $\sigma = S(n)$ has a coupling degree far greater than $d+1$ (perhaps an “oligarch” with many dependencies, or conversely no dependencies while $i$ had many). Other axioms do not forbid that scenario: A22 (SSR) only assures some agent has $S(n)$, but says nothing about their degree. STC-5 and NRPP only apply to agents of equal standing (which $i$ and that $j$ are not, since $j$ has higher standing). Bounded drift (A20) concerns changes within one operation, not the comparability of different agents. So, absent A23, it’s possible to satisfy all core axioms with a model in which any time you look at the next standing rung, you only find agents whose dependency count is vastly higher or lower, introducing a large structural gap. Such a model violates the spirit of “gradualism” that LSR is meant to enforce, but does not directly violate any other axiom.

Conclusion: Axiom 23 is independent (within the extended system). It ensures a finer-gradation of the standing structure incorporating dependency measures, a condition not mandated by any other axiom. Without it, the framework allows jumps in coupling structure when moving between levels of standing.

Axiom 24 (Coupling Exhaustiveness – Typed Coupling):

Formal:

Role: This extension axiom requires that every instance of structural coupling be classified under a recognized type $k \in K$ (where $K$ is a finite set of coupling “kinds” such as IntDep, Comp, Emerg, etc., representing different modes of dependence). In other words, there are no “mystery” couplings – any dependency of $i$ on $j$ must belong to one of the defined categories (interdependence, compositional, emergency, role-based, teleological, etc., as introduced in the extended signature). Coupling Exhaustiveness means the list of coupling types is complete for the model: untyped $Coupled(i,j)$ is true if and only if there exists a specific kind $k$ for which the typed coupling $Coupled_k(i,j,k)$ is true. This axiom ensures structural transparency of influence: no domination can hide outside the taxonomy of coupling types.

Countermodel: Take a model with the coupling-kind sort $K$ and the $Coupled_k$ predicates, but drop Axiom 24. This allows a scenario where an agent $x$ is coupled to $y$ in the untyped sense ($Coupled(x,y)$ holds), but that coupling is not assigned any specific type in $K$ (no $Coupled_k(x,y,k)$ holds for any $k$). For example, $K$ might list only two kinds of coupling (“financial” and “informational”), and we have $Coupled(x,y)$ representing some other kind of influence (say, physical coercion) which is not labeled as either financial or informational, and we leave $Coupled_k$ false for all $k$. All other axioms can remain true: $deg(y)$ would count this coupling in the usual (untyped) way, ALRP, STC5, etc., are indifferent to the presence or absence of coupling types, and so on. Yet the model contains a hidden domination channel ($x$ influences $y$) that is invisible to the type-specific reasoning. Because $Coupled(x,y)$ holds but no particular $Coupled_k$ is true, certain extension axioms (like those that assign obligations or constraints to specific types of coupling) would not trigger. No base axiom detects this, because the base axioms (Tier-1 and Tier-2) don’t require couplings to be typed.

Conclusion: Axiom 24 is independent (in any extended theory that includes coupling types). Only this axiom forces every dependency to be “seen” in terms of a known mode of coupling. Without Axiom 24, an otherwise valid model could have arbitrary or illegitimate power relations that lie outside the regulatory scope of other axioms, effectively reintroducing a form of hidden domination.

Axiom 25 (Unique Dominant Coupling):

Formal: Each agent has a unique dominant coupling type that imposes the greatest constraints on it: Here $DomCoupling(i,k)$ is a defined property meaning that for every agent $j$ with $Coupled(j,i)$, the coupling kind is $k$ (intuitively, $k$ is $i$’s single biggest dependency category).

Role: This extension axiom asserts that even if an agent is involved in multiple kinds of coupling relations, one specific coupling kind can be identified as dominant for that agent’s state. This is useful in reasoning about worst-case dependency: for any given agent, we know which dependency modality is the most restricting or significant for them (e.g. maybe their “role-based” dependency is the greatest among all their dependencies, making role-type coupling dominant for them). The axiom prevents ambiguity in defining what that dominant mode is (the exclamation mark denotes uniqueness). Without this, an agent might have two different coupling types that are incomparable or equally significant, complicating reasoning about ensuring its exit or remedy.

Countermodel: If A25 is removed, one can imagine an agent $i$ that has two (or more) different coupling types that are equally constraining, with no single one clearly dominant. For example, agent $i$ might simultaneously be in an intensive interdependence (IntDep) with agent $a$ and a compositional dependence (Comp) with agent $b$, such that neither relationship is strictly “stronger” – perhaps $i$ is exactly equally constrained by both. All other axioms (e.g. exit-preservation, A28, which presupposes a dominant coupling kind, or others like capacity/standing constraints) could still be satisfied if we carefully design the scenario (the conflict is only in selecting a unique dominant coupling). By dropping A25, the system could have trouble deciding which dependency to address first in a repair or exit context, but it wouldn’t outright violate any remaining single axiom. In particular, the existence of multiple coupling types for $i$ doesn’t violate ALRP, STC5, etc., it just violates the assumption needed for certain Tier-3 rules (like A28’s formulation of exit along the dominant coupling).

Conclusion: Axiom 25 is independent (within the extended theory that includes coupling typologies). It provides a simplifying assumption (a well-order on coupling severity for each agent) that is not guaranteed by other axioms. Removing A25 does not cause an immediate logical contradiction with other axioms, as one can have models with multiple equally dominant couplings per agent, which the rest of the framework does not forbid.

Axiom 26 (Risk-Load Monotonicity):

Formal: If an operation $F$ makes any agent incur risk or bear a new burden, that agent’s cumulative risk load cannot decrease as a result of $F$. In symbols: Here $RB(F,i)$ (“risk-bearer”) means that agent $i$’s situation is worsened or altered by $F$ in any autonomy-relevant way (standing lowered, new coupling imposed, exit made less viable, etc.), and $RiskLoad(i)$ is a numerical measure of the total “autonomy risk” or burden agent $i$ carries.

Role: This axiom enforces a kind of conservation of risk: an operation cannot reduce an agent’s overall risk exposure unless it is truly a repair that addresses root issues. In practical terms, it prevents “risk laundering” or concealment: you cannot simply shuffle risks around or hide them – unless the risk is actually alleviated (which usually requires a repair operation), the total burden on each individual must stay the same or increase. This guarantees accountability: any operation that puts an agent in a vulnerable or burdened position cannot claim to have lowered that agent’s aggregate risk. It is crucial in ensuring that the system cannot fake improvements by transferring harm or risk in ways that aren’t real mitigations.

Countermodel: Remove Axiom 26 and consider a scenario in which an operation $F$ appears to reduce an agent’s risk without actually repairing anything – essentially a risk-laundering operation. For example, imagine an operation $F$ that redistributes responsibilities or danger from agent $x$ to others in such a way that $x$’s measured $RiskLoad$ drops, even though the overall situation hasn’t improved (the risk is just shifted or hidden). Without A26, nothing in the other axioms forbids an admissible $F$ from doing this, as long as $F$ doesn’t lower standing (ALRP), doesn’t break symmetry among equals (STC5), etc. Indeed, risk metrics are part of the extension; core axioms are silent about them. As a concrete model: let $RiskLoad(i)$ be some function that is normally non-decreasing, but define a particular admissible operation $F$ that artificially sets $RiskLoad(F(x))$ to 0 for some $x$ (clearing that agent’s risk record) while not actually changing any structural conditions for $x$. All other invariants like ALRP, NRPP, etc., could be maintained (maybe $F$ does nothing else but manipulate the risk accounting). No core axiom would catch this, because risk is outside their scope. Thus $F$ could be admissible and even legitimate by core standards while violating the intent that risk should not magically disappear.

Conclusion: Axiom 26 is independent (in any theory with the risk-load concept). It alone binds the behavior of the $RiskLoad$ function to the structural effects captured by $RB(F,i)$. Without A26, a model could allow “free” risk removal or concealment without contradiction – meaning the principle of risk accountability would fail.

Axiom 27 (Risk-Sensitive Symmetry):

Formal: Strengthening STC5 with attention to risk loads: among agents of equal standing and capacity, an agent with a higher risk load should not lose more standing than one with a lower risk load. Formally one can express it as:

Role: This axiom introduces a fairness criterion based on historical or contextual risk exposure. It refines the symmetry condition (STC5) by saying if two agents are otherwise equal, the one that has already endured more risk or burden should not be treated worse (in terms of losing standing or receiving a smaller increase) than one with less prior risk. In essence, it ensures that the system is sensitive to the distribution of past burdens: it will not pile additional disadvantages on those who have already been more heavily burdened, at least not when comparing them to similarly situated peers. This is a formal expression of a “levelling” or compensatory fairness principle.

Countermodel: Without A27, a legitimate operation could inadvertently or intentionally prefer agents who had less prior risk, undermining fairness. For example, consider two agents $i$ and $j$ with equal standing and capacity, but suppose $i$ has a higher $RiskLoad$ (perhaps $i$ has been subjected to more past burdens or dangers in the system than $j$ has). If A27 is removed, it is possible for a legitimate operation $F$ to reduce $i$’s standing (or fail to increase it) while increasing $j$’s, even though $i$ was the more at-risk agent. This would create or exacerbate an imbalance. A concrete scenario: $i$ and $j$ both have $\sigma=5$, $cap=5$, but $RiskLoad(i)=3$ (higher past exposure) and $RiskLoad(j)=1$. An operation $F$ might keep $\sigma(F(i))=5$ but raise $\sigma(F(j))$ to 6. If ALRP (A15) is enforced, $i$ didn’t lose standing (so okay by ALRP), STC5 doesn’t strictly apply because $cap(i)=cap(j)$ and $\sigma$ were equal initially *and remain equal in that $i$’s $\sigma$ didn’t change? Actually in this scenario, $\sigma(j)$ increased and $\sigma(i)$ stayed same, so now $\sigma(F(i)) < \sigma(F(j))$, meaning STC5 is violated because $i,j$ started equal. Perhaps better: imagine $i$ and $j$ had equal capacity but $i$ had slightly higher standing initially – STC5 wouldn’t relate them because their standing isn’t equal, and $F$ might raise the lower-risk agent’s standing to catch up, but not raise the higher-risk agent’s standing, achieving equality in standing while the risk loads differ.) In any event, if STC5 is satisfied or not triggered, the operation could slip through as legitimate by core criteria, yet it clearly disadvantages the one who already bore more risk. None of the core axioms incorporate $RiskLoad$ or this kind of historical sensitivity, so they wouldn’t object. Only A27 addresses this.

Conclusion: Axiom 27 is independent. It adds a nuance of fairness not accounted for by the other invariants. Without it, even a system that obeys ALRP and STC5 might still allocate upgrades or resources in a way that neglects past burdens, which is a scenario the core theory permits in the absence of A27.

Axiom 28 (Exit-Preservation for Dominant Coupling):

Formal: Whenever an operation affects an agent who is dominantly coupled, it must preserve that agent’s ability to exit from its dominant dependency. In formal terms, if $k$ is agent $i$’s unique dominant coupling type (from A25) and $F$ is any operation, then Here $ExitPreserved_k(F,i)$ means that after operation $F$, agent $i$ either remains uncoupled in mode $k$ or still has the option to sever any new $k$-type coupling introduced by $F$ (precisely defined in the extension as an “exit viability” condition specific to coupling kind $k$).

Role: This axiom is a specialized safeguard of exit rights: it ensures that if an operation $F$ involves agent $i$ in its most critical dependency (in the mode $k$ that constrains $i$ the most), then $F$ cannot take away $i$’s ability to exit that dependency structure. In other words, even if $F$ might impose some change on $i$ (e.g., put $i$ under an authority in mode $k$), it cannot permanently trap $i$ in that state – $i$ must retain the structural possibility of uncoupling from that dominant relation. This is important to prevent operations from locking an agent into a subservient role without recourse. A28 extends the basic exit/repair principles to each category of coupling: it’s a promise that for each type of domination, the agent can find a way out.

Countermodel: If Axiom 28 is omitted, one can conceive a scenario where an operation $F$ introduces a new dominant coupling for some agent $i$ and simultaneously eliminates $i$’s ability to sever or escape that coupling. For example, suppose $k$ is $i$’s dominant dependency type (say $i$ is now in an “Emerg” emergency chain under another agent’s control). If $F$ creates this emergency coupling and also removes any alternative options or future transformations that would allow $i$ to exit (perhaps by altering the structure so that no repair in mode $k$ is available), then $i$ is effectively locked in. Without A28, no axiom explicitly forbids this: ALRP (A15) only cares about standing, STC5 (A17) is about symmetric treatment of equals, Rerunnability (A18) and drift (A20) concern quantitative changes, and even A19 (Repair) does not guarantee that a repair exists, only constrains what a repair does if one is performed. A25 gave us a dominant coupling but without A28, there is no rule that that dominant coupling must be escapable. Thus we could have a model where, say, an emergency authority $F$ temporarily suspends some invariants and puts $i$ under control of $j$ (dominant “Emerg” coupling) and closes all doors for $i$ to exit that emergency (no repair or alternative provided). Other axioms can still be satisfied in this emergency scenario except for the missing exit guarantee.

Conclusion: Axiom 28 is independent (in any system where exit rights are considered). It is the only axiom that formally guarantees an agent’s escape hatch from its worst domination. Without A28, an agent could be structurally stuck in a dominant-subordinate relation with no path out, even if other constraints (no one reduced its standing, etc.) were respected.

Axiom 29 (Emergent Wrong Repair Obligation):

Formal:

Role: This axiom addresses independently emergent wrongs – situations where a harmful or autonomy-undermining state arises from structural factors or system dynamics rather than a particular agent’s action. Axiom 29 imposes a duty that whenever such a state occurs, there must exist a repair operation to correct it. In other words, the system is not allowed to admit a harmful condition for which it has no remedy merely because no single agent “caused” it. This axiom ensures the remediability of structural problems: even if a harm (like a drastic loss of autonomy or safety) emerges without direct culpability, the system must still provide a fix. It is a way of saying the system takes responsibility for adverse conditions that “just happen” (e.g., systemic risks or failures), by guaranteeing that a remedy is available.

Countermodel: Without A29, one could have a model where certain states of the system are recognized as violating autonomy or safety (the predicate $EmergentWrong(s)$ holds for some state $s$ – meaning, for example, that an agent’s basic needs or autonomy are compromised by external circumstances), yet no repair operation exists to rectify that situation. For instance, consider a system state $P$ in which, due to an environmental disaster or an unintended side-effect of many small actions, an agent $u$’s basic autonomy is below acceptable levels (an “emergent wrong”), and assume this occurred without any single agent’s direct wrongdoing. If we do not require a repair, the system might simply say “this is unfortunate but no one violated a rule, so no fix is mandated.” All other axioms could still hold: ALRP, STC5, etc., govern how operations can or cannot reduce standing or create asymmetries, but they don’t guarantee that an operation to increase someone’s standing or restore their autonomy exists. In this countermodel, $EmergentWrong(P)$ is true (so $u$ is, say, below survival-level autonomy), yet for every operation $R \in O$, either $R$ is not a repair or $R(P)$ is still in a state of emergent wrong for $u$. Without A29, this situation – a persistent harm with no available fix – does not violate any other axiom; it’s just an absence of a positive remedy rather than a forbidden action.

Conclusion: Axiom 29 is independent (in any theory that includes the concept of emergent wrongs). Only A29 compels the existence of a remedy for harm that arises without direct violation of other rules. Without it, the system can satisfy all “don’t do harm” rules and still end up in a condition where harm has occurred and there’s no path to recovery – a scenario A29 was formulated to avoid.

Axiom 30 (Structural Debt Accumulation):

Formal:

Role: This axiom defines how the system tracks structural debt, which is essentially a measure of unresolved autonomy reduction or accrued “domination damage” that an agent $i$ has suffered. Axiom 30 says that if an operation $F$ introduces any Autonomy-Reducing Variable (ARV) for agent $i$ (i.e., if $F$ in some way reduces $i$’s future options or autonomy, such as by forcing a choice, blocking exit, creating an inescapable dependency, etc.), then $i$’s structural debt is incremented (one successor step higher) in the resulting state. The idea is to count any instance of autonomy reduction as a debt that the system must eventually “pay back” (via repairs or other measures). This mechanism ensures that even if a temporary exception or harm is allowed (like in an emergency), it is accounted for and not forgotten.

Countermodel: If Axiom 30 is removed, the system might allow autonomy-reducing actions without tallying any debt. For example, consider a model where ARV conditions (Autonomy-Reducing Variables such as forced choice or exit blockage) can occur, yet the function $StructuralDebt(i)$ is interpreted as always zero (or is not incremented by those ARVs). All other axioms can remain true: ALRP might be suspended in an emergency situation (or the ARV could be something like forced choice that doesn’t technically lower $σ$ so ALRP isn’t violated), STC5 doesn’t speak to this situation, and so on. Without A30, the theory imposes no “memory” of the event. Thus you could have an agent’s autonomy reduced (say, temporarily locking them in a building during an emergency – an ARV condition) with no record that anything is amiss once the immediate situation passes. This violates the intent of structural accountability, but no other axiom would register a violation, since ALRP forbids only standing decreases (our scenario might not reduce $σ$), and others like A28 (exit preservation) might technically hold if eventually the agent is let out. The key difference is that without A30, the system doesn’t accumulate any obligation to fix what happened.

Conclusion: Axiom 30 is independent (for systems that include the structural debt concept). It is the unique rule that memorializes autonomy reductions. If omitted, one can construct scenarios where autonomy is chipped away or temporarily suppressed without any lasting metric of that suppression, and no other axiom will impose a penalty or acknowledge the harm.

Axiom 31 (Debt Dissipation by Repair):

Formal:

Role: This axiom complements A30 by requiring that any true repair action must reduce the structural debt of every agent it affects. In essence, each repair should “pay down” the autonomy debt that was previously accumulated. Together with A30, this ensures that any temporary violation of autonomy (which increased $StructuralDebt$) is eventually compensated: a valid repair always lessens the debt (for example, by restoring lost autonomy or resolving dependencies) rather than leaving it unchanged. It guarantees that repairs are effective in making forward progress toward restoring full autonomy and are not merely stopping further damage. Without A31, a so-called repair could be a no-op with respect to structural debt – meaning it doesn’t actually mend the prior harms – which would allow an illusion of compliance.

Countermodel: Without A31, one could label an operation $R$ as a Repair even if it does not improve structural debt. For example, consider a system where $StructuralDebt(i)$ is increased whenever $i$ suffers an autonomy reduction (if A30 is present), but imagine a “repair” operation $R$ that does something inconsequential – say, it changes some unrelated variable or provides a minor benefit that does not actually reduce any agent’s dependencies or increase their standing. This operation could be designated as Repair(R) (satisfying A19 by not harming anyone further), but if A31 is absent, there is no requirement that $StructuralDebt$ decrease. Thus the debt counts (the measure of unresolved domination) might remain high or unchanged after what is nominally a “repair,” meaning the underlying asymmetry wasn’t really fixed. Yet all other axioms could be satisfied: ALRP and others allow standing to stay the same or increase; STC5, idempotence, drift are not violated if $R$ essentially does nothing structurally; even A30 (if present) would allow structural debt to persist or increase until a real repair occurs, but without A31 it’s possible no operation actually reduces the debt. Hence a model could obey everything except the obligation to actually reduce debt when repairing.

Conclusion: Axiom 31 is independent (in any system using structural debt accounting). It uniquely enforces that repairs must make tangible progress. Without it, the system could acknowledge autonomy debts (via A30) but never require paying them off – a scenario not prevented by any other single axiom.

Axiom 32 (Public Frame (PFA) Requirement – Contestability):

Formal: If an operation is a public act (i.e. a decision that affects multiple agents and is meant to have collective, binding force) and it is not an emergency, then a public frame agreement must be resolved before the act can be taken. In logical form:

Role: This axiom comes from the extension dealing with contestability and shared frames. It requires that for any collective decision or public policy (PublicAct), there must be an agreed-upon justificatory frame (a shared context or rationale $f$ that has been endorsed by the agents, often through a Public Frame Agreement process) in place before that action can proceed. In effect, Axiom 32 says “no public action without public justification/agreement.” This ensures that the system cannot take a unilateral public action (that affects everyone) without going through a process of establishing a common reasoning frame or gathering the necessary endorsements from participants. It’s a formal way to secure transparency and participatory legitimacy for collective decisions.

Countermodel: Take a system without A32. It’s easy to imagine a model where a certain operation $F$ is a major policy applied to all agents (so $PublicAct(F)$ is true) and no emergency is declared, yet $F$ is implemented without any agreed public frame. For instance, one could have $PFAResolved(F)$ be false (no shared agreement on $F$’s justification), and simply not include any check for that in the admissibility conditions. If other axioms hold, $F$ might still satisfy ALRP (suppose $F$ doesn’t reduce anyone’s standing), STC5 (it treats equals equally, say it affects all agents uniformly or only one class of agents with a good reason but that reason isn’t mutually agreed), and so on. Idempotence, drift, and repair could also be satisfied. Nothing in ALRP or STC5 demands a public deliberation or agreement; those axioms are silent about the process by which $F$ was chosen. In this countermodel, the system essentially behaves as a benevolent dictator: it enforces all the structural protections (no one’s standing drops, etc.) but does not allow debate or contestation – decisions are made unilaterally. This does not violate any core invariant except the public framing requirement (since we removed it).

Conclusion: Axiom 32 is independent (in any system implementing contestability features). Only A32 mandates the deliberative aspect of legitimacy.
