The other axioms guarantee non-domination in outcomes (e.g. no loss of standing), but not the process of decision-making. Without A32, a model can obey all the non-domination constraints yet still impose policies autocratically without a shared frame – a scenario inconsistent with the full pluralist vision but not ruled out by the rest of the axioms.

Axiom 33 (Contestation Condition – Appeal/Frame Failure Blocks Admissibility):

Formal:

Role: This final extension axiom is a direct complement to A32: it states that if the required public frame or contestation process has not been successfully completed (i.e. $F$ lacks proper justification or unresolved objections remain), then $F$ cannot be considered admissible. In plain terms, if the system hasn’t achieved consensus or properly handled dissent for a public decision, that decision is structurally disallowed. Axiom 33 thus encodes a strict “no un-consented policy changes” rule: any operation that should be contested or justified but isn’t, is automatically illegitimate. This axiom, together with A32, embeds the principle of contestability and transparency into the logic of Σᴿ.

Countermodel: Without A33, even if one assumes A32 (requiring a frame for public acts), that requirement could be violated without automatically stopping the operation. For example, consider a model where public actions normally are supposed to have a frame but there is no rule linking the absence of a frame to inadmissibility. One can then have a public operation $F$ for which $PFAResolved(F)$ is false (no consensus frame) but still treat $F$ as admissible and even legitimate. If A33 is not present, $F$ could proceed as long as it doesn’t violate ALRP, STC5, etc. Imagine a scenario: a new policy $F$ is enacted by a central authority without consulting others (so no public agreement). If $F$ doesn’t reduce anyone’s standing (ALRP ok), perhaps even increases some standings, treats all equals the same (so STC5 ok), and is idempotent and drift-bounded (maybe $F$ is a one-time policy change), then $F$ would satisfy all structural invariants except the missing public contestation. The system would thereby allow an uncontested policy change, a form of procedural domination, but one that wouldn’t necessarily violate the other axioms.

Conclusion: Axiom 33 is independent (when contestation requirements are part of the theory). It alone provides the link between the process of contestation and the admissibility of outcomes. Without A33, the absence of a PFA resolution or appeal mechanism does not inherently trigger any other axiom’s violation – thus an autocratic decision could slip through the structural net. A33 closes that gap by declaring unframed or uncontestable acts as inadmissible.

Independence Summary and Notes

Each Tier-1 axiom (Axioms 1–13) is independent. Removing any one of the Tier-1 axioms results in a model of Σᴿ₁ that violates the intended property of that axiom while still satisfying the others. For example, without Nullity (A1) one can have no initial zero-standing agents; without Non-Dilution (A5) one can define standing aggregation arbitrarily, etc. Each foundational axiom addresses a unique aspect of the standing algebra (successor arithmetic, standing measurement, or category of agents) that is not enforced by the rest. In particular, the arithmetic properties of $S$ (having a 0, being injective, etc.) are not guaranteed unless explicitly axiomatised – a model that violates them can often be concocted without breaking other axioms. Definitions like Prime/Composite are likewise independent stipulations (the theory wouldn’t know what “Prime” means or that every entity must be prime/composite unless we assert it).

Each Tier-2 axiom (Axioms 14–20) is independent. As a set, these invariants collectively ensure non-domination (see Theorem 21.1), but if any single one is removed, a domination scenario becomes possible without contradicting the remaining axioms. We have provided explicit constructions to show how domination (or a violation of the intuitions of autonomy preservation) can occur when each invariant is omitted in turn. For example, dropping ALRP allows “slow erosion” of standing; dropping STC-5 allows arbitrary favoritism among equals; dropping Rerunnability or Drift allows gradual or immediate buildup of domination through iterative or large-step changes; dropping Repair means asymmetries need not be corrected. Each axiom thus addresses a distinct dimension of structural autonomy, and none is redundant. Moreover, Tier-2 axioms are not derivable from Tier-1 axioms (which deal with the standing algebra, not with dynamic transformations), and conversely Tier-1 axioms are not derivable from Tier-2 (Tier-2 doesn’t constrain the arithmetic of standing or basic definitions). The two tiers govern different aspects and neither implies the other; this separation of concerns is deliberate and ensured by design.

Each extension axiom (Axioms 22–33) is independent of the core axioms and of each other. The extended axioms introduce additional constraints (coupling typology, risk accounting, contestability, etc.) that are not consequences of Tier-1 or Tier-2 alone. We have outlined how, by removing each such axiom, one can find models or scenarios that satisfy the rest of the axioms but violate the intended principle of the removed axiom. For instance, without Coupling Exhaustiveness (A24), a dependency can exist outside the typology; without Risk Monotonicity (A26), risk could be shuffled off an agent without true mitigation; without the PFA/contestability axioms (32–33), a system could enforce decisions without any collective agreement or possibility of appeal, all while obeying the other structural constraints. The optional axioms, when included, each add a unique restriction that is not implied by the others. If any such axiom were removed, the specific failure mode it is meant to prevent would become possible again (e.g., hidden domination channels without A24, unbounded risk-shifting without A26, uncontestable authority without A32–33, etc.).

In summary, no axiom of Σᴿ (or its extensions) can be derived from the remaining ones. Each axiom plays an “non-redundant” role in ruling out a class of undesirable models or transformations, and for each axiom we can demonstrate a model (or transformation) that violates that axiom while respecting all others. This confirms the logical independence of the axioms, a hallmark of a well-designed axiomatic system.

Appendix Q: Closure-Theoretic Semantics for Domination-Constrained Interaction

Q.1 Primitive Structure

Let \(S\) be a set of states.
Let \(\mathcal C \subseteq \mathcal P(S)\) be a closure system (Moore family), i.e.:
\(S \in \mathcal C\);

\(\mathcal C\) is closed under arbitrary intersections.

No other primitives are assumed.

Q.2 Induced Closure Operator

Definition Q.2.1 (Closure Operator)

Define \(\mathrm{Cl} : \mathcal P(S) \to \mathcal P(S)\) by \[ 
\mathrm{Cl}(X)\ :=\ \bigcap\{\,C \in \mathcal C \mid X \subseteq C\,\}. 
\]

Lemma Q.2.2 (Closure Laws)

\(\mathrm{Cl}\) is extensive, monotone, and idempotent. Moreover, \[ 
\mathcal C \;=\; \{\, C \subseteq S \mid \mathrm{Cl}(C)=C \,\}. 
\]
Proof. Standard Moorefamily construction. ∎

Q.3 Closure Lattice

Define the closure lattice \[ 
\mathcal L\ :=\ (\mathcal C,\ \subseteq). 
\]
All semantic structure introduced below is internal to this lattice.

Q.4 Interaction (Composition)

Definition X.4.1 (Interaction)

For \(X,Y \subseteq S\), define \[ 
X \otimes Y\ :=\ \mathrm{Cl}(X \cup Y). 
\]
For points \(x,y \in S\), write \[ 
x \otimes y\ :=\ \mathrm{Cl}(\{x,y\}). 
\]
This operation is uniquely induced by the closure system and corresponds to finite generation in the closure lattice.

Q.5 Closure Neighborhood Filters

Definition Q.5.1 (Neighborhood Filter)

For each \(x \in S\), define the closure neighborhood filter \[ 
\mathcal F_x\ :=\ \{\, C \in \mathcal C \mid x \in C \,\}. 
\]
\(\mathcal F_x\) is a principal filter in \(\mathcal L\).

Q.6 Specialization Preorder (Domination)

Definition Q.6.1 (Specialization Preorder)

Define a preorder \(\preceq\) on \(S\) by \[ 
x \preceq y 
\;\Longleftrightarrow\; 
\mathcal F_y \subseteq \mathcal F_x. 
\]
Equivalently, every closed region admissible for \(y\) is also admissible for \(x\).

Lemma Q.6.2

\(\preceq\) is reflexive and transitive.
Proof. Immediate from filter inclusion. ∎
This preorder coincides with the specialization order induced by the closure space.

Q.7 Interaction Refinement and Relevance

Definition Q.7.1 (Relevance)

The interaction between \(x,y \in S\) is relevant if \[ 
\mathcal F_{x \otimes y} 
\;\subsetneq\; 
\mathcal F_x \cap \mathcal F_y. 
\]
Equivalently, joint presence strictly refines the closure semantics: \[ 
\mathrm{Cl}(\{x,y\}) 
\;\neq\; 
\mathrm{Cl}(\{x\}) \cap \mathrm{Cl}(\{y\}). 
\]

Q.8 Minimality and Fixed Points

Proposition Q.8.1 (Canonical Minimality)

For any \(X \subseteq S\), \(\mathrm{Cl}(X)\) is the least element of \(\mathcal C\) containing \(X\).
Consequently, selecting any closed set strictly larger than \(\mathrm{Cl}(X)\) imposes strictly stronger constraints than required by the closure system.

Q.9 Summary (ClosureOnly Semantics)

Given a closure system \((S,\mathcal C)\):
Admissible regions are exactly the closed sets \(\mathcal C\);

Interaction is closure of unions;

Constraint comparison is given by the specialization preorder;

Relevance is strict refinement under interaction.

No numeric valuation, ranking, optimization principle, procedural iteration, or auxiliary operator is required.
All semantic structure is uniquely induced by closure.

Q.10 Normalization Remark

All terminology such as “domination,” “constraint,” or “relevance” is purely interpretive. 
Formally, the construction consists of a closure space together with its induced lattice and specialization preorder. No additional semantic assumptions are introduced beyond closure, inclusion, and filter containment.

Q.11 Scope

This construction is conditional on the choice of closure system \(\mathcal C\). 
Given \(\mathcal C\), all other structure is uniquely determined.


The structure defined here is that of a closure space (equivalently, a Moore family or Alexandrov topology); interaction corresponds to closuregenerated joins, and domination coincides with the specialization preorder.
